case_summary.text: ST : Procedural lapses and absence of all particulars are rectifiable errors, hence, credit was to be allowed subject to rectification by assessee; further, credit is allowable even if invoices are in name of head office

II. Credit may be taken in one factory based on duty paying documents addressed to main office of company or documents in old name of company assessee, subject to utilization of input services for dutiable goods.
Cenvat credit available even if challan and invoices were in name of head office

Cenvat Credit : Credit may be taken on basis of invoices issued by manufacturer or importer or their distributor/dealer and said requirement is mandatory; since endorsement of invoice is not provided in rules, hence, job-worker cannot take credit on basis of invoices endorsed by principal-manufacturer

Cenvat Credit : It is natural that Customs House Agent (CHA) invoice would be in name of Head Office where clearance of goods through Customs is centralized; hence, in absence of doubt as to actual receipt of services, credit cannot be denied merely because Head Office is not registered as Input Service Distributor (ISD)
ST : Credit of input service cannot be denied merely because invoice was in name of assessee's Head Office, especially when receipt and utilization of input service were not under challenge

Excise/ST/VAT: Cenvat Credit could not be denied to branch office merely because bill of entry was in name of head office when capital goods had been used in branch office and head office had not availed Cenvat Credit on such goods
Credit can't be denied to input service distributor even if its invoices bear name of head office

II. CENVAT Credit, otherwise admissible, cannot be denied merely on ground that it was availed on basis of invoices raised by their head office, which was not registered under central registration during material period

ST : In case of centralized purchases of capital goods by Head Office, credit can be allowed to individual units/branch only if Cenvat credit was passed to such unit/branch under proper authorisation and there is no multiple claim by other units

Cenvat Credit : Where lessee is manufacturing goods under lease agreement with lessor and lessor supplies capital goods to lessee, lessee may take credit on basis of supplier's invoice in name of lessor but endorsed by lessor in favour of lesse.
Cenvat Credit can not be denied to branch office just because bill of entry was in name of head office: CESTAT
GST/CENVAT : Cenvat credit of service tax paid by assessee could not be denied on ground that in invoices address given was that of Head Office, Delhi and not of registered premises at NOIDA

Cenvat Credit : Credit of duty-paid returned goods can be allowed only if invoice is in name of person availing credit or invoice is endorsed in favour of assessee; credit cannot be taken on invoice in name of a third party

Cenvat Credit : Where two units are located adjacent to each other and have common service tax registration, practice of taking credit belonging to either of units without considering whether invoice was addressed to Head Office or to units is valid; department cannot seek segregation of credit along with separate registration

ST : Where receipt of input service and use thereof along with identity of service provider and service recipient are established, credit cannot be denied merely because invoice thereof bears address of Head Office, which is not registered as ISD.
No denial of Cenvat Credit even if invoices are in name of employees: Mumbai CESTAT
Credit of ST couldn't be denied merely on ground that address of registered office wasn't mentioned in invoice
Credit of CHA service allowable even if bill is issued to Head Office which isn’t ‘Input Service Distributor’
EXICSE/ST/VAT : Cenvat credit taken by assessee not on basis of invoices issued to their Mumbai office but on ISD invoice; Further, credit cannot be denied on ground of nexus; Matter remanded.

CENVAT : Cenvat credit can be availed by manufacturer on strength of invoices issued by supplier for clearance of inputs or capital goods, showing manufacturer's name as consignee and name of dealers as buyer
Cenvat credit on capital goods purchased by HO would be allowed on prorated basis to each unit

Cenvat Credit : If particulars relating to payment of tax on input services are genuine, then, credit cannot be denied merely because input service provider had quoted incorrect address of assessee in invoice.
Manufacture can claim Cenvat credit even on basis of invoice showing him as consignee

Cenvat Credit : Where three separately registered units are using a common input in continuous, interconnected and integrated process for common share, they constitute a single factory and CENVAT cannot be denied on ground that credit is being availed by one factory and material inputs are used by three factories

GST/Cenvat: Where invoices were in name of appellant themselves and receipt of service by appellant had not been challenged, credit on same could not be denied merely because of a different address being shown

Cenvat Credit : Where imported consignment is directly received in factory of job-worker, job-worker may take credit of CVD paid on imports, on strength of bill of entry, even if said bill of entry is in name of principal manufacturer
No credit can be taken on basis of invoices neither addressed to assessee nor endorsed in his favour

Cenvat Credit: Where applicant gas transporter will engage contractor to lay pipelines and contractor will procure pipes and valves from manufacturer who will issue invoice to contractor showing applicant as consignee and pipes will be delivered directly at applicant's work-site, applicant can avail cenvat credit on pipes and valves on basis of invoice issued by contractor, if contractor is a registered dealer

Cenvat Credit : Where supplier factories and recipient factories, both, belonged to assessee only, demand of Cenvat reversal from recipient factories on ground of excess duty payment by supplier factories, was dropped on undertaking from supplier factories that they would not claim refund of such excess duty

GST: Where a manufacturer with regular registration in Tamil Nadu and separate ISD registration for its Head Office received common input service invoices in the name of regular registration and distributed ITC based on Board circular till March 2025, amendments effective 1 April 2025 mandate that such ITC can only be received and distributed through ISD registration, making invoice receipt in regular registration and subsequent credit transfer to ISD impermissible.

Cenvat Credit : Where there is no dispute that assessee had received input services and utilised them for providing output services, credit cannot be denied merely on ground that address of assessee was not mentioned on invoices on which credit was availed

Excise & Customs : Word "factory" includes "all units/premises at same place"; therefore, if steam/electricity generated out of fuel (furnace oil) is used for more than one units (DTA & EOU) in same "factory", entire fuel/furnace oil would be eligible for input credit

CENVAT : Where expenditure was incurred by assessee company, even though invoices were not in name of company but in name of directors/employees and same had been booked as expenditure in books of assessee, Cenvat credit could not have been denied

ST : Being a manufacturer having one factory and setting up second factory, assessee can easily and correctly take credit of services availed at Unit-2 in Unit-1 also, but since assessee took a separate registration for Unit-2, credit could only be taken in Unit-2

CENVAT : Where manufacturer had intimated department about shifting of machines to rented premises near factory and submitted proper documents and no job work was done, Cenvat credit could not be denied
Cenvat Credit: Non-mentioning of address of ISD in LOP could not be a ground to deny credit
Cenvat Credit : Where there is no dispute about receipt of material and payment of duty thereon, credit taken based on 'endorsed bill of entry' is valid
Manufacturer entitled to credit of ST paid on outward transportation from factory to customer's premises : SC

Cenvat Credit : Credit cannot, prima facie, be allowed on unsigned invoices especially when there is no correspondence or certificate from supplier/service provider that said invoices were issued by them

EXCISE/ST/VAT : Refund was admissible in respect of ISD invoices issued by head office of appellant for portion of services received in Gurugram for authorised operations of appellant in its SEZ unit in Indore

EXCISE/CENVAT : Supplier was duly registered with Central excise department and paid Central excise duty on capital goods and cleared same from his factory; since receipt of capital goods was also not in dispute, Cenvat credit on same could not be denied to recipient unit
Cenvat credit can be allowed only if assessee holds valid invoice
EXCISE : Cenvat credit on capital goods used in beneficiation plant cannot be denied on ground of separate registration as it is an integral part of factory
CENVAT: Where there was specific inclusion of input services for construction of factory, assessee-manufacturer would be eligible to avail credit of service tax paid on such input services
Credit of ST paid on transport of employees to factory not admissible after 1-4-2011: HC
EXCISE/ST/VAT : Debit note issued by importer in respect of import of machines and CVD paid thereon can also be valid document for availing credit

Cenvat Credit : Prior to 1-4-2011, services used in relation to setting up of factory were eligible for input service credit because factory is setup for manufacture of final products which are liable to Central Excise duty

GST : Where applicant company procures various goods/services directly used for air transportation services (including passenger and cargo) for all other States at its Head Office (HO), input GST credit pertaining to services only on procurement made by HO towards maintenance of aircraft (including lease thereof) shall be distributed by way of input service distributor mechanism and credit pertaining to goods (including capital goods) shall be distributed by way of normal registration mechanism

Cenvat Credit : Where purchase order shows that goods are to be delivered on FOR basis and assessee had complied with other conditions of Circular, dated 23-8-2007, assessee is entitled to credit of 'outward transportation' upto customer's premises

digest.text:
HEADNOTE: Modvat credit cannot be denied on account of some minor procedural lapses in duty-paying documents Rule 57A read with rule 57G of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 - Cenvat credit - Allowability of - Whether Modvat credit can be denied on account of some minor procedural lapses in duty-paying documents - Held, no - Whether benefit of modvat credit could be denied to assessee merely on ground that in invoice there was change in address - Held, no Circulars and Notifications - Notification No. 7/1999 - C.E. (NT), dated 9-2-1999 - Circular No. 441/7/1999-CX, dated 23-2-1999

FACT: The assessee, namely, ‘G’, Ghaziabad availed MODVAT credit on the strength of invoice, which was in the name of ‘G’, Kota. The assessee also availed MODVAT credit on the strength of other invoice in which the buyer’s name was ‘P’, Faridabad; whereas the goods had been consigned to the assessee at Delhi. The Commissioner (Appeals) allowed the MODVAT credit taken by the assessee on the strength of the aforesaid invoices. He held that though there was cutting in consignees’ address but the same had been authenticated by the same person who had prepared the invoice and the address was changed from Kota to Ghaziabad.

He further held that a certificate issued by ‘P’ was also brought on record to show that the goods had been supplied by it to the assessee at Delhi address.

On appeal to the Tribunal by the revenue:

HELD: The benefit of MODVAT credit could not be denied to the assessee merely on the ground that there was change in the address from Kota to Ghaziabad. Further, it had not been disputed by the revenue that the inputs sent by ‘P’ were duty-paid and the same were received in the factory for being used in the manufacture of the final products. Thus, in view of the subsequent amendment made in rule 57G by Notification No. 7/1999-CE (NT) dated 9-2-1999, the MODVAT credit cannot be denied on account of some minor procedural lapses in the duty-paying documents. The Board had also clarified, vide Circular No. 441/7/1999-CX dated 23-2-1999, that Notification No. 7/1999-CE (NT), has been issued so as to empower the Assistant Commissioner, having jurisdiction over the factory of the manufacturer, to allow the credit ignoring minor procedural lapses provided the inputs have suffered duty and are being used in the process of manufacture. Hence, the appeal was liable to be rejected. [Para 3]

HEADNOTE: Rule 2(l), read with rule 15, of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - Cenvat credit - Input service - Period October, 2005 to March, 2006 - Assessee availed credit of service tax on basis of invoices which were in name of head office - Original authority denied said credit on ground that invoices were not in name of factory - On appeal, Commissioner (Appeals) held that mistake was only a procedural omission and dropped demand - However, he imposed a penalty under rule 15(1) - Whether since there was no allegation of non-receipt of input service in factory or no allegation that input service was not relatable to factory and further since invoice was in name of head office of same factory and not in name of some one else, Commissioner (Appeals) was justified in holding that assessee was eligible for Cenvat credit - Held, yes - Whether since assessee was eligible for credit and there was no suppression of facts and extended period was not invocable, question of imposing penalty did not arise - Held, yes [Para 4]

FACT: The assessee was engaged in the manufacture of polyester filament yarn. It availed credit of service tax during the period from October, 2005 to March, 2006 on the basis of invoices which were not in the name of its factory. In the impugned order, the Commissioner (Appeals) had held that it was only a procedural omission and therefore, the credit taken by the assessee was in order. On that ground as well as on the ground of limitation, he had dropped the demand and also set aside the penalty but had imposed a penalty of Rs. 10,000 under rule 15(1).

On cross-appeals :

HELD: The Commissioner (Appeals) had rightly followed the decision of the Tribunal in the case of CCE&CE v. DNH Spinners [2010] 25 STT 295 (Ahd. - CESTAT). Even though the assessee had multiple divisions, in the absence of any dispute about the receipt of the services in question by the factory to whom credit had been passed on, the ratio of the cited decision was applicable. In fact, the Commissioner(Appeals) proceeded to say that the assessee should have followed the procedure of issue of invoices by the head office as an input service distributor but observed that as far as the present appeal was concerned, the proceedings were limited by the ground taken in the show-cause notice and the order-in-original which had held that assessee had taken credit wrongly since invoice was not in its name but in the name of its head office. In view of the fact that the invoice was in the name of the head office and there was no dispute raised in the show-cause notice as to the admissibility of input service credit to the factory on the ground that the input service was not relatable to the factory, the omission became a totally curable defect and was a condonable one. Under those circumstances, the conclusion reached by the Commissioner (Appeals) to drop the demand could not be found fault with. The Commissioner (Appeals) also had taken a view that merely because the assessee did not disclose to the department that it had availed credit on the basis of documents not prescribed under rule 9(2), it could not be said that there was suppression of fact, wilful misstatement, etc. He had relied upon the decision of the Supreme Court in the case of Larsen & Toubro Ltd. v. CCE 2007 (211) ELT 513. In view of the fact that there was no allegation of non-receipt of input service or the allegation of service not relatable to the factory and also in view of the fact that invoice was in the name of head office of the same factory and not in the name of someone else, the decision of the Commissioner (Appeals) that extended period was not invocable also had to be upheld. Since the assessee was eligible for the credit and there was no suppression of facts, extended period was not invocable and, hence, the question of penalty did not arise. Accordingly, the penalty imposed was to be set aside. In view of the above, the appeal filed by the revenue was to be rejected and appeal filed by the assessee was to be allowed. [Para 2]

HEADNOTE: Section 57F of the Central Excise Act, 1944 - Modvat Credit - Manner of utilisation and credit allowed in respect of duty there on

HELD: Merger/Amalgamation of factories - MODVAT--Transfer of credit - Matter to be disposed of in terms of CBEC letter dt. 23.12.1992.

HEADNOTE: Rule 9, read with Rules 2(a), 3 and 4 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004, Rule 4A and Rule 4B of the Service Tax Rules, 1994 and Rule 11 of the Central Excise Rules, 2002 - Cenvat Credit - Documents on which credit may be taken - Assessee was manufacturing dutiable products under lease agreement with DSM - DSM had provided capital goods to assessee and said capital goods were installed and used by assessee - Assessee took credit of duty paid on capital goods on basis of supplier's invoice, which was in name of DSM and was endorsed by DSM to effect that 'goods covered under these invoices are transferred to assessee in view of lease agreement' - Department denied credit on ground that Endorsed invoices which are in name of DSM Sugars cannot be held to be proper Cenvatable document - HELD : Since there was no dispute that said capital goods were : (a) received by assessee, (b) duly installed in their factory and (c) used for manufacture of final product cleared by assessee, revenue's objection that such CENVAT credit is not available on basis of endorsed invoices cannot be upheld - Since this was not a case of 'sale' by one manufacturer to another and was a case of lessor buying and supplying capital goods to assessee-lessee's factory, certificate by lessor DSM as endorsement on invoice would be sufficient to take credit [Para 4] [In favour of assessee]Cenvat Credit : Where lessee is manufacturing goods under lease agreement with lessor and lessor supplies capital goods to lessee, lessee may take credit on basis of supplier's invoice in name of lessor but endorsed by lessor in favour of lesse.

FACT: Facts

The assessee is engaged in the manufacture of mould steel ingots and runners and risers under an agreement entered into by them with DSM Sugar Asmoli.

Under the said lease agreement dated 26-09-2002, the facility of land and machinery stands provided by DSM Sugar, Asmoli and the capital goods were received by them are required to be installed by the assessee and the duty on the final product required to be paid by the assessee.

DSM Sugars, Asmoli had endorsed the said invoices indicating as "certified that the goods covered under these invoices transferred to Kailash Steel, Asmoli in view of lease agreement dated 20-09-2002".

The Department denied CENVAT credit to the assessee on the ground that the invoices issued by the supplier are in the name of DSM Sugars, Asmoli, though there is no dispute that the said capital goods were received by the assessee and were duly erected and installed in their premises and were used for the manufacture of dutiable and excisable goods.

Revenue's Arguments

Endorsed invoices which are in the name of DSM Sugars cannot be held to be proper Cenvatable document so as to allow the CENVAT credit in respect of the same, to the assessee.

Assessee's Arguments

Even though DSM Sugars are the owners of the capital goods in question, there is no sale purchase of the capital goods and the same only stands transferred to their unit under the lease agreement, in which case, the effect of endorsement would not be of much relevance.

HELD: In as much as there is no dispute that the said capital goods stand received by the assessees and further duly installed in their factory and were being used for the manufacture of the final product, which was being cleared by the assessee, the revenue's objection that such CENVAT credit is not available in as much as the same was taken on the basis of the endorsed invoices cannot be upheld.

Admittedly, this is not a case of sale of capital goods from one manufacturer unit to another. It is a case where the capital goods are bought by the lessor and transferred to the lessee's factory, under lease agreement for further manufacture of the final product. As such, the certificate given by DSM Sugars, Asmoli on the invoices indicating that are being transferred and in the absence of any dispute to the factual aspect, the assessee is entitled to the CENVAT credit involved in the present appeal. [Para 4]

HEADNOTE: Section 73 of the Finance Act, 1994 read with section 11A of the Central Excise Act, 1944 and section 28 of the Customs Act, 1962 - Recovery - Of duty or tax not levied/paid or short-levied/paid or erroneously refunded - Scope of Show-cause Notice - Assessee took credit of capital goods in year 2005-06 on basis of invoices issued by its head office - Department issued a letter/corrigendum dated 17-7-2007 stating that said credit was not in order and sought to recover said amount - HELD : There has been no show cause notice given to assessee for showing cause as to why cenvat credit was inadmissible to them and how same was recoverable under what provision of law and how it was not hit by time bar inspite of having been taken in year 2005-06 - Even if said letter/corrigendum is taken as notice, it falls fatally short of requirement of a notice under section 73 inasmuch as it does not even mention section 73 ibid anywhere at all and it also does not contain any grounds to allege as to how recovery was not hit by time bar [Para 2] [In favour of assessee]Service Tax : While confirmed demand can be adjusted from amount of refund, there is no provision to adjust unconfirmed demand from amount of refund

Rule 9, read with Rule 7A of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004, read with Rule 4A and 4B of the Service Tax Rules, 1994 and Rule 11 of the Central Excise Rules, 2002 - CENVAT Credit - Documents on which credit may be taken - Assessee took credit of capital goods on basis of invoices issued by its head office - Department sought to deny said credit - HELD : Prima facie, credit was admissible as has been held in several cases of assessee themselves [Para 3] [In favour of assessee]

Section 11, read with section 11E of the Central Excise Act, 1944, sections 87 and 88 of the Finance Act, 1994 and sections 142 and 142A of the Customs Act, 1962 - Recovery - Of sums due to Government - Department sanctioned refund of Rs. 11.8 lakhs - Simultaneously, department issued a letter seeking adjustment of refund against proposed denial of credit of Rs. 11.2 lakhs - HELD : While confirmed demand can be adjusted from amount of refund, there is no provision to adjust unconfirmed demand from amount of refund - Having sanctioned full amount, there was no legal authority to adjust amount of Rs. 11.2 lakhs, as same cannot be held to be a confirmed demand - Hence, department was directed to refund back Rs. 11.2 lakhs [Paras 2 to 5] [In favour of assessee]

FACT: Facts

The assessee was given a show cause notice dated 17-1-2007 asking them to show cause as to why their refund claim of Rs. 11,79,720 should not be rejected. The assessee submitted their reply dated 25-5-2007. The Assistant Commissioner sanctioned said refund claim.

However, the Assistant Commissioner issued a corrigendum (dated 17-7-2007) to the earlier show cause notice -

stating that as the assessee had taken credit to the tune of Rs. 11,18,182 on the strength of the invoices for capital goods issued by their Head Office, the same was not admissible as their Head Office was not registered as a registered dealer and

therefore asking why their refund should not be rejected to the extent of Rs. 11,18,182.

The assessee contended that -

the refund sought was of the excess amount paid by them which should be sanctioned and that the amount of cenvat credit on capital goods (Rs. 11,18,182) was rightly taken on the strength of the documents issued by their Head Office in respect of the capital goods actually used by them for providing the output service and

they and their Head Office are not separate entities.

Issue Involved

Whether unconfirmed demand can be set-off against unconfirmed refund claim ?

HEADNOTE: Rule 9 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - Cenvat credit - Documents and accounts - Assessee took Cenvat credit of inputs/capital goods on basis of invoices wherein supplier had mentioned its brand name and address - Adjudicating authority denied said credit on ground that invoices did not bear assessee’s name - Whether since there was no dispute that inputs/capital goods had suffered duty and were used in manufacture of final products and further since brand name of assessee with its address instead of companies’ name in invoices established ownership of goods, Commissioner (Appeals) had rightly allowed credit - Held, yes [Para 4] Circulars & Notifications : CBEC Circular No. 441/7/99-CX, dated 23-2-1999.

FACT: The assessee availed Cenvat credit on inputs/capital goods on basis of the invoices, wherein the suppliers had mentioned the brand name and address of the assessee. The adjudicating authority denied credit on the ground that the invoices did not bear the assessee’s name. The Commissioner (Appeals) set aside the adjudication order.

On appeal :

HELD: There was no dispute that the goods in question were received by the assessee and were used in the manufacture of the final product and duly recorded in the register. The Central Board of Excise & Customs vide Circular No. 441/7/99-CX, dated 23-2-1999 clarified that in terms of sub-rule (11) in rule 57G, and sub-rule (13) of rule 57T of the erstwhile Central Excise Rules, 1944, the Assistant Commissioner of Central Excise may allow the credit of duty paid on inputs/capital goods in minor procedural lapses in filing the declaration or in the invoices/documents, based on which credit is to be taken. However, the Assistant Commissioner should ensure that inputs/capital goods have suffered duty and are being used/are to be used in the process of manufacture. In the instant case, there was no dispute that inputs/capital goods had suffered duty and were used in the manufacture of final products. In any event, brand name of the assessee with its address instead of company’s name in the invoices established ownership of the goods. So, the Commissioner (Appeals) had rightly allowed the credit. Accordingly, no reason was found to interfere with the order of the Commissioner (Appeals). The appeal filed by the revenue was to be rejected. [Para 4]

A.K. Rastogi for the Appellant. V.K. Agarwal for the Respondent.

HEADNOTE: Rule 57A of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 - Modvat credit - Depot sales -Registered dealer - invoices issued by Depots of manufacturer on the basis of inter-depot stock transfer invoices are not the invoices issued by third stage or subsequent stage dealer - credit admissible - Revenue appeal rejected.

FACT: "In fact the invoices issued by T1SC0 Depots (though registered as dealers) for effecting inter-depot transfers are merely stock transfer invoices and can not be categorized as Dealer's invoices, because there is no sale by one Depot to another depot. The sale from TISCO to the appellants constitutes the first sale. Hence the establishments of TISCO issuing the inter depot transfer invoices would be categorized as the stockists or Depots and the status of the invoices issued from these establishment would merit categorization as "invoice issued from the Depot of the manufacturer." (Para 5)

HEADNOTE: Rule 57G of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 - CENVAT credit - Procedure to be observed by manufacturer - Assessee was availing MODVAT credit on basis of invoices issued by dealers/traders - MODVAT credit was denied to assessee on ground that duty paying documents did not show required details - On appeal, Commissioner (Appeals) confirmed said order - As per relevant Board Circular, Assistant Commissioner should ignore minor procedural lapses as long as it is verified that inputs/capital goods have suffered duty and are being used in manufacturing process - Whether Commissioner (Appeals), while disposing of appeal, should have considered Board’s Circular - Held, yes - Whether since assessee demonstrated that it had received duty paid inputs and consumed same in its factory, assessee was eligible for MODVAT credit - Held, yes [Para 5] Circular and notification : Circular No. 441/7/99-CX dated 23-2-1999

FACT: The assessee availed MODVAT credit on the invoices issued by the dealers/traders during the period July, 1994 to December, 1994. A show-cause notice was issued to the assessee denying the MODVAT credit on the ground that these dealers/traders were not registered dealers with the Central Excise department. Though the assessee contested the show-cause notice on the ground that these dealers/traders got themselves registered, the adjudicating authority confirmed the demand on the assessee and imposed penalty on the ground that addresses of the traders were different and duty paying documents did not show the required details. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals), in respect of the credit availed by the assessee on the invoices issued by Indian Oil Corporation, allowed the appeal but in respect of other dealers/traders, denied the MODVAT credit and upheld imposition of penalty. He, however, reduced the quantum of penalty.

On appeal :

HELD: It was undisputed that the inputs covered under all the orders were received in the factory of the assessee and consumed by it in its factory. From the plain reading of the Board’s Circular No. 441/7/99-CX dated 23-2-1999, it is very clear that the Assistant Commissioner should ignore minor procedural lapses as long as it is verified that inputs/capital goods have suffered duty and are being used in the manufacturing process. The Board, in the above Circular had clearly mentioned for disposal of pending cases accordingly. The Commissioner (Appeals), while disposing of the appeal, should have considered the Board’s Circular while dismissing the appeal filed by the assessee. Accordingly, the assessee demonstrated that it had received the duty paid inputs and consumed the same in its factory and, hence, it was eligible for MODVAT credit. [Para 5]

HEADNOTE: Rule 57G of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 - Modvat credit - Procedure to be observed by manufacturer- ‘E’ Ltd. imported a consignment of shredded steel which was cleared under bill of entry on payment of countervailing duty - A portion of said goods imported was given as loan to appellant - Appellant availed credit of duty on goods received from ‘E’ Ltd. - Revenue denied credit of duty to appellant on ground that bill of entry was not endorsed in its name - However, Superintendent of Central Excise issued certificate that ‘E’ Ltd. had not taken credit of duty paid on goods which were given as loan to appellant and goods received by appellant were used in its factory as input - Whether since rule 57G does not require that for taking credit of duty, bill of entry should be endorsed in name of claimant, credit of duty could not be denied on that ground to appellant - Held, yes - Whether, further, since bill of entry together with certificate issued by authority clearly showed that goods imported and cleared under bills of entry on payment of duty, were received and utilized by appellant as inputs in its factory and that assessee had not utilized credit of duty paid on said goods, authorities below were not justified in denying credit of duty to appellant - Held, yes

FACT: E Ltd. had imported a consignment of shredded scrap and cleared the same on payment of duty. Out of the said consignment, ‘E’ Ltd. gave certain quantity of shredded scrap to the appellant as a loan. On receipt of said goods, the appellant took credit of duty of the amount equivalent to customs duty paid by ‘E’ Ltd. on those goods. However, the revenue denied credit of duty to the appellant on the ground that it had taken credit of duty on basis of delivery challans issued by ‘E’ Ltd. but credit of duty could not be taken under rule 57G on that basis. On adjudication, the Commissioner confirmed the demand of duty on the appellant along with penalty. On appeal, the Tribunal also confirmed the demand on the ground that bills of entry were not endorsed in the name of the appellant.

On appeal :

HELD: Rule 57G clearly shows that the credit of duty can be taken on inputs by establishing that the duty has been paid on the said inputs on the basis of documents such as invoice, AR-1, Bill on Entry, etc. In the instant case, it was not in dispute that the appellant had received imported shredded steel scrap from ‘E’ Ltd. on which countervailing duty had been paid by ‘E’ Ltd. It was also not in dispute that ‘E’ Ltd. had not taken credit of the duty paid on shredded steel scrap which was given on loan to the appellant. It was also not in dispute that the appellant had used the said shredded steel scrap taken on loan from ‘E’ Ltd. as inputs in its factory. The certificate issued by a Superintendent of Central Excise to the effect that ‘E’ Ltd. had not taken credit of duty paid on the said shredded steel scrap, was not doubted by the Excise authorities. Similarly, the certificate issued by another Superintendent to the effect that the quantity of shredded steel scrap received by the appellant from ‘E’ Ltd. had been used as inputs in the factory of the appellant, was also not doubted by the Excise authorities. In these circumstances, the appellant had established that the credit of duty on receipt of imported shredded steel scrap from ‘E’ Ltd. had been taken in accordance with law. [Para 9]

scrap, was not doubted by the Excise authorities. Similarly, the certificate issued by another Superintendent to the effect that the quantity of shredded steel scrap received by the appellant from ‘E’ Ltd. had been used as inputs in the factory of the appellant, was also not doubted by the Excise authorities. In these circumstances, the appellant had established that the credit of duty on receipt of imported shredded steel scrap from ‘E’ Ltd. had been taken in accordance with law. [Para 9] For availing the credit of duty, what is required to be established under rule 57G is that the inputs received are in fact duty paid. The procedure set out in rule 57G is to ensure that the credit is taken on the basis of duty paid documents. The bill of entry is one such document set out in rule 57G. The said rule does not require that the bill of entry should be in the name of the person claiming credit of duty. It is not in dispute that the goods imported and cleared on payment of duty by one person can be used as inputs and credit of duty can be claimed by another person by establishing that the imported duty paid goods have been received as inputs and that the importer has not taken credit of that duty. In the instant case, it was established that the duty paid goods were received as inputs, however, the credit was denied on the ground that the Bill of entry was not endorsed in the name of the appellant. Rule 57G does not require that for taking credit of duty, the bill of entry should be endorsed in the name of the claimant. In the absence of any provision regarding endorsement on the bill of entry, the credit of duty cannot be denied on the ground that the bill of entry is not endorsed in the name of the claimant. In the facts of the instant case, the evidence on record i.e., the bills of entry together with the certificates issued by excise authorities, clearly showed that the goods imported and cleared under the bills of entry on payment of duty were received and utilized by the appellant as inputs in its factory and that the importer had not utilized the credit of duty paid on the said goods. Thus, the appellant had established that the inputs received under the bills of entry were duty paid and, therefore, the authorities below were not justified in denying the credit of duty to the appellant. [Para 10]

As per rule 4A(1)(ii), the invoices should indicate the name and address of the person who is receiving the taxable services. There was a strong force in the contention of the assessee that the provisions of rule were very clear; it only requires person receiving the taxable services and only address where the taxable services are provided. [Para 7] It could be seen from the impugned order that the Commissioner (Appeals) had tried to apply rule 2(1)(ii ) to deny Cenvat credit. That allegation was not made out in the show-cause notice and the finding recorded by the Commissioner (Appeals) to reject the appeal filed by the assessee, on that ground, was beyond the allegations made in the show-cause notice. In sum, the assessee had made out a case for credit of service tax paid on the service to its branch offices. In view of the foregoing reasoning, the impugned order was unsustainable and was to be set aside. The appeal was to be allowed. [Para 9]

It has been further held that the Tribunal is correct in allowing Modvat credit on capital goods received when endorsement is made in the Bill of Entry by the importer. In the present case, Cenvat invoices were consigned in favour of SISCOL. [Para 64.1] Power plant supplying exclusively to factory for manufacture - Treated as part of factory : Capital goods/input/input service used on power plant situated at a different premises CENVAT credit is admissible subject to exclusive supply of power by the impugned plant to the assessee manufacturing unit. In the present case, the capital goods were used to set up power plant for generation of electricity primarily for use in the manufacture of the final product within the factory of SISCOL. [Para 64.4]

Lease agreement : On perusal of the lease agreement, it is seen that the Lessor (SISCOL) requested to the Lessee (JSWPL) to set up a power plant in the premises of the Lessor (SISCOL) to take care of the power generation of the Lessor to which Lessee has agreed. The lease of the immovable property is determined for a limited period conditionally on the happenings of some events. The tenure of the lease agreement depends upon the happenings of the future events. In the instant case, it is a conditional transfer of the property with an interest created on a transfer of the property and dependent upon the fulfilment of the condition. Thus, it is clearly evident that SISCOL had provided their land to JSWPL with a condition to set up a power plant and the electricity generated would be consumed in manufacturing activities of SISCOL. [Para 68.1]

Lease agreement was financing arrangement : An agreement should also be examined with actual state of affairs and its implementation from the records. In the present case, it may be seen from the documents and records that in 2004, SISCOL was declared as sick unit under SICA, 1985. CDR Cell report would show that SJG came forward for financing the sick unit SISCOL, as finance acts as an engine of growth. It appears from the Show Cause Notices that JSWPL, one of the companies of SJG, have expertise in constructing and operating Power Plants and JSW Steel Ltd. another company of SJG, is one of the purchasers of the final product of SISCOL. It is recorded in the CDR Cell report that there was proposal of merger of SISCOL with SJG, which is corroborated by Director's report dated 26-4-2005 of JSWPL balance sheet. It is mentioned in "Unit III Debentures Trust Deed" dated 22-9-2005 of JSWPL that with a view to finance its 2 x 30 MW plant at SISCOL, the company has approached the Debenture holders. JSWPL declared to TNEB by letter dated 6-1-2005 that Captive Power Plant is installed inside the SISCOL premises to meet the present and future power requirements of SISCOL. Further, TNEB approved as SISCOL Captive Power Plant located in the company's premises. [Para 68.2]

Rule 4(3) - Capital goods were acquired under loan/lease agreement : Rule 4 (3) of CCR 2004 provides that the Cenvat credit in respect of the capital goods shall be allowed to a manufacturer, even if the capital goods are acquired by him on lease, hire purchase or loan agreement, from a financing company. Rule 4(3) has a wide amplitude in so far as it would cover the cases of various types of financial arrangements for availing credit on the capital goods. It is contemplated that under this sub-rule (3) of rule 4 would cover the cases where the ownership of the capital goods does not vest in the manufacturer until the loan is repaid. There must be an agreement for the purpose of acquiring the capital goods. Variations/unusual features in the agreement covering the lease agreement were not relevant for determining the eligibility of credit. It is clear that title of the property is not relevant for availing Cenvat credit on capital goods. [Para 68.3]

Plant was captive power plant : Even prior to 31-8-2006, it was a Captive Power Plant of SISCOL as approved by TNEB under the Electricity Act. SISCOL was a sick unit. They entered into lease agreement with JSWPL, a relationship had already been developed prior to October 2005, as evident from CDR Cell report, JSWPL balance sheet etc., for financial accommodation to get loan from UTI Bank Ltd. for setting up C.P.P. and one of the considerations is that electricity would be supplied to SISCOL, which is an integral part of manufacturing activities of SISCOL. [Para 68.4]

contended that -

the refund sought was of the excess amount paid by them which should be sanctioned and that the amount of cenvat credit on capital goods (Rs. 11,18,182) was rightly taken on the strength of the documents issued by their Head Office in respect of the capital goods actually used by them for providing the output service and

they and their Head Office are not separate entities.

Issue Involved

Whether unconfirmed demand can be set-off against unconfirmed refund claim ? HELD: It is seen that vide Order-in-original No. 44/R/2007, the Assistant Commissioner sanctioned the entire amount of refund sought by them. In other words, the Assistant Commissioner sanctioned the refund of Rs.11,79,720. Having sanctioned the entire amount as refund, the Assistant Commissioner, recording that Rs.11,18,182 availed and utilised by the assessee was not found admissible on the ground of its availment on the strength of improper documents under rule 9 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, went ahead and deducted Rs.11,18,182 from the sanctioned amount.

In this regard, it is pertinent to state that while confirmed demand can be adjusted from the amount of refund, there is no provision to adjust unconfirmed demand from the amount of refund.

There has been no show cause notice given to the assessee for showing cause as to why the cenvat credit amount of Rs.11,18,182 (adjusted from the amount of refund sanctioned) was inadmissible to them and how the same was recoverable under what provision of law and how it was not hit by time bar inspite of having been taken in the year 2005-06.

Even if the corrigendum issued on 17-7-2007 is attempted to be treated as a show cause notice, the said corrigendum falls fatally short of the requirement of a notice under section 73 of the Finance Act, 1994 inasmuch as the said corrigendum does not even mention section 73 ibid anywhere at all and it also does not contain any grounds to allege as to how the recovery, even if the said credit was held to be inadmissible, was not hit by time bar. Indeed the said corrigendum nowhere requires the assessee to show cause as to why the said amount should not be held inadmissible and why / how the same is recoverable without being hit by time bar. It merely stated that the said amount appeared to be not admissible to them and then straightaway called upon the assessee to show cause as to why the refund claim should not be rejected to the extent of Rs. 11,18,182. [Para 2]

While it is arguable that the amount of Rs. 11,18,182 taken as cenvat credit on the strength of the document received by the Head Office of the assessee is clearly admissible as has been held in several cases of the assessee themselves, in the instant case, this point is beside the issue. [Para 3]

Having sanctioned the full amount, there was no legal authority to adjust the amount of Rs. 11,18,182 as the same cannot be held to be a confirmed demand. [Para 4]

In view of the above, the impugned order was set aside and refund of the remaining amount of Rs. 11,18,182 was granted alongwith applicable interest. [Para 5]

HEADNOTE: Rule 57G of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 - Modvat Credit - Gate pass endorsements--procedure cannot deny Mod vat so long as duty has been paid on the inputs. Three endorsements on original gate pass accepted

FACT: The appellants had taken Modvat credit for goods received against GP J, after it had been endorsed three times by different parties and a demand for Rs. 1,02,600.00 was confirmed. Their appeal was also rejected by the Collector (Appeals).

HELD: Modvat--cannot be denied in routine or by mechanical approach even if documentation is defective so long as duty has been paid on inputs, "... we are unable to appreciate the routine and mechanical approach of the authorities below in rejecting the claim of the Modvat credit only on the ground that more than one endorsement has been made. When the Board themselves have taken a decision to relax the procedural requirement by way of administrative instruction it should be the endeavour of the authorities to extend Modvat credit wherever the duty-paid nature of the goods is evident from the gate passes produced and quantum of duty paid on the inputs could be ascertained from them. A positive approach is called for in this regard."

2. Modvat--credit for goods received against GP I, after three endorsements by different parties can be allowed as long as duty-paid nature of the goods is established. "Rule 57G of the Central Excise Rules stipulates that inputs are to be received under the cover of a gate pass, an AR-I, a Bill of Entry or any other document as may be prescribed by the Board. ...However, when this requirement created some difficulties in the ease of Small Scale units to obtain the inputs through intermediaries, the Board appears to have made relaxation to this requirement by permitting one endorsement in the gate pass initially and subsequently based on the representations permitting upto two endorsements in the gate passes. This relaxation made by the Board appears to be purely of administrative nature based on considerations of implementing the Modvat scheme, so long as the duty-paid nature of the goods and duty paid thereon could be established. As seen from the Trade Notice cited by the learned advocate, it is evident that the Government is keen to extend the Modvat credit so long as the goods in factory packed condition as are covered by the gate passes are received by the parties intending to avail Modvat credit...... the department is entitled to make verification or investigation with regard to the genuineness of the gate pass and also on the question whether gate pass has been utilised for availment of Modvat credit at the earliest stages. In this case, no such enquiry appears to have been conducted and the Modvat credit has-been denied only on the ground that more than that of permitted endorsements have been made in the gate passes. Such an order cannot be sustainable in the context of the scheme of Modvat credit read along with the relaxation made by the Board. We, therefore, set aside the order passed by the authorities below and permit availment of credit and while doing so, we allow the liberty to the Assistant Collector to cause any inquiry or investigation to satisfy himself about the genuine nature of the gate passes and also about non-utilisation of the gate passes at the earlier stages of endorsements for availment of Modvat credit."

HEADNOTE: Rule 57 of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 - Cenvat Credit (Modvat) - Modvat - Raw material can be transferred to another unit which can get credit - Inputs need not be used directly as per settled law, as there is no requirement of direct use if inputs are fully utilised - CE Rule 57F(2)

FACT: The appellants have their factory at Mandideep in M.P. They have another factory at Ankleshwar in Gujarat. They manufacture Cephalexin and Cephadroxil falling under Chapter 29 of CETA. Penicillin GK is the main input for the final product, which the appellants import as also procure locally. With the approval of the Assistant Collector they sent Penicillin to Ankleshwar factory direct where the same was converted into "7ADCA", which was then received at the factory at Mandideep for manufacture of the final product. They had similar approval in respect of other raw materials used in the manufacture of "7ADCA" for being sent to the factory at Ankleshwar. They were availing of the Modvat credit in respect of all the raw materials at Mandideep when "7ADCA" along with other documents was received from Ankleshwar. The Collector of CE, Indore after issuing a show cause notice and hearing the appellants, held that appellants had wrongly availed of the Modvat credit at Mandideep by deliberately suppressing the fact by not making a proper declaration of use of inputs in as much as "7ADCA" was never declared as an input. According to the Collector, in the absence of such a declaration they were not entitled to Modvat credit which could have been availed of by the Ankleshwar factory which received the declared raw materials. He therefore disallowed Modvat credit of Rs. 79,38,597.50 and also imposed a penalty of Rs. 5 lakhs.

HELD: The appellants were legally entitled to send the raw material to Ankleshwar factory and to avail of Modvat credit when "7ADCA" was received at Mandideep factory. "Since the appellant had filed the declaration the appellant was legally entitled to send the raw materials to Ankleshwar factory and avail of the credit in respect of such raw materials when 7ADCA manufactured by the appellant at its Ankleshwar factory from such raw materials was received by the appellant at its Mandideep factory."

2. Since there was no requirement to use raw material directly in the manufacture of final product the denial of Modvat credit was uncalled for and contrary to judicial pronouncements. "Since there was no requirement to use raw materials directly in the manufacture of final product the denial of modvat credit by the Collector was clearly uncalled for and contrary to judicial pronouncements which has settled this position beyond any pale of doubt."

3. There was no violation of Rule 57F(2). "We, therefore, hold that there was no violation of Rule 57F(2) which postulates that a manufacturer assessee engaged in the manufacture of final product can send the raw materials directly to a job worker, request such job worker to convert the raw materials into an intermediate product and then receive such intermediate product in his factory for manufacture of final dutiable products."

4. No justification for denying the credit because all raw materials were used in the manufacture of final product. "There is no justification for denying the credit because it was not in dispute that the entirety of the raw materials were, in fact, used in the manufacture of final dutiable product. The appellant had filed before the Collector a certificate from the Chartered Accountant certifying that the total quantity of raw materials received at Ankleshwar was used in the manufacture of 7ADCA which, in turn, was used in the manufacture of Cephalexin at Mandideep. Every ounce of the material was thus fully accounted for."

5. Appellants entitled to Modvat credit of Rs. 79,38,597.50. Penalty imposed set side. "We, therefore, hold that the appellants are entitled to the benefit of modvat credit of Rs. 79,38,597.50. For the same reason, we also set aside the penalty imposed by the adjudicating authority."

HEADNOTE: Rule 57G of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 - Cenvat Credit - Modvat - Declaration within time--Benefit cannot be denied. Error in recording declaration date rectified

FACT: The Tribunal denied Modvat to the applicant for 1.4.1986 on the ground that its declaration under Rule 57G was acknowledged by the Assistant Collector on 2.4.1986. The applicant has requested for rectification of the error in the Tribunal's order because its declaration was filed on 31.3.1986 and duly acknowledged by the Superintendent.

HELD: Modvat--the applicant is eligible for Modvat for 1.4.1986 because its declaration under Rule 57G was filed with the Range Supdt. on 31.3.1986. "The Tribunal has given a finding in the impugned order that the petitioner would not be entitled to the Modvat benefit for the inputs in question for the period prior to 2.4.1986 on the ground that the declaration under Rule 57-G has been acknowledged by the jurisdictional Collector only on 2.4.1986 and under Rule 57G(2) a manufacturer who has filed a declaration under sub-rule (1) may after obtaining the acknowledgement of the Asst. Collector take the credit of the duty paid on the inputs received by him. On going through the records we find that on 31.3.1986 the petitioner has addressed a communication to the Asst. Collector purporting to be a declaration under Rule 57-G of the Modvat Rules. This was presented with the Range Supdt., Hyderabad and has been acknowledged by him on 31.3.1986. It has been forwarded to the Asst. Collector, Hyderabad who had received it on 2.4.1986. It is not disputed that the inputs in question have suffered duty and the petitioner would be otherwise eligible to Modvat credit in respect of the inputs in question. Filing of a declaration under Rule 57-G is a procedural formality and in the present case the same has been done on 31.3.1986 itself to the Range Supdt. The fact that the Range Supdt. forwarded the same to the Assistant Collector in the same place only on 2.4.1986 cannot be a reason to deny the petitioner the benefit of Modvat credit. The Board has also given a clarification in this regard.........the impugned order is amended by rectifying the error holding that the petitioner would be entitled to the Modvat credit in respect of the inputs in question taken on 1.4.1986. The impugned order would stand modified accordingly after rectification of this mistake."

However, the adjudicating authority rejected said claim of the assessee and confirmed the demand along with interest and penalty. Appeal of the assessee before the Commissioner (Appeals) was allowed.

On appeal : HELD: It was an admitted fact that the lorryloads of HR Coils which were received at the assessee's factory were weighed on its weighbridge and the net weights of the materials were recorded in the ‘HR Coil receipt register' maintained by the assessee. Often these weights were found to be less than the quantities mentioned in the corresponding invoices. In some cases, the weight entered in the said register was higher than that indicated in the invoice. In both the cases, the MODVAT/CENVAT credit was availed of the duty paid on the materials as indicated in the invoices. These facts, noted by the lower appellate authority, were also not in dispute. The only dispute was with regard to the credit availed on the differential quantity of input where the weight of material entered in the material receipt register was less than that mentioned in the corresponding invoice. According to the revenue that differential quantity of input was not received in the factory and was not used in the manufacture of the final product and, hence, was not eligible for the MODVAT/CENVAT credit as per the relevant rules. According to the assessee, the variation in the weight was on account of two different weighbridges having been used for weighing the materials, one at the supplier's end and another in its own factory. These weighbridges were of different capacities and their tolerance limits worked out to be 0.075 per cent to 0.1 per cent. The actual shortage of material, as found on comparison of the invoices with the ‘HR Coil receipt register', was from 0.02 per cent to 0.04 per cent only, which variations were within the abovesaid tolerance limit. These facts pleaded by the assessee and accepted by the lower appellate authority had not been disputed by the revenue. The contention of the revenue was that the rules did not permit any tolerance limits of weighbridges to be taken into account in the determination of admissibility of the MODVAT/CENVAT credit. A similar contention of the revenue was considered by the Larger Bench in the case of CCE v. Bhuwalka Steel Industries Ltd. [2010] 24 STT 436 (Chennai - CESTAT) wherein it was held that minor variations arising due to weighment on different machines will have to be ignored, if such variations are within tolerance limits. [Para 6]

In the instant case, the variations due to weighment on different weighbridges, undisputedly, were only from 0.02 per cent to 0.04 per cent and were within tolerance limits prescribed under the Standards of Weights & Measures Act and the Standards of Weights & Measures (General) Rules, 1987 and, hence, could be ignored as held by the Larger Bench in the above case. As it was not the case of the revenue that the so-called differential quantity of HR Coil was lost in the transit or had been diverted or that it was not duty paid, it was to be held that the entire quantity of the material covered by the invoices was received in the assessee's factory and was used in the manufacture of the final product and, therefore, credit of the duty paid on such quantity would be admissible to it. [Para 7]

Therefore, the decision of the Commissioner (Appeals) was to be sustained and the instant appeal was to be dismissed. [Para 10]

HELD: Cenvat Credit on dry dock

The definition of 'input service' under rule 2(l) precisely covers any service used by a provider of taxable service for providing an output service, any service used by a manufacturer in or in relation to manufacture of final product and inclusive part of the definition, services used in relation to setting up, modernisation, renovation or repair of a factory, premises of a provider of output service or an office relating to such factory or premises, etc. The expression 'any service' read with 'for providing an output service' would cover wide encompass of the definition of input service. The Supreme Court in the case of Indian Chamber of Commerce v. CIT AIR 1976 SC 348 observed that the expression 'for' has to be interpreted as 'for the purpose of'. Cenvat credit availed on input service, input and capital goods for setting up dry dock would be allowed for providing output service namely repair/refit service. This is also covered in the inclusive part of the definition of 'input service'. Hence, the finding of the adjudicating authority, that the appellant is exclusively engaged in the manufacture of exempted final product 'Ships' and Cenvat credit on input, capital goods is inadmissible, cannot be sustainable. [Para 7]

Thus, any item which is covered by the list of the items mentioned in rule 2(a) of the Cenvat Credit Rules, except for office equipment or office appliances, and is used in any manner in the factory of the manufacturer of the final products, would be covered by the definition of the capital goods and, accordingly, would be eligible for Cenvat credit. There is absolutely no requirement that the capital goods at the time of receipt must be owned by manufacturer or that the same would cease to be capital goods, if they are installed in the factory and become fixed to earth. In fact, most of the capital goods the machinery, equipment or instruments covered by Chapters 84, 85 and 90, pipes and tubes, pollution control equipment refractories, and storage tanks are required to be installed and after installation, the same put together constitute a manufacturing plant, which is fixed to earth structure. Just because after being installed in the factory, the capital goods put together become a plant which is fixed to earth structure, the Cenvat credit cannot be denied on the basis that the plant which is fixed to earth structure, is not excisable. This preposition of the Department is, in fact absurd, as there is no such condition in rule 2(a) for capital goods.

For capital goods Cenvat credit, the items must be among those mentioned in this rule and should have been used in the factory of the manufacturer and how the items are not used relevant. The words used in rule 2(a) are "used in the factory of manufacturer of the final product" not "used in the manufacture of final product". Therefore, once any item received in the factory is 'capital goods' in terms of Rule 2(a) of the Cenvat Credit Rules, and is used in the factory, the manufacturer would be entitled to Cenvat credit of excise duty paid in respect of the same.

If the logic of the Commissioner in the impugned order is accepted, no capital goods Cenvat credit can be allowed in respect of any item of capital goods enumerated in rule 2(a) of the Cenvat Credit Rules, as all the items - various items of machinery covered under Chapters 84, 85 and 90 of the Tariff, pipes and tubes, tanks, pollution control equipments refractories, etc., have to be installed in the factory before being put to use and after installation, the same would become fixed to earth plant. Reading the impugned order gives an impression that the same has been passed without any application of mind.

Therefore, prima facie, impugned order is not sustainable and as such the assessee have strong prima facie case in their favour. The requirement of pre-deposit of the Cenvat credit demand, interest thereon and penalty is, therefore, waived for hearing of the appeal and recovery thereof is stayed till the disposal of the appeal. HEADNOTE: Rule 9 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - Cenvat credit - Documents and Accounts - Period 1-4-2005 to 31-5-2005 - Whether branch offices are not registered with service tax authorities and they do not discharge service tax liability - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, if a person discharges service tax liability from registered premises for services provided by branches, benefit of Cenvat credit on service tax cannot be denied only on ground that invoices are in name of branch offices - Held, yes [Para 7]

FACT: The assessee was registered as provider of advertisement services. According to the adjudicating officer, it had contravened the provisions of rule 9 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 inasmuch as it had availed credit on the documents which were not addressed to its registered premises but addressed to the branch office of the assessee. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the order of the adjudicating authority. Before the Tribunal, the assessee’s case was that it had taken service tax registration with the authorities on the ground that it had got centralized accounting system and centralized billing was done from the address of its registered premises.

HELD: The assessee was not having any service tax registration in respect of branch office on whose name the invoices were issued by the service provider; it had centralized billing and centralized accounting system at its registered office. Rule 4 of the Service Tax Rules, 1994 provides for an assessee to get himself registered as service provider. It was seen that in the instant case, the assessee had taken registration under the category of ‘Service provider of advertising services’.

It can be seen from rule 4(2) that an option is given to an assessee to register the premises where centralized billing or centralized accounting systems are located. It was found from the records that there was no dispute that the assessee’s office at Manipal had got the centralized billing and accounting systems. If that be so, registration taken by the assessee was in accordance with the Rules. [Para 6]

If a person is discharging service tax liability from his registered premises, the benefit of Cenvat credit on the service tax paid cannot be denied only on the ground that the said invoices are in the name of branch office. There was no dispute that the branch office was not registered with the service tax authorities and it was not discharging the service tax liability, obviously, as the assessee was discharging service tax liability on the services provided by branch. [Para 7]

It was found that though the document on basis of which the assessee had taken the service tax credit was in the name of branch office, tax was actually paid from the premises wherein the service tax registration had been taken. [Para 8]

In view of the findings, the impugned order was unsustainable and the same was to be set aside and the appeal was to be allowed. [Para 9]

HEADNOTE: Rule 57G of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 - Modvat credit - Procedure to be observed by manufacturer - Appellant availed Modvat credit on basis of gate pass of goods consigned to job worker - Though duplicate copy of gate pass contained name of consignee, i.e., job worker, in original copy name of appellant was written after scoring out name of job worker - For said irregularities original authority denied Modvat credit to appellants and made demand of that amount - However, appellant stated that in order to avoid problem during transportation, said correction was made in gate pass - Whether when material had not been received by appellant, but by job worker, taking credit on such goods by changing name of consignee in original copy of gate pass was serious matter and such scant regard to rules could not be ignored - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, appellant would not be entitled for Modvat credit - Held, yes

FACT: The appellant availed Modvat credit on the strength of a gate pass which was not consigned to them but to their job worker. However, in the original gate pass the name of the job worker was scored out and name of the appellant was written but in duplicate gate pass name of the job worker was written. In these circumstances the department proceeded against the appellant for irregular availment of credit and the original authority disallowed the Modvat credit and demanded that amount with penalty.

In appeal the appellant contended that in order to avoid any problem during transportation, the correction was made by the consigner in original gate pass.

HELD: The goods, on which Modvat credit had been taken by the appellants irregularly, were consigned to the job worker. In other words the goods were not received by the appellant but by his job worker. The duplicate copy of the gate pass which had accompanied the goods contain the name of the job worker. However, the original which was sent to the appellants contains the name of the appellant, which was written after scoring out the original consignee i.e., the job worker. The adjudicating authority had given a very detailed finding to indicate that there had been manipulation of the consignee’s name in the original copy of the gate pass. But for that manipulation, the appellant would not have got the Modvat credit. In fact actual consignee was only the job worker. Further the adjudicating authority had found that there was no endorsement in name of appellant as rightly found in the duplicate copy of the gate pass in question. The adjudicating authority had observed that Modvat credit can be taken only when both the material as well as duty paying documents are received by the consignee as indicated in the gate pass. In this case, no fraudulent motive was found which could be attributed to the appellant. The appellant along with consigner have taken recourse to certain devices of expediency to avoid irksome procedures. However, when the material had not been received by the appellant and only by some job worker, taking credit on the goods received by the job worker by changing the name of the consignee in the original copy of the gate pass, was serious matter and such scant regard to rules could not be ignored. The appellant was not entitled for the Modvat credit. [Para 6]

The appeal of the manufacturer was, accordingly, allowed and it was held that the MODVAT credit was allowable on the use of the explosives in the manufacture of cement irrespective of the fact that the explosives were used directly in the mines and never entered the factory of the manufacturer of cement. [Para 8] In 2000, the MODVAT Rules were replaced by the CENVAT Rules by the Central Excise (Second Amendment) Rules, 2000. Basically there was a re-arrangement of the earlier rules which in substance remained the same.

It is clear that sub-rule (d ) of rule 57AA (as introduced in 2000) had merely reframed rule 57B to include all the ingredients of inputs while at the same time broadening the base not only by referring to ‘all goods’ but also by using the word ‘includes’. [Para 9]

Rule 57AC provides for the conditions for allowing CENVAT credit in respect of inputs received in the factory of the manufacturer. [Para 10]

Initially, rule 57J of the MODVAT Rules was deleted. Consequently, with the intention of re-introducing the benefit granted earlier under rule 57J, rule 57AB was introduced under the heading ‘CENVAT credit’. [Para 11]

Rule 57AB effectively duplicates the substance of rule 57J(1) and (2) and deals with a situation where inputs are received by a job worker for production of intermediate goods which are used in the manufacture of a final product. [Para 12]

In J.K. Udyog Ltd.’s case (supra), three reasons were given by the Supreme Court for holding that credit could be taken only on inputs received in the factory of the manufacturer of the final product. First, the Court held that the definition of input given in sub-rule(d) of rule 57AA was entirely different from the manner in which the said word had been expounded in the Explanation to rule 57A of the MODVAT Rules. However, there was only a re-arrangement of the several provisions of rule 57B in rule 57AA. Rule 57AA is in fact more broad based than rule 57B.

Second, the Court proceeded on the basis that under the CENVAT scheme, there was no provision similar to rule 57J of the MODVAT scheme. However, rule 57J was replaced in substance by rule 57AB. That provision was overlooked.

Another reason given by the Court in J.K. Udaipur Udyog case (supra ) for holding that the CENVAT scheme was different from the MODVAT Scheme was rule 57AC(1). However, that rule was limited to inputs received in the factory of the manufacturer and did not impinge on rule 57AB at all.

The schemes of MODVAT and CENVAT Credit are not, therefore, different and the conclusion of the Court in J.K. Udaipur Udyog that the decision in Jaypee Rewa Cement (supra ) would have no application to CENVAT Rules could not be accepted. [Para 14]

The CENVAT Rules in effect substitute the MODVAT Rules and the decision in Jaypee Rewa Cement would continue to apply. The decision in CCE v. J.K. Udaipur Udyog Ltd. (supra ) holding to the contrary, was not good law. [Para 15]

Issue Involved

When the assessee who manufacture the steam, use the same in the factory of manufacturing and also utilized the steam in its another unit which is situated in the same compound, is he entitled to CENVAT Credit proportionately to the extent which was used in the other unit ? HELD: The definition of "input" makes it clear that, "input" means all goods used in or in relation to the manufacture of final products whether directly or indirectly and whether contained in the final products or not and includes lubricating oils, greases, cutting oils, coolants, accessories of the final products cleared along with the final product, goods used as paint, or as packing material, or as fuel, or for generation of electricity or steam used in or in relation to manufacture of final products or for any other purpose, within the factory of production. [Para 8]

The word "factory" has been defined in the Central Excise Act at section 2(e). It is an inclusive definition. For the purpose of Central Excise Act, a 'factory' means more than one premises. [Para 9]

Rule 6, of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004 makes it clear that the CENVAT Credit shall not be allowed on such quantity of goods which is used in the manufacture of exempted goods. However, exception is carved out in sub-Rule (2). Sub-Rule (2) of Rule 6 provides- where a manufacturer or provider of output service avails CENVAT Credit in respect of any inputs except the input intended to be used as fuel and manufactures such final products or provides such output service which are chargeable to duty or tax as well as exempted goods or services, then, an obligation is cast on the assessee to maintain separate accounts for receipt, consumption and inventory or input and input service meant for use in the manufacture of dutiable final products or in providing output service and the quantity of input meant for use in the manufacture of exempted goods or services. However he would be entitled to CENVAT credit only on that quantity of input or input service which is intended for use in the manufacture of dutiable goods. Therefore, it is clear that the assessee manufacturer is entitled to CENVAT Credit on "inputs" which is used in the manufacture of dutiable goods. [Para 11]

In view of clear language in the statutory provisions coupled with the fact that the factory includes more than one premises to be eligible for CENVAT Credit, an assessee has to use the input in the manufacture of dutiable goods in his factory. If the factory includes more than one unit and if the assessee uses this input in the manufacturing of excisable goods in both the units, he would be entitled to CENVAT Credit. [Para 12]

The definition of 'input' brings within its fold the inputs used for generation of electricity or steam, provided such electricity or steam is used within the factory of production for manufacture of final products or for any other purpose. Therefore, it follows the term "within the factory of production" cannot be confined to a single unit. In view of the definition of factory in the act which means more than one premises, it has to be construed as the factory owned by the assessee. If the assessee owns more than one unit, all the units if they are situated at a place would constitute "a factory". If the electricity or steam generated within the factory of production means within the factory premises which may include more than one unit. If such electricity or steam generated within the factory of production is utilized by the assessee in more than one unit and if those units are manufacturing excisable goods, then, the assessee would be entitled to the benefit of CENVAT credit to the entire extent of utilization of such electricity or steam in all the units of its factory premises. Therefore, whatever goes into generation of electricity or steam which is placed within the factory which may consists of more than one unit would be an input for the purposes of obtaining credit on the duty payable thereon. [Para 15]

In the instant case, the assessee is having two units; one DTA unit and another EOU unit. Both are situated in the same factory premises. Both are manufacturing excisable goods. The assessee has purchased furnace oil from which, the steam is generated within the said factory premises. The said steam is utilized by the assessee in manufacturing excisable goods in both the units which are situated within the same compound, which falls within the definition of the word "factory" and therefore, the assessee is entitled to CENVAT credit in respect of entire volume of steam used in the manufacture of excisable goods by both the units. That is precisely what the appellate authorities have held and granted relief to the assessee. [Para 16]

Hence, impugned order was confirmed. [Para 17]

Scheme : Under the Cenvat Credit Scheme a manufacturer of excisable goods is allowed to take credit of excise duty paid on inputs and capital goods used in the manufacture of excisable goods and utilize such credit for payment of excise duty on final products manufactured by him. [Para 36]

Rule 4(4) - Credit only by person paying value/duty : There is no specific provision in the Rules to the effect that credit can be taken by a manufacturer only if duty is paid by him to the supplier of goods. There is a provision in rule 4(4) to the effect that CENVAT credit in respect of capital goods shall not be allowed in respect of that part of the value of capital goods which represents the amount of duty on such capital goods, which the manufacturer claims as depreciation under section 32 of the Income-tax Act, 1961. So prima facie it would appear that the person who is paying for the value of goods and duty thereon is relevant for taking credit. [Para 38]

Receipt in factory : On the other hand definition of capital goods as given in rule 2 (a) and the rule 3 (1) and rule 4 (2) (a) allowing taking of credit are clear enough that credit is to be taken on capital goods received in the factory of the manufacturer. Interestingly there has been amendment to rule 2(a) and rule 4(2) (a) by Notification 3/2011-NT dated 1-3-2011 to the effect that in the case of captive power plants credit can be taken even if the plants are outside the factory. [Para 39]

Payment of value and duty was made by JSWPL - JSWPL neither holding-subsidiary no job-worker : In this case Cenvat credit was taken by SISCOL during the period Sep 05 to July 06. (From 31-08-2006, SISCOL had taken over the power plant from JSWPL.). SISCOL had not paid for the value of the goods or excise duty payable thereon when credit was taken. Such payments could not be seen in the books of account of SISCOL, when credit was taken. The value of the goods and excise duty thereon were paid by JSWPL on the date on which credit was taken by SISCOL. These are two different companies. There is no relationship of one as the holding company of the other which fact existed in some of the decisions relied upon. There is no relationship of SISCOL as job-worker of JSWPL which was the fact in cases where persons not paying for the goods along with duty were allowed to take credit of duty. [Para 40]
