As regards the Board's circular he submits that it is admitted fact that their invoice in question has not been endorsed by their head office in [sic] their factory and as such the conditions of the circular are not satisfied. If the goods were transported by a taxi they could have mentioned the taxi number etc. in the invoice itself. In the circumstances he submits that there is no case made up for grant of stay to the applicants. 4. I have considered the submissions made from both the sides. The dispute is limited to only one invoice in question. The Modvat credit has been disallowed by not accepting the said invoice on the ground that the same shows the address of their head office instead of the factory and there is no endorsement by the head office. Further the department has also doubted the actual receipt of the goods in their factory premises because the applicants have failed to produce any documents showing the actual receipt and [since] the transporters' column in the invoices [having been]left blank. However, I find that the applicants have explained before the Assistant Commissioner, vide their reply to the show cause notice, that the input in question was transported personally by one of their employees in asmuchas the same was only 115.3 K.gs. of stainless steel wire for which a regular transport was not required. They had also produced the good's receipt report. I have seen the photocopy of the report produced on record. The same is carrying a printed serial number and is duly signed by their store-keeper. I also find that the cardex maintained by them reflects the receipt of the above material. Further, there is no dispute or doubt about the fact that the said material was duly entered in their RG-23A Part-I record. Having entered the goods in their Modvatable raw material register, the applicants could not have escaped to show the utilisation of the same in the manufacture of final product and to clear the final product on payment of duty. It is not a case where the applicants have availed the Modvat credit in their Part-II register without the corresponding receipt of raw material in their part I register. As such I find that the failure on the part of the applicants to show the transporters' mode in the invoice, to take the goods first to their head office, got the invoice endorsed in their factory and then transport the goods to their factory are no reasons for denial of benefit of Modvat credit to them. Endorsement of the invoice by their own head office is a rectifiable defect in any case. Taking all these issues into consideration I hold that the applicants had made out a prima facie case for granting them unconditional stay. I Order accordingly.

5. As only above points are involved in the appeal, I take up the appeal itself and allow the same. The impugned order is set aside.

Per Archana Wadhwa :

Modvat credit of Rs. 2,560/- has been disallowed and penalty of Rs. 500/- has been imposed on the applicant/appellant by the authorities below. The reason for disallowing the credit on the stainless steel wire received by the applicant from M/s. Hindustan Wire Ltd. under cover of invoice No. A-1158 dt. 24.9.94 is that the same mentions the address of the head office of the applicant company instead of mentioning the factory address. It has also been alleged that the column meant for transporter in the invoice has been left blank. The said invoice has not been further endorsed by the applicants' head office in favour of their factory, thus showing the receipt of the inputs in the factory premises.

2. Shri B.N. Chattopadhyay, Ld. Consultant appearing for the applicant/appellant submits that the invoice in question shows the address of the head office because the Order was placed from their head office and the goods were transported from the input manufacturer's premises to their factory premises directly by one of their employee in a taxi and that is the reason that the transporters mode has not been reflected in the invoice. He submits that to meet the department's allegations that the inputs have not been received by them in their factory, they had produced serial numbered goods receipt report and cardex maintained by them in the ordinary course of their business. These documents have been discarded by the adjudicating authority as well as by the first appellate authority on the basis of assumptions and presumptions and by observing that these are private documents of the Company. He further submits that the goods were duly entered in their RG-23A part-I register on the same day i.e. on the day of receipt of the goods in their factory. He submits that there is absolutely no ground for doubting these documents and giving the findings that the goods were not received in their factory. He submits that the applicants are paying revenue to the tune of six crores from their P.L.A. apart from paying duty from their RG-23A Part-II account. As such it is not expected from the appellant to manipulate the documents for a small amount of Rs. 2,560/-. He also makes reference to the Board's circular No. 211/45/96-CX dt. 14.5.96, wherein the invoices raised in the name of registered Office/head office have [been] recognised as proper invoices for the purposes of availing of Modvat credit in the factory premises. He also submits that the non-endorsement of the invoice issued in the name of head office by the head office is only a rectifiable defect on the basis of which Modvat credit should not be disallowed to them. He explains that this endorsement could not be made because the inputs were directly transported from the manufacturer's factory to the appellants' factory without ever going to the head office. In the circumstances he prays for allowing the stay petition unconditionally.

3. Countering the arguments Shri T.P. Kumar, Ld. SDR submits that the Assistant Commissioner had allowed the Modvat in respect of two other invoices where the applicants had produced the evidence of transportation of the inputs to their factory. However, in respect of the invoice in question, the applicant failed to substantiate their submission of transportation of the goods to their factory premises directly. As regards other co-lateral evidences produced by them he submitted that these are in the nature of private records maintained by the applicant themselves and entries made for the same cannot be accepted as reflecting the actual position. As regards the Board's circular he submits that it is admitted fact that their invoice in question has not been endorsed by their head office in [sic] their factory and as such the conditions of the circular are not satisfied. If the goods were transported by a taxi they could have mentioned the taxi number etc. in the invoice itself. In the circumstances he submits that there is no case made up for grant of stay to the applicants.

to the said assessees. I also observe that there is no danger of the invoices being misutilised as the procedure for endorsement had been done away with after 1994 with the introduction of the new system of the invoices. In the circumstances, I hold that there was no infirmity in the invoices stamped with rubber stamp and the ground of denial of modvat credit was not a valid ground. Accordingly, I set aside this part of the order and allow the appeal to that extent. 4. The second point requiring consideration of the Tribunal is whether modvat credit can be disallowed on the ground when the invoice is in the name of the branch office of the appellant whereas the inputs were received in the factory premises of the appellants and were utilised therein. The department's objection is that as per the Trade Notice No. 18/95 dated 21.2.1995 issued by the Allahabad Collectorate goods covered under a particular invoice should be delivered only at the place of destination reflected in the said invoice and in the instant case the goods have been delivered in the factory premises of the appellant whereas the address shown in the invoice is that of their branch office. I find that the same issue had come up earlier before the Tribunal in the case of Larsen & Toubro, Orissa Vs. Collector of Central Excise, Bhubaneswar reported in 1994 (3) RLT 215 (ERB) wherein it was held that modvat credit should not be on the ground that the duty paying documents were in the name of the office whereas the inputs were received and utilised in the factory. In the instant case, there is no dispute that the invoice is in the name of the same appellant. Further, the department also does not dispute the duty-paid character of the inputs, their receipt in the appellants' factory and its utilisation in the manufacture of final product or the clearance of the final product on payment of duty. In nutshell, the availability of the modvat credit to the appellant on all other counts is not denied by the department. The appellants' reliance on Board's Circular No. 96/7/95-CX dated 13.2.1995 which is to the effect that in case of transit sale, invoices which may be in the assessees registered office can be endorsed by them in the name of their factory premises, is appropriate. In the instant case, the documents were in the name of branch office. The branch office could have endorsed the same in their own factory address. In the circumstances, it is only a procedural lapse, if at all, on the part of the appellants and cannot be made the basis for denial of modvat credit to the appellants. Accordingly, I allow this part of the appeal also by setting aside the order of the lower authority to that extent.

5. As regards the denial of modvat credit on the ground that dealers invoices are defective in character, I find that the original adjudicating authority in his impugned order has himself observed that as the goods were sold to the appellants as 'transit sale', the manufacturer's invoices bearing end-user's name would have been sufficient and proper documents to enable the appellant to take the credit. However, after observing so, he goes further to the dealers invoices and refers some defects in the said invoices and by holding the dealers invoices as defective disallowed the modvat credit. I find sufficient force in the submission of Shri Dutta that having himself observed that manufacturer's invoices were sufficient to extend the benefit of modvat credit to the appellants, the Assistant Collector has erred in relying on dealers invoices and rejecting the appellants claim for modvat by holding the same to be improper documents. I find that the Assistant Collector should have looked into the manufacturer's invoices and should have allowed the benefit of modvat after satisfying himself about the correctness of the same. As the manufacturer's invoices have not been looked into by the Assistant Collector from that angle, I set aside the impugned order and remand the case to the original adjudicating authority with the directions to verify the particulars required to be mentioned in the manufacturer's invoices under the law and to extend the benefit, if available, on the basis of the manufacturer's invoices.

6. In view of the foregoing discussions, penalty of Rs. 5,000/- is also set aside.

7. Appeal disposed of in the above terms.

Per Gowri Shankar : The question for consideration in this appeal is the eligibility to modvat credit by the appellant of the duty that is shown to have been paid on the invoices issued by the dealers of the inputs. After hearing both sides, we deal with each of the grounds on which modvat has been denied, as follows:-

2. A sum of Rs. 2.21 lakhs had been denied on the ground that the invoice bore the address of the appellant's head office and not that of the factory. Counsel for the appellant says that there was only one manufacturing unit located at Pune, the head office being in Mumbai. The head office could not have taken the credit, not being a factory. Endorsement of invoices is also not permissible. The goods had been received in the appellant's factory and utilised in the manufacture. Therefore the failure, if any, is most technical and should not stand in the way. The departmental representative emphasises that the invoice is not in the name of the manufacturing unit.

3. In a situation of this kind where there is only one factory, we are of the view that the drawback in the invoice that it did not contain the factory's name, should not result in the invoice being held invalid. The head office was not a factory and so could not have utilised the credit. The provisions of Rule 57F (1), permitting removal of the inputs for home consumption as such, would also not be available to it. It is not as if, by containing the heading office's name, credit could have been taken by the recipient in more than one factory; as we have noted, the factory was only one. There is no dispute that the goods were not received and utilised in the factory. In this situation, we do not think that the credit should be denied.

4. Invoices issued by dealers for a total of Rs. 7.49 lakhs have been held invalid on the ground that they were not marked duplicate or original and they were "extra copies". The invoices were issued between the period from 3rd August 1994 to 4th January 1995. The contention of the counsel for the appellant is that the requirement that credit must be been taken on duplicate invoices came on the statute book by way of amendment of sub-rule (4) of Rule 57GG on 19.1.1995. The trade notice that was issued in November 1994 by the Commissioner, Pune, insisting upon this requirement had no legal authority.

5. Although the departmental representative relies on the trade notice, the appellant's contention has to be accepted. In the absence of any legal authority, the denial of the credit is not justified. This is the view taken by the Tribunal in its decisions in Lauls Ltd. Vs. CCE 2000 (41) RLT 213 and Parikh Chemical Industries Vs. CCE 1997 (95) ELT 598. Another objection raised with regard to these invoices is that they did not contain details of the mode of transport and time. The Commissioner has confirmed that these invoices did not indicate the mode and time of transport. Counsel for the appellant points out, rightly, that the proforma prescribed under sub-rule (4) of Rule 57GG did not contain time and mode of transport. Column 1 (i) of the proforma specifies "date and time of issue both in words and figures of the invoice of registered person issuing the invoice." This refers to the date of issue of the invoice and not the date and time of despatch of the goods from the premises. The contention of the departmental representative that some of the invoices did not contain this also may be true; that however was not the basis for proposing to disallow these invoices. The basis was very clear that time and mode of transport had not been shown. We therefore do not think that this was a valid objection and credit ought not to have been denied.

6. The credit of 36000/- has been objected to on the ground that it was a customer copy of an invoice issued by Steel Authority of India Ltd. (SAIL for short) and not a duplicate. We do not see how reliance made on a Circular 86/86/94-CX dated 22.12.1994 of the Board helps the appellant. This only provides that SAIL can issue invoices from the depot recognised for modvat credit purposes and has anything to do with any copy. There being no other ground, the denial of the credit is in order.

7. The appeal is accordingly allowed in part.

Per S.L. Peeran : This appeal arises from Order-in-Appeal No. 86/2003-CE, dated 31.1.2003 by which the Modvat Credit has been denied on invoices which has been endorsed in favour of the Head Office. The department has taken a stand that there is no endorsement in favour of factory for the purpose of availing of Modvat Credit by the factory. It is, therefore, a demand of Rs. 39,530/- under Rule 57I of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 has been invoked. The appellant has relied on large number of judgments, which are noted in para 3 (e), of Commissioner (Appeals) order, which are reproduced herein below:-

(a)

Amai Rasayan Ltd. Vs. CCE - 1993 (67) ELT 133 (T)

(b)

Eicher Tractors Vs. CCE - 1996 (87) ELT 252 (T)

(c)

Bansal Containers P. Ltd. Vs. CCE - 1996 (83) ELT 425 (T)

(d)

Subros Ltd. Vs. Commr. - 1997 (96) ELT 602 (T)

(e)

Chamundi Rolling Mills Vs. Commr. - 1994 (3) RLT 855 (CEGAT-B)=1996 (81) ELT 563 (T)

(f)

Shree Acids Chemicals Vs. Commr. - 1997 (95) ELT 114 (T)

(g)

Commr. Vs. Jay Enn Castings Ltd. - 1997 (22) RLT 210 (CEGAT)=1997 (95) ELT 82 (T)

(h)

Ramgarh Chini Mills Vs. Commr. of Central Excise, Kanpur - 1998 (26) RLT 169 (CEGAT)=1998 (103) ELT 65 (T).

Despite these citations the Commissioner (Appeals) did not accept the plea and proceeded to decide on the basis of Trade Notice No. 57/96, dated 4.6.96 to deny the taking of Modvat Credit.

2. Ld. Advocate Shri Hasan Khan submit that the ratio of the judgments rendered in the case of Ramgarh Chini Mills Vs. Commissioner of Central Excise, Kanpur reported in 1998 (26) RLT 169 (CEGAT)=1998 (103) ELT 65 (Tri.) and Chrome Chemical Industries Vs. Commissioner of Central Excise, Calcutta-IV reported in 2001 (135) ELT 405 (Tri. Kolkata) directly applies to the facts of the case and all the citations already noted. He submits that the invoices being in the Head Office name, it has been held to be condonable procedural lapse. As, it is not the dispute that the inputs were actually received and utilised in the manufacture of final products and there is no allegation of malafide. He submits that the appeal is required to be allowed in the light of these judgments.

3. Ld. JDR Shri C. Mani, reiterates the view expressed by the authorities. In so far as the citations are concerned, he leaves the matter to the discretion of the Bench.

4. On a careful consideration, I notice that there is no allegation of any malafides against the appellants in misusing the inputs. 2. The appeal relates to denial of Modvat credit to the tune of Rs. 1,69,302/- and imposition of penalty Rs. 15,000/- under Rule 173Q. The invoice issued by M/s. Transpeck India, the goods were purchased for their Ratnagiri factory. However, the invoice was prepared in the name of head office. So far as this ground is concerned, I find that the credit cannot be disallowed on the basis that the invoice is not in the name of the factory. The diversion of the entire consignment initially invoiced in the name of head office does not affect the entitlement of Modvat credit, the discrepancy is curable. The provision of Rule 57G (11) also take care of the situation of applying correction to such defects. There is no dispute as regards the duty payment on the inputs and their utilisation in the finished goods production. Therefore, the credit cannot be disallowed on this ground.

So far as the credit taken on the basis of original invoices is concerned, it is noted that, there are large number of invoices which are spread over different dates and relate to different manufacturer namely Hindustan Petroleum, ILC and BPCL wherein it is claimed that duplicate copy is lost in transit. It is obvious that several transporters would be involved in the process of transporting these goods and it cannot be a case that, all the transporters have lost the duplicate copy of invoice in transit. Therefore, I hold that appellants are not in position justify their claim for Modvat on the basis of original documents. Therefore, the claim against original invoices is rejected.

So far as the invoices issued by Metco services and trading are concerned, I notice that the critical particulars as prescribed by Notification Nos. 32/94 and 33/94-CE (NT) are not incorporated therein. Therefore, the credit taken against the invoices issued by the said dealer is also correctly held as inadmissible by the lower authorities.

5. Accordingly, I hold that, except for allowing the credit pertaining to the consignment diverted to Dombivili from the head office, relating to the credit of Rs. 39,668/-, the claim for the remaining amount is disallowed. Accordingly, the appeal is rejected partly and partly allowed for the claim to the extent of Rs. 39,668/-.

The Tribunal in the case of Chrome Chemical Industries vs. Commissioner of Central Excise (Calcutta-IV (Supra) after considering this Circular held that manufacturing Unit is entitled for credit where the invoices were in the name of Registered office in case the invoices were not endorsed by the Head office which is only a procedural lapse. Neither this Rule nor any of other Central Excise Rule requires that the duty paying document should be made only in the name of the manufacturer using the inputs. All that is required according to both the spirit and the letter of the Rule is that the document should evidence the payment of duty on the input. Indeed, as held by the CEGAT in Collector Vs. Good lass Nerolac Paints -1986 (26) ELT 57 (T) - not only is it not necessary for the duty paying document to show the manufacturer as the Consignee, even the endorsement in favour of the manufacturer is not required. Therefore for claiming the modvat credit the end user of the goods covered by the invoices has to satisfy the two conditions. Firstly, that the dealer who issued the invoice or invoices is a registered one, under Rule 174 of the Central Excise Rules and secondly that the goods covered by the invoice or invoices were intended to be used or had been actually used in the production of final product. If the very first condition regarding the registration of the dealer does not stand proved, the end user of the goods cannot claim modvat credit on the basis of the invoices on the simple ground that the goods were intended to be used or had been actually used in the product of final product, as in the invoice proforma under Rule 57-G or 57-T appended by the Board as annexure '2E' to the Central Excise Rules, the details regarding the Central Excise registration No., Sales Tax Registration, Income Tax Registration numbers besides other details regarding the goods, had to be mentioned by the dealer issuing the invoice. It is for end user of the goods before making the purchase to satisfy himself that the dealer with whom he is dealing is registered under the Central Excise Act. If he purchases the goods from an unregistered dealer, then he has to blame himself and not the Revenue department, when he is disallowed modvat credit in respect thereof. He cannot be legally permitted to take the benefit of modvat credit scheme for having simply shown that the goods had been used by him in the manufacture of the final product. The question for consideration in this appeal is the eligibility to modvat credit which was taken by Indoco Remedies Pvt. Ltd., the respondent to this appeal. The notice issued to it proposed denial on two grounds. The first was that it could not take modvat credit of the duty paid on invoices which were issued in the name of a "loan licensee" i.e. person who utilised machinery and other facilities in the respondent's factory for manufacture of medicaments out of their own raw material and employing their skill. The second was that the respondent had taken modvat credit on the basis of invoices of the manufacturer of the inputs which had been endorsed. Credit was proposed to be denied on the ground that there was no provision in law for such endorsement. The Asstt. Commissioner, who adjudicated on the show cause notice confirmed the proposal in the notice and denied the credit, and also imposed a penalty. The assessee appealed the order. The Commissioner (Appeals) was persuaded by the points made in the appeal and permitted credit and set aside the penalty. Hence this appeal by the department.

2. I have heard both sides.

3. As far as the first issue is concerned, the matter is clearly in the department's favour. The Commissioner has been swayed by the fact that the actual place where the goods were manufactured was respondent's factory. That is however not relevant. The credit is to be taken by the manufacturer, that manufacturer was the "loan licensee", the person who utilised the respondent's factory for manufacture by it of the medicaments. It is that person who paid the duty on these goods and it is in his name the invoice has been issued. Therefore, while that manufacturer, the loan licensee may be entitled to the credit, the respondent would not be. The order of the Asstt. Commissioner in this regard will have to be restored.

4. As to the second point, counsel for the respondent says that the invoices which were endorsed to it were issued by the manufacturers for clearance of their goods either to their own depots or to the dealer. He says that the respondent was in fact in possession of the invoices for the same goods which were issued by the depot or by the dealer and credit could validly be taken on this invoice. If that is the case, the respondent would be entitled to credit notwithstanding that it would not be entitled to credit on the basis of endorsed invoice. This point however has been raised for the first time before me and I think it appropriate to remand the matter to the Asstt. Commissioner for considering these document and reviewing on the eligibility to credit.

5. The appeal is therefore allowed and the impugned order set aside. So far as the credit taken on invoice issued to a "loan licensee" is concerned, the Asstt. Commissioner's order is restored. The remaining matter is remanded to the Asstt. Commissioner. He shall consider the documents that the respondent may produce within a month from the order and pass orders on the eligibility to credit in accordance with law. I however set aside the penalty imposed on the appellant. The credit was taken in April 1994 shortly after the invoice system was introduced and there was considerable lack of clarity both in the department and outside as to various aspects of the system. I therefore think that the respondent deserves the benefit of doubt in this case.

" The main issue to be decided in this appeal is whether the denial of modvat credit in respect of inputs received under gate passes endorsed in favour of the appellants after passing through more than two hands, is sustainable. Gate pass is a document prescribed for removal of the goods from the factory of manufacturer to the first destination. This is evident from the provisions of Rule 52A and Rule 173G of the Central Excise Rules. Hence, when there is a stipulation in Rule 57G that the inputs are to be received under gate pass by the claimant of modvat credit, it should be normally taken to mean that the said Rule contemplates receipt of inputs straight from the factory of manufacturer under gate pass. In that case, the consignee is necessarily to be the modvat claimant and consignor being the manufacturer of inputs, However, when this requirement created some difficulties in the case of Small Scale Units to obtain the inputs through intermediaries the Board appears to have made relaxation to this requirement, by permitting one endorsement in the gate passes initially and subsequently based on the representations permitting up to two endorsements in the gate passes. Per P.S. Bajaj : Heard.

2. From the record, I find that the appellants have a strong, prima facie, case as the modvat credit has been disallowed to them of the disputed amount on technical ground. Therefore, the stay application is allowed.

3. With the consent of both sides, I proceed to decide the appeal itself on merits.

4. This appeal has been filed by the appellants against a part of the impugned order-in-appeal dated 8.5.2002 vide which the Commissioner (Appeals) has disallowed the modvat credit of Rs. 8,36,297.

5. The appellants are engaged in the manufacture of steel tubes and pipes. They during the period March 1998 to June 1999 availed the modvat credit of Rs. 8,36,297/- on the invoices/B.Es, but they were served with a show cause notice for recovery of this amount on the ground that the invoices/B.Es did not contain their name and address and there were also no endorsements on those documents in their favour. After getting their reply to the show cause notice, the adjudicating authority confirmed the demand through the order-in-original. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) has also upheld that order through the impugned order.

6. I have heard both sides.

7. The learned counsel has contended that there is no cogent evidence to substantiate the allegations as alleged in the show cause notice against the appellants. He has also referred to the letter issued by the SAIL from whom the goods were purchased in respect of which the modvat credit has been claimed, clarifying all the objections raised by the Department in the show cause notice. But the same, according to the learned counsel, has been overlooked by the Commissioner (Appeals). Therefore, the impugned order of the Commissioner (Appeals) disallowing the modvat credit of the disputed amount deserves to be set aside.

8. On the other hand, the learned SDR, has simply reiterated the correctness of the impugned order. The perusal of the record shows that the modvat credit of the disputed amount has been taken by the appellants on the strength of 15 invoices and one Bill of Entry. The invoices were issued by the registered dealer i.e. SAIL. On the invoices, initially the factory address of the appellants was not mentioned, but address of the Head Office was recorded therein. But, later on, this position was clarified by the SAIL through letter (refer page 41) dated 18.12.1998 and address on the invoices was corrected. There is no dispute regarding the duty paid character of the goods as they were sold to the appellants by the SAIL. There is no evidence to suggest that the goods were not delivered at the factory premises by the SAIL. The observations of the Commissioner (Appeals) in para 13 of the impugned order that there was no endorsement in favour of the factory by the Head/Regd. Offices of the appellants and that there was no balance in the quantity of the raw materials issued vis-a-vis final product/waste/burning losses, while disallowing the modvat credit claimed by the appellants, had been based on no evidence whatsoever. No endorsement of the Head Office was required when the address on the invoices itself was corrected by the SAIL, the supplier of the goods, through letter dated 18.12.1998, referred to above. No material has been brought on record to show that there was no balance in the quantity of the raw-materials issued vis-a-vis final product. When the duty paid character of the goods stands amply established and there had been also receipt of the goods in the factory, the modvat credit claimed, could not be legally denied to the appellants. In this context, reference may be made to Aradhana Beverages Food Co. Ltd. Vs. CCE, Bolpur, 1999 (35) RLT 152, wherein in similar circumstances, this view has been taken by the Tribunal.

9. In the light of the discussion made above, the impugned order of the Commissioner (Appeals) disallowing the modvat credit of disputed amount of Rs. 8,36,297/- to the appellants, cannot be sustained and the same is ordered to be set aside. The appeal of the appellants is accordingly allowed with consequential relief, if any, permissible under the law.

[Notification No. 15/94-C.E.(N.T.), dated 30.3.1994] It is seen that in a contingency where the goods were received not directly from the manufacturer but through the agency of the dealer, facility for taking modvat was taken care of by authorising the taking of MOD VAT Credit based on the invoice to be issued by the wholesaler, dealer, distributor etc. and for that reason it would appear the Government did not feel it necessary to issue any notification for acceptance of the endorsed invoices as was the case in case of Gate Passes. Even in the case of Gate Passes, a provision was earlier made for acceptance of subsidiary gate passes also. Thus, simultaneously the provision of acceptance of subsidiary gate passes and also endorsed gate passes was available. It is seen that at the time when the change over took place in the Central Excise documentation as above, there was some' confusion and some hardship and the Government issued Notification 16/94 dated 30th March, 1994 under which the endorsed Gate Pass, Subsidiary Gate Pass and certain certificates were notified as authorised documents for taking MODVAT Credit till 30th June, 1994. It would thus appear that upto 30th June, 1994 this facility of accepting endorsed Gate Pass was available along with the amended provisions in regard to taking of MODVAT Credit based on the invoices issued by the manufacturer or by the dealer. In the present case what has happened is that the full consignment as received by the dealer has been sent to the Respondents and the dealer has not issued any invoice of his own but has made an endorsement for the sale of the goods to the Respondents and sent the goods under the cover of this endorsed invoice. The question that arises is that whether in the circumstances which prevailed at the relevant time such a course was acceptable. It is observed that at the relevant time the dealers were not required to register while they were authorised to issue invoices as would be seen from Notification 15/94. In the present case what has happened is that instead of the dealer issuing invoice, he has made the endorsement in the invoice in respect of the goods he has received from the manufacturer. It is in the above context that the matter should have been examined by the learned lower authority. The learned lower authority does not appear to have examined the whole issue in depth and has held that the endorsements made later in the Gate Passes was adequate enough to give cover to the appellants for the purpose of MODVAT Credit. This, I am afraid, is not the correct way to look at things with the change of law and with the changed parameters and facilities which had been made available at the relevant time. The position should have been examined in the context of the same. This having not been done, I hold that the order of the learned lower authori ty is not proper and therefore set aside the same and remand the matter for denovo consideration of the factors set out above and after affording the Respondents an opportunity of being heard. The appeal is therefore allowed by remand.

Provided that no credit shall be taken unless the inputs are received in the factory under the cover of a Gate Pass, an AR-1, a Bill of Entry or any other documents as may be prescribed by the Central Board of Excise and Customs, (constituted under the Central Board of Revenue Act, 1963, (54 of 1963) in this behalf evidencing the payment of duty on such inputs)." Gate pass is a prescribed document under Rule 52A in respect of excisable goods cleared from a factory and this has been described as GP-1. Among other particulars in this form are - Name and address of the consignee, manner of transport, date and time of removal which should be shown in figures and words. All these particulars have been prescribed to ensure that the gate pass is not misused for double or treble transport of excisable goods and the gate pass is valid for transport of the goods in respect of consignees to whom these are consigned and the mode of transport etc. prescribed. We observe that the moment the goods have been received at the consignee's end the validity of the gate pass so far as the transport of the goods is concerned, can be taken to have run out and the gate pass only remains as evidence of clearance of the goods on payment of duty and the same gate pass can only be revived by following the procedure prescribed in this regard as set out under Rule 57G. Re-endorsement of gate pass in respect of part of the consignment sold is not one of the prescribed modes. For bringing the goods for MODVAT purposes, the proper course for the assessee was to have had the gate pass re-endorsed by the jurisdictional Central Excise officer after getting the particulars regarding consignment verified with reference to the gate pass if such a course had been prescribed under Rule 57G. This admittedly had not been done. We observe that a strict view has to be taken in regard to the documents under the cover of which the goods are brought in a factory for MODVAT purposes. The documents as have been prescribed are with a view to ensure that duty paid goods alone are received in the factory and it is obligatory that statutory documents as set out under Rule 57G alone are taken into consideration for the purpose of MODVAT Credit. There is possibility of misuse in case consignees on their own are allowed to endorse the gate pass after the goods have been cleared from the factory and received by them and a part of the same are resold. It would he difficult to verify the identity of the goods after the original consignment is broken up for sale. In this view of the matter we hold that the learned lower appellate authority has been in error in allowing the appeal of the Respondents. We, therefore, set aside the impugned order and allow the Departmental appeal.

The appellant company has four units all situated in Silvassa. Further, for the sake of convenience, they can be called Unit I to Unit 4.

2. During the period 30.06.03 to 24.01.04, four duty paying invoices were issued by the concerned manufacturer of POY in favour of Unit 3 of the company. However, as the said material was proposed to be used in the present appellant's unit i.e. Unit 2, the said raw material was delivered in the appellant's factory under the cover of invoices with the remark by the Unit 3 that entire consignment stand transferred to the appellant's unit. The said goods were re-directed to the appellant's unit without receiving in Unit 3. The appellant took the credit of the same in their record on the basis of the said invoices.

3. Only objection of Revenue is that the invoices were in the name of Unit 3, who could not have endorsed the same. On the other hand, it is the appellant's contention that all the units are belonging to the same appellant and it is not a case of sale of input requiring any endorsement etc. For the above proposition, they have relied upon Tribunal's decision in case of CCE, Coimbatore Vs. Coimbatore Murugan Mills 2003 (56) RLT 84 (CEGAT-Che.)=2003 (160) ELT 825 (Tri-Chennai).

4. After hearing the learned SDR Shri J.S. Negi, I find that there is no dispute about the factual position. The inputs were actually received by the appellant and utilised by them in manufacture of final product. Admittedly, the inputs were duty paid and covered by the invoices, which were in the name of M/s Raj Rayon only. There was difference in the address of the recipient inasmuch as the address of Unit 3 was shown instead of Unit 2. As per the remarks on the invoices, Unit 3 diverted the entire consignment to the present appellant who actually received in their factory. As such, it cannot be said to be a case of endorsement of invoices. Tribunal in case of Zenith Weaves Pvt. Ltd Vs. CCE, Surat 2004 (178) ELT 1029 (Tri.-Del.)=2004 (177) ELT 251 (Tri-Mum.), has held that invoices addressed in respect of assessee's kim factory, but goods delivered at Surat factory, cannot be made basis for denial of Modvat credit. To the same effect, is Tribunal's decision in case of CCE, Noida Vs. Flex Industries Ltd. 2004 (178) ELT 1029 (Tri-Del.).

5. In view of the above and in absence of any doubt about the duty paid character of the input, their receipt in the appellant's factory, utilisation of the same in manufacture of final product, cleared on payment of duty, I find no justification for denial of Modvat credit to the appellant.

6. The impugned order is accordingly set aside and appeal allowed with consequential relief to the appellant.

Computation of input tax credit

26. (1) Input tax credit on the opening stock of the tax paid goods purchased between 1.4.2005 and Appointed Day—

After the commencement of the Act, where any dealer registered as a VAT dealer or where the authority prescribed registers any dealer as a VAT dealer under rule 3, such dealer shall be eligible for input tax credit as provided under section 20 of the Act. The goods on which the input tax credit 5[and] claimed or allowed shall be available as on the Appointed Day, on stock of tax-paid goods excluding the goods mentioned in Part-E of Schedule-II of the Act, and shall be admissible within nine months from the appointed date on the following conditions:—

(a)

The dealer claiming such input tax credit must be registered under the Act.

(b)

The VAT dealer claiming input tax credit, shall make an inventory of all goods in hand, on the Appointed Day, which has suffered the incidence of tax under the Repealed Act, and shall file his claim for input tax credit in Form JVAT 401 along with the evidences, including the 6[statement of] purchase or sale invoice(s) 7[or] 8[***] copies of the Declaration (s) in Form IX-C issued/received under the Repealed Act.

(c)

The VAT dealer claiming input tax credit, in the circumstances he is a manufacturer or a miner and has purchased his Inputs or the raw-materials under sub-section (1) of section 13 of the Repealed Act, shall make an inventory of all such goods in hand, on the Appointed Day, which has suffered the incidence of tax under the Repealed Act, and shall file his claim for input tax credit in Form JVAT 401 along with the evidences, including the purchase or sale invoice(s) and the evidences/copies of the Declaration (s) in Form IX issued/received under the Repealed Act.

(d)

In the circumstances, the tax paid purchase invoices reflect the amount of taxes realised and paid separately, input tax credit to the extent of 100% of such amount of tax shall be admissible.

(e)

In the circumstances, the tax paid purchase invoices are inclusive of tax, the amount of tax shall be derived by an under-mentioned formula and input tax credit to the extent of 75% of such calculated tax amount shall be admissible:—

Tax Amount = R x Purchase/100 + R

Where, R is equal to "Rate of tax"; "Purchase" is "Purchase Value" or "Opening Stock Value" inclusive of tax amount. (If rate of tax is 10%, 'R' is 10)

(f)

The claim for such input tax credit shall be filed before the prescribed authority, within a period of thirty days from the date of commencement of the Act. The claim of such input tax credit shall be verified and allowed in Form JVAT 402, not later than a period of 1[eight months], from the date of receipt of Form JVAT 401.

(g)

In the circumstances, if the input tax credit is claimed and availed under this sub-rule, in any manner with an intention to evade the tax payable, the same shall be treated as an offence under sub-section (7) of section 84 of the Act.

(h)

The burden of proving, that the input tax credit claimed under this sub-rule is true and correct, shall be on such dealer.

Subject to this sub-rule, if the input tax credit as allowed in Form JVAT 402 and claimed in the return(s) by such dealer, remains unadjusted from the output tax for that month, the same shall be carried forward for the next month(s).

4. Section 10 of the Tripura Value Added Tax Act provides inputs tax credit. Taxes paid on inputs used for producing taxable goods or purchases are deductible from the tax payable on the taxable sales whether the inputs or purchases are used only partly for production or sale of taxable goods, credit would be given for a fraction of input tax equal to the proportion of the taxable sales to total sales:

Provided credit for input tax may be enjoyed under the following circumstances:—

(1) Purchasers and sellers shall be registered under the Tripura Value Added Tax Act, 2004;

(2) Tax credit should be provided for production input and goods for sale;

(3) In case of production, tax credit may be allowed for not only raw materials and components, but also for plant, machinery and equipments:

Provided purchases of such plant, machinery and equipment could be made eligible for input tax credit if these are acquired for use exclusively for taxable production, manufacturing or processing activities:

Provided further that no input tax credit will be allowed for office equipment and building materials for use in residential or commercial construction. Though materials for factory construction may be eligible for tax credit. Tax credit will be denied for transportation of equipments and supplies (as transportation services are exempt from the tax).

(4) Manufacturers and producers (including mining companies) are eligible to claim tax credit for the tax paid on virtually all of the materials used in their production or manufacturing processes. This would include raw materials, component, parts, packaging materials, consumables, chemicals, additives, lubricants and explosives but would not include motor fuels (petroleum and diesels but not furnace fuel) and coal and coke.

(5) Goods brought from outside the State shall not be entitled to get input tax credit in respect of tax paid in the other State.

RG 23A Register

9. Dina Mahabir Re-Rollers (P.) Ltd. v. CCE [Final Order No. A-112/Kol./2010, dated 12-2-2010. As per rule 9, a challan evidencing payment of service tax by the persons liable to pay service tax is a valid duty paying document. Before the lower authorities, the appellant pleaded that the credit was taken on the strength of debit entry made in RG 23A, Pt.II of the statutory record showing the payment of service tax. In reply to the show-cause notice also the appellant specifically mentioned that the service tax was paid through CENVAT credit register and, hence, on the basis of entry made in the register, the credit was availed. It was also the submission of the appellant that a consolidated entry was made in respect of the payment of service tax.

The Tribunal found that in the absence of any challan, no verification can be done regarding the service received by the appellant or where the service tax was paid regarding the service received by the assessee. The Tribunal found that there was no infirmity in the impugned order.

Private challans

10. In CCE v. Stelko Strips Ltd. 2010 (255) ELT 397 (Punj. & Har.), the Tribunal had referred the question of law for adjudication of the High Court, namely, - Whether the private challans other than the prescribed documents are valid for taking MODVAT credit under Central Excise Rules, 1944?

The High Court held that the Punjab and Haryana High Court in ‘ CCE v. Gujarat Medicraft (P.) Ltd. held that once duty payment is not disputed and it is found that documents are genuine and not fraudulent, then the manufacturer would be entitled to MODVAT credit on duty paid inputs. The Division Bench of Punjab & Haryana High Court in CCE v. Ralson India Ltd. 2006 (202) ELT 759 held that if the duty paid character of inputs and their receipt in manufacturer’s factory and utilization for manufacturing a final product is not disputed, then credit cannot be denied.

In this case, the High Court held that the respondent-manufacturer would be entitled to claim MODVAT credit on the strength of private challans as the same were not found to be false and there was a proper certification that duty had been paid.

Xerox copy

11. In CCE&C v. Steelco Gujarat Ltd. 2010 (255) ELT 518 (Guj.), the original/duplicate invoices had been lost in transit. As such, the assessee availed CENVAT credit on the basis of xerox copy of the triplicate copy of the invoice, duly attested by the Jurisdictional Range Superintendent at the suppliers end to evidence the duty payment character of the said invoice in question.

The Commissioner of Central Excise (Appeals) observed that there was no dispute about the duty paid character of the input, receipt of the same in the appellant’s factory and utilization for manufacture of final product. Therefore, the Commissioner of Central Excise (Appeals) came to the conclusion that the legitimate right of the appellants cannot be denied just because the original/duplicate invoices were lost in transit. The department could at best, as a precaution to prevent availment of double credit in the case of appellants recover the original document and insist for an undertaking or indemnity bond from the appellants.

The Tribunal while confirming the order of the Commissioner of Central Excise (Appeals) observed that mere xerox copy by itself should not be made the basis of allowing the credit but where the assessee had made efforts to get the said xerox copy attested by the Range Superintendent at the supplier’s end and had established beyond doubt that the duty, stood paid on the goods and the goods stood received by him, denial of credit on the procedural irregularity would not be justified.

The High Court did not find any infirmity in the order passed by the Tribunal and Commissioner of Central Excise (Appeals).

Invoices issued in the name of branch office

allowing the credit but where the assessee had made efforts to get the said xerox copy attested by the Range Superintendent at the supplier’s end and had established beyond doubt that the duty, stood paid on the goods and the goods stood received by him, denial of credit on the procedural irregularity would not be justified.

The High Court did not find any infirmity in the order passed by the Tribunal and Commissioner of Central Excise (Appeals).

Invoices issued in the name of branch office 12. In ‘Manipal Advertising Services (P.) v. CCE [2010] 25 STT 30 (Bang. - CESTAT), the issue as to the eligibility of invoice to avail credit which was issued in the name of the branch office is discussed. In this case, it was undisputed that—

u the appellant was not having any service tax registration in respect of branch offices on whose name the invoices were issued by the service providers;

u the appellant had got centralized billing and centralized accounting system.

The Tribunal held that if a person is discharging service tax liability from his registered office, the benefit of CENVAT credit on the service tax paid by the service provider cannot be denied to him only on the ground that the said invoices were in the name of the branch office. There was no dispute that the said invoices were in the name of the Branch Office. There was no dispute that the branch offices were not registered with the service tax authorities and they were not discharging the service tax liability, obviously, the appellant was discharging service tax liability on the services provided by branches.

The Tribunal found that the documents on which the appellant had taken the service tax credit, though in the name of the Branch Office, were actually being paid from the premises wherein the service tax registration had been taken. In view of the above finding, the impugned order was unsustainable and the Tribunal set aside the same and allowed the appeal with consequential relief, if any.

Invoice not in the name of the assessee

13. In ‘Kitply Industries Ltd. v. CCE [2010]26 STT 369 (New Delhi - CESTAT), two elements are involved—

u disallowance of CENVAT credit in respect of service tax paid on cellular phone service availed while bills thereof were not in the name of the assessee; and

u disallowance of credit on account of payment of service tax for availing insurance services on the strength of photocopy of insurance policy.

The Tribunal held that so far as the demand raised disallowing the CENVAT credit of service tax on the cellular phones was concerned, integrity, dependability and relevancy test was applied by adjudicating authority to reach the conclusion. Accordingly, the Adjudicating Authority was justified to disallow the claim.

So far as the service tax on insurance was concerned, if the appellant would produce relevant documents having force of evidence, the authority would reconsider the claim. If the authority founds that service tax was paid on the input service meeting all the three tests aforesaid, the claim would be admissible.

Conclusion

14. From the above discussion, it is clear that the assessee in order to avail CENVAT credit has to maintain documents as required under rule 9. However, in cases where such documents could not be maintained and other sorts of documents are with the assessee by which he availed credit, then the following requirements are to be fulfilled—

u There shall be no dispute about the duty paid character of the input;

u Receipt of the goods in the factory of the assessee;

u Utilization for manufacture of the final product.

The authority, in such cases, has to satisfy the three tests, viz., integrity, dependability and relevancy as held in Kitply Industries Ltd. (supra). The Tribunal in Stelco Gujarat Ltd. case (supra) rightly held that the denial of credit on the procedural irregularity would not be justified. Even though favourable judgments are there, the assessee should try to maintain documents for availing credit in accordance with the rule with utmost care to avoid unnecessary litigations.

It was found from the records that there was no dispute that the assessee’s office at Manipal had got the centralized billing and accounting systems. If that be so, registration taken by the assessee was in accordance with the Rules. u There was no dispute that the branch office was not registered with the service tax authorities and it was not discharging the service tax liability, obviously, as the assessee was discharging service tax liability on the services provided by branch. It was found that though the document on basis of which the assessee had taken the service tax credit was in the name of branch office, yet tax was actually paid from the premises wherein the service tax registration had been taken. In view of the findings, the impugned order was unsustainable and the same was to be set aside and the appeal was to be allowed.

Even though the final product may be exempted from payment of excise duty, yet the assessee could not be asked to reverse the Modvat credit already taken by it

12.6 The assessee was engaged in manufacture of vegetable products and was taking credit of duties paid on inputs used in manufacture of final products. The final product was exempted from payment of excise duty vide Notification No. 16/96-CE, dated 23-7-1996. The revenue issued a show-cause notice requiring the assessee to reverse the Modvat credit on the inputs in hand and in process as well as on the inputs contained in the final products as on 23-7-1996. The assessee contested the notice on the ground that once the credit had been taken, the same could not be disallowed since in the books it had already been used and there was no legal provision which provided for recovery of such credit. The Assistant Commissioner rejected the assessee’s contention and disallowed the credit. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the order of the Assistant Commissioner. On appeal, the Tribunal, however, allowed the credit. On revenue’s appeal:

Held that the Supreme Court in Collector of Central Excise v. Dai Karkaria Ltd. 1999 (7) SCC 448 held that where a manufacturer obtains credit for the excise duty paid on raw material to be used by him in the production of an excisable product immediately, it should make the requisite declaration and obtain an acknowledgement thereof. It is entitled to use the credit at any time thereafter while making payment of excise duty on the excisable product. There is no provision in the Rules which provides for a reversal of the credit by the Excise Authorities, except where it has been illegally or irregularly taken, in which event it stands cancelled or, if utilized, has to be paid for. Where the credit has been validly taken, its benefit is available to the manufacturer without any limitation in time or otherwise, unless the manufacturer itself chooses not to use the raw material in its excisable product. The credit is, therefore, indefeasible. It should also be noted that there is no correlation of the raw material and the final product, that is to say, it is not as if credit can be taken only on a final product, that is, manufactured out of the particular raw material to which the credit is related. The credit may be taken against the excise duty on a final product manufactured on the very day it becomes available.

Applicability of proviso to Rule 11(2) of Central Excise Rules

3. Rule 9(1)(iv) of Cenvat Credit Rules states that invoice issued by a first stage dealer or a second stage dealer, as the case may be, in terms of the provisions of Central Excise Rules, 2002.

Rule 11 of Central Excise Rules makes provisions in respect of invoice issued by manufacturer.

Rule 11(7) of Central Excise Rules states that the provision of rule 11 shall apply mutatis mutandis (i.e., after making necessary changes) to goods supplied by a first stage dealer or second stage dealer.

Rule 11(1) of Central Excise Rules are applicable for removal of goods from the factory. As per rule 11(2) of Central Excise Rules, the invoice is required to contain various details like, range, classification, time and date of removal, mode of transport and registration number, rate of duty etc.

Thus the rule expected that goods should be dispatched from the godown of the registered dealer (so that time and date of removal, mode of transport etc. can be indicated in the invoice).

Thus, a registered dealer was required to bring goods to his godown and then dispatch goods to his customer under his Cenvatable invoice.

This required double transport of goods, which increased transportation costs. Hence, as a facility to registered dealer, direct dispatch of goods has been permitted vide proviso to rule 11(2) of Central Excise Rules, w.e.f. 1-3-2015.

Thus, the proviso is applicable only to invoice issued by registered dealer, who is issuing invoice under rule 9(1)(iv) of Cenvat Credit Rules.

The new proviso only provides that Cenvat credit can be availed on basis of invoice of registered dealer even in case of transit sale. Of course, Cenvat credit can be availed on basis of invoice of original manufacturer also.

Eligibility of Transit sale – In case of transit sale, the Cenvat credit can be availed on basis of invoice of original manufacturer, which is eligible document under rule 9(1)(a)(i)(I) of Cenvat Credit Rules. "It is a cardinal principle of construction that efforts should be made in construing the different provisions, so that, each provision will have its play and in the event of any conflict a harmonious construction should be given. Background

1. In industries like pharmaceuticals and agro-chemicals many times near-about expired goods, defective goods or damaged goods (for the sake of convenience let us say "defective goods") are sent again by various marketing depots (not registered under excise) for reprocessing. Usually it happens that the original goods have been manufactured by let us say factory A, B and C but the defective goods are returned to only one factory, let us say factory D for reprocessing. This is so because it will be impractical to send the defective goods for reprocessing to the very same factory which had manufactured the original goods due to logistical costs as well as difficulties in identifying them on one-to-one basis.

In such scenario, only document available will be copy of excise invoice issued by the original factory. Had the defective goods been returned to the same factory, manufacturer could have easily claimed CENVAT credit on the basis of originally issued invoice (as the excise invoice was issued by the same factory). However, here the case is different. Factory D wants to claim CENVAT credit of returned defective goods on the basis of excise invoice issued by other factories.

Critical Issues

2. Following critical issues arise in this set-up:

2.1 Whether CENVAT credit can be claimed by factory D when the invoices on the basis of which credit will be claimed has been issued by factory A, B and C ?

2.2 W.e.f. 11-07-2014, third proviso has been added to rule 4(1) of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004 which provides that credit cannot be claimed after a period of six months from the date of issuance of any document (in our case excise invoice) on the basis of which credit is claimed. In our case, as we are dealing with near-expired or defective goods, in all likelihood excise invoice issued by original manufacturer would have been dated beyond statutory period of six months. Issue is whether the third proviso will apply to the present case ?

2.3 What are the procedures one needs to follow to claim the said credit ?

3. Legal Analysis

3.1 To answer the first question, i.e., whether factory D can avail CENVAT credit on the basis of invoices issued by factory A, B and C for defective goods which are received back, one has to refer to rule 16 of the Central Excise Rules, 2002. Relevant extract is reproduced below for ready reference:

"Rule 16. Credit of duty on goods brought to the factory.—(1) Where any goods on which duty had been paid at the time of removal thereof are brought to any factory for being re-made, refined, re-conditioned or for any other reason, the assessee shall state the particulars of such receipt in his records and shall be entitled to take CENVAT credit of the duty paid as if such goods are received as inputs under the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2002 and utilize this credit according to the said rules.

(2) If the process to which the goods are subjected before being removed does not amount to manufacture, the manufacturer shall pay an amount equal to the CENVAT credit taken under sub-rule (1) and in any other case the manufacturer shall pay duty on goods received under sub-rule (1) at the rate applicable on the date of removal and on the value determined under sub-section (2) of section 3 or section 4 or section 4A of the Act, as the case may be.

[Explanation.—The amount paid under this sub-rule shall be allowed as CENVAT credit as if it was a duty paid by the manufacturer who removes the goods.]

3.2 Careful reading of above rule provides that CENVAT credit will be available of any goods on which duty has been paid and are brought to any factory for re-making, refining, re-conditioning or for any other reason as inputs. Thus, only condition to be fulfilled for claiming credit is that duty should have been paid on said goods. It is not necessary that goods should be received back in the same factory. It can be received in any factory. Further, goods can be brought back for reprocessing under rule 16 even if shelf life has expired (CCE v. Rako Agrochem (P.) Ltd. 2010 (260) ELT 479 (Trib. - Delhi)). Thus, credit can be claimed of goods received by factory D on the basis of invoices issued by original manufacturers. One may also refer to Board's Circular 607/44/2001-CX, dated 13-12-2001 which confirms the above view. Thus, CENVAT credit can be claimed on basis of manufacturers invoice available with depot to the extent of quantity received by factory D.

One may also refer to Board's Circular 607/44/2001-CX, dated 13-12-2001 which confirms the above view. Thus, CENVAT credit can be claimed on basis of manufacturers invoice available with depot to the extent of quantity received by factory D. 3.3 As far as second question is concerned, w.e.f. 11-07-2014 third proviso has been inserted in rule 4(1) of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004 which provides that CENVAT credit shall not be allowed after a period of six months from the date of issuance of invoice. Claim of CENVAT credit under Rule 16 discussed above will not be hit by the new proviso as rule 16 is a specific provision made for allowance of CENVAT credit in cases involving remaking. It is cardinal rule of interpretation that specific provisions will always override general provisions. If third proviso is universally operative, rule 16 will become inoperative as for remaking or reconditioning, return of goods can never be within a period of six months. That can never be the intention of legislators. Reliance is also placed on decision of the Mumbai CESTAT in case of Arihant Domestic Appliances Ltd. v. CCE 2012 (279) ELT 449 which has held that there is no time-limit for taking the credit under rule 16.

3.4 To claim the above discussed CENVAT credit as per para 14.2 of Circular No. 224/37/2005-CX. 6, dated 24-12-2008, factory D will have to intimate the department of receipt of duty paid goods. Factory D will also have to maintain the register duly recording the incoming goods so that only proportionate CENVAT credit is claimed.

Conclusion

4. From the foregoing analysis, a different manufacturer (factory D) can claim proportionate CENVAT credit, i.e., to the extent of goods received back on the basis of original manufacturer's invoice.

INPUT SERVICE DISTRIBUTOR AND CONTENTS OF INVOICE

6. Clause 2(m ) defines ‘input service distributor’ as an office of the manufacturer or provider of output service which receives invoice issued under rule 4A of the Service-tax Rules. Rule 4A(1) specifies the nature of invoices to be issued by the provider of taxable service, which should be serially numbered and signed by such person or a person authorized by him and shall contain,

(i)the name, address and registration number,

(ii)the name and address of the person receiving taxable service,

(iii)description, classification and value of taxable service,

(iv)the service tax payable thereon.

Sub-rule (2) of rule 4A provides that the input service distributor, distributing credit of taxable service shall also incorporate the details as per sub-rules (1)(i), (ii), (iii ) and (iv) of the amount of the credit distributed.

7. Rule 3 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 provides types of taxes and duties allowed for Cenvat Credit, the manner in which and extent to which such credit can be utilized. Credit is allowable on

(vii)service-tax leviable under section 66 of the finance act, paid on

(1)any input or capital goods received in the factory of manufacturer of final product or premises of the provider of output service on or after 10th day of September, 2004 and

UTILISATION OF CREDIT

8. Sub-rule (4) of rule 3 provides for the utilization of the credit availed above for the payment of

(a)any duty of excise on any final product, or

(b) and (c) credit taken on inputs or capital goods if such inputs or capital goods are removed as such or partially processed in the case of inputs,

(d)an amount under sub-rule (2) of rule 16 of the central excise rules, 2002, or

(e)service-tax on any output service.

Sub-rule 5 of rule 3 provides the payment of equal credit availed on the input or capital goods when they are removed as such from the factory or premises of the service provider, under cover of an invoice. Such payment shall not be made where the inputs are removed from the premises of the provider of output service for providing the output service.

Sub-rule 5 further provided that such payment shall not be made when any capital goods are removed for providing an output service and such capital goods are brought back within 180 days with the permission of Deputy or Assistant Commissioner.

V S DATEY

There is controversy raging in respect of eligibility of Cenvat credit in respect of transit sale through dealer not registered under Central Excise and also through dealer registered under Central Excise. The issues discussed in this article.

Background of the issue

1. Often the end user (manufacturer consumer) purchases goods through dealer and not through the original manufacturer. If the goods are purchased by dealer and then sold on piecemeal basis, there is provision to issue Cenvatable invoice by first stage dealer and second stage dealer.

However, when entire consignment is to be sold as it is, the dealer instruct the original manufacturer of excisable goods to dispatch the goods directly to the end used (consumer manufacturer). Invoice of Manufacturers invoice is in name of dealer as the buyer. Name and address of end user (manufacturer consumer) is shown as consignee.

The end user (consumer manufacturers) avail CENVAT credit on the basis of such invoice of original manufacturer.

This is standard practice, going on at least since 1995.

In the recent budget, a proviso has been added to rule 11(2) of Central Excise Rules w.e.f. 1-3-2015, which reads as follows - "Provided also that if the goods are directly sent to any person on the direction of the registered dealer, the invoice shall also contain the details of the registered dealer as the buyer and the person as the consignee, and that person shall take CENVAT credit on the basis of the registered dealer's invoice:"

1.1 Controversy arising out of this proviso: On the basis of this proviso inserted w.e.f. 1-3-2015, a view has been expressed that the Cenvat credit cannot be availed in case of transit sale, if the intermediate buyer is not registered under Central Excise.

A view is also expressed by some assessees that Cenvat credit cannot be availed on basis of invoice of original manufacturer, if sale is through registered dealer. The registered dealer has to issue another Cenvatable invoice.

In my view, there is no such change in rules. In case of transit sale, Cenvat credit can be availed on basis of invoice of original manufacturer, even if the intermediate buyer is not registered dealer. Even if intermediate buyer is registered dealer, he need not issue Cenvatable invoice as Cenvat credit can be availed on basis of invoice of original manufacturer.

Reasons for my view are stated below.

Statutory provisions

2. Rule 9(1) of Cenvat Credit Rules prescribes that Cenvat Credit can be taken on the basis of any of the documents prescribed in that sub-rule. The relevant extract from the rule are as follows –

Rule 9(1) Documents and accounts - The CENVAT credit shall be taken by the manufacturer or the provider of output service or input service distributor, as the case may be, on the basis of any of the following documents, namely:–

(a)

An invoice issued by -

(i)

a manufacturer for clearance of— (I) inputs or capital goods from his factory or depot or from the premises of the consignment agent of the said manufacturer or from any other premises from where the goods are sold by or on behalf of the said manufacturer (II) inputs or capital goods as such

(ii)

not relevant

(iii)

not relevant

(iv)

a first stage dealer or a second stage dealer, as the case may be, in terms of the provisions of Central Excise Rules, 2002.

2.1 Invoice of manufacturer is eligible document for Cenvat credit: It can be seen that invoice issued by manufacturer for clearance of inputs or capital goods from his factory is eligible document for availing Cenvat credit, as per rule 9(1)(a)(i)(I) of Cenvat Credit Rules.

The rule does not state that the invoice should be in name of buyer-manufacturer or consumer-manufacturer. The rule even does not state that name of end user (final consumer-manufacturer) should be shown in the invoice.

Of course, it has to be 'input' or 'capital goods' of the consumer-manufacturer.

2.2 Transit Sale through dealer not registered under Central Excise: In transit sale, goods are despatched directly from place of original manufacturer to final user manufacturer (end user) though invoice is in name of the intermediary dealer.

In that case, Cenvat credit is available on basis of invoice of manufacturer under rule 9(1)(a)(i)(I) of Cenvat Credit Rules itself.

It is learnt that in some cases, the department is taking a view that in such cases, registration as Input Service Distributor and distribution of credit is mandatory.

The issue involved is whether such registration and/or distribution is compulsory or optional. Who is Input Service Distributor ?

2. As per rule 2(m ) of CENVAT Credit Rules, an entity is ‘input service distributor’ if it satisfies the following three conditions—

"(a )office managing the business of manufacturer or producer of final products or provider of output service,

(b )which receives invoices issued under rule 4A of the Service Tax Rules, 1994 towards purchases of input services and

(c )issues invoice, bill or, as the case may be, challan for the purposes of distributing the credit of service tax paid on the said services to such manufacturer or producer or provider, as the case may be."

The word used is ‘and’. Thus, an entity is ‘input service distributor’ only if all the three conditions are satisfied. If an assessee has office or premises which receives invoices and it does not issue any invoice, bill or challan for distributing credit of service tax, it is not ‘Input Service Distributor’.

Service Tax (Registration of Special Category of Persons) Rules, 2005 issued vide Notification No. 27/2005-ST, dated 7-6-2005 provide for registration of ‘Input Service Distributor’. Rule 2(c) of these Rules states that ‘input service distributor’ shall have the meaning assigned to it in rule 2(m) of CENVAT Credit Rules.

It is, thus, clear that the Service tax (Registration of Special Category of Persons) Rules, 2005 apply when an entity falls within the definition of rule 2(m). If the office or main factory does not issue any invoice or challan for distribution of CENVAT credit, it does not fall within the definition of ‘Input Service Distributor’. In such case, the rules in respect of registration and issue of invoice by Input Service Distributor do not apply at all.

Provision is not a mandatory requirement

3. Rule 7 of the CENVAT Credit Rules uses the words ‘Input Service Distributor may distribute credit’. ‘May’ cannot be read as ‘must’.

Rule 9(1) of CENVAT Credit Rules gives list of seven types of documents eligible for availing CENVAT credit, out of which invoice of input service distributor is one of the eligible documents. Thus, the invoice of input service distributor is not the only eligible document for availing CENVAT credit. Credit can be availed on basis of other eligible documents also.

As discussed below, distribution can be in any ratio. Thus, even if main factory is registered as ‘Input Service distributor’ it can legally allocate entire CENVAT credit to itself, which would be an exercise in futility.

Facility cannot be a compulsion

4. ‘Input Service Distributor’ is a facility provided to assessee. It is nowhere stated that it is a mandatory requirement. This ‘facility’ cannot be thrust upon an unwilling assessee.

In CIT v. Mahendra Mills [2000] 243 ITR 56/109 Taxman 225 (SC), it was observed, ‘A privilege cannot be to a disadvantage and an option cannot become an obligation’.

How can it lead to complete denial of CENVAT credit?

CENTRALISED OPERATIONS We are a Gas Distribution Company based at Gujarat. We are having CNG Station at various locations. We obtain excise Separate Registration of each CNG Station. Our queries are (1) Whether we are able to take CENVAT Credit on Excise Payable for Capital Goods? (2) Shall we claim excise on common pipe line which is partly used for CNG and partly for domestic gas, inspite of fact that domestic gas is not excisable goods? (3) Whether regarding the supplier invoice, the address of CNG Station has to be mentioned or not on that invoice or invoice made to Head Office address is sufficient to take Cenvat Credit?

(1) Since you have separate registration for each location, it is advisable to take separate credit only for each unit in respect of capital goods installed there. (2) Check tariff heading of pipeline. Mostly, it is 72 or 73 and, hence, does not fall within the definition of ‘capital goods’, as defined in the Cenvat Credit Rules. However, if some equipment does fall within the definition, you can take credit even if it is only partly used for taxable service. (3) It is highly advisable to mention address of CNG station in supplier’s invoice to avoid disputes and harassment from department. If this is not possible, invoice should be endorsed by HO in favour of CNG station with clear remark that these goods are for the particular unit and they have not taken any Cenvat credit at HO.

One of my clients has centralised registration. He has placed capital goods at various sites of the clients. Can the unit shift the capital goods to other sites of the clients after work at one site is completed ?

In respect of capital goods on which there was no credit taken, obviously no question arises. In other cases, if each unit is registered separately, then the first unit should pay ‘amount’ as per Cenvat credit rules and then other unit can take credit. However, in this case, since there is centralised registration, there is no problem, since there is no question of one unit paying duty and other unit taking credit. At the most, you may write letter informing department suitably (Don’t ask for permission. That will create a mess).

A unit having centralised registration is procuring inputs and input services at the sites where the work of the clients is going on. In view of the fact that the unit has taken centralized registration, will it be able to get credit of inputs and input services in the centralized office, if the billing of the supplier is addressed to this centralized office and inputs/input services are directly received at the work site? Or will the unit be required to avail service tax registration as a distributor for all these sites separately and then transfer the credit to centralized office? Here we would like to clarify that service tax registration certificate at present mentions the addresses of various sites at which work is going on.

Really, input service distributor is a facility and not compulsion. Further, Cenvat Credit Rules do not require one to one relationship. If there is centralised accounting and all records are available in HO, credit can be taken at HO. Of course, harassment from department cannot be ruled out. Hence, it is better to write a letter to the department about informing the procedure you are following.

We have branches at various places. Each branch is separately registered for purpose of service tax. In some cases, capital goods installed in one branch have to be shifted to other branch for various purposes like shortages, urgency, etc. We have received a demand that in such cases, Cenvat credit has to be reversed. Please advise.

It is true that technically, you should pay ‘amount’ while removing capital goods from one branch under ‘invoice’ and then take credit in other branch. However, practically, at operational level, such deep knowledge of service tax laws is difficult. You can argue that paying ‘amount’ in one branch and taking credit in other branch will be a revenue neutral exercise. There are many Tribunal decisions that substantive benefit cannot be lost for procedural lapses, particularly when the whole exercise is revenue neutral.

Often, an assessee has office at a place different from the factory or place from which service is provided. Such small offices maintain only basic information. The accounting records including invoices, etc., are sent to main factory and final accounting and record-keeping is done in the main factory/office. Sometimes, office and main factory is at one place, but there are factories or places for provision of service in another places. This article examines the statutory provisions and concludes that Input Service Distributor is a facility, not a compulsion.
