CENVAT CREDIT RULES

13. Increase in time-limit for availment of Cenvat credit from six months to one year

Till 10.07.2014, there was no restriction on availment of Cenvat credit. From 11.07.2014, the Cenvat credit can be taken only upto six months from the date of issue of document as contained in rule 9(1) of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004. From 01.03.2015, the time-limit for availment of Cenvat credit has been increased from six months to one year.

14. Credit on goods directly dispatched to job worker

As per rule 4(1) of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004, 'the CENVAT credit in respect of inputs may be taken immediately on receipt of the inputs in the factory of the manufacturer or in the premises of the provider of output service'.

In case where the goods are directly dispatched to the premises of job worker on the direction of the manufacturer or the provider of output service, credit can be taken only when the said goods are received in the factory of the manufacturer or in the premises of the provider of output service. This was the interpretation done by the department and various Courts.

In order to streamline the said provision, rule 4(1) of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 w.e.f 01.03.2015 states that the CENVAT credit in respect of inputs may be taken immediately on receipt of the inputs in the factory of the manufacturer or in the premises of the provider of output service or in the premises of the job worker, in case goods are sent directly to the job worker on the direction of the manufacturer or the provider of output service, as the case may be;

Similarly, w.e.f 01.03.2015, with respect of capital goods, rule 4(2)(a) now states that the CENVAT credit in respect of capital goods received in a factory or in the premises of the provider of output service or outside the factory of the manufacturer of the final products for generation of electricity for captive use within the factory or in the premises of the job worker, in case capital goods are sent directly to the job worker on the direction of the manufacturer or the provider of output service, as the case may be at any point of time in a given financial year shall be taken only for an amount not exceeding fifty per cent of the duty paid on such capital goods in the same financial year.

1.2 Service need not be received in factory or premises from where output service provided - In case of inputs and capital goods, Cenvat credit is available to manufacturer only if these are received in the factory. However, in case of input service, there is no such requirement. Input service need not be received in factory or premises of service provider.

In case of service provider, even there is no requirement that inputs and capital goods should be received in premises of service provider.

Coverage beyond manufacturing/service provision stage

2. Inclusive definition clause of rule 2(l) extends scope of ‘input services’ even beyond stage of ‘manufacture’ or ‘provision of service’. The inclusive clause makes it clear that services much earlier to manufacture or provision of service or even after manufacture and after provision of provision of service will be eligible for service tax credit.

Services which do not have even any casual relation with manufacture of goods or provision of service have been covered by the definition of ‘input service’. In fact, any service in relation to business of assessee is ‘input service’.

Thus, though the words used in rule 2(l)(ii) are ‘used by the manufacturer, whether directly or indirectly, in or in relation to the manufacture of final products and clearance of final products from the place of removal’, in view of the word ‘includes’, the scope of definition is much wider than ‘in or in relation to manufacture’ and would cover even services unrelated to ‘manufacture’. This is also clear from the fact that service tax paid at Head Office and branches/depots can be utilised as Cenvat credit through the mechanism of ‘input service distributor’.

(a)Setting up, modernization, renovation or repairs of a factory, premises of provider of output service or an office relating to such factory or premises

We have two units – one unit is paying duty and other unit is in Himachal Pradesh, which is exempt from duty. Is it required that Cenvat credit of services received at HO should be taken on proportionate basis? Please advise.

There is no provision to take credit on ‘proportionate basis’. You cannot apply costing principles for Cenvat credit when rule 7 or any other rule of Cenvat Credit Rules makes no such provision. Further, rule 7(b) of Cenvat Credit Rules provides that if some expenses are exclusively related to exempted product, then no credit is available. Thus, so long as expenses are not exclusively related to exempted final product, Cenvat credit is available. Hence, in my view, entire credit of service tax can be availed at HO, except that which is exclusively related to the unit manufacturing exempted goods.

We have Head Office at Mumbai and factories in Pune and Goa. All our HO expenses are accounted for in our factory in Pune and all credit of service tax is taken at Pune. We have received a letter from department that Cenvat credit cannot be availed since Mumbai office is not registered as Input Service Distributor. Please advise, if the objection of service tax department is correct.

Input Service Distributor is a facility and not compulsion. Even rule 7 of Cenvat Credit Rules uses the words ‘may distribute the Cenvat credit’. Thus, law does not say that credit can be availed only through mechanism of Input Service Distributor. Moreover, you can distribute credit in any ratio. Thus, technically, even if you register your HO as input service distributor, you can take entire credit at Pune factory, itself. Cenvat Rules do not require one to one relationship.

To avoid litigation and petty disputes, it may be advisable to register HO as Input Service Distributor, though not legally required.

It was also undisputed that the inputs covered under all the orders were received in the factory of the assessee and consumed by it in its factory. The Tribunal further held that from the plain reading of the Board’s Circular No. 441/7/99-CX dated 23-2-1999, it is very clear that the Assistant Commissioner should ignore minor procedural lapses as long as it is verified that inputs/capital goods have suffered duty and are being used in the manufacturing process. Input service distributor

6. What is meant by the term ‘input service distributor’?

If the goods were sent directly to job worker, goods should be received by purchasing manufacturer after job work, within 180 days from the date at which inputs were received by first job worker – proviso to rule 4(5)(a)(i) of Cenvat Credit Rules w.e.f. 1-3-2015.

T 340 (Punj. & Har.)

Documents and Accounts - Shared Service Center

4.3 The assessee availed Cenvat credit on the basis of ISD invoice issued by its shared service center. The revenue denied credit on the grounds that shared service center was not registered as Input Service Distributor and that the ISD invoices were not valid documents as they did not contain the information as required under rule 4A(2) of the Service Tax Rules, 1994. The Tribunal held that the credit was taken by the assessee almost after more than two months of applying for centralized registration and it showed that the revenue had enough time to take a decision. Thereafter, the application was wrongly rejected and, later restored, based on the clarification issued by the Board. As regards other defects, they were mainly procedural and rectifiable. The Tribunal further held that in view of catena of decisions, invoices need not have to contain all the details. Further, the effective date of validity of the registration certificate is also required to be considered in terms of the statute. It is also necessary for the Commissioner to decide whether the defects are rectifiable and if yes, have been rectified. Accordingly, the Tribunal remanded the matter to the Commissioner to reconsider the issue after giving an opportunity to the assessee to represent the case in the light of judicial precedence, legal provisions and other relevant factors.

Philips Electronics (India) Ltd. v. CCE [2009] 22 STT 332 (Ahd. - CESTAT)

SECTION 65(76 b) OF THE FINANCE ACT, 1994, READ WITH SECTION 2(f) OF THE CENTRAL EXCISE ACT, 1944 - PACKAGING ACTIVITY - MANUFACTURE

5. The assessee purchased bottles of country spirit from the licensees who were engaged in the manufacture and supply of country liquor in sealed bottles pursuant to the license issued by the competent authority of the State Government under the provisions of the M.P. Excise Act, 1915 and the Rules framed therein. The rectified spirit was manufactured by the process of distillation in the distillery. It was blended in the warehouses, bottled, sealed, labelled and was supplied to the retail contractors. The assessee was granted a bottling license in respect of the excise year 2005-06 for supply in respect of the areas mentioned therein. Service tax was demanded from the assessee for activity of bottling of liquor as packaging activity under section 65(76b). The assessee challenged the validity of said section in writ petition. In the course of hearing, the assessee contended that the Division Bench in Vindhyachal Distilleries (P.) Ltd. v. State of MP [2006] 5 STT 254 (MP) had not appropriately considered the decision rendered in case of Som Distilleries & Breweries (P.) Ltd. v. State of MP 1997 (1) JLJ 319 and various other aspects which deserved consideration. The Division Bench thought it apposite to refer the matter to a Larger Bench referring the question as to whether bottling of liquor amounts to manufacture of liquor or only packaging so as to attract service tax.

The High Court held that on a scrutiny of the definition of ‘packaging activity’, it is quite clear that packaging activity means packaging of goods including pouch-filling, bottling, labelling or imprinting of the package but the definition does not stop there, as the provision expressly shows that it does not include any packaging activity that amounts to manufacture within the meaning of clause (f) of section 2 of the 1944 Act. In Circular No. 249/1/2006, it was mentioned that as alcohol beverages are not covered under the Central Excise Law, the production of beverages would not fall within the meaning of the term ‘manufacture’ as conceptualized under clause (f) of section 2. The Board re-examined the matter in detail after receipt of the response and issued Circular F. No. 249/1/2006-CX.4, dated 27-10-2008 which relates to levy of service tax on production of alcoholic beverages on job work basis.

As per High Court, the basic aspect of manufacture as contained in section 2(f) conveys that the term ‘manufacture’ would include ‘any process incidental or ancillary with the completion of manufactured product’. The definition clause further expands the scope of manufacture to include certain goods which are specified in the section. The first limb of the inclusive definition of the term ‘manufacture’ under section 2(f) has a very wide connotation. As the definition clause lays down an inclusive facet, the term ‘manufacture’ has to be construed in a natural and plain manner and would include any process incidental or ancillary to the completion of a manufactured product. Keeping in view the context in which the term ‘manufacture’ has been used, it would take in its fold the incidental or ancillary process in the manufacture or finishing of any manufactured product. It does not leave any room for doubt that an allied process should be an integral and inextricable part of manufacture for completeness and presentability of the manufactured product.

T 242 (CESTAT), it was held that credit of duty paid on inputs meant for ‘matador’ vehicle can be used for payment of duty on other motor vehicle ‘tempo-traveller’.

CBE&C, vide para 2(viii) of Circular No. 33/33/94-CX dated 4-5-1994 has confirmed that there is no one to one correlation between input and final product under the CENVAT scheme for utilisation of credit. Definition of ‘input service’ expanded

8. Definition of ‘input service’ as per rule 2(1) of CENVAT Credit Rules is very wide in view of the inclusive part of the definition. Any service in relation to business is ‘input service’.

The second part of the definition of ‘input service’ covers various services like advertisement or sales promotion, market research, activities relating to business, such as accounting, auditing, financing, recruitment and quality control, coaching and training, computer networking, credit rating, share registry and security.

These input services have hardly any relation with ‘manufacture’ or ‘provision of output service’.

Main factory can ‘distribute’ entire credit to itself

9. In some cases, office and main factory are situated at one place and other factories are situated at different places. In such case, if the office is registered as ‘Input Service Distributor’, it is perfectly legal to distribute all CENVAT credit to the main factory itself. Thus, registering office as ‘Input Service Distributor’ and ‘distributing’ all CENVAT credit to the main factory itself is an exercise in futility. Instead of that, the credit of services at office can be utilised in main office itself. As explained above, definition of ‘input service’ does not require any relation with ‘manufacture’ or ‘provision of output service’. CENVAT Credit Rules do not require one-to-one relationship.

What is not required in the main definition cannot be brought in through the mechanism of ‘input service distributor’.

All provisions have to be read in cohesive manner

10. Any provision in law cannot be read in isolative manner. The provision of ‘Input Service Distributor’ cannot be read in isolation of other provisions relating to CENVAT credit.

Interpretation must depend on the text and the context . They are the basis of interpretation. One may well say, if the text is the texture, context is what gives the colour. Neither can be ignored. The interpretation is best which makes the textual interpretation match the contextual. A statute is best interpreted when we know why it is enacted. With this knowledge, the statute must be read, first as a whole and then section by section, clause by clause, phrase by phrase and word by word. If a statute is looked at, in the context of its enactment, with the glasses of the statute-maker, provided by such context, its scheme, the sections, clauses, phrases and words may take colour and appear different than when statute is looked at without the glasses of context. With those glasses, we must look at the Act as a whole and discover what each section, each clause, each phrase and each word is meant and designed to say as to fit into the scheme of the entire Act. No part of a statute can be construed in isolation. Statutes have to be construed so that every word has a place and everything is in its place - RBI v. Peerless General Finance & Investment Co. Ltd. AIR 1987 SC 1023/[1987] 1 SCC 424/[1987] 61 Comp. Cas. 663 (SC) - quoted with approval in J.K. Industries Ltd. v. Chief Inspector of Factories [1996] 89 Taxman 321 (SC), Indian Handicrafts Emporium v. UOI AIR 2003 SC 3240/[2003] 7 SCC 589, National Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Swaran Singh AIR 2004 SC 1531/[2004] 3 SCC 257, Prakash Kumar v. State of Gujarat AIR 2005 SC 1075.

Conclusion

11. In conclusion, it can be stated as follows—

u Input Service Distributor is a facility, not a compulsion.

u CENVAT Credit Rules do not require one-to-one relationship.

u Provision of ‘Input Service Distributor’ also does not envisage one-to-one relationship.

u Any service in relation to business of assessee is his ‘input service’.

u CENVAT credit can be utilised at one place without distributing it.

u Even if distribution is done, ‘distribution’ of credit can be in any ratio. Entire credit can be allocated to one of the factories/places of provision of output services, if assessee so desires.

u The only requirement is that ‘input service’ should be in relation to business of assessee. Any relation with ‘manufacture’ or ‘provision of output service’ is not required.

[2009] 23 STT 22 (MAG)

CENVAT CREDIT

PL SUBRAMANIAN*

INPUT SERVICE DISTRIBUTOR

In this article, the author has discussed the provisions relating to ‘input service distributor’ including amendment carried out in 2008.

Introduction

1. ‘Input service distributor’ is the beautiful and utilitarian concept introduced by the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004. In this article, we shall discuss the provisions relating to ‘input service distributor’.

Definition

2. Rule 2(m ) of the Rules defines ‘input service distributor’ as under :—

"(m)‘Input service distributor’ means an office of the manufacturer or producer of final products or provider of output service, which receives invoices issued under rule 4A of the Service Tax Rules, 1994 towards purchases of input services and issues invoice, bill or, as the case may be, challan for the purposes of distributing the credit of service tax paid on the said services to such manufacturer or producer or provider, as the case may be;"

Important criteria for input service provider

3. Important criteria for input service provider are :—

(i)It has an office as the manufacturer or producer of final products or provider of output service. In other words, an office of manufacturer of excisable goods or taxable service provider can be registered as input service distributor.

(ii)It has to receive invoices towards purchase of services. The services might have been received by one of the units manufacturing goods or premises providing services or other offices.

(iii)It can issue invoice or bill or challan for the purpose of distributing the credit of service tax paid on the services to the manufacturing unit or service providing unit.

It is to be noted that the input service provider can be registered as head office, registered office, branch, depot, regional office, zonal office, etc.

Regional marketing office was registered as input service distributor and credit was distributed to manufacturing units. It was held by the Tribunal in its prima facie view, that the distribution was in order in Jaypee Rewa Plant v. CCE 2007 (218) ELT 576 (Delhi - Trib.).

It is possible that one company may have many input service distributors.

Example

4. ABC Ltd. has three manufacturing units. Its head office has taken Fire Insurance Policy covering the manufacturing units and paid insurance premium and service tax of Rs. 10,300. Head Office can distribute the service tax paid by it to the manufacturing units and manufacturing units can take the credit on receipt of Invoice from the head office and utilise this amount like any other Cenvat credit.

Conditions

5. Rule 7 deals with distribution of credit by input service distributor. The input service provider can distribute service tax paid by it subject to the following conditions :—

(i)The credit distributed shall not exceed the amount of service tax paid by it. (Is it possible to distribute more than the credit availed?)

(ii)The credit of service tax attributable to service used in an unit exclusively engaged in manufacture of exempted goods or providing of exempted services shall not be distributed.

It is important to note that there is no requirement to distribute the credit proportionately. The input service distributor can distribute to various units as the circumstances warrants. There is no rule regarding periodicity of distribution and it is advisable to distribute monthly.

Registration

6. Input service distributors have to obtain registration from the service tax authorities. They have to apply in Form No. ST-1 and have to obtain Registration Certificate in Form No. ST-2.

Maintenance of records

7. Rule 9 of the Rules deals with maintenance of records by the input service distributor. The records maintained by it must contain the following :—

(i)Serial number and date of the document on which the Cenvat credit is availed.

(ii)Service tax registration number and name of input service provider.

(iii)Description and value of input service.

(iv)Service tax credit availed.

(v)Basis of allocation/apportionment of credit amount.

(vi)Service tax utilised for distributing the credit.

(vii)Balance credit available for distribution.

Issue of Invoice

8. After making the payment of service charges and service tax, input service distributor can avail the credit provided service received is input service and distribute it to various manufacturing units or service providing units.

Rule 4A(2) of the Service Tax Rules, 1994 deals with the issue of invoice by the input service distributor. The invoice shall be serially numbered and contain the following particulars :

(i)the name, address and registration number of the person providing input services and the serial number and date of invoice;

(ii)the name and address of the input service distributor;

(iii)the name and address of the recipient of the credit distributed; and

(iv)the amount of the credit distributed.

41.3-4 Supplementary Invoice by supplier-manufacturer or service provider for differential excise duty/service tax

It is possible that a manufacturer who had supplied input/capital goods and who had paid duty on such inputs/capital goods may have to pay further duty on these inputs/capital goods on account of any demand or audit objection or finalisation of provisional assessment or on account of cost escalation granted by buyer or for any other reason. Similarly, a service provider may be liable to pay additional service tax at a later stage.

In such cases, the other manufacturer who is using that input/capital goods will get further credit of additional duty paid by the supplier of inputs/capital goods or additional service tax paid by service provider.

The manufacturer (supplier) or service provider should issue supplementary invoice to buyer for this purpose, which is document eligible for availing Cenvat Credit [rule 9(1)(b) as existing right from 10-9-2004 and 9(1)(bb) as introduced w.e.f. 1-4-2011]

41.3-5 GAR-7 challan when service tax paid by person other than service provider

In some cases, service tax is payable by service receiver instead of service provider.

In such case, the recipient of service/insurance company will pay service tax by way of GAR-7 challan. Such challan is eligible for availing Cenvat credit [rule 9(1)(e) of Cenvat Credit Rules] - same view in CCE v. Ambika Overseas (2012) 278 ELT 524 (CESTAT SMB).

10.1-1 Concept of Input Service Distributor is compulsory w.e.f. 1-4-2012 if assessee has more than one factories or places of provision of service

As per Rule 7 of Cenvat Credit Rules as existing upto 31-3-2012, the Cenvat Credit could be distributed by Input Service Distributor in any ratio. Only restriction was that Cenvat credit distributed should not be more than available credit.

Assessee having only one factory or place of provision of service - Sometimes, an assessee has offices at various places but accounting is done centrally in the factory. Sometimes, there are various factories of assessee but accounting is done in main factory.

In such cases, in my opinion, if assessee has only one factory and/or one centralised registration of service tax, the HO or branches need not be registered and all Cenvat credit can be availed in the factory or place where centralised registration has been taken.

The reason is that Rule 7 of Cenvat Credit Rules reads, 'The input service distributor may distribute the Cenvat credit'. 'May' cannot be read as 'must'. It is nowhere stated that the utilisation should be only through mechanism of Input Service Distributor. A facility cannot be a compulsion.

It may be noted that depot/consignment of manufacturer/importer is not a 'first stage dealer'. Similarly, 'importer' is not a first stage dealer.

Second Stage dealer - Second stage dealer means a dealer who purchases goods from a first stage dealer. - Rule 2(s) of Cenvat Credit Rules. Dealer of any subsequent stage after second stage cannot issue Cenvatable Invoice. If a dealer purchases goods from another person, he is 'second stage dealer' even if the name of dealer is shown as 'Consignee' in the invoice of original manufacturer - Gautam Steel Traders v. CCE (2011) 265 ELT 77 (CESTAT SMB)

Dealer need not be authorised dealer of manufacturer - There is no requirement that the dealer should be authorised dealer of manufacturer. - CCE v. Uttam Ind 1997(89) ELT 87 = 18 RLT 613 (CEGAT), followed in CCE v. Beekay Engineering 2001(129) ELT 543 (CEGAT).

Invoice of depot/importer - A depot or consignment agent or importer is required to be registered.

Depots, consignment agents and importers should be registered with CE. However, they are not 'first stage dealers'. Hence, purchaser who is purchasing from such depot or consignment agent will still be a 'first stage dealer'. Invoice of depot/consignment agent of manufacturer is eligible for Cenvat under rule 9(1)(a)(i)(I). In such case, another depot will not become 'dealer'.

Input Credit Distributor

26.1-2 Often invoices and bills in respect of inputs and capital goods are received at the head office while service is provided from some other place or site. In such case, the head office can distribute the credit of duty paid on such inputs and capital goods to the service provider by issuing an invoice. Such office will have to be registered with Central Excise and submit returns etc. similar to first stage dealer and second stage dealer [Rule 7A of Cenvat Credit Rules, inserted w.e.f. 1-4-2008].

Distribution of credit by warehouse of manufacturer

26.1-3 A manufacturer may have central warehouse from which he may be distributing inputs to his various factories.

In such case, the warehouse can get registered under Central Excise and issue invoices like those issued by first stage dealer or second stage dealer. The manufacturing unit can take Cenvat credit on basis of such invoice - [Rule 7B of Cenvat Credit Rules, inserted w.e.f. 1-4-2016].

12.2-2 Supplementary Invoice by supplier-manufacturer or service provider for differential excise duty/service tax

It is possible that a manufacturer who had supplied input/capital goods and who had paid duty on such inputs/capital goods may have to pay further duty on these inputs/capital goods on account of any demand or audit objection or finalisation of provisional assessment or on account of cost escalation granted by buyer or for any other reason. Similarly, a service provider may be liable to pay additional service tax at a later stage.

In such cases, the other manufacturer who is using that input/capital goods will get further credit of additional duty paid by the supplier of inputs/capital goods or additional service tax paid by service provider.

Suppose, S is a manufacturer of an input supplied to B. S had paid duty of Rs. 50,000 while supplying the input to B. On the basis of the duty paid by S, B had utilised Cenvat credit of Rs. 50,000. Now, if S has to pay further duty of say Rs. 15,000, B will be entitled to avail of extra Cenvat credit of Rs. 15,000.

The manufacturer (supplier) or service provider should issue supplementary invoice to buyer for this purpose, which is document eligible for availing Cenvat Credit [rule 9(1)(b) as existing right from 10-9-2004 and 9(1)(bb) as introduced w.e.f. 1-4-2011]

Such supplementary invoice can be issued by manufacturer from his factory or depot, dealer, consignment agent or importer. The supplementary invoice can be in respect of excise duty or CVD paid subsequently.

Similarly, a service provider can issue supplementary invoice.

If supplementary invoice is issued by manufacturer on account of price rise given by buyer, the buyer can avail Cenvat credit - Ispat Industries v. CCE (2008) 221 ELT 540 (CESTAT).

In Andhra Petrochemicals v. CCE (2005) 1 STT 195 = 183 ELT 377 (CESTAT), it was held that Cenvat credit can be taken on the basis of supplementary invoice even if differential duty was paid on the directions of Supreme Court.

In CCE v. Himalaya Drug Co. Ltd. (2012) 36 STT 715 = 25 taxmann.com 165 (Karn HC DB), assessee did not pay duty initially as goods were non-excisable. Later, on insistence of department, duty was paid to buy piece of mind and supplementary invoice was issued. It was held that Cenvat credit is available at the end of customer.

In CCE v. MRF Ltd. (2009) 244 ELT 601 (CESTAT), supplementary invoice was issued to rectify incorrect adoption of rate of duty at the time of clearance. Department contended that supplementary invoice is recognised only if it arises from provisional assessment or price escalation. However, it was held that substantial benefit cannot be denied for procedural irregularities and Cenvat credit is available. Basic proposition is that credit has to be varied if amount of duty paid is varied.

26.5 In certain cases, direct dispatch of goods without bringing in the premises of dealer is permitted.

Direct despatch from manufacturer to final buyer, but sale is through dealer i.e. Transit sale - If whole consignment is despatched to buyer from manufacturer, Cenvat will be permissible, if name of the final buyer is shown as consignee. COMMENTS

10.1

Input Service Distributor

A manufacturer or service provider may have head office/regional office at different place/s. The services may be received at head office/regional office, but ultimately, these will be indirectly used for manufacture or providing output service.

Similarly, a principal manufacturer (brand name owner) may send inputs to job worker who is manufacturing goods under brand name of brand name owner. These goods will be supplied by job worker to principal manufacturer. If the goods are covered under MRP valuation provisions, duty will be payable by job worker on basis of MRP. However, many of input services received by principal manufacturer are indirectly used by the job worker.

Provision has been made to avail Cenvat credit of services received and paid for at head office/regional office. Such head office/regional office can be registered with Central Excise as 'Input Service Distributor' and it can issue invoice on the manufacturer or producer or service provider or outsourced manufacturing unit [The words in italics inserted w.e.f. 1-4-2016]

If assessee intends to use the facility, he has to apply for registration in form ST-1.

Provision for registration was introduced w.e.f. 7-6-2005. Hence, during 10-9-2004 to 7-6-2005, the HO could distribute credit even without registration - prima facie view in Hindustan Coca Cola Beverages v. CCE (2011) 32 STT 176 (Mag) = 266 ELT 347 (CESTAT).

In fact, in my view, registration and distribution of Cenvat credit are independent aspects. Even if registration was obtained later, Cenvat credit of prior period at HO/branches can be distributed, if otherwise eligible.

Who is 'input service distributor' - As per rule 2(m) of Cenvat Credit Rules, "input service distributor" means (a) an office managing the business of manufacturer or producer of final products or provider of output service, (b) which receives invoices issued under rule 4A of the Service Tax Rules, 1994 towards purchases of input services (c) issues invoice, bill or, as the case may be, challan for the purposes of distributing the credit of service tax paid on the said services to such manufacturer or producer or provider or an outsourced manufacturing unit, as the case may be. [The words in italics inserted w.e.f. 1-4-2016].

An office of assessee (manufacturer or service provider) is 'Input Service Distributor' if it satisfies all the three aforesaid requirements. It is not that each and every office of assessee is 'Input Service Distributor' and must register. The office should be registered as 'Input Service Distributor' only if it wants to distribute. There is no law that 'distribution' is the only way of availing Cenvat credit of services received at office of assessee. There are various documents eligible for availing Cenvat credit. Invoice/challan issued by 'Input Service Distributor' is only one of the specified document.

In Jaypee Rewa Plant v. CCE (2007) 218 ELT 576 (CESTAT SMB), regional marketing office was registered as Input Service Distributor and credit was distributed to manufacturing units. In prima facie view, the distribution was held as correct.

Outsourced manufacturing unit - 'Outsourced manufacturing unit' means a job-worker who is liable to pay duty on the value determined under rule 10A of the Central Excise Valuation (Determination of Price of Excisable Goods) Rules, 2000 on the goods manufactured for the input service distributor or a manufacturer who manufactures goods, for the input service distributor under a contract, bearing the brand name of such input service distributor and is liable to pay duty on the value determined under section 4A of the Excise Act. [Explanation 4 to rule 7 of Cenvat Credit Rules inserted w.e.f. 1-4-2016]

Document eligible for Cenvat credit - As per rule 9(1)(g); 'invoice, bill or challan' issued by an 'input service distributor' under rule 4A of Service Tax Credit Rules is an eligible document for purpose of taking Cenvat credit.

In Shriram Pistons v. CCE (2012) 281 ELT 90 (CESTAT), it was held that Cenvat credit is allowable on the basis of letter issued by Head Office (as Input Service Distributor) even if not mentioned as invoice or challan, if it contains all required details.

In Jaypee Rewa Plant v. CCE (2007) 218 ELT 576 (CESTAT SMB), regional marketing office was registered as Input Service Distributor and credit was distributed to manufacturing units. In prima facie view, the distribution was held as correct.

Outsourced manufacturing unit - 'Outsourced manufacturing unit' means a job-worker who is liable to pay duty on the value determined under rule 10A of the Central Excise Valuation (Determination of Price of Excisable Goods) Rules, 2000 on the goods manufactured for the input service distributor or a manufacturer who manufactures goods, for the input service distributor under a contract, bearing the brand name of such input service distributor and is liable to pay duty on the value determined under section 4A of the Excise Act. [Explanation 4 to rule 7 of Cenvat Credit Rules inserted w.e.f. 1-4-2016]

Document eligible for Cenvat credit - As per rule 9(1)(g); 'invoice, bill or challan' issued by an 'input service distributor' under rule 4A of Service Tax Credit Rules is an eligible document for purpose of taking Cenvat credit.

In Shriram Pistons v. CCE (2012) 281 ELT 90 (CESTAT), it was held that Cenvat credit is allowable on the basis of letter issued by Head Office (as Input Service Distributor) even if not mentioned as invoice or challan, if it contains all required details.

Distribution of credit even if invoices prior to registration as ISD - There is no bar in rule 7 of Cenvat Credit Rules for distributing of credit of invoices prior to date of registration as Input Service Distributor - Beico Industries v. In Autoline v. CCE (2015) ELT 610 (CESTAT), it was held that valuation of process rejection materials at lower than purchase price for balance sheet purposes, does not amount to write off of inputs. Reversal under rule 3(5B) of Cenvat Credit Rules is not required. Removal of obsolete inputs is removal 'as such' - Removal of obsolete inputs is removal 'as such' and entire Cenvat credit is required to be reversed. Mere paying excise duty on scrap price is not sufficient - Panasonic AVC Networks India Co. Ltd. v. CCE (2014) 301 ELT 624 (CESTAT SMB).

Recovery if the 'amount' not paid - If the 'amount' payable under rule 3(5), 3(5A) or 3(5B) of Cenvat Credit Rules is not paid, the same can be recovered in the manner provided in rule 14 of Cenvat Credit Rules, as if it is recovery of Cenvat credit wrongly taken - Explanation to rule 3(5B) of Cenvat Credit Rules, inserted w.e.f. 1-3-2013.

Storage of inputs outside the factory

21.2-2 Inputs should be stored within the factory. However, if manufacturer is unable to store the inputs inside the factory for want of space, hazardous nature of goods etc., he can store the inputs outside the premises. The storage point will be treated as extension of the factory. Permission from Assistant / Deputy Commissioner is necessary. [Rule 8 of Cenvat Credit Rules].

Supervision charges or MOT (Merchant Overtime Charges) are not required to be collected from assessee for storage of finished goods outside the factory. However, any other condition to safeguard revenue may be imposed by Jurisdictional Commissioner before granting permission for storage of non-duty paid goods. - CBE&C circular No. 709/25/2003-CX dated 23-4-2003. [Instructions in case of storage of finished goods, but principle will apply to storage of inputs outside the factory also].

As per Pune Commissionerate TN No. 67/96 dated June 96, a register in prescribed form has to be maintained at the godown as well as factory. Inputs from outside godown should move under challan in prescribed form. As per Chandigarh-II Commissionerate TN 13/97-CE dated 17-11-1997, intimation in D-3 form is necessary within 24 hours of receipt of each consignment. Monthly stock statement should be submitted to Range Office. Cenvat credit can be taken only when entire inputs covered by an invoice are received in the factory - similar procedure in CCE, Ahmedabad II TN 93/2004 [179 ELT T15].

No assessee would like to store goods outside factory except under compelling circumstances as storage outside is open to many vagaries of nature including theft, pilferage etc. Hence, shortage of space outside factory is an exceptional circumstance, and application for storage of goods outside factory should be considered, as per guidelines of CBE&C vide circular No. 206/40/96-CE dated 1-5-1996 - Anutone Accoustics v. CCE (2010) 250 ELT 590 (CESTAT).

Even if permission is not obtained, confiscation is not sustainable if there was no mala fide, but penalty for technical breach of law without intent to evade duty is sustainable - Sanchit Polymers v. CCE (2009) 241 ELT 240 (CESTAT SMB).

In British Biologicals v. CCE (2011) 266 ELT 217 (CESTAT), inputs were stored outside in rented premises without even reversing Cenvat credit. It was held that no demand is sustainable as situation similar to sending inputs to job worker.

In Priyadarshini Polysacks v. CCE (2014) 307 ELT 136 (CESTAT), it was held that Cenvat credit is available even if permission was not obtained for taking out inputs outside the factory.

If permission is refused, appeal can be filed, as it is adjudication order - GKN Sinter Metals v. CCE (2015) 324 ELT 153 (CESTAT).

Input Credit Distributor

21.2-3 Often invoices and bills in respect of inputs and capital goods are received at the head office while service is provided from some other place or site. In such case, the head office can distribute the credit of duty paid on such inputs and capital goods to the service provider by issuing an invoice. Such office will have to be registered with Central Excise and submit returns etc. similar to first stage dealer and second stage dealer [Rule 7A of Cenvat Credit Rules, inserted w.e.f. 1-4-2008].

21.2-3A Distribution of credit by warehouse of manufacturer

A manufacturer may have central warehouse from which he may be distributing inputs to his various factories.

In such case, the warehouse can get registered under Central Excise.

CCE 2001(128) ELT 496 (CEGAT SMB), it was held that Cenvat credit being a beneficial piece of legislation, department is expected to take a liberal view in case of technical violations but certainly guard against violations of grave nature.

Majestic Auto (2010) 25 STT 293 (CESTAT SMB), the invoice mentioned name of brand name owned of manufacturer (e.g. Hero Puch or Hero Motors) and the address, and not name of the company. It was held that when there is no dispute that goods suffered duty and are used in manufacture and invoice indicates ownership of goods, minor defect is ignorable and Cenvat is allowable.

Invoice in different name - Name of service recipient is not an essential requirement for availment of Cenvat credit. Cenvat credit cannot be denied on that count - Akshar Courier Service v. CCE (2013) 42 GST 293 = 33 taxmann.com 410 (CESTAT).

Mistake in description of goods - In Omax Autos v. CCE (2012) 35 STT 379 = 20 taxmann.com 772 (CESTAT), invoice described the goods as CR sheets though goods actually received were HR sheets. It was held that Cenvat credit cannot be denied on this ground.

Invoice damaged in fire and particulars not legible - In Supreme Industries Ltd. v. CCE 2005 (180) ELT 28 (CESTAT SMB), copies of invoices were badly damaged in fire and necessary particulars of payment were not legible. It was held that credit cannot be denied on this technical ground.

Assessee cannot be penalised for mistake of supplier - In Elveety Industries v. CCE 2001(130) ELT 199 (CEGAT SMB), assessee had taken Cenvat credit on basis of dealer's invoice. Serial number generated on computer - Cenvat credit cannot be denied on basis of invoice generated on computers having serial number generated by computer. Capital goods used in EPC project

23.4 Capital goods are used in EPC projects by service provider. Issue is how service receiver can avail Cenvat credit of capital goods used by the service provider in the works contract (EPC project).

This is possible with some planning. The invoice of machinery supplier will be in name of service provider (contractor). If the service receiver (principal) intends to avail Cenvat credit of capital goods used in works contract, the invoice should show name of service receiver as consignee, so that he can avail Cenvat credit. Strictly legally, even endorsed invoice is sufficient for availing Cenvat credit.

In Rajarambhau Patil SSK Ltd. v. CCE 2007 (208) ELT 372 (CESTAT), components and equipments required for sugar plants were purchased/manufactured by contractor and brought to the factory. Name of assessee was shown on the invoices. The sugar plant was erected at site and commissioned. It was held that Cenvat credit is available to assessee.

In appeal by assessee, Bombay High Court has quashed the order and matter has been remanded to Tribunal for fresh consideration [263 ELT A139]. In my opinion, the decisions that credit can be taken on basis of endorsed bill of entry are correct as there is no provision that bill of entry must be in name of the person claiming Cenvat. In CCE v. National Leather Cloth 1999 (113) ELT 299 (CEGAT), it was observed that 'Bill of Entry' has been specified as a valid document. It is never specified that it should not be endorsed. Hence, endorsed Bill of Entry is eligible.

System of endorsement by customs dispensed with - As per public notice No. 16/2006 dated 22-3-2006 (196 ELT T4) issued by CC (Imp), Mumbai, new Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 do not specify for endorsement of Bill of Entry by customs officers. Hence, practice of endorsement by customs officer has been dispensed with and earlier public notices stand withdrawn.

Bill of Entry endorsed by importer is permissible. There is no prescription under customs law of endorsement by port authorities (in customs) - Hindustan Zinc Ltd. v. CCE (2012) 282 ELT 453 (CESTAT SMB).

Sale on high seas - In case of high sea sales, Cenvat credit can be taken on basis of endorsed Bill of Entry - Maharaja International Ltd. v. CCE - (1996) 84 ELT 466 (CEGAT). If Bill of Entry indicates name of person who has purchased goods on high seas sale and has cleared goods from harbour, further endorsement or certificate from customs authorities is not necessary. Cenvat credit can be taken on such Bill of Entry - Mayura Caps v. CCE 1997(95) ELT 493 (CEGAT).

Import through Courier - If goods are imported through Courier, he submits a consolidated Bill of Entry. Individual importer who gets the goods from courier cannot avail Cenvat credit on basis of such Bill of Entry. If an importer wants to avail Cenvat credit, he should file a normal individual Bill of Entry, which can then be used to avail Cenvat credit - CBE&C circular No. 31/2007-Cus dated 29-8-2007.

However, in Controls & Drives Coimbatore v. CCE (2008) 222 ELT 470 = 2008-TIOL-284-CESTAT (SMB), Courier had filed consolidated Bill of Entry containing imports 4/5 importers, since individual value was small. He gave photocopy of Bill of Entry (Xerox) to each importer and importer took Cenvat credit. It was held that Cenvat credit cannot be denied only on the ground that it has been taken on basis of photocopy of Bill of Entry, when there is no dispute about receipt and eligibility of goods. In similar case, in Macneill Engg v. CCE (2009) 234 ELT 345 (CESTAT SMB), Cenvat credit was allowed as a special case.

Loss of duplicate/triplicate copy of Bill of Entry - New Cenvat rules do not specify any particular copy of Bill of Entry for availing Cenvat credit. In Industrial Cables (I) Ltd. v. 4.2-2 Storage of inputs outside the factory

Inputs should be stored within the factory. However, if manufacturer is unable to store the inputs inside the factory for want of space, hazardous nature of goods etc., he can store the inputs outside the premises. The storage point will be treated as extension of the factory. Permission from Assistant/Deputy Commissioner is necessary. [Rule 8 of Cenvat Credit Rules].

Supervision charges or MOT (Merchant Overtime Charges) are not required to be collected from assessee for storage of finished goods outside the factory. However, any other condition to safeguard revenue may be imposed by Jurisdictional Commissioner before granting permission for storage of non-duty paid goods. - CBE&C Circular No. 709/25/2003-CX dated 23-4-2003. [Instructions in case of storage of finished goods, but principle will apply to storage of inputs outside the factory also].

As per Pune Commissionerate TN No. 67/96 dated June 96, a register in prescribed form has to be maintained at the godown as well as factory. Inputs from outside godown should move under challan in prescribed form. As per Chandigarh-II Commissionerate TN No. 13/97-CE dated 17-11-1997, intimation in D-3 form is necessary within 24 hours of receipt of each consignment. Monthly stock statement should be submitted to Range Office. Cenvat credit can be taken only when entire inputs covered by an invoice are received in the factory - similar procedure in CCE, Ahmedabad II TN No. 93/2004 [179 ELT T15].

40.4

Input Service Distributor

A manufacturer or service provider may have head office/regional office at different place/s. The services may be received at head office/regional office, but ultimately, these will be indirectly used for manufacture or providing output service.

Similarly, a principal manufacturer (brand name owner) may send inputs to job worker who is manufacturing goods under brand name of brand name owner. These goods will be supplied by job worker to principal manufacturer. If the goods are covered under MRP valuation provisions, duty will be payable by job worker on basis of MRP. However, many of input services received by principal manufacturer are indirectly used by the job worker.

Provision has been made to avail Cenvat credit of services received and paid for at head office/regional office. Such head office/regional office can be registered with Central Excise as 'Input Service Distributor' and it can issue invoice on the manufacturer or producer or service provider or outsourced manufacturing unit [The words in italics inserted w.e.f. 1-4-2016]

If assessee intends to use the facility, he has to apply for registration in form ST-1.

In my view, registration and distribution of Cenvat credit are independent aspects. Even if registration was obtained later, Cenvat credit of prior period at HO/branches can be distributed, if otherwise eligible.

Who is 'input service distributor' - As per rule 2(m) of Cenvat Credit Rules, "input service distributor" means (a) an office managing the business of manufacturer or producer of final products or provider of output service, (b) which receives invoices issued under rule 4A of the Service Tax Rules, 1994 towards purchases of input services (c) issues invoice, bill or, as the case may be, challan for the purposes of distributing the credit of service tax paid on the said services to such manufacturer or producer or provider or an outsourced manufacturing unit, as the case may be. [The words in italics inserted w.e.f. 1-4-2016].

An office of assessee (manufacturer or service provider) is 'Input Service Distributor' if it satisfies all the three aforesaid requirements. It is not that each and every office of assessee is 'Input Service Distributor' and must register. The office should be registered as 'Input Service Distributor' only if it wants to distribute. There is no law that 'distribution' is the only way of availing Cenvat credit of services received at office of assessee. There are various documents eligible for availing Cenvat credit. Invoice/challan issued by 'Input Service Distributor' is only one of the specified document.

Outsourced manufacturing unit - ' Outsourced manufacturing unit' means a job-worker who is liable to pay duty on the value determined under rule 10A of the Central Excise Valuation (Determination of Price of Excisable Goods) Rules, 2000 on the goods manufactured for the input service distributor or a manufacturer who manufactures goods, for the input service distributor under a contract, bearing the brand name of such input service distributor and is liable to pay duty on the value determined under section 4A of the Excise Act. [Explanation 4 to rule 7 of Cenvat Credit Rules inserted w.e.f. 1-4-2016]

Document eligible for Cenvat credit - As per rule 9(1)(g); 'invoice, bill or challan' issued by an 'input service distributor' under rule 4A of Service Tax Credit Rules is an eligible document for purpose of taking Cenvat credit.

As per Rule 7 of Cenvat Credit Rules as existing upto 31-3-2012, the Cenvat Credit could be distributed by Input Service Distributor in any ratio. Only restriction was that Cenvat credit distributed should not be more than available credit.

However, after 1-4-2012, the distribution is required to be on basis of turnover.

Assessee having only one factory or place of provision of service - Sometimes, an assessee has offices at various places but accounting is done centrally in the factory. Sometimes, there are various factories of assessee but accounting is done in main factory.

In such cases, in my opinion, if assessee has only one factory and/or one centralised registration of service tax, the HO or branches need not be registered and all Cenvat credit can be availed in the factory or place where centralised registration has been taken.

The reason is that Rule 7 of Cenvat Credit Rules reads, 'The input service distributor may distribute the Cenvat credit'. 'May' cannot be read as 'must'. It is nowhere stated that the utilisation should be only through mechanism of Input Service Distributor. A facility cannot be a compulsion.

In Durferrit Asea v. CCE (2010) 258 ELT 414 (CESTAT SMB), it was held that if assessee has only one manufacturing unit, HO need not be registered and Cenvat credit can be taken at factory even if invoices are with address of Head Office. Rule 7 is not compulsory if assessee is not inclined to do so.

In Manipal Advertising Services v. CCE (2010) 25 STT 30 (CESTAT), branch offices were not registered with service tax authorities. Invoices were with address of branch, but payment of made from registered premises. It was held that Cenvat credit is available at HO which had Centralised registration as it had centralised accounting system. It was held that Cenvat credit is available even if address on invoice is of branch office.

Invoice of service in name of HO is eligible. It is not necessary that HO should be registered as Input Service Distributor (when there is only one factory) - CCE v. Samita Conductors (2012) 278 ELT 492 (CESTAT SMB) * Valco Industries Ltd. v. CCE (2013) 42 GST 165 = 31 taxmann.com 360 = 286 ELT 54 (CESTAT SMB).

If assessee has only one manufacturing unit, registration as Input Service Distributor is not required. Assessee can take Cenvat credit even if invoice is with address of Head Office - National Plastic Industries v. CCE (2012) 35 STT 193 = 20 taxmann.com 132 (CESTAT) * Bloom Dekor v. CCE (2013) 38 STT 336 = 29 taxmann.com 357 (CESTAT SMB).

In Doshion Ltd. v. CCE (2013) 288 ELT 291 (CESTAT), it was held that since assessee could distribute Cenvat Credit in any ratio upto 31-3-2012, the HO could distribute credit to its unit without registration as Input Service Distributor.

In WNS Global Services v. CCE (2013) 30 taxmann.com 208 (CESTAT), it was held that Cenvat credit is allowable even if assessee was not registered as Input Service Distributor.

(now or GAR-7 challan also) is not a specified document for availing credit.

In Avanti Kopp Electricals v. CCE 2006 (193) ELT 581 (CESTAT), duty was paid on moulds and press tools manufactured by them, under TR-6 challan. Subsequently, Cenvat credit was taken on the basis of that TR-6 challan. It was held as admissible (now GAR-7 challan also). In my opinion, even if duty is paid by TR-6 or GAR-7 challan, duty/tax paying document like invoice or supplementary invoice should be prepared. It is never advisable to pay duty/tax on ad hoc basis.

Debit Note issued by service provider

25.2-6 In Chemplast Sanmar Ltd. v. CCE (2009) 21 STT 283 = 2009 TIOL 443 (CESTAT), assessee availed Cenvat credit on basis of debit note. The document contained all the required details as required in invoice or challan. It was prima facie held that Cenvat credit cannot be denied solely on the basis that document was titled as 'debit note' - same view in Pharmalab Process v. CCE (2009) 242 ELT 467 (CESTAT SMB) * Pallipalayam Spinners v. CCE (2010) 28 STT 424 (CESTAT SMB) * CCE v. Jalaram Plastic Pack (2012) 35 STT 94 = 19 taxmann.com 187 (CESTAT SMB) * Trident Ltd. v. CCE (2012) 35 STT 99 = 19 taxmann.com 184 (CESTAT SMB) * A P Coal Washeries P Ltd. v. CCE (2013) 38 STT 316 = 29 taxmann.com 327 (CESTAT) * HCL Commet Services v. CCE (2015) 60 taxmann.com 410 (CESTAT).

There is contrary view in Godrej Consumer Products Ltd. v. CCE (2011) 30 STT 48 (CESTAT SMB).

In Shriram Pistons v. CCE (2012) 281 ELT 90 (CESTAT), it was held that Cenvat credit is allowable on the basis of letter issued by Head Office (as Input Service Distributor) even if not mentioned as invoice or challan, if it contains all required details.

In CCE v. Graphite (I) (2007) 212 ELT 54 (CESTAT SMB), Cenvat credit on basis of 'cash memo' was held as admissible. It was observed that hyper technicalities should not be made to disallow Cenvat credit.

In CCE v. Gwalior Chemicals (2011) 274 ELT 97 (CESTAT SMB), it was held that Cenvat credit can be taken on basis of document titles 'Debit Note cum Bill'.

The view seems correct for the following reasons.

The words used in rule 4A(1) of Service Tax Rules are 'invoice, challan or Bill'. Rule 11 of Central Excise Rules specified the document as 'Invoice'. This indicates that in case of service tax, specific nomenclature is not essential.

In fact, first and second proviso to rule 4A(1) uses the term 'any document, by whatever name called'. Thus, rules do envisage flexibility in nomenclature depending on trade and business practices. Different practices are followed in different trades. Nomenclature can vary from trade to trade or business to business.

As per rule 5(1) of Service Tax Rules, the records maintained by assessee including computerised data maintained by assessee in accordance with various other laws are acceptable. Thus, private documents maintained in normal course of business are acceptable. No special records or registers or change in business practices is envisaged. This also indicates that law does not envisage that trade should change its normal business practices.

As per Explanation (c) to section 67 of Finance Act, 1994, "Gross amount charged" includes payment by cheque, credit card, deduction from account and any form of payment by issue of credit notes or debit notes and book adjustment. Thus, charging of any amount by debit note and credit note has been accepted.

Invoice - A list of goods shipped or services rendered, with prices and charges; a bill - Concise Oxford Dictionary, 8th edition * A list of goods sent, with prices - Collins English Gem Dictionary * An invoice is a written account of particulars of goods delivered to a purchaser, and of their prices, and the charges concerning them - Law Lexicon by P Ramanatha Aiyar, 1999 edition.

Bill - A printed or written statement of charges for goods supplied or services rendered - - Concise Oxford Dictionary, 8th edition * Note of charges - Collins English Gem Dictionary * A note of charges for goods delivered or services rendered - Law Lexicon by P Ramanatha Aiyar, 1999 edition.

Challan - This is a typical word used in India, not found in any English Dictionary.

case_summary.text: ST : Procedural lapses and absence of all particulars are rectifiable errors, hence, credit was to be allowed subject to rectification by assessee; further, credit is allowable even if invoices are in name of head office

II. Credit may be taken in one factory based on duty paying documents addressed to main office of company or documents in old name of company assessee, subject to utilization of input services for dutiable goods.
Cenvat credit available even if challan and invoices were in name of head office

Cenvat Credit : Credit may be taken on basis of invoices issued by manufacturer or importer or their distributor/dealer and said requirement is mandatory; since endorsement of invoice is not provided in rules, hence, job-worker cannot take credit on basis of invoices endorsed by principal-manufacturer

Cenvat Credit : It is natural that Customs House Agent (CHA) invoice would be in name of Head Office where clearance of goods through Customs is centralized; hence, in absence of doubt as to actual receipt of services, credit cannot be denied merely because Head Office is not registered as Input Service Distributor (ISD)
ST : Credit of input service cannot be denied merely because invoice was in name of assessee's Head Office, especially when receipt and utilization of input service were not under challenge

Credit can't be denied to input service distributor even if its invoices bear name of head office

II. CENVAT Credit, otherwise admissible, cannot be denied merely on ground that it was availed on basis of invoices raised by their head office, which was not registered under central registration during material period

ST : In case of centralized purchases of capital goods by Head Office, credit can be allowed to individual units/branch only if Cenvat credit was passed to such unit/branch under proper authorisation and there is no multiple claim by other units

Cenvat Credit : Where lessee is manufacturing goods under lease agreement with lessor and lessor supplies capital goods to lessee, lessee may take credit on basis of supplier's invoice in name of lessor but endorsed by lessor in favour of lesse.
Cenvat Credit can not be denied to branch office just because bill of entry was in name of head office: CESTAT
GST/CENVAT : Cenvat credit of service tax paid by assessee could not be denied on ground that in invoices address given was that of Head Office, Delhi and not of registered premises at NOIDA

Cenvat Credit : Where two units are located adjacent to each other and have common service tax registration, practice of taking credit belonging to either of units without considering whether invoice was addressed to Head Office or to units is valid; department cannot seek segregation of credit along with separate registration

ST : Where receipt of input service and use thereof along with identity of service provider and service recipient are established, credit cannot be denied merely because invoice thereof bears address of Head Office, which is not registered as ISD.
No denial of Cenvat Credit even if invoices are in name of employees: Mumbai CESTAT
Credit of ST couldn't be denied merely on ground that address of registered office wasn't mentioned in invoice
Credit of CHA service allowable even if bill is issued to Head Office which isn’t ‘Input Service Distributor’
EXICSE/ST/VAT : Cenvat credit taken by assessee not on basis of invoices issued to their Mumbai office but on ISD invoice; Further, credit cannot be denied on ground of nexus; Matter remanded.

CENVAT : Cenvat credit can be availed by manufacturer on strength of invoices issued by supplier for clearance of inputs or capital goods, showing manufacturer's name as consignee and name of dealers as buyer
Cenvat credit on capital goods purchased by HO would be allowed on prorated basis to each unit

Cenvat Credit : If particulars relating to payment of tax on input services are genuine, then, credit cannot be denied merely because input service provider had quoted incorrect address of assessee in invoice.
Manufacture can claim Cenvat credit even on basis of invoice showing him as consignee

Cenvat Credit : Where three separately registered units are using a common input in continuous, interconnected and integrated process for common share, they constitute a single factory and CENVAT cannot be denied on ground that credit is being availed by one factory and material inputs are used by three factories

GST/Cenvat: Where invoices were in name of appellant themselves and receipt of service by appellant had not been challenged, credit on same could not be denied merely because of a different address being shown

Cenvat Credit : Where imported consignment is directly received in factory of job-worker, job-worker may take credit of CVD paid on imports, on strength of bill of entry, even if said bill of entry is in name of principal manufacturer
No credit can be taken on basis of invoices neither addressed to assessee nor endorsed in his favour

Cenvat Credit: Where applicant gas transporter will engage contractor to lay pipelines and contractor will procure pipes and valves from manufacturer who will issue invoice to contractor showing applicant as consignee and pipes will be delivered directly at applicant's work-site, applicant can avail cenvat credit on pipes and valves on basis of invoice issued by contractor, if contractor is a registered dealer

Cenvat Credit : Where supplier factories and recipient factories, both, belonged to assessee only, demand of Cenvat reversal from recipient factories on ground of excess duty payment by supplier factories, was dropped on undertaking from supplier factories that they would not claim refund of such excess duty

GST: Where a manufacturer with regular registration in Tamil Nadu and separate ISD registration for its Head Office received common input service invoices in the name of regular registration and distributed ITC based on Board circular till March 2025, amendments effective 1 April 2025 mandate that such ITC can only be received and distributed through ISD registration, making invoice receipt in regular registration and subsequent credit transfer to ISD impermissible.

Cenvat Credit : Where there is no dispute that assessee had received input services and utilised them for providing output services, credit cannot be denied merely on ground that address of assessee was not mentioned on invoices on which credit was availed

Excise & Customs : Word "factory" includes "all units/premises at same place"; therefore, if steam/electricity generated out of fuel (furnace oil) is used for more than one units (DTA & EOU) in same "factory", entire fuel/furnace oil would be eligible for input credit

CENVAT : Where expenditure was incurred by assessee company, even though invoices were not in name of company but in name of directors/employees and same had been booked as expenditure in books of assessee, Cenvat credit could not have been denied

ST : Being a manufacturer having one factory and setting up second factory, assessee can easily and correctly take credit of services availed at Unit-2 in Unit-1 also, but since assessee took a separate registration for Unit-2, credit could only be taken in Unit-2

CENVAT : Where manufacturer had intimated department about shifting of machines to rented premises near factory and submitted proper documents and no job work was done, Cenvat credit could not be denied
Cenvat Credit: Non-mentioning of address of ISD in LOP could not be a ground to deny credit
Cenvat Credit : Where there is no dispute about receipt of material and payment of duty thereon, credit taken based on 'endorsed bill of entry' is valid
Manufacturer entitled to credit of ST paid on outward transportation from factory to customer's premises : SC

Cenvat Credit : Credit cannot, prima facie, be allowed on unsigned invoices especially when there is no correspondence or certificate from supplier/service provider that said invoices were issued by them

EXCISE/ST/VAT : Refund was admissible in respect of ISD invoices issued by head office of appellant for portion of services received in Gurugram for authorised operations of appellant in its SEZ unit in Indore

EXCISE/CENVAT : Supplier was duly registered with Central excise department and paid Central excise duty on capital goods and cleared same from his factory; since receipt of capital goods was also not in dispute, Cenvat credit on same could not be denied to recipient unit
Cenvat credit can be allowed only if assessee holds valid invoice
EXCISE : Cenvat credit on capital goods used in beneficiation plant cannot be denied on ground of separate registration as it is an integral part of factory
CENVAT: Where there was specific inclusion of input services for construction of factory, assessee-manufacturer would be eligible to avail credit of service tax paid on such input services
Credit of ST paid on transport of employees to factory not admissible after 1-4-2011: HC
EXCISE/ST/VAT : Debit note issued by importer in respect of import of machines and CVD paid thereon can also be valid document for availing credit

GST : Where applicant company procures various goods/services directly used for air transportation services (including passenger and cargo) for all other States at its Head Office (HO), input GST credit pertaining to services only on procurement made by HO towards maintenance of aircraft (including lease thereof) shall be distributed by way of input service distributor mechanism and credit pertaining to goods (including capital goods) shall be distributed by way of normal registration mechanism
