HEADNOTE: Rule 57A of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 - Modvat Credit - Modvat - Procedural lapses cannot deny credit (substantive right) - Remanded for removal of omissions

FACT: The appellants availed Modvat credit for certain inputs used in the manufacture of their final product. The Asstt. Collector ordered reversal of credit taken on grounds that the original Gate Passes were not endorsed properly. The Collector (Appeals) rejected their appeal. Hence this appeal.

HELD: Modvat-Technicalities cannot deny a substantive right-credit admissible on removal of defects. Matter remanded for fresh decision. "........the defects referred to in the Show Cause Notices, on the basis of Modvat Credit has been denied, are remediable defects. On a query by this Bench Shri Willingdon Christian undertakes to get the defects rectified and also produce the requisite certificates from the suppliers about the fact of non-availment of Modvat Credit by them. In the circumstances, we hold that this technical requirement cannot come in the way in availment of the substantive benefit of Modvat Credit. Hence we set aside the order and remand the case back to the Assistant Collector before whom the appellants should produce the Gate Passes after rectifying the defects pointed out by the Department. The Assistant Collector may, thereupon decide the issue. So long as he is satisfied that the inputs has been received in the factory and utilised in the manufacture, modvat credit cannot be denied only on these technical aberrations."

HEADNOTE: Section 16 of the Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017/Rule 3 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - Input tax credit -  Period March, 2009 to March, 2015 - Assessee availed cenvat credit on photocopies of invoices - Adjudicating Authority denied cenvat credit - Whether photocopies of invoices were not valid documents for availing cenvat credit - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, assessee could not avail cenvat credit on photocopies of invoices - Held, yes [Para 9.6] [In favour of revenue]GST/Cenvat : Photocopies of invoices are not valid documents for availing cenvat credit and, therefore, assessee cannot avail cenvat credit on photocopies of invoices

FACT: The assessee was engaged in the manufacture of crushing machines and screening machines.

It availed cenvat credit on certain input services.

The Adjudicating Authority denied cenvat credit on input services.

On appeal to Tribunal:

HELD: The Adjudicating Authority has denied cenvat credit alleging that the assessee has not obtained registration as Input Service Distributor (ISD). The assessee has submitted that it has obtained ISD registration in 2008. A copy of the ISD registration is also furnished. Therefore, the disallowance of credit for the reason that the assessee has not obtained ISD registration is unjustified and requires to be set aside. [Paras 9.1 and 9.2]

The Adjudicating Authority has further denied cenvat credit stating that the invoices were raised in the address of Bangalore and Pune office and the credit has been availed in Hosur Unit. The assessee has taken centralized registration incorporating Bangalore and Pune units. In such circumstances, the revenue cannot deny the credit availed on invoices raised in the address of Bangalore and Pune unit. [Para 9.3]

The Adjudicating Authority has also denied cenvat credit on the plea that clearing and forwarding agent services are availed by the assessee outside the factory/place of removal. The definition of input service does not state that the services have to be availed within the factory. The Board Circular No. 999/6/2015-CX, dated 28-1-2015 has also clarified this point. Therefore, the disallowance of credit is unjustified. [Para 9.4]

The assessee has availed credit on debit notes which has been disallowed on plea that these are not valid documents to avail credit. Debit notes can be considered to be valid documents for availing credit when there is no dispute with regard to the service tax paid and the services consumed. In the instant case, the department does not have a contention that the assessee has not discharged the service tax on the said services on which credit has been availed. Therefore, the disallowance of credit on this ground is unjustified. [Para 9.5]

The assessee has availed cenvat credit on photocopies of invoices. The assessee has submitted that the original invoices were misplaced and, therefore, it has availed credit on photocopies. This submission does not find favour. The assessee cannot avail credit on photocopies. These are not valid documents for availing credit. Further if such practice of availing credit on photocopies of invoices is allowed, then it will lead to false claims of credit made by assessees. The claim of assessee on this ground is disallowed. [Para 9.6]

The Adjudicating Authority has disallowed credit on various input services stating that these services are not availed in relation to the activity of manufacture. The assessee has submitted that these services include services like membership charges which are paid for taking membership in industrial association, exhibition stall charges, delegate fee, sales commission, etc. According to assessee, all these services have an integral connection with the manufacture of finished products. These services were consumed to carry out the activity of manufacture effectively and also to provide export of services/goods. The Adjudicating Authority has not made adequate discussion in this regard. The assessee has submitted that it would be able to establish the nexus of the services with the output services/manufacturing activity, if it is given a further chance. Therefore, this issue requires to be remanded to the Adjudicating Authority. [Para 9.7]

In the result, the impugned order is modified to the extent of allowing the credit in respect of the services availed except on photocopies of invoices. The issue with regard to credit disallowed alleging that the services do not have nexus with the manufacturing activity is remanded to the Adjudicating Authority leaving this issue open. [Para 10]

items, it cannot be argued that the Government had used its general powers under section 37(1), in excess of the specific powers under section 37(2)(xvia), to grant such credit for the earlier period prior to the amendment. Therefore, the powers under section 37(1) were not used to grant credit in respect of goods for which credit cannot be otherwise allowed under specific powers under section 37(2)(xvia). [Para 36]

CENVAT Scheme The Cenvat Credit Rules allow credit of duty paid on (i ) capital goods used in the factory of the manufacturer of the final products and (ii) inputs used in or in relation to the manufacture of final products. There are provisions in the Cenvat Credit Rules which deny credit of duty paid on inputs and capital goods if the same are used for manufacturer of exempted final products. The Cenvat scheme enables a manufacturer to take credit of duty paid on the inputs and capital goods and utilize the same for paying duty on excisable goods manufactured by him which are called ‘final products’. If the scheme was to be limited to granting credit only on capital goods and inputs, it would be advantageous for a manufacturer to buy capital goods on payment of duty but it would be disadvantageous if he manufactured the capital goods himself by procuring inputs for the same (such as parts and components) on payment of duty as he would not be able to take credit of duty paid on such inputs because these are not inputs used for manufacturing the final products. It is clear that to obviate such a disadvantageous situation, the scope of ‘input’ has been extended to include goods used in the manufacture of capital goods, which are further used in the factory of the manufacturer. This provision has been made by way of inserting Explanation 2 to the definition of ‘input’ under rule 2(k ), of the Cenvat Credit Rules and, thus, the scheme provides for credit of duty paid on :-

(i)Capital goods used in the factory of the manufacturer of the final products;

(ii)inputs used in or in relation to the manufacture of final products; and

(iii)inputs used in the manufacture of capital goods which are further used in the factory of the manufacturer. [Para 38]

Capital goods

There are other details to the Cenvat scheme and the definition of ‘capital goods’ primarily includes machinery items; components, spares and accessories of the same; and a few other things which have been specifically added such as pollution control equipment; moulds, dies, etc.; refractories; tubes and pipes and fittings thereof; and storage tank. The moulds, dies, refractories, tubes and tank have been specifically added as they would not get classified and included as machinery items, but the rule makers in their wisdom have specifically and additionally included these perhaps considering their functional utility to the manufacturing process. By specifically including these items, credit in respect of duty paid on such items has been allowed which would not otherwise get coverage under the term ‘capital goods’. Secondly, credit of duty paid on inputs used in the manufacture of such specifically listed items has also been allowed. However, factory shed, building foundation and structures (in the manufacture of which the goods, namely, cement and steel items are used) have not been specifically listed under the definition of ‘capital goods’. [Para 39]

Capital goods v. capital assets

HEADNOTE: Rule 57G of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 - Modvat credit - Procedure to be observed by manufacturer - Whether gate-passes issued prior to 1-4-1994, but endorsed after that date, would fall under coverage of Entry No. 10 in Table to Notification No. 16/94-CE (NT), dated 30-3-1994 and would, consequently be eligible documents for taking credit under Modvat Scheme - Held, yes [Para 3] Circulars and Notifications : Notification No. 16/94-CE(NT), dated 30-3-1994, Circular No. 600/37/2001-CX, dated 19-11-2001

FACT: The Tribunal held that the gate-passes issued prior to 1-4-1994, but endorsed after that date, would fall under the coverage of Entry No. 10 in the Table to the Notification No. 16/94-CE(NT), dated 30-3-1994 and would, consequently, be eligible documents for taking credit under the Modvat Scheme. It rejected the objection of the revenue that the endorsement should also have been made on the gate-passes on or before 1-4-1994, by observing that endorsed gate-pass was not comparable to the issue of gate-pass because what is mentioned in the proviso to the Notification is that documents should have been issued, which meant that gate-passes should have been issued on or before 1-4-1994.

On reference :

HELD: As per the position prevailing prior to 30-3-1994, when the purchaser resold inputs to third party, he would make an endorsement on the gate pass issued by the manufacturer of the input. Procedure had changed and instead of endorsement on the gate-passes, invoice was required to be produced as per Notification No. 16/94-CE(NT), dated 30-3-1994. Certain documents were prescribed for the purpose of giving credit of Modvat under the Rules. In Column No. 3 to the Entry No. 10 of the aforesaid Notification, prescribed documents were endorsed gate-passes/subsidiary gate-passes/certificates. Admittedly, gate-passes were required to be issued by the manufacturer under the procedure then prevailing and as and when the purchaser of the inputs resold inputs to third party, he would make an endorsement on the gate-pass, which would authorise the purchaser to take benefit of the credit of the duties paid on the goods. From the language of the said Notification, it is clear that benefit could be given if the documents would have been issued before 1-4-1994 and credit had been taken on or before 30-6-1994. From this, it was clear that gate-passes could be issued before 1-4-1994 and the benefit of credit could be taken on or before 30-6-1994. Transaction of sale or re-sale could take place any time prior to 30th June and on endorsement of same being made, benefit could be taken on or before 30-6-1994. The language of the Notification nowhere requires that the endorsement should also be made before 1-4-1994. [Para 1]

Therefore, gate-passes issued prior to 1-4-1994 but endorsed after that date would fall under the coverage of Entry No. 10 in the Table to the Notification No. 16/94-CE(NT), dated 30-3-1994 and would, consequently, be eligible documents for taking credit under the Modvat Scheme. [Para 3]

facts.text:
The assessee, namely, ‘G’, Ghaziabad availed MODVAT credit on the strength of invoice, which was in the name of ‘G’, Kota. The assessee also availed MODVAT credit on the strength of other invoice in which the buyer’s name was ‘P’, Faridabad; whereas the goods had been consigned to the assessee at Delhi. The Commissioner (Appeals) allowed the MODVAT credit taken by the assessee on the strength of the aforesaid invoices. He held that though there was cutting in consignees’ address but the same had been authenticated by the same person who had prepared the invoice and the address was changed from Kota to Ghaziabad.

He further held that a certificate issued by ‘P’ was also brought on record to show that the goods had been supplied by it to the assessee at Delhi address.

On appeal to the Tribunal by the revenue:

Facts

The assessee is engaged in the manufacture of mould steel ingots and runners and risers under an agreement entered into by them with DSM Sugar Asmoli.

Under the said lease agreement dated 26-09-2002, the facility of land and machinery stands provided by DSM Sugar, Asmoli and the capital goods were received by them are required to be installed by the assessee and the duty on the final product required to be paid by the assessee.

DSM Sugars, Asmoli had endorsed the said invoices indicating as "certified that the goods covered under these invoices transferred to Kailash Steel, Asmoli in view of lease agreement dated 20-09-2002".

The Department denied CENVAT credit to the assessee on the ground that the invoices issued by the supplier are in the name of DSM Sugars, Asmoli, though there is no dispute that the said capital goods were received by the assessee and were duly erected and installed in their premises and were used for the manufacture of dutiable and excisable goods.

Revenue's Arguments

Endorsed invoices which are in the name of DSM Sugars cannot be held to be proper Cenvatable document so as to allow the CENVAT credit in respect of the same, to the assessee.

Assessee's Arguments

Even though DSM Sugars are the owners of the capital goods in question, there is no sale purchase of the capital goods and the same only stands transferred to their unit under the lease agreement, in which case, the effect of endorsement would not be of much relevance.

Facts

There was no dispute with regard to the compliance with the substantial conditions for availing the Modvat Credit viz., inputs have suffered Central Excise duty, such duty paid goods were received into the factory under the cover of the duty paying document and the said inputs were used in the manufacture of the final product.

Since the goods in question, covered under single invoice, could not be transported as a single consignment, the same were split up into smaller consignments and transported as per the convenience of the supplier. The various split up consignments were transported under the cover of the photocopy of the original invoice.

The Department denied the Modvat Credit to relating to the inputs received from Visakhapatnam Steel Plant, a Government of India undertaking, merely on the ground that the inputs covered under single invoice were transported by various vehicles by splitting up the consignment, as a matter of convenience for the supplier in transporting such inputs.

The Department also denied the Modvat Credit taken on the basis of Original copy of the invoice, as the duplicate for the transporter was lost, though the inputs were received into the factory of manufacture and used in the manufacture.

Issue Involved

Whether denial of Modvat Credit merely on procedural lapses was valid ?

The assessee availed Cenvat credit on inputs/capital goods on basis of the invoices, wherein the suppliers had mentioned the brand name and address of the assessee. The adjudicating authority denied credit on the ground that the invoices did not bear the assessee’s name. The Commissioner (Appeals) set aside the adjudication order.

On appeal :

The appellants have their factory at Mandideep in M.P. They have another factory at Ankleshwar in Gujarat. They manufacture Cephalexin and Cephadroxil falling under Chapter 29 of CETA. Penicillin GK is the main input for the final product, which the appellants import as also procure locally. With the approval of the Assistant Collector they sent Penicillin to Ankleshwar factory direct where the same was converted into "7ADCA", which was then received at the factory at Mandideep for manufacture of the final product. They had similar approval in respect of other raw materials used in the manufacture of "7ADCA" for being sent to the factory at Ankleshwar. They were availing of the Modvat credit in respect of all the raw materials at Mandideep when "7ADCA" along with other documents was received from Ankleshwar. The Collector of CE, Indore after issuing a show cause notice and hearing the appellants, held that appellants had wrongly availed of the Modvat credit at Mandideep by deliberately suppressing the fact by not making a proper declaration of use of inputs in as much as "7ADCA" was never declared as an input. According to the Collector, in the absence of such a declaration they were not entitled to Modvat credit which could have been availed of by the Ankleshwar factory which received the declared raw materials. He therefore disallowed Modvat credit of Rs. 79,38,597.50 and also imposed a penalty of Rs. 5 lakhs.

Facts

The assessee was given a show cause notice dated 17-1-2007 asking them to show cause as to why their refund claim of Rs. 11,79,720 should not be rejected. The assessee submitted their reply dated 25-5-2007. The Assistant Commissioner sanctioned said refund claim.

However, the Assistant Commissioner issued a corrigendum (dated 17-7-2007) to the earlier show cause notice -

stating that as the assessee had taken credit to the tune of Rs. 11,18,182 on the strength of the invoices for capital goods issued by their Head Office, the same was not admissible as their Head Office was not registered as a registered dealer and

therefore asking why their refund should not be rejected to the extent of Rs. 11,18,182.

The assessee contended that -

the refund sought was of the excess amount paid by them which should be sanctioned and that the amount of cenvat credit on capital goods (Rs. 11,18,182) was rightly taken on the strength of the documents issued by their Head Office in respect of the capital goods actually used by them for providing the output service and

they and their Head Office are not separate entities.

Issue Involved

Whether unconfirmed demand can be set-off against unconfirmed refund claim ?

The appellant availed Modvat credit on the strength of a gate pass which was not consigned to them but to their job worker. However, in the original gate pass the name of the job worker was scored out and name of the appellant was written but in duplicate gate pass name of the job worker was written. In these circumstances the department proceeded against the appellant for irregular availment of credit and the original authority disallowed the Modvat credit and demanded that amount with penalty.

In appeal the appellant contended that in order to avoid any problem during transportation, the correction was made by the consigner in original gate pass.

The assessee availed MODVAT credit on the invoices issued by the dealers/traders during the period July, 1994 to December, 1994. A show-cause notice was issued to the assessee denying the MODVAT credit on the ground that these dealers/traders were not registered dealers with the Central Excise department. Though the assessee contested the show-cause notice on the ground that these dealers/traders got themselves registered, the adjudicating authority confirmed the demand on the assessee and imposed penalty on the ground that addresses of the traders were different and duty paying documents did not show the required details. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals), in respect of the credit availed by the assessee on the invoices issued by Indian Oil Corporation, allowed the appeal but in respect of other dealers/traders, denied the MODVAT credit and upheld imposition of penalty. He, however, reduced the quantum of penalty.

On appeal :

The assessee was engaged in the manufacture of Vinyl Chloride Monomer, Poly Vinyl Chloride, High Density Polyethylene, Mono-Ethylene Glycol, Polyester Oriented Yarn, etc. at its integrated manufacturing under known as 'H'.

During the set up of 'H', the assessee purchased the complete Single Point Mooring System [SPM system] along with anchor chain, chain stoppers, anchor piles and anchor pipes and other items such as offshore bands, half shell brackets, anode pipes, etc.

SPM system was located by the assessee outside the factory.

It availed Modvat credit of duty paid on SPM system stating that it was capital goods in terms of rule 57Q.

The lower authorities including the Tribunal disallowed the Modvat credit.

On appeal to High Court:

The assessee was engaged in the manufacture of automobile parts. It registered itself with Central Excise Department on 28-11-2006 for manufacture of automobile components. The assessee set up its new factory by awarding the contract of construction thereof to a contractor. During the period from January 2007-08, the assessee availed cenvat credit on service tax paid on the construction services on the strength of 12 invoices issued by the contractor. Out of 12 invoices, invoices involving cenvat credit were issued prior to 28-11-2006 and remaining were issued after 28-11-2006, i.e. the date on which the assessee was registered with the Central Department. The Commissioner allowed the credit relating to the invoices which were issued subsequent to 28-11-2006, however, disallowed the credit in relation to the invoices which were issued prior to 28-11-2006 on the ground that the assessee was not registered with the Department at the time of issuance of those invoices and secondly, on the ground that the invoices were issued in the earlier name of assessee and not in the current name of the assessee.

On appeal:

The assessee was engaged in the manufacture of carbon black. It was availing the facility of modvat credit under rule 57A. On scrutiny of RT-12 returns, filed by the assessee, it was noticed that the assessee had taken modvat credit on the strength of original copies of invoices without taking/applying for permission from the competent authority under rule 57G(2A). Hence, the adjudicating authority disallowed the modvat credit and confirmed the demands under rule 57-I along with penalties. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) remanded the matter to adjudicating authority for de novo proceedings. In remand proceedings, the adjudicating authority allowed the modvat credit, holding that there was no dispute regarding the duty paid character of the inputs and their receipt/utilization in manufacture of final product. Being aggrieved, the revenue successfully took the matter in appeals to the Commissioner against which assessee preferred appeal before the Tribunal, which was allowed.

On appeal :

The appellants availed Modvat credit for certain inputs used in the manufacture of their final product. The Asstt. Collector ordered reversal of credit taken on grounds that the original Gate Passes were not endorsed properly. The Collector (Appeals) rejected their appeal. Hence this appeal.

The assessee installed in its factory duty paid imported capital goods which were to be used in manufacture of dutiable final products. The assessee availed Modvat credit. Subsequently, CBI conducted investigation in the assessees’ premises and seized various documents. Whether the assessee was eligible for CENVAT Credit on input services ?

On appeal :

held.text: The Commissioner (Appeals) had rightly followed the decision of the Tribunal in the case of CCE&CE v. DNH Spinners [2010] 25 STT 295 (Ahd. - CESTAT). Even though the assessee had multiple divisions, in the absence of any dispute about the receipt of the services in question by the factory to whom credit had been passed on, the ratio of the cited decision was applicable. In fact, the Commissioner(Appeals) proceeded to say that the assessee should have followed the procedure of issue of invoices by the head office as an input service distributor but observed that as far as the present appeal was concerned, the proceedings were limited by the ground taken in the show-cause notice and the order-in-original which had held that assessee had taken credit wrongly since invoice was not in its name but in the name of its head office. In view of the fact that the invoice was in the name of the head office and there was no dispute raised in the show-cause notice as to the admissibility of input service credit to the factory on the ground that the input service was not relatable to the factory, the omission became a totally curable defect and was a condonable one. Under those circumstances, the conclusion reached by the Commissioner (Appeals) to drop the demand could not be found fault with. The Commissioner (Appeals) also had taken a view that merely because the assessee did not disclose to the department that it had availed credit on the basis of documents not prescribed under rule 9(2), it could not be said that there was suppression of fact, wilful misstatement, etc. He had relied upon the decision of the Supreme Court in the case of Larsen & Toubro Ltd. v. CCE 2007 (211) ELT 513. In view of the fact that there was no allegation of non-receipt of input service or the allegation of service not relatable to the factory and also in view of the fact that invoice was in the name of head office of the same factory and not in the name of someone else, the decision of the Commissioner (Appeals) that extended period was not invocable also had to be upheld. Since the assessee was eligible for the credit and there was no suppression of facts, extended period was not invocable and, hence, the question of penalty did not arise. Accordingly, the penalty imposed was to be set aside. In view of the above, the appeal filed by the revenue was to be rejected and appeal filed by the assessee was to be allowed. [Para 2]

Rules permit taking of credit under a common pool and permit the use of the credit from common pool for different purposes and there is no restriction placed to the effect that credit accounts should be maintained for use for manufacture of excisable goods and for use for providing services. The restriction on utilisation of Cenvat credit stipulated relates only for specific type of duties, i.e., education cess on excisable goods or payment of education cess on output service. There is no restriction for utilisation of common input credit availed on the inputs and also on input service for payment of excise duty or service tax. Hence, there is no reason to deny the input service credit on the ground that it was shown in the ER-1 return. [Para 13]

Cenvat credit on crane in dry dock

The adjudicating authority denied Cenvat credit on capital goods, being inadmissible used in immovable property come into existence. The Andhra Pradesh High Court in the case of CCE v. Sai Sahmita Storages (P.) Ltd. [2012] 17 taxmann.com 107/34 STT 306 held that storage and warehousing service could not have been rendered without creating a warehouse and, consequently, the credit on TMT bars used for construction of warehouse would be admissible. Similarly, in the instant case, the appellant is unable to render the repair/refit service without the crane in dry dock and which can be treated as capital goods. [Para 14]

Cenvat credit on basis of invoices issued by ISD

There is a denial of Cenvat credit availed on input service on the ground that credit was taken on the strength of invoices issued by the appellant's head office at Mumbai as ISD (Input Service Distributor). It is observed by the adjudicating authority that the head office address was not mentioned in the LOP issued by the DGFT. There is no dispute that the head office is registered as ISD with the Service Tax authorities. As per Cenvat Credit Rules, the appellants are eligible to avail the credit on the invoices issued by the ISD. There is no reason to deny the credit on the ground that the address of the ISD was not mentioned in the LOP. [Para 15]

In view of the above discussion, the denial of Cenvat credit along with interest and penalties cannot be sustained. Accordingly, the impugned order is set aside. [Para 16]

Modvat--cannot be denied in routine or by mechanical approach even if documentation is defective so long as duty has been paid on inputs, "... we are unable to appreciate the routine and mechanical approach of the authorities below in rejecting the claim of the Modvat credit only on the ground that more than one endorsement has been made. When the Board themselves have taken a decision to relax the procedural requirement by way of administrative instruction it should be the endeavour of the authorities to extend Modvat credit wherever the duty-paid nature of the goods is evident from the gate passes produced and quantum of duty paid on the inputs could be ascertained from them. A positive approach is called for in this regard."

2. Modvat--credit for goods received against GP I, after three endorsements by different parties can be allowed as long as duty-paid nature of the goods is established. "Rule 57G of the Central Excise Rules stipulates that inputs are to be received under the cover of a gate pass, an AR-I, a Bill of Entry or any other document as may be prescribed by the Board. ...However, when this requirement created some difficulties in the ease of Small Scale units to obtain the inputs through intermediaries, the Board appears to have made relaxation to this requirement by permitting one endorsement in the gate pass initially and subsequently based on the representations permitting upto two endorsements in the gate passes. This relaxation made by the Board appears to be purely of administrative nature based on considerations of implementing the Modvat scheme, so long as the duty-paid nature of the goods and duty paid thereon could be established. As seen from the Trade Notice cited by the learned advocate, it is evident that the Government is keen to extend the Modvat credit so long as the goods in factory packed condition as are covered by the gate passes are received by the parties intending to avail Modvat credit...... the department is entitled to make verification or investigation with regard to the genuineness of the gate pass and also on the question whether gate pass has been utilised for availment of Modvat credit at the earliest stages. In this case, no such enquiry appears to have been conducted and the Modvat credit has-been denied only on the ground that more than that of permitted endorsements have been made in the gate passes. Such an order cannot be sustainable in the context of the scheme of Modvat credit read along with the relaxation made by the Board. We, therefore, set aside the order passed by the authorities below and permit availment of credit and while doing so, we allow the liberty to the Assistant Collector to cause any inquiry or investigation to satisfy himself about the genuine nature of the gate passes and also about non-utilisation of the gate passes at the earlier stages of endorsements for availment of Modvat credit."

The benefit of MODVAT credit could not be denied to the assessee merely on the ground that there was change in the address from Kota to Ghaziabad. Further, it had not been disputed by the revenue that the inputs sent by ‘P’ were duty-paid and the same were received in the factory for being used in the manufacture of the final products. Thus, in view of the subsequent amendment made in rule 57G by Notification No. 7/1999-CE (NT) dated 9-2-1999, the MODVAT credit cannot be denied on account of some minor procedural lapses in the duty-paying documents. The Board had also clarified, vide Circular No. 441/7/1999-CX dated 23-2-1999, that Notification No. 7/1999-CE (NT), has been issued so as to empower the Assistant Commissioner, having jurisdiction over the factory of the manufacturer, to allow the credit ignoring minor procedural lapses provided the inputs have suffered duty and are being used in the process of manufacture. Hence, the appeal was liable to be rejected. [Para 3]

In as much as there is no dispute that the said capital goods stand received by the assessees and further duly installed in their factory and were being used for the manufacture of the final product, which was being cleared by the assessee, the revenue's objection that such CENVAT credit is not available in as much as the same was taken on the basis of the endorsed invoices cannot be upheld.

Admittedly, this is not a case of sale of capital goods from one manufacturer unit to another. It is a case where the capital goods are bought by the lessor and transferred to the lessee's factory, under lease agreement for further manufacture of the final product. As such, the certificate given by DSM Sugars, Asmoli on the invoices indicating that are being transferred and in the absence of any dispute to the factual aspect, the assessee is entitled to the CENVAT credit involved in the present appeal. [Para 4]

There was no dispute that the goods in question were received by the assessee and were used in the manufacture of the final product and duly recorded in the register. The Central Board of Excise & Customs vide Circular No. 441/7/99-CX, dated 23-2-1999 clarified that in terms of sub-rule (11) in rule 57G, and sub-rule (13) of rule 57T of the erstwhile Central Excise Rules, 1944, the Assistant Commissioner of Central Excise may allow the credit of duty paid on inputs/capital goods in minor procedural lapses in filing the declaration or in the invoices/documents, based on which credit is to be taken. However, the Assistant Commissioner should ensure that inputs/capital goods have suffered duty and are being used/are to be used in the process of manufacture. In the instant case, there was no dispute that inputs/capital goods had suffered duty and were used in the manufacture of final products. In any event, brand name of the assessee with its address instead of company’s name in the invoices established ownership of the goods. So, the Commissioner (Appeals) had rightly allowed the credit. Accordingly, no reason was found to interfere with the order of the Commissioner (Appeals). The appeal filed by the revenue was to be rejected. [Para 4]

The goods, on which Modvat credit had been taken by the appellants irregularly, were consigned to the job worker. In other words the goods were not received by the appellant but by his job worker. The duplicate copy of the gate pass which had accompanied the goods contain the name of the job worker. However, the original which was sent to the appellants contains the name of the appellant, which was written after scoring out the original consignee i.e., the job worker. The adjudicating authority had given a very detailed finding to indicate that there had been manipulation of the consignee’s name in the original copy of the gate pass. But for that manipulation, the appellant would not have got the Modvat credit. In fact actual consignee was only the job worker. Further the adjudicating authority had found that there was no endorsement in name of appellant as rightly found in the duplicate copy of the gate pass in question. The adjudicating authority had observed that Modvat credit can be taken only when both the material as well as duty paying documents are received by the consignee as indicated in the gate pass. In this case, no fraudulent motive was found which could be attributed to the appellant. The appellant along with consigner have taken recourse to certain devices of expediency to avoid irksome procedures. However, when the material had not been received by the appellant and only by some job worker, taking credit on the goods received by the job worker by changing the name of the consignee in the original copy of the gate pass, was serious matter and such scant regard to rules could not be ignored. The appellant was not entitled for the Modvat credit. [Para 6]

Modvat credit; that the duplicate copy of manufacturer's invoice under rule 52A will serve as cover for transport and for availment of Modvat by the end-user. As per the position prevailing prior to 30-3-1994, when the purchaser resold inputs to third party, he would make an endorsement on the gate pass issued by the manufacturer of the input. Procedure had changed and instead of endorsement on the gate-passes, invoice was required to be produced as per Notification No. 16/94-CE(NT), dated 30-3-1994. Certain documents were prescribed for the purpose of giving credit of Modvat under the Rules. In Column No. 3 to the Entry No. 10 of the aforesaid Notification, prescribed documents were endorsed gate-passes/subsidiary gate-passes/certificates. Admittedly, gate-passes were required to be issued by the manufacturer under the procedure then prevailing and as and when the purchaser of the inputs resold inputs to third party, he would make an endorsement on the gate-pass, which would authorise the purchaser to take benefit of the credit of the duties paid on the goods. From the language of the said Notification, it is clear that benefit could be given if the documents would have been issued before 1-4-1994 and credit had been taken on or before 30-6-1994. From this, it was clear that gate-passes could be issued before 1-4-1994 and the benefit of credit could be taken on or before 30-6-1994. Transaction of sale or re-sale could take place any time prior to 30th June and on endorsement of same being made, benefit could be taken on or before 30-6-1994. The language of the Notification nowhere requires that the endorsement should also be made before 1-4-1994. [Para 1]

Therefore, gate-passes issued prior to 1-4-1994 but endorsed after that date would fall under the coverage of Entry No. 10 in the Table to the Notification No. 16/94-CE(NT), dated 30-3-1994 and would, consequently, be eligible documents for taking credit under the Modvat Scheme. [Para 3]

One of the documents on which Cenvat credit is allowed as mentioned in clause (a) of subject rule 9(1) is an invoice issued by manufacturer for clearance of inputs or capital goods from his factory. In the instant case, invoices, on which credit was disputed was issued by manufacturer and the appellant's name is clearly appearing as consignee. Therefore, the invoices in question squarely covered by clause (a) of sub-rule 1 of Rule 9. The Revenue's contention that in case of purchase of input from dealer, invoices should be issued by first stage dealer or second stage dealer, is not agreeable. Only in case where the input is purchased directly from a dealer on his invoices and the manufacturer invoices does not indicate the name of the recipient as consignee, the first stage dealer or second stage dealer, as case may be, who is registered with Central Excise, should issue invoices as provided under rule 11 of Central Excise Rules, 2002. However, in the instant case invoices on which credit was taken issued by manufacturer and appellant's name is appearing as consignee, in such cases credit is admissible on these invoices and there is no need of separate invoices to be issued by the registered dealer for taking credit. The contention of the Revenue that since appellant has not made payment for purchase of the input of the manufacturer supplier, Cenvat credit is not admissible, is absurd for the reason that manufacturer supplier as per the invoices, sold the goods to the dealers and in turn dealers sold the goods to appellant in such transactions there are sale purchase transactions is involved, i.e., one from manufacturer supplier to dealers and second from dealers to the appellant. Therefore, the appellant made payment to dealers and cannot make payment of the bills to manufacturer supplier. Therefore, contention of the Revenue on this count is not acceptable. However, for taking Cenvat credit on input it is not mandatory that payment towards purchase of the input has to be made. There are number of transactions in the trade such as procurement input from group company, sister concern on payment of duty, procurement of input for job work, etc. In such transaction there is no transaction of any payments towards supply of inputs. Despite this position, Cenvat credit is admissible and cannot be disputed so long input is duty paid, received in the factory and used in the manufacture. The appellant has correctly and legally availed the Cenvat credit on the invoices wherein appellant name is appearing as consignee and name of the dealers as buyer; therefore, the impugned order is set aside. [Para 5]

So, if the power plant is situated outside the factory premises, Cenvat credit on capital goods used for setting up power plant cannot be denied as the electricity is captively consumed within the factory of SISCOL. Lease agreement : On perusal of the lease agreement, it is seen that the Lessor (SISCOL) requested to the Lessee (JSWPL) to set up a power plant in the premises of the Lessor (SISCOL) to take care of the power generation of the Lessor to which Lessee has agreed. The lease of the immovable property is determined for a limited period conditionally on the happenings of some events. The tenure of the lease agreement depends upon the happenings of the future events. In the instant case, it is a conditional transfer of the property with an interest created on a transfer of the property and dependent upon the fulfilment of the condition. Thus, it is clearly evident that SISCOL had provided their land to JSWPL with a condition to set up a power plant and the electricity generated would be consumed in manufacturing activities of SISCOL. Lease agreement was financing arrangement : An agreement should also be examined with actual state of affairs and its implementation from the records. In the present case, it may be seen from the documents and records that in 2004, SISCOL was declared as sick unit under SICA, 1985. CDR Cell report would show that SJG came forward for financing the sick unit SISCOL, as finance acts as an engine of growth. It appears from the Show Cause Notices that JSWPL, one of the companies of SJG, have expertise in constructing and operating Power Plants and JSW Steel Ltd. another company of SJG, is one of the purchasers of the final product of SISCOL. Rule 4(3) - Capital goods were acquired under loan/lease agreement : Rule 4 (3) of CCR 2004 provides that the Cenvat credit in respect of the capital goods shall be allowed to a manufacturer, even if the capital goods are acquired by him on lease, hire purchase or loan agreement, from a financing company. Rule 4(3) has a wide amplitude in so far as it would cover the cases of various types of financial arrangements for availing credit on the capital goods. It is contemplated that under this sub-rule (3) of rule 4 would cover the cases where the ownership of the capital goods does not vest in the manufacturer until the loan is repaid. There must be an agreement for the purpose of acquiring the capital goods. Variations/unusual features in the agreement covering the lease agreement were not relevant for determining the eligibility of credit. It is clear that title of the property is not relevant for availing Cenvat credit on capital goods. [Para 68.3]

The High Court in the case of Ambuja Cements Ltd. v. UOI [2009] 20 STT 182 (Punj. & Har.) had upheld the Board Circular No. 97/6/2007-ST, dated 23-8-2007 and held that the conditions laid down therein should be fulfilled by a manufacturer claiming the benefit of CENVAT credit on outward transportation of finished goods from the factory. The High Court considered three conditions :-

(a)The ownership of the goods and the property therein to remain with the seller of the goods till delivery of the goods in acceptable condition to the purchaser at his doorstep.

(b)The seller to bear the risk of loss or damage to the goods during transit to the destination.

(c)The freight charges to be included in the assessable value of the goods.

In the written submissions filed by the assessee, it had been claimed that all these conditions were fulfilled and, therefore, CENVAT credit of service tax paid on outward transportation of cement from the factory to depots/customers’ premises should be allowed. Therefore, the orders of the lower authorities were to be set aside and the matter was to be remanded to the original authority to take a fresh decision. [Para 2]

The MODVAT Scheme was introduced by the Finance Minister with effect from 1-3-1986. The nature of the MODVAT Scheme is intended to be a revenue neutral. It was not the purpose to use the MODVAT to give substantial relief of excise. The shifting the effective burden of excise taxation away from inputs and on the final products is the heart of the said scheme. In short, the MODVAT Scheme allows the manufacturer to obtain instant and complete reimbursement of the excise duty paid on the components and raw materials which will result in considerable reduction in the cost of final product. The benefit of MODVAT is available only in respect of such raw material/components actually consumed in production of final goods actually sold. In the instant case, since only 50 per cent of inputs covered by the MODVAT Scheme were consumed in respect of which gate passes were obtained, MODVAT benefit available was only 50 per cent. Moreover, the issue had come up before the Tribunal in the assessee’s case for the assessment year 1987-88 where the Tribunal had upheld the deletion made by the Commissioner (Appeals).

In the light of above discussion and in the absence of additional material/evidence, the Commissioner (Appeals) was right in holding that there was no impact on the profit whether cost of raw material was debited at gross or at net of MODVAT. Therefore, the Commissioner (Appeals) had rightly deleted the said additions pertaining to the MODVAT.

During the period of dispute, the assessee availed GTA service for outward transportation of liquefied gases (final products) from its factory to buyers’ premises. Rule 57G clearly shows that the credit of duty can be taken on inputs by establishing that the duty has been paid on the said inputs on the basis of documents such as invoice, AR-1, Bill on Entry, etc. In the instant case, it was not in dispute that the appellant had received imported shredded steel scrap from ‘E’ Ltd. on which countervailing duty had been paid by ‘E’ Ltd. It was also not in dispute that ‘E’ Ltd. had not taken credit of the duty paid on shredded steel scrap which was given on loan to the appellant. It was also not in dispute that the appellant had used the said shredded steel scrap taken on loan from ‘E’ Ltd. as inputs in its factory. The certificate issued by a Superintendent of Central Excise to the effect that ‘E’ Ltd. had not taken credit of duty paid on the said shredded steel scrap, was not doubted by the Excise authorities. Similarly, the certificate issued by another Superintendent to the effect that the quantity of shredded steel scrap received by the appellant from ‘E’ Ltd. had been used as inputs in the factory of the appellant, was also not doubted by the Excise authorities. In these circumstances, the appellant had established that the credit of duty on receipt of imported shredded steel scrap from ‘E’ Ltd. had been taken in accordance with law. [Para 9]

For availing the credit of duty, what is required to be established under rule 57G is that the inputs received are in fact duty paid. The procedure set out in rule 57G is to ensure that the credit is taken on the basis of duty paid documents. The bill of entry is one such document set out in rule 57G. The said rule does not require that the bill of entry should be in the name of the person claiming credit of duty. It is not in dispute that the goods imported and cleared on payment of duty by one person can be used as inputs and credit of duty can be claimed by another person by establishing that the imported duty paid goods have been received as inputs and that the importer has not taken credit of that duty. In the instant case, it was established that the duty paid goods were received as inputs, however, the credit was denied on the ground that the Bill of entry was not endorsed in the name of the appellant. Rule 57G does not require that for taking credit of duty, the bill of entry should be endorsed in the name of the claimant. In the absence of any provision regarding endorsement on the bill of entry, the credit of duty cannot be denied on the ground that the bill of entry is not endorsed in the name of the claimant. In the facts of the instant case, the evidence on record i.e., the bills of entry together with the certificates issued by excise authorities, clearly showed that the goods imported and cleared under the bills of entry on payment of duty were received and utilized by the appellant as inputs in its factory and that the importer had not utilized the credit of duty paid on the said goods. Thus, the appellant had established that the inputs received under the bills of entry were duty paid and, therefore, the authorities below were not justified in denying the credit of duty to the appellant. [Para 10]

In the instant case, there was no doubt that the assessee was required to maintain a canteen in its factory as per the Factories Act and to provide canteen facilities to its workers to run its factory which was a statutory requirement. In M.M.R. Khan v. Union of India AIR 1990 SC 937, the Apex Court had given a clear-cut findings that providing canteen was an integral part of the manufacturing activity of the assessee and as per the decision in Maruti Suzuki Ltd.'s v. CCE [2009] 22 STT 54 (SC) also any input which has gone into manufacturing of the final product directly or indirectly is entitled to input credit. Relying on both the decisions, it was to be held in the instant case also that the assessee was entitled to input credit on LPG used in the canteen, which as per the Factories Act was necessarily required to run its manufacturing activity. Accordingly, there was no infirmity in the impugned order and the same was to be upheld and the appeal filed by the revenue was to rejected. [Para 6]

The charges only on classification of the input under heading 72.30 and not under the machinery or fuel storage tank or steel tanks headings, would not deter from granting capital goods credit; as the incorrect classification done by the supplier cannot be a ground for denial of Modvat credit. The credit can be obtained if the input is used in relation to the manufacture of the goods. Fuel storage tanks have been held to be eligible capital goods by catena of decisions of the Tribunal. Therefore, there was no reason to deny the credit on fuel storage tanks eligibility. [Para 4]

Modvat--Limitation for taking credit--Rule 57G does not lay down any time limit for taking credit after the inputs have been received in the factory. "........the procedure for taking MODVAT Credit has been set out in Rule 57G of the Central Excise Rules, 1944. The requirement is that the assessees are required to file declaration in respect of final products manufactured in the factory and the inputs intended to be used in each of the said final products and thereafter take the credit in respect of the duty paid on the inputs. There is no provision specifying any time limit for taking the MODVAT Credit in the MODVAT Rules on receipt of the goods inside the factory. ......We do not see as to how the interests of the Revenue are prejudiced if the assessees choose to take the credit after a lapse of time after the date of receipt of the goods inside the factory. It is in fact the assessees who will be foregoing the benefit of the credit in case they choose to take the credit after a lapse of time as they will be deprived of the benefit of the MODVAT Credit due till they take the credit. In view of the above and in the absence of any specific provision in the Central Excise Rules in regard to time limit for taking MODVAT Credit, we hold that the plea of the Revenue is not maintainable in law."

The case of the assessee was that TISCO did not supply original challans but only gave the carbon copies and same must be regarded as original within meaning of rule 57G. The appellate authority after considering various pieces of evidence had recorded a categorical finding in its order that it was incorrect to claim by the assessee that TISCO only issued carbon copies. The Tribunal in its finding observed that there were other manufacturers also who were receiving original challans issued by the stockyards of TISCO. [Para 3]

In the wake of the aforesaid findings, it was not possible to conclude that carbon copy was required to be regarded as original copy as per the claim made by the assessee.

A perusal of the provisions of the rule 57G shows that in order to claim Modvat credit, the original copy of the invoice is required to be produced. There is no provision for granting Modvat credit on the basis of carbon copy. If it is to be presumed that carbon copy in a case like the one in hand could be treated as original, then the finding of fact by the appellate authority or Tribunal has to be on the record. In the instant case, the finding of fact was against the dealer that TISCO did not issue invoice on a carbon copy so as to be treated as original for the purpose of rule 57G. The contention of the assessee that carbon copy had been properly verified and defaced was not impressive as in the instant case adjudication had to be only on the question of law. No merit was found in the contention raised by the assessee. Moreover, laying down a blanket principle permitting Modvat credit on carbon copy may result into setting up of false claims. On such a possibility of availing Modvat credit by many persons against one transaction would not be ruled out which will be highly damaging to the revenue. [Para 4]

Therefore, on the facts and circumstances of the case, the Tribunal was right in disallowing credit for Modvat on carbon copy of challans furnished by the assessee evidencing payment of duty. [Para 5]
