[Notification No. 15/94-C.E.(N.T.), dated 30.3.1994] It is seen that in a contingency where the goods were received not directly from the manufacturer but through the agency of the dealer, facility for taking modvat was taken care of by authorising the taking of MOD VAT Credit based on the invoice to be issued by the wholesaler, dealer, distributor etc. and for that reason it would appear the Government did not feel it necessary to issue any notification for acceptance of the endorsed invoices as was the case in case of Gate Passes. Even in the case of Gate Passes, a provision was earlier made for acceptance of subsidiary gate passes also. Thus, simultaneously the provision of acceptance of subsidiary gate passes and also endorsed gate passes was available. It is seen that at the time when the change over took place in the Central Excise documentation as above, there was some' confusion and some hardship and the Government issued Notification 16/94 dated 30th March, 1994 under which the endorsed Gate Pass, Subsidiary Gate Pass and certain certificates were notified as authorised documents for taking MODVAT Credit till 30th June, 1994. It would thus appear that upto 30th June, 1994 this facility of accepting endorsed Gate Pass was available along with the amended provisions in regard to taking of MODVAT Credit based on the invoices issued by the manufacturer or by the dealer. In the present case what has happened is that the full consignment as received by the dealer has been sent to the Respondents and the dealer has not issued any invoice of his own but has made an endorsement for the sale of the goods to the Respondents and sent the goods under the cover of this endorsed invoice. The question that arises is that whether in the circumstances which prevailed at the relevant time such a course was acceptable. It is observed that at the relevant time the dealers were not required to register while they were authorised to issue invoices as would be seen from Notification 15/94. In the present case what has happened is that instead of the dealer issuing invoice, he has made the endorsement in the invoice in respect of the goods he has received from the manufacturer. It is in the above context that the matter should have been examined by the learned lower authority. The learned lower authority does not appear to have examined the whole issue in depth and has held that the endorsements made later in the Gate Passes was adequate enough to give cover to the appellants for the purpose of MODVAT Credit. This, I am afraid, is not the correct way to look at things with the change of law and with the changed parameters and facilities which had been made available at the relevant time. The position should have been examined in the context of the same. This having not been done, I hold that the order of the learned lower authori ty is not proper and therefore set aside the same and remand the matter for denovo consideration of the factors set out above and after affording the Respondents an opportunity of being heard. The appeal is therefore allowed by remand.

Provided that no credit shall be taken unless the inputs are received in the factory under the cover of a Gate Pass, an AR-1, a Bill of Entry or any other documents as may be prescribed by the Central Board of Excise and Customs, (constituted under the Central Board of Revenue Act, 1963, (54 of 1963) in this behalf evidencing the payment of duty on such inputs)." Gate pass is a prescribed document under Rule 52A in respect of excisable goods cleared from a factory and this has been described as GP-1. Among other particulars in this form are - Name and address of the consignee, manner of transport, date and time of removal which should be shown in figures and words. All these particulars have been prescribed to ensure that the gate pass is not misused for double or treble transport of excisable goods and the gate pass is valid for transport of the goods in respect of consignees to whom these are consigned and the mode of transport etc. prescribed. We observe that the moment the goods have been received at the consignee's end the validity of the gate pass so far as the transport of the goods is concerned, can be taken to have run out and the gate pass only remains as evidence of clearance of the goods on payment of duty and the same gate pass can only be revived by following the procedure prescribed in this regard as set out under Rule 57G. Re-endorsement of gate pass in respect of part of the consignment sold is not one of the prescribed modes. For bringing the goods for MODVAT purposes, the proper course for the assessee was to have had the gate pass re-endorsed by the jurisdictional Central Excise officer after getting the particulars regarding consignment verified with reference to the gate pass if such a course had been prescribed under Rule 57G. This admittedly had not been done. We observe that a strict view has to be taken in regard to the documents under the cover of which the goods are brought in a factory for MODVAT purposes. The documents as have been prescribed are with a view to ensure that duty paid goods alone are received in the factory and it is obligatory that statutory documents as set out under Rule 57G alone are taken into consideration for the purpose of MODVAT Credit. There is possibility of misuse in case consignees on their own are allowed to endorse the gate pass after the goods have been cleared from the factory and received by them and a part of the same are resold. It would he difficult to verify the identity of the goods after the original consignment is broken up for sale. In this view of the matter we hold that the learned lower appellate authority has been in error in allowing the appeal of the Respondents. We, therefore, set aside the impugned order and allow the Departmental appeal.

2. During the period 30.06.03 to 24.01.04, four duty paying invoices were issued by the concerned manufacturer of POY in favour of Unit 3 of the company. However, as the said material was proposed to be used in the present appellant's unit i.e. Unit 2, the said raw material was delivered in the appellant's factory under the cover of invoices with the remark by the Unit 3 that entire consignment stand transferred to the appellant's unit. The said goods were re-directed to the appellant's unit without receiving in Unit 3. The appellant took the credit of the same in their record on the basis of the said invoices.

3. Only objection of Revenue is that the invoices were in the name of Unit 3, who could not have endorsed the same. 4. After hearing the learned SDR Shri J.S. Negi, I find that there is no dispute about the factual position. The inputs were actually received by the appellant and utilised by them in manufacture of final product. Admittedly, the inputs were duty paid and covered by the invoices, which were in the name of M/s Raj Rayon only. The Commissioner (Appeals) had rightly followed the decision of the Tribunal in the case of CCE&CE v. DNH Spinners [2010] 25 STT 295 (Ahd. - CESTAT). Even though the assessee had multiple divisions, in the absence of any dispute about the receipt of the services in question by the factory to whom credit had been passed on, the ratio of the cited decision was applicable. In fact, the Commissioner(Appeals) proceeded to say that the assessee should have followed the procedure of issue of invoices by the head office as an input service distributor but observed that as far as the present appeal was concerned, the proceedings were limited by the ground taken in the show-cause notice and the order-in-original which had held that assessee had taken credit wrongly since invoice was not in its name but in the name of its head office. In view of the fact that the invoice was in the name of the head office and there was no dispute raised in the show-cause notice as to the admissibility of input service credit to the factory on the ground that the input service was not relatable to the factory, the omission became a totally curable defect and was a condonable one. Under those circumstances, the conclusion reached by the Commissioner (Appeals) to drop the demand could not be found fault with. The Commissioner (Appeals) also had taken a view that merely because the assessee did not disclose to the department that it had availed credit on the basis of documents not prescribed under rule 9(2), it could not be said that there was suppression of fact, wilful misstatement, etc. He had relied upon the decision of the Supreme Court in the case of Larsen & Toubro Ltd. v. CCE 2007 (211) ELT 513. In view of the fact that there was no allegation of non-receipt of input service or the allegation of service not relatable to the factory and also in view of the fact that invoice was in the name of head office of the same factory and not in the name of someone else, the decision of the Commissioner (Appeals) that extended period was not invocable also had to be upheld. Since the assessee was eligible for the credit and there was no suppression of facts, extended period was not invocable and, hence, the question of penalty did not arise. Accordingly, the penalty imposed was to be set aside. In view of the above, the appeal filed by the revenue was to be rejected and appeal filed by the assessee was to be allowed. [Para 2]

HELD: The Commissioner (Appeals) had rightly followed the decision of the Tribunal in the case of CCE&CE v. DNH Spinners [2010] 25 STT 295 (Ahd. - CESTAT). Even though the assessee had multiple divisions, in the absence of any dispute about the receipt of the services in question by the factory to whom credit had been passed on, the ratio of the cited decision was applicable. In fact, the Commissioner(Appeals) proceeded to say that the assessee should have followed the procedure of issue of invoices by the head office as an input service distributor but observed that as far as the present appeal was concerned, the proceedings were limited by the ground taken in the show-cause notice and the order-in-original which had held that assessee had taken credit wrongly since invoice was not in its name but in the name of its head office. In view of the fact that the invoice was in the name of the head office and there was no dispute raised in the show-cause notice as to the admissibility of input service credit to the factory on the ground that the input service was not relatable to the factory, the omission became a totally curable defect and was a condonable one. Under those circumstances, the conclusion reached by the Commissioner (Appeals) to drop the demand could not be found fault with. The Commissioner (Appeals) also had taken a view that merely because the assessee did not disclose to the department that it had availed credit on the basis of documents not prescribed under rule 9(2), it could not be said that there was suppression of fact, wilful misstatement, etc. He had relied upon the decision of the Supreme Court in the case of Larsen & Toubro Ltd. v. CCE 2007 (211) ELT 513. In view of the fact that there was no allegation of non-receipt of input service or the allegation of service not relatable to the factory and also in view of the fact that invoice was in the name of head office of the same factory and not in the name of someone else, the decision of the Commissioner (Appeals) that extended period was not invocable also had to be upheld. Since the assessee was eligible for the credit and there was no suppression of facts, extended period was not invocable and, hence, the question of penalty did not arise. Accordingly, the penalty imposed was to be set aside. In view of the above, the appeal filed by the revenue was to be rejected and appeal filed by the assessee was to be allowed. [Para 2]

Depots, consignment agents and importers should be registered with CE. However, they are not 'first stage dealers'. Hence, purchaser who is purchasing from such depot or consignment agent will still be a 'first stage dealer'. Invoice of depot/consignment agent of manufacturer is eligible for Cenvat under rule 9(1)(a)(i)(I). Invoice of depot/consignment agent of importer is eligible document for Cenvat as per rule 9(1)(a)(iii).

Transfer of goods from one depot to another - If goods are transferred from one depot to another, the second depot will still be a 'depot', as the second depot is not 'purchasing' goods from first depot - the goods are only being 'transferred'. As per section 2(h) of CEA, 'purchase' requires transfer from one person to another for valuable consideration. Hence, transfer from one depot to another on the basis of invoice is permissible. In such case, another depot will not become 'dealer'.

u disallowance of CENVAT credit in respect of service tax paid on cellular phone service availed while bills thereof were not in the name of the assessee; and

If the authority founds that service tax was paid on the input service meeting all the three tests aforesaid, the claim would be admissible.

Conclusion

14. From the above discussion, it is clear that the assessee in order to avail CENVAT credit has to maintain documents as required under rule 9. However, in cases where such documents could not be maintained and other sorts of documents are with the assessee by which he availed credit, then the following requirements are to be fulfilled—

u There shall be no dispute about the duty paid character of the input;

u Receipt of the goods in the factory of the assessee;

u Utilization for manufacture of the final product.

The authority, in such cases, has to satisfy the three tests, viz., integrity, dependability and relevancy as held in Kitply Industries Ltd. (supra). The Tribunal in Stelco Gujarat Ltd. case (supra) rightly held that the denial of credit on the procedural irregularity would not be justified. Even though favourable judgments are there, the assessee should try to maintain documents for availing credit in accordance with the rule with utmost care to avoid unnecessary litigations.

Held that the Supreme Court in Collector of Central Excise v. Dai Karkaria Ltd. 1999 (7) SCC 448 held that where a manufacturer obtains credit for the excise duty paid on raw material to be used by him in the production of an excisable product immediately, it should make the requisite declaration and obtain an acknowledgement thereof. It is entitled to use the credit at any time thereafter while making payment of excise duty on the excisable product. There is no provision in the Rules which provides for a reversal of the credit by the Excise Authorities, except where it has been illegally or irregularly taken, in which event it stands cancelled or, if utilized, has to be paid for. Where the credit has been validly taken, its benefit is available to the manufacturer without any limitation in time or otherwise, unless the manufacturer itself chooses not to use the raw material in its excisable product. The credit is, therefore, indefeasible. It should also be noted that there is no correlation of the raw material and the final product, that is to say, it is not as if credit can be taken only on a final product, that is, manufactured out of the particular raw material to which the credit is related. The credit may be taken against the excise duty on a final product manufactured on the very day it becomes available.

Applicability of proviso to Rule 11(2) of Central Excise Rules

3. Rule 9(1)(iv) of Cenvat Credit Rules states that invoice issued by a first stage dealer or a second stage dealer, as the case may be, in terms of the provisions of Central Excise Rules, 2002.

Rule 11 of Central Excise Rules makes provisions in respect of invoice issued by manufacturer.

Rule 11(7) of Central Excise Rules states that the provision of rule 11 shall apply mutatis mutandis (i.e., after making necessary changes) to goods supplied by a first stage dealer or second stage dealer.

Rule 11(1) of Central Excise Rules are applicable for removal of goods from the factory. As per rule 11(2) of Central Excise Rules, the invoice is required to contain various details like, range, classification, time and date of removal, mode of transport and registration number, rate of duty etc.

Thus the rule expected that goods should be dispatched from the godown of the registered dealer (so that time and date of removal, mode of transport etc. can be indicated in the invoice).

Thus, a registered dealer was required to bring goods to his godown and then dispatch goods to his customer under his Cenvatable invoice.

This required double transport of goods, which increased transportation costs. Hence, as a facility to registered dealer, direct dispatch of goods has been permitted vide proviso to rule 11(2) of Central Excise Rules, w.e.f. 1-3-2015.

Thus, the proviso is applicable only to invoice issued by registered dealer, who is issuing invoice under rule 9(1)(iv) of Cenvat Credit Rules.

The new proviso only provides that Cenvat credit can be availed on basis of invoice of registered dealer even in case of transit sale. Of course, Cenvat credit can be availed on basis of invoice of original manufacturer also.

3.1 Providing additional facility does not mean that earlier facility withdrawn: In UOI v. Rajasthan Spg. & Wvg. Mills 2004 (174) ELT 42 (Raj.), it was held that merely providing an alternative method or additional method for availing Cenvat Credit does not take away the entitlement to avail Cenvat credit on the basis of original document evidencing payment of duty on inputs.

In this case, the issue was relating to eligibility of Cenvat credit on basis of endorsed invoice. However, the principle is fully applicable here.

Thus, proviso to rule 11(2) of Central Excise Rules is only additional method of availing Cenvat credit on basis of invoice of registered dealer, in case of transit sale.

Conclusion

4. On the basis of aforesaid case law and statutory, it can be concluded as follows.

Eligibility of Transit sale – In case of transit sale, the Cenvat credit can be availed on basis of invoice of original manufacturer, which is eligible document under rule 9(1)(a)(i)(I) of Cenvat Credit Rules. That rule does not require that invoice should be in name of the end user.This has been confirmed in the CBE&C circulars issued in 1995 and 1996. These circulars are not statutory provisions. The circulars only explain and confirm the legal provision. These are still valid as there is no change in that rule.

Intermediary dealer need not be registered - Since Cenvat credit is available on basis of invoice of manufacturer itself, the intermediary dealer is not required to issue any Cenvatable invoice. Hence, he need not be registered under Central Excise.

Invoice need not be in name of manufacturer – Tribunal has consistently held that invoice need not be in name of manufacturer, Even showing name of end user as consignee is not a statutory requirement. There is no such requirement of rule 9(1)(a)(i)(I) of Cenvat Credit Rules.

Proviso to rule 11(2) is only additional facility to registered dealer – The proviso to rule 11(2) of Central Excise Rules inserted w.e.f. 1-3-2015 is only additional facility to registered dealer. That rule is applicable only to registered dealers and not to unregistered dealers. The additional facility does not mean that the earlier provisions become invalid.

The proviso is added 'to increase ease of doing business' and not to create more hurdles in business.

If assessee intends to be safe, he may inform department accordingly, though there is no such legal requirement.

COMMENTS

10.1

Input Service Distributor

A manufacturer or service provider may have head office/regional office at different place/s. The services may be received at head office/regional office, but ultimately, these will be indirectly used for manufacture or providing output service.

Similarly, a principal manufacturer (brand name owner) may send inputs to job worker who is manufacturing goods under brand name of brand name owner. These goods will be supplied by job worker to principal manufacturer. If the goods are covered under MRP valuation provisions, duty will be payable by job worker on basis of MRP. However, many of input services received by principal manufacturer are indirectly used by the job worker.

Provision has been made to avail Cenvat credit of services received and paid for at head office/regional office. Such head office/regional office can be registered with Central Excise as 'Input Service Distributor' and it can issue invoice on the manufacturer or producer or service provider or outsourced manufacturing unit [The words in italics inserted w.e.f. 1-4-2016]

If assessee intends to use the facility, he has to apply for registration in form ST-1.

Provision for registration was introduced w.e.f. 7-6-2005. Hence, during 10-9-2004 to 7-6-2005, the HO could distribute credit even without registration - prima facie view in Hindustan Coca Cola Beverages v. CCE (2011) 32 STT 176 (Mag) = 266 ELT 347 (CESTAT).

In fact, in my view, registration and distribution of Cenvat credit are independent aspects. Even if registration was obtained later, Cenvat credit of prior period at HO/branches can be distributed, if otherwise eligible.

Who is 'input service distributor' - As per rule 2(m) of Cenvat Credit Rules, "input service distributor" means (a) an office managing the business of manufacturer or producer of final products or provider of output service, (b) which receives invoices issued under rule 4A of the Service Tax Rules, 1994 towards purchases of input services (c) issues invoice, bill or, as the case may be, challan for the purposes of distributing the credit of service tax paid on the said services to such manufacturer or producer or provider or an outsourced manufacturing unit, as the case may be. [The words in italics inserted w.e.f. 1-4-2016].

An office of assessee (manufacturer or service provider) is 'Input Service Distributor' if it satisfies all the three aforesaid requirements. It is not that each and every office of assessee is 'Input Service Distributor' and must register. The office should be registered as 'Input Service Distributor' only if it wants to distribute. There is no law that 'distribution' is the only way of availing Cenvat credit of services received at office of assessee. There are various documents eligible for availing Cenvat credit. Invoice/challan issued by 'Input Service Distributor' is only one of the specified document.

In Jaypee Rewa Plant v. CCE (2007) 218 ELT 576 (CESTAT SMB), regional marketing office was registered as Input Service Distributor and credit was distributed to manufacturing units. In prima facie view, the distribution was held as correct.

Outsourced manufacturing unit - 'Outsourced manufacturing unit' means a job-worker who is liable to pay duty on the value determined under rule 10A of the Central Excise Valuation (Determination of Price of Excisable Goods) Rules, 2000 on the goods manufactured for the input service distributor or a manufacturer who manufactures goods, for the input service distributor under a contract, bearing the brand name of such input service distributor and is liable to pay duty on the value determined under section 4A of the Excise Act. [Explanation 4 to rule 7 of Cenvat Credit Rules inserted w.e.f. 1-4-2016]

Document eligible for Cenvat credit - As per rule 9(1)(g); 'invoice, bill or challan' issued by an 'input service distributor' under rule 4A of Service Tax Credit Rules is an eligible document for purpose of taking Cenvat credit.

In Shriram Pistons v. CCE (2012) 281 ELT 90 (CESTAT), it was held that Cenvat credit is allowable on the basis of letter issued by Head Office (as Input Service Distributor) even if not mentioned as invoice or challan, if it contains all required details.

The Collector of CE, Indore after issuing a show cause notice and hearing the appellants, held that appellants had wrongly availed of the Modvat credit at Mandideep by deliberately suppressing the fact by not making a proper declaration of use of inputs in as much as "7ADCA" was never declared as an input. According to the Collector, in the absence of such a declaration they were not entitled to Modvat credit which could have been availed of by the Ankleshwar factory which received the declared raw materials. Direct dispatch of goods by manufacturer i.e. transit sale

In certain cases, direct dispatch of goods without bringing in the premises of dealer is permitted.

Direct despatch from manufacturer to final buyer, but sale is through dealer i.e. Transit sale - If whole consignment is despatched to buyer from manufacturer, Cenvat will be permissible, if name of the final buyer is shown as consignee. (Invoice will be in name of dealer). The consignee can avail Cenvat on the basis of duplicate copy of manufacturer issued under rule 11 (that time rule 52A). In such cases, the goods need not be brought to the premises of registered person. Invoice of Registered person (dealer) is not required for availing Cenvat by the consignee -CBE&C Circular No. 96/7/95-CX dated 13-2-1995.

This was also held permissible in CCE v. SSPE Cotton 1999 (106) ELT 102 (CEGAT), SWILL Ltd. v. CCE (2008) 232 ELT 802 (CESTAT SMB), CCE v. REC Ispat (2009) 240 ELT 101 (CESTAT).

In Century Dyeing v. CCE (2012) 35 STT 196 = 19 taxmann.com 281 (CESTAT SMB), it was held that Cenvat credit can be taken on basis of endorsed invoices (by dealers) even if name of manufacturer was not shown as consignee on the invoice, as name of consignee is not one of the essential requirements of rule 9(2) of Cenvat Credit Rules.

It has been clarified that in case of direct despatch from manufacturer to the end user, the indenting dealer need not be registered with Central Excise, even if his name and address is mentioned in the Invoice. Cenvat can be taken by the buyer on the basis of invoice of manufacturer - CBE&C Circular No. 218/52/96-CX dated 4-6-1996 [Similar instructions were given in earlier MF(DR) Circular No. 207/11/96-CX dated 1-5-1996 and 137/48/95-CX dated 18-7-1995.] - same view in Stadmed P Ltd. v. CCE 1998(102) ELT 466 (CEGAT) * Dr. Curies Labs Ltd. v. CCE 1999(112) ELT 539 (CEGAT) * CCE v. Transformers and Rectifiers (2012) 281 ELT 670 (Guj HC DB).

In CCE v. Balaji Iron (2009) 236 ELT 595 (CESTAT), original manufacturer has consigned goods to unregistered dealer who had consigned the same to the registered dealer. It was held that in such case, the dealer whose name is shown as consignee is 'first stage dealer'. He can take credit and issue Dealer's invoice on the basis of invoice issued by manufacturer (where his name was shown as 'consignee').

Dealer (registered person) should not issue Cenvatable Invoice for transit sales. Such invoices can be issued only when goods are physically received in the godown of dealer. Dealer can issue Non-Cenvatable invoice in case of transit sales. They should maintain different series of Invoice Book for this purpose. Such Invoice should not contain the details which are required for Cenvatable Invoice of dealer. - Pune Commissionerate TN No. 76/95 dated 20-7-1995.

In UOI v. Rajasthan Spinning & Weaving Mills 2004 (174) ELT 42 (Raj HC DB), it was held that credit can be taken on basis of endorsed invoice. Input Service Distributor

22.6 A manufacturer or service provider may have head office/regional office at different place/s. The services may be received at head office/regional office, but ultimately, these will be indirectly used for manufacture or providing output service.

Similarly, a principal manufacturer (brand name owner) may send inputs to job worker who is manufacturing goods under brand name of brand name owner. These goods will be supplied by job worker to principal manufacturer. If the goods are covered under MRP valuation provisions, duty will be payable by job worker on basis of MRP. However, many of input services received by principal manufacturer are indirectly used by the job worker.

Provision has been made to avail Cenvat credit of services received and paid for at head office/regional office. Such head office/regional office can be registered with Central Excise as 'Input Service Distributor' and it can issue invoice on the manufacturer or producer or service provider or outsourced manufacturing unit [The words in italics inserted w.e.f. 1-4-2016]

Who is 'input service distributor' - As per rule 2(m) of Cenvat Credit Rules, "input service distributor" means (a) an office managing the business of manufacturer or producer of final products or provider of output service, (b) which receives invoices issued under rule 4A of the Service Tax Rules, 1994 towards purchases of input services (c) issues invoice, bill or, as the case may be, challan for the purposes of distributing the credit of service tax paid on the said services to such manufacturer or producer or provider or an outsourced manufacturing unit, as the case may be. [The words in italics inserted w.e.f. 1-4-2016].

An office of assessee (manufacturer or service provider) is 'Input Service Distributor' if it satisfies all the three aforesaid requirements. It is not that each and every office of assessee is 'Input Service Distributor' and must register. The office should be registered as 'Input Service Distributor' only if it wants to distribute. There is no law that 'distribution' is the only way of availing Cenvat credit of services received at office of assessee. There are various documents eligible for availing Cenvat credit. Invoice/challan issued by 'Input Service Distributor' is only one of the specified document.

In Jaypee Rewa Plant v. CCE (2007) 218 ELT 576 (CESTAT SMB), regional marketing office was registered as Input Service Distributor and credit was distributed to manufacturing units. In prima facie view, the distribution was held as correct.

Outsourced manufacturing unit - 'Outsourced manufacturing unit' means a job-worker who is liable to pay duty on the value determined under rule 10A of the Central Excise Valuation (Determination of Price of Excisable Goods) Rules, 2000 on the goods manufactured for the input service distributor or a manufacturer who manufactures goods, for the input service distributor under a contract, bearing the brand name of such input service distributor and is liable to pay duty on the value determined under section 4A of the Excise Act. [Explanation 4 to rule 7 of Cenvat Credit Rules inserted w.e.f. 1-4-2016]

Document eligible for Cenvat credit - As per rule 9(1)(g); 'invoice, bill or challan' issued by an 'input service distributor' under rule 4A of Service Tax Credit Rules is an eligible document for purpose of taking Cenvat credit.

In Shriram Pistons v. CCE (2012) 281 ELT 90 (CESTAT), it was held that Cenvat credit is allowable on the basis of letter issued by Head Office (as Input Service Distributor) even if not mentioned as invoice or challan, if it contains all required details.

Distribution of credit even if invoices prior to registration as ISD - There is no bar in rule 7 of Cenvat Credit Rules for distributing of credit of invoices prior to date of registration as Input Service Distributor - Beico Industries v. Dashion Ltd. (2016) 54 GST 32 = 66 taxmann.com 31 (Guj HC DB).

It should also be noted that there is no correlation of the raw material and the final product, that is to say, it is not as if credit can be taken only on a final product, that is, manufactured out of the particular raw material to which the credit is related. That being so ultimate clearance of goods at nil rate due to contingency existing at the time of removal does not affect the entitlement that legally arises long before that date.

Storage of inputs outside the factory

21.2-2 Inputs should be stored within the factory. However, if manufacturer is unable to store the inputs inside the factory for want of space, hazardous nature of goods etc., he can store the inputs outside the premises. The storage point will be treated as extension of the factory. Permission from Assistant / Deputy Commissioner is necessary. [Rule 8 of Cenvat Credit Rules].

Supervision charges or MOT (Merchant Overtime Charges) are not required to be collected from assessee for storage of finished goods outside the factory. However, any other condition to safeguard revenue may be imposed by Jurisdictional Commissioner before granting permission for storage of non-duty paid goods. - CBE&C circular No. 709/25/2003-CX dated 23-4-2003. [Instructions in case of storage of finished goods, but principle will apply to storage of inputs outside the factory also].

As per Pune Commissionerate TN No. 67/96 dated June 96, a register in prescribed form has to be maintained at the godown as well as factory. Inputs from outside godown should move under challan in prescribed form. As per Chandigarh-II Commissionerate TN 13/97-CE dated 17-11-1997, intimation in D-3 form is necessary within 24 hours of receipt of each consignment. Monthly stock statement should be submitted to Range Office. Cenvat credit can be taken only when entire inputs covered by an invoice are received in the factory - similar procedure in CCE, Ahmedabad II TN 93/2004 [179 ELT T15].

No assessee would like to store goods outside factory except under compelling circumstances as storage outside is open to many vagaries of nature including theft, pilferage etc. Hence, shortage of space outside factory is an exceptional circumstance, and application for storage of goods outside factory should be considered, as per guidelines of CBE&C vide circular No. 206/40/96-CE dated 1-5-1996 - Anutone Accoustics v. CCE (2010) 250 ELT 590 (CESTAT).

Even if permission is not obtained, confiscation is not sustainable if there was no mala fide, but penalty for technical breach of law without intent to evade duty is sustainable - Sanchit Polymers v. CCE (2009) 241 ELT 240 (CESTAT SMB).

In Priyadarshini Polysacks v. CCE (2014) 307 ELT 136 (CESTAT), it was held that Cenvat credit is available even if permission was not obtained for taking out inputs outside the factory.

If permission is refused, appeal can be filed, as it is adjudication order - GKN Sinter Metals v. CCE (2015) 324 ELT 153 (CESTAT).

HEADNOTE: Rule 9, read with Rules 2(a), 3 and 4 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004, Rule 4A and Rule 4B of the Service Tax Rules, 1994 and Rule 11 of the Central Excise Rules, 2002 - Cenvat Credit - Documents on which credit may be taken - Assessee was manufacturing dutiable products under lease agreement with DSM - DSM had provided capital goods to assessee and said capital goods were installed and used by assessee - Assessee took credit of duty paid on capital goods on basis of supplier's invoice, which was in name of DSM and was endorsed by DSM to effect that 'goods covered under these invoices are transferred to assessee in view of lease agreement' - Department denied credit on ground that Endorsed invoices which are in name of DSM Sugars cannot be held to be proper Cenvatable document - HELD : Since there was no dispute that said capital goods were : (a) received by assessee, (b) duly installed in their factory and (c) used for manufacture of final product cleared by assessee, revenue's objection that such CENVAT credit is not available on basis of endorsed invoices cannot be upheld - Since this was not a case of 'sale' by one manufacturer to another and was a case of lessor buying and supplying capital goods to assessee-lessee's factory, certificate by lessor DSM as endorsement on invoice would be sufficient to take credit [Para 4] [In favour of assessee]Cenvat Credit : Where lessee is manufacturing goods under lease agreement with lessor and lessor supplies capital goods to lessee, lessee may take credit on basis of supplier's invoice in name of lessor but endorsed by lessor in favour of lesse.

FACT: Facts

The assessee is engaged in the manufacture of mould steel ingots and runners and risers under an agreement entered into by them with DSM Sugar Asmoli.

Under the said lease agreement dated 26-09-2002, the facility of land and machinery stands provided by DSM Sugar, Asmoli and the capital goods were received by them are required to be installed by the assessee and the duty on the final product required to be paid by the assessee.

DSM Sugars, Asmoli had endorsed the said invoices indicating as "certified that the goods covered under these invoices transferred to Kailash Steel, Asmoli in view of lease agreement dated 20-09-2002".

The Department denied CENVAT credit to the assessee on the ground that the invoices issued by the supplier are in the name of DSM Sugars, Asmoli, though there is no dispute that the said capital goods were received by the assessee and were duly erected and installed in their premises and were used for the manufacture of dutiable and excisable goods.

Revenue's Arguments

Endorsed invoices which are in the name of DSM Sugars cannot be held to be proper Cenvatable document so as to allow the CENVAT credit in respect of the same, to the assessee.

Assessee's Arguments

Even though DSM Sugars are the owners of the capital goods in question, there is no sale purchase of the capital goods and the same only stands transferred to their unit under the lease agreement, in which case, the effect of endorsement would not be of much relevance.

HELD: In as much as there is no dispute that the said capital goods stand received by the assessees and further duly installed in their factory and were being used for the manufacture of the final product, which was being cleared by the assessee, the revenue's objection that such CENVAT credit is not available in as much as the same was taken on the basis of the endorsed invoices cannot be upheld.

Admittedly, this is not a case of sale of capital goods from one manufacturer unit to another. It is a case where the capital goods are bought by the lessor and transferred to the lessee's factory, under lease agreement for further manufacture of the final product. As such, the certificate given by DSM Sugars, Asmoli on the invoices indicating that are being transferred and in the absence of any dispute to the factual aspect, the assessee is entitled to the CENVAT credit involved in the present appeal. Removal of obsolete inputs is removal 'as such' - Removal of obsolete inputs is removal 'as such' and entire Cenvat credit is required to be reversed. Mere paying excise duty on scrap price is not sufficient - Panasonic AVC Networks India Co. Ltd. v. CCE (2014) 301 ELT 624 (CESTAT SMB).

Recovery if the 'amount' not paid - If the 'amount' payable under rule 3(5), 3(5A) or 3(5B) of Cenvat Credit Rules is not paid, the same can be recovered in the manner provided in rule 14 of Cenvat Credit Rules, as if it is recovery of Cenvat credit wrongly taken - Explanation to rule 3(5B) of Cenvat Credit Rules, inserted w.e.f. 1-3-2013.

4.2-2 Storage of inputs outside the factory

Inputs should be stored within the factory. However, if manufacturer is unable to store the inputs inside the factory for want of space, hazardous nature of goods etc., he can store the inputs outside the premises. The storage point will be treated as extension of the factory. Permission from Assistant/Deputy Commissioner is necessary. [Rule 8 of Cenvat Credit Rules].

Supervision charges or MOT (Merchant Overtime Charges) are not required to be collected from assessee for storage of finished goods outside the factory. However, any other condition to safeguard revenue may be imposed by Jurisdictional Commissioner before granting permission for storage of non-duty paid goods. - CBE&C Circular No. 709/25/2003-CX dated 23-4-2003. [Instructions in case of storage of finished goods, but principle will apply to storage of inputs outside the factory also].

As per Pune Commissionerate TN No. 67/96 dated June 96, a register in prescribed form has to be maintained at the godown as well as factory. Inputs from outside godown should move under challan in prescribed form. As per Chandigarh-II Commissionerate TN No. 13/97-CE dated 17-11-1997, intimation in D-3 form is necessary within 24 hours of receipt of each consignment. Monthly stock statement should be submitted to Range Office. Cenvat credit can be taken only when entire inputs covered by an invoice are received in the factory - similar procedure in CCE, Ahmedabad II TN No. 93/2004 [179 ELT T15].

See Appendix for text of circular issued by CCE, Ahmedabad.

No assessee would like to store goods outside factory except under compelling circumstances as storage outside is open to many vagaries of nature including theft, pilferage etc. Hence, shortage of space outside factory is an exceptional circumstance, and application for storage of goods outside factory should be considered, as per guidelines of CBE&C vide Circular No. 206/40/96-CE dated 1-5-1996 - Anutone Accoustics v. CCE (2010) 250 ELT 590 (CESTAT).

Even if permission is not obtained, confiscation is not sustainable if there was no mala fide, but penalty for technical breach of law without intent to evade duty is sustainable - Sanchit Polymers v. CCE (2009) 241 ELT 240 (CESTAT SMB).

In British Biologicals v. CCE (2011) 266 ELT 217 (CESTAT), inputs were stored outside in rented premises without even reversing Cenvat credit. It was held that no demand is sustainable as situation similar to sending inputs to job worker.

In Priyadarshini Polysacks v. CCE (2014) 307 ELT 136 (CESTAT), it was held that Cenvat credit is available even if permission was not obtained for taking out inputs outside the factory.

If permission is refused, appeal can be filed, as it is adjudication order - GKN Sinter Metals v. CCE (2015) 324 ELT 153 (CESTAT).

4.2-3 Input Credit Distributor

Often invoices and bills in respect of inputs and capital goods are received at the head office while service is provided from some other place or site. In such case, the head office can distribute the credit of duty paid on such inputs and capital goods to the service provider by issuing an invoice. Such office will have to be registered with Central Excise and submit returns etc. similar to first stage dealer and second stage dealer [Rule 7A of Cenvat Credit Rules, inserted w.e.f. 1-4-2008].

4.2-3A Distribution of credit by warehouse of manufacturer

A manufacturer may have central warehouse from which he may be distributing inputs to his various factories.

40.4

Input Service Distributor

A manufacturer or service provider may have head office/regional office at different place/s. The services may be received at head office/regional office, but ultimately, these will be indirectly used for manufacture or providing output service.

Similarly, a principal manufacturer (brand name owner) may send inputs to job worker who is manufacturing goods under brand name of brand name owner. These goods will be supplied by job worker to principal manufacturer. If the goods are covered under MRP valuation provisions, duty will be payable by job worker on basis of MRP. However, many of input services received by principal manufacturer are indirectly used by the job worker.

Provision has been made to avail Cenvat credit of services received and paid for at head office/regional office. Such head office/regional office can be registered with Central Excise as 'Input Service Distributor' and it can issue invoice on the manufacturer or producer or service provider or outsourced manufacturing unit [The words in italics inserted w.e.f. 1-4-2016]

If assessee intends to use the facility, he has to apply for registration in form ST-1.

In my view, registration and distribution of Cenvat credit are independent aspects. Even if registration was obtained later, Cenvat credit of prior period at HO/branches can be distributed, if otherwise eligible.

Who is 'input service distributor' - As per rule 2(m) of Cenvat Credit Rules, "input service distributor" means (a) an office managing the business of manufacturer or producer of final products or provider of output service, (b) which receives invoices issued under rule 4A of the Service Tax Rules, 1994 towards purchases of input services (c) issues invoice, bill or, as the case may be, challan for the purposes of distributing the credit of service tax paid on the said services to such manufacturer or producer or provider or an outsourced manufacturing unit, as the case may be. [The words in italics inserted w.e.f. 1-4-2016].

An office of assessee (manufacturer or service provider) is 'Input Service Distributor' if it satisfies all the three aforesaid requirements. It is not that each and every office of assessee is 'Input Service Distributor' and must register. The office should be registered as 'Input Service Distributor' only if it wants to distribute. There is no law that 'distribution' is the only way of availing Cenvat credit of services received at office of assessee. There are various documents eligible for availing Cenvat credit. Invoice/challan issued by 'Input Service Distributor' is only one of the specified document.

Outsourced manufacturing unit - ' Outsourced manufacturing unit' means a job-worker who is liable to pay duty on the value determined under rule 10A of the Central Excise Valuation (Determination of Price of Excisable Goods) Rules, 2000 on the goods manufactured for the input service distributor or a manufacturer who manufactures goods, for the input service distributor under a contract, bearing the brand name of such input service distributor and is liable to pay duty on the value determined under section 4A of the Excise Act. [Explanation 4 to rule 7 of Cenvat Credit Rules inserted w.e.f. 1-4-2016]

Document eligible for Cenvat credit - As per rule 9(1)(g); 'invoice, bill or challan' issued by an 'input service distributor' under rule 4A of Service Tax Credit Rules is an eligible document for purpose of taking Cenvat credit.

In Shriram Pistons v. CCE (2012) 281 ELT 90 (CESTAT), it was held that Cenvat credit is allowable on the basis of letter issued by Head Office (as Input Service Distributor) even if not mentioned as invoice or challan, if it contains all required details.

Distribution of credit even if invoices prior to registration as ISD - There is no bar in rule 7 of Cenvat Credit Rules for distributing of credit of invoices prior to date of registration as Input Service Distributor - Beico Industries v. CCE (2012) 286 ELT 689 (CESTAT SMB) * Dagger Forst Tools v. CCE (2013) 42 GST 225 = 32 taxmann.com 353 (CESTAT) * Bhansali Engg v. CCE (2015) 49 GST 697 = 53 taxmann.com 448 (CESTAT).

3) 288 ELT 291 (CESTAT), it was held that since assessee could distribute Cenvat Credit in any ratio upto 31-3-2012, the HO could distribute credit to its unit without registration as Input Service Distributor.

In WNS Global Services v. CCE (2013) 30 taxmann.com 208 (CESTAT), it was held that Cenvat credit is allowable even if assessee was not registered as Input Service Distributor. Assessee having more than one factory or place of provision of service - If assessee has more than one factories or registered places of provision of service, the Cenvat credit of HO and branches can be availed in factories/registered places of service provider only if the HO/branch is registered as Input Service distributor. Thus, distribution is mandatory w.e.f. 1-4-2012.

Assessee having Centralised registration for service tax - Assessee having Centralised registration for service tax (and either having no manufacturing unit or having manufacturing unit only at the place where assessee has centralized registration for service tax) can avail entire Cenvat Credit of input services at one place. In my view, in such cases, distribution of Cenvat credit is not required, as he has centralized accounting.

In case of Centralised registration, the Cenvat credit is also centralised and that credit can be utilised by any of taxable output services - ratio of B E Billimoria & Co. Ltd. v. CST (2013) 39 STT 315 = 29 taxmann.com 271 (CESTAT).

Distribution of credit without registration - In Doshion Ltd. v. CCE (2013) 288 ELT 291 (CESTAT), it was held that since assessee could distribute Cenvat Credit in any ratio upto 31-3-2012, the HO could distribute credit to its unit without registration as Input Service Distributor [In my view, the principle will be valid even after 1-4-2012, if assessee has only one factory].

In WNS Global Services v. CCE (2013) 30 taxmann.com 208 (CESTAT), it was held that Cenvat credit is allowable even if assessee was not registered as Input Service Distributor.

In a contrary view, in Khaitan Electricals v. CCE (2011) 32 STT 234 (Mag) = 12 taxmann.com 338 (CESTAT SMB), it was held that manufacturing unit cannot avail Cenvat credit of services availed at depot if depot is not registered as Input Service Distributor.

Cenvat credit available even if a particular unit was not included in Centralised Registration - In Tech Mahindra Ltd. v. CCE (2013) 39 STT 785 = 33 taxmann.com 354 (CESTAT), it was held that even if a unit was not registered under centralised registration, the Cenvat credit is available of input services received by such unit.

Position till 31-3-2012 - Till 31-3-2012, in my view, the main factory could directly take Cenvat credit of service tax on the basis of documents, even if there were more than one factories or places of provision of service of the assessee.

Till 31-3-2012, law did not even specify that there must be distribution of Cenvat credit or that the distribution should be in some specified ratio. If no 'distribution' is necessary, there should not be any need of 'Input Service Distributor'.

10.1-2 Invoice for distribution of credit by input service distributor

The 'input service distributor' should issue a 'Invoice, Bill or Challan' on monthly basis after consolidating the service tax paid on services received during the month.

Requirements of Invoice, Bill or Challan - As per rule 4A(2) of Service Tax Rules, requirements of the Invoice, Bill or Challan of input service distributor are as follows :

It shall be signed by authorised person.

The document should be for each recipient of the credit distributed.

Document should be serially numbered.

The invoice should contain following details :

(i)

Name, address and registration number of the person providing input services and Serial Number and date of invoice, Bill or challan issued by service provider under rule 4A(1)

(ii)

Name and address of input service distributor

(iii)

Name and address of the recipient of the credit distributed

(iv)

Amount of credit distributed

Thus, details of all invoices of input services are required to be given, which is going to be very cumbersome for large offices and will be administratively difficult.

For example, a company with HO at Nariman Point, Mumbai has factories at Pune and Chennai and has a premise providing services at Delhi. If the turnover ratio of the three units in 40:35:25, it will have to distribute Cenvat credit of service tax on input services in the ratio of 40:35:25, by preparing three invoices every month. In each invoice, details of all input invoices and ratio to which tax on input services have been allocated to each unit should be given.

The view seems correct for the following reasons.

The words used in rule 4A(1) of Service Tax Rules are 'invoice, challan or Bill'. Rule 11 of Central Excise Rules specified the document as 'Invoice'. This indicates that in case of service tax, specific nomenclature is not essential.

In fact, first and second proviso to rule 4A(1) uses the term 'any document, by whatever name called'. Thus, rules do envisage flexibility in nomenclature depending on trade and business practices. Different practices are followed in different trades. Nomenclature can vary from trade to trade or business to business.

As per rule 5(1) of Service Tax Rules, the records maintained by assessee including computerised data maintained by assessee in accordance with various other laws are acceptable. Thus, private documents maintained in normal course of business are acceptable. No special records or registers or change in business practices is envisaged. This also indicates that law does not envisage that trade should change its normal business practices.

5.1 Rule of harmonious construction - In Jagdish Singh v. Lt. Governor [1997] AIR SCW 2106 = AIR 1997 SC 2239, it was observed -

"It is a cardinal principle of construction that efforts should be made in construing the different provisions, so that, each provision will have its play and in the event of any conflict a harmonious construction should be given. Further, a statute or a rule made thereunder should be read as a whole and one provision should be construed with reference to the other provision so as to make the rule consistent and any construction which would bring any inconsistency or repugnancy between one provision and the other should be avoided. One rule cannot be used to defeat another rule in the same Rules, unless it is impossible to effect harmonisation between them. - - A construction that reduces one of the provisions to a ‘dead letter’ is not a harmonious construction as one part is being destroyed and consequently, Court should avoid such construction". - similar views in British Airways Plc.v. 7. In CCE v. Sai Ram Industries 2010 (255) ELT 256 (Trib. - Delhi), the goods had been manufactured by Swastika Pipes Ltd., Rohtak who had sold goods to Rameswar Das Devi Dayal, Faridabad. The invoice issued by Swastika Pipes Limited mentioned that the goods were sold to Rameswar Das Devi Dayal, though the same were consigned to Gautam Steel Trader.

As per the definition of ‘First stage dealer’ given in rule 2(ii) of Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004, the ‘First stage dealer’ means the dealer who purchases the goods directly from the manufacturer or from the depots of the manufacturers or the premises of consignment agent of the said manufacturer or from any premises from where the goods are sold by or on behalf of the said manufacturer or from an importer or from the premises of consignment agent of such importer. In this case, Gautam Steel Trader had not purchased the goods directly from the manufacturer but had purchased the same from Rameswar Das Devi Dayal and the manufacturer’s invoice mentioned Rameswar Das Devi Dayal as the buyer, and, thus, Gautam Steel Trader cannot be called ‘First stage dealer’ within the meaning defined in rule 2(ii) of CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004.

Since Golden Steel Co. had purchased the goods from Gautam Steel Trader and Gautam Steel Trader was not ‘First stage dealer’, Golden Steel Co. would not be covered by the definition of ‘Second stage dealer’ as the term ‘Second stage dealer’ as defined in rule 2(s) of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 means a dealer who purchases goods from the first stage dealer.

In view of this, the invoice issued by Golden Steel Co. cannot be said to be a valid duty paying document for taking credit in terms of rule 9. Therefore, the Commissioner of Central Excise (Appeals)’s order permitting CENVAT credit on the basis of this invoice was not correct.

The High Court held that even as a matter of first principle on a plain and literal construction of rule 3(1) the Tribunal was not justified in holding that Deepak Fertilisers was not entitled to avail of the CENVAT credit in respect of services utilized in relation to ammonia storage tanks on the ground that they were situated outside the factory premises. The High Court further observed that rule 2(l) initially provides that input service means any services of the description falling in sub-clauses (i) and (ii). Rule 2(l) then provides an inclusive definition by enumerating certain specified services. Among those services were services pertained to the procurement of inputs and inward transportation of inputs. The first part of rule 2(l), inter alia , covers any services used by the manufacturer directly or indirectly, in or in relation to the manufacture of final products. The inclusive part of the definition enumerates certain specified categories of services. Whereas rule 3(1) allows a manufacturer of final products to take credit of excise duty and service tax among others paid on any input or capital goods received in the factory of manufacture of the final product, insofar as any input service is concerned, the only stipulation is that it received the final product. This was needed to be read with the broad and comprehensive meaning of the expression 'input service' in rule 2(l).

The Court finally held that the input services in this case were used by Deepak Fertilisers, whether directly or indirectly, in or in relation to the manufacture of the final products and the storage and use of Ammonia was an intrinsic part of that process.

Background

1. In industries like pharmaceuticals and agro-chemicals many times near-about expired goods, defective goods or damaged goods (for the sake of convenience let us say "defective goods") are sent again by various marketing depots (not registered under excise) for reprocessing. Usually it happens that the original goods have been manufactured by let us say factory A, B and C but the defective goods are returned to only one factory, let us say factory D for reprocessing. This is so because it will be impractical to send the defective goods for reprocessing to the very same factory which had manufactured the original goods due to logistical costs as well as difficulties in identifying them on one-to-one basis.

In such scenario, only document available will be copy of excise invoice issued by the original factory. Had the defective goods been returned to the same factory, manufacturer could have easily claimed CENVAT credit on the basis of originally issued invoice (as the excise invoice was issued by the same factory). However, here the case is different. Factory D wants to claim CENVAT credit of returned defective goods on the basis of excise invoice issued by other factories.

Critical Issues

2. Following critical issues arise in this set-up:

2.1 Whether CENVAT credit can be claimed by factory D when the invoices on the basis of which credit will be claimed has been issued by factory A, B and C ?

2.2 W.e.f. 11-07-2014, third proviso has been added to rule 4(1) of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004 which provides that credit cannot be claimed after a period of six months from the date of issuance of any document (in our case excise invoice) on the basis of which credit is claimed. In our case, as we are dealing with near-expired or defective goods, in all likelihood excise invoice issued by original manufacturer would have been dated beyond statutory period of six months. Issue is whether the third proviso will apply to the present case ?

2.3 What are the procedures one needs to follow to claim the said credit ?

3. Legal Analysis

3.1 To answer the first question, i.e., whether factory D can avail CENVAT credit on the basis of invoices issued by factory A, B and C for defective goods which are received back, one has to refer to rule 16 of the Central Excise Rules, 2002. Relevant extract is reproduced below for ready reference:

"Rule 16. Credit of duty on goods brought to the factory.—(1) Where any goods on which duty had been paid at the time of removal thereof are brought to any factory for being re-made, refined, re-conditioned or for any other reason, the assessee shall state the particulars of such receipt in his records and shall be entitled to take CENVAT credit of the duty paid as if such goods are received as inputs under the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2002 and utilize this credit according to the said rules.

(2) If the process to which the goods are subjected before being removed does not amount to manufacture, the manufacturer shall pay an amount equal to the CENVAT credit taken under sub-rule (1) and in any other case the manufacturer shall pay duty on goods received under sub-rule (1) at the rate applicable on the date of removal and on the value determined under sub-section (2) of section 3 or section 4 or section 4A of the Act, as the case may be.

[Explanation.—The amount paid under this sub-rule shall be allowed as CENVAT credit as if it was a duty paid by the manufacturer who removes the goods.]

3.2 Careful reading of above rule provides that CENVAT credit will be available of any goods on which duty has been paid and are brought to any factory for re-making, refining, re-conditioning or for any other reason as inputs. Thus, only condition to be fulfilled for claiming credit is that duty should have been paid on said goods. It is not necessary that goods should be received back in the same factory. It can be received in any factory. Further, goods can be brought back for reprocessing under rule 16 even if shelf life has expired (CCE v. Rako Agrochem (P.) Ltd. 2010 (260) ELT 479 (Trib. - Delhi)). Thus, credit can be claimed of goods received by factory D on the basis of invoices issued by original manufacturers. One may also refer to Board's Circular 607/44/2001-CX, dated 13-12-2001 which confirms the above view. Thus, CENVAT credit can be claimed on basis of manufacturers invoice available with depot to the extent of quantity received by factory D.

There is controversy raging in respect of eligibility of Cenvat credit in respect of transit sale through dealer not registered under Central Excise and also through dealer registered under Central Excise. The issues discussed in this article.

Background of the issue

1. Often the end user (manufacturer consumer) purchases goods through dealer and not through the original manufacturer. If the goods are purchased by dealer and then sold on piecemeal basis, there is provision to issue Cenvatable invoice by first stage dealer and second stage dealer.

However, when entire consignment is to be sold as it is, the dealer instruct the original manufacturer of excisable goods to dispatch the goods directly to the end used (consumer manufacturer). Invoice of Manufacturers invoice is in name of dealer as the buyer. Name and address of end user (manufacturer consumer) is shown as consignee.

The end user (consumer manufacturers) avail CENVAT credit on the basis of such invoice of original manufacturer.

This is standard practice, going on at least since 1995.

In the recent budget, a proviso has been added to rule 11(2) of Central Excise Rules w.e.f. 1-3-2015, which reads as follows - "Provided also that if the goods are directly sent to any person on the direction of the registered dealer, the invoice shall also contain the details of the registered dealer as the buyer and the person as the consignee, and that person shall take CENVAT credit on the basis of the registered dealer's invoice:"

1.1 Controversy arising out of this proviso: On the basis of this proviso inserted w.e.f. 1-3-2015, a view has been expressed that the Cenvat credit cannot be availed in case of transit sale, if the intermediate buyer is not registered under Central Excise.

A view is also expressed by some assessees that Cenvat credit cannot be availed on basis of invoice of original manufacturer, if sale is through registered dealer. The registered dealer has to issue another Cenvatable invoice.

In my view, there is no such change in rules. In case of transit sale, Cenvat credit can be availed on basis of invoice of original manufacturer, even if the intermediate buyer is not registered dealer. Even if intermediate buyer is registered dealer, he need not issue Cenvatable invoice as Cenvat credit can be availed on basis of invoice of original manufacturer.

Reasons for my view are stated below.

Statutory provisions

2. Rule 9(1) of Cenvat Credit Rules prescribes that Cenvat Credit can be taken on the basis of any of the documents prescribed in that sub-rule. The relevant extract from the rule are as follows –

Rule 9(1) Documents and accounts - The CENVAT credit shall be taken by the manufacturer or the provider of output service or input service distributor, as the case may be, on the basis of any of the following documents, namely:–

(a)

An invoice issued by -

(i)

a manufacturer for clearance of— (I) inputs or capital goods from his factory or depot or from the premises of the consignment agent of the said manufacturer or from any other premises from where the goods are sold by or on behalf of the said manufacturer (II) inputs or capital goods as such

(ii)

not relevant

(iii)

not relevant

(iv)

a first stage dealer or a second stage dealer, as the case may be, in terms of the provisions of Central Excise Rules, 2002.

2.1 Invoice of manufacturer is eligible document for Cenvat credit: It can be seen that invoice issued by manufacturer for clearance of inputs or capital goods from his factory is eligible document for availing Cenvat credit, as per rule 9(1)(a)(i)(I) of Cenvat Credit Rules.

The rule does not state that the invoice should be in name of buyer-manufacturer or consumer-manufacturer. The rule even does not state that name of end user (final consumer-manufacturer) should be shown in the invoice.

Of course, it has to be 'input' or 'capital goods' of the consumer-manufacturer.

2.2 Transit Sale through dealer not registered under Central Excise: In transit sale, goods are despatched directly from place of original manufacturer to final user manufacturer (end user) though invoice is in name of the intermediary dealer.

In that case, Cenvat credit is available on basis of invoice of manufacturer under rule 9(1)(a)(i)(I) of Cenvat Credit Rules itself.

The adjudicating authority confirmed the demand as proposed in show-cause notice and also imposed penalty under rule 15. The Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the order of the adjudicating authority.

The assessee was engaged in the manufacture of excisable goods and provision of output services.

Issue Involved

•

Whether the assessee was eligible for CENVAT Credit on input services ?

As per the position prevailing prior to 30-3-1994, when the purchaser resold inputs to third party, he would make an endorsement on the gate pass issued by the manufacturer of the input. Procedure had changed and instead of endorsement on the gate-passes, invoice was required to be produced as per Notification No. 16/94-CE(NT), dated 30-3-1994. Certain documents were prescribed for the purpose of giving credit of Modvat under the Rules. In Column No. 3 to the Entry No. 10 of the aforesaid Notification, prescribed documents were endorsed gate-passes/subsidiary gate-passes/certificates. Admittedly, gate-passes were required to be issued by the manufacturer under the procedure then prevailing and as and when the purchaser of the inputs resold inputs to third party, he would make an endorsement on the gate-pass, which would authorise the purchaser to take benefit of the credit of the duties paid on the goods. From the language of the said Notification, it is clear that benefit could be given if the documents would have been issued before 1-4-1994 and credit had been taken on or before 30-6-1994. From this, it was clear that gate-passes could be issued before 1-4-1994 and the benefit of credit could be taken on or before 30-6-1994. Transaction of sale or re-sale could take place any time prior to 30th June and on endorsement of same being made, benefit could be taken on or before 30-6-1994. The language of the Notification nowhere requires that the endorsement should also be made before 1-4-1994. [Para 1]

Therefore, gate-passes issued prior to 1-4-1994 but endorsed after that date would fall under the coverage of Entry No. 10 in the Table to the Notification No. 16/94-CE(NT), dated 30-3-1994 and would, consequently, be eligible documents for taking credit under the Modvat Scheme. [Para 3]

The issue involved is whether such registration and/or distribution is compulsory or optional. Who is Input Service Distributor ?

2. As per rule 2(m ) of CENVAT Credit Rules, an entity is ‘input service distributor’ if it satisfies the following three conditions—

"(a )office managing the business of manufacturer or producer of final products or provider of output service,

(b )which receives invoices issued under rule 4A of the Service Tax Rules, 1994 towards purchases of input services and

(c )issues invoice, bill or, as the case may be, challan for the purposes of distributing the credit of service tax paid on the said services to such manufacturer or producer or provider, as the case may be."

The word used is ‘and’. Thus, an entity is ‘input service distributor’ only if all the three conditions are satisfied. If an assessee has office or premises which receives invoices and it does not issue any invoice, bill or challan for distributing credit of service tax, it is not ‘Input Service Distributor’.

Service Tax (Registration of Special Category of Persons) Rules, 2005 issued vide Notification No. 27/2005-ST, dated 7-6-2005 provide for registration of ‘Input Service Distributor’. Rule 2(c) of these Rules states that ‘input service distributor’ shall have the meaning assigned to it in rule 2(m) of CENVAT Credit Rules.

It is, thus, clear that the Service tax (Registration of Special Category of Persons) Rules, 2005 apply when an entity falls within the definition of rule 2(m). If the office or main factory does not issue any invoice or challan for distribution of CENVAT credit, it does not fall within the definition of ‘Input Service Distributor’. In such case, the rules in respect of registration and issue of invoice by Input Service Distributor do not apply at all.

Provision is not a mandatory requirement

3. Rule 7 of the CENVAT Credit Rules uses the words ‘Input Service Distributor may distribute credit’. ‘May’ cannot be read as ‘must’.

Rule 9(1) of CENVAT Credit Rules gives list of seven types of documents eligible for availing CENVAT credit, out of which invoice of input service distributor is one of the eligible documents. Thus, the invoice of input service distributor is not the only eligible document for availing CENVAT credit. Credit can be availed on basis of other eligible documents also.

As discussed below, distribution can be in any ratio. Thus, even if main factory is registered as ‘Input Service distributor’ it can legally allocate entire CENVAT credit to itself, which would be an exercise in futility.

Facility cannot be a compulsion

4. ‘Input Service Distributor’ is a facility provided to assessee. It is nowhere stated that it is a mandatory requirement. This ‘facility’ cannot be thrust upon an unwilling assessee.

In CIT v. Mahendra Mills [2000] 243 ITR 56/109 Taxman 225 (SC), it was observed, ‘A privilege cannot be to a disadvantage and an option cannot become an obligation’.

Can CENVAT credit be denied in such cases

5. Even assuming for the sake of argument that registration as Input Service Distributor and distribution of credit is mandatory (though really it is not), non-registration and non-distribution may at the most lead to penalty for violation of rules. How can it lead to complete denial of CENVAT credit?

Is there any provision to deny CENVAT credit for violation of such a procedural provision?

The procedure set out in rule 57G is to ensure that the credit is taken on the basis of duty paid documents. The bill of entry is one such document set out in rule 57G. The said rule does not require that the bill of entry should be in the name of the person claiming credit of duty. It is not in dispute that the goods imported and cleared on payment of duty by one person can be used as inputs and credit of duty can be claimed by another person by establishing that the imported duty paid goods have been received as inputs and that the importer has not taken credit of that duty. In the instant case, it was established that the duty paid goods were received as inputs, however, the credit was denied on the ground that the Bill of entry was not endorsed in the name of the appellant. Rule 57G does not require that for taking credit of duty, the bill of entry should be endorsed in the name of the claimant. In the absence of any provision regarding endorsement on the bill of entry, the credit of duty cannot be denied on the ground that the bill of entry is not endorsed in the name of the claimant. In the facts of the instant case, the evidence on record i.e., the bills of entry together with the certificates issued by excise authorities, clearly showed that the goods imported and cleared under the bills of entry on payment of duty were received and utilized by the appellant as inputs in its factory and that the importer had not utilized the credit of duty paid on the said goods. Thus, the appellant had established that the inputs received under the bills of entry were duty paid and, therefore, the authorities below were not justified in denying the credit of duty to the appellant. CENVAT CREDIT

Input Service Distributor - Facility or compulsion

V.S. DATEY

Often, an assessee has office at a place different from the factory or place from which service is provided. Such small offices maintain only basic information. The accounting records including invoices, etc., are sent to main factory and final accounting and record-keeping is done in the main factory/office. Sometimes, office and main factory is at one place, but there are factories or places for provision of service in another places. In such cases, the input services received at main factory are recorded there itself and credit is availed in the main factory without ‘distributing’ to other factories or other places providing output services. It is learnt that in some cases, the department is taking a view that in such cases, registration as Input Service Distributor and distribution of credit is mandatory. This article examines the statutory provisions and concludes that Input Service Distributor is a facility, not a compulsion. Even ‘distribution’ of credit is a facility and not compulsion and the only requirement is that input service should be in relation to the business of the assessee.

Introduction

1. Often, an assessee has office at a place different from the factory or place from which service is provided. Such small offices maintain only basic information. The accounting records including invoices, etc., are sent to main factory and final accounting and record-keeping is done in the main factory/office.

Sometimes, office and main factory is at one place, but there are factories or places for provision of service in another places. 13. Increase in time-limit for availment of Cenvat credit from six months to one year

Till 10.07.2014, there was no restriction on availment of Cenvat credit. From 11.07.2014, the Cenvat credit can be taken only upto six months from the date of issue of document as contained in rule 9(1) of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004. From 01.03.2015, the time-limit for availment of Cenvat credit has been increased from six months to one year.

14. Credit on goods directly dispatched to job worker

As per rule 4(1) of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004, 'the CENVAT credit in respect of inputs may be taken immediately on receipt of the inputs in the factory of the manufacturer or in the premises of the provider of output service'.

In case where the goods are directly dispatched to the premises of job worker on the direction of the manufacturer or the provider of output service, credit can be taken only when the said goods are received in the factory of the manufacturer or in the premises of the provider of output service. This was the interpretation done by the department and various Courts.

In order to streamline the said provision, rule 4(1) of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 w.e.f 01.03.2015 states that the CENVAT credit in respect of inputs may be taken immediately on receipt of the inputs in the factory of the manufacturer or in the premises of the provider of output service or in the premises of the job worker, in case goods are sent directly to the job worker on the direction of the manufacturer or the provider of output service, as the case may be;

Similarly, w.e.f 01.03.2015, with respect of capital goods, rule 4(2)(a) now states that the CENVAT credit in respect of capital goods received in a factory or in the premises of the provider of output service or outside the factory of the manufacturer of the final products for generation of electricity for captive use within the factory or in the premises of the job worker, in case capital goods are sent directly to the job worker on the direction of the manufacturer or the provider of output service, as the case may be at any point of time in a given financial year shall be taken only for an amount not exceeding fifty per cent of the duty paid on such capital goods in the same financial year.

2. Inclusive definition clause of rule 2(l) extends scope of ‘input services’ even beyond stage of ‘manufacture’ or ‘provision of service’. The inclusive clause makes it clear that services much earlier to manufacture or provision of service or even after manufacture and after provision of provision of service will be eligible for service tax credit.

Services which do not have even any casual relation with manufacture of goods or provision of service have been covered by the definition of ‘input service’. In fact, any service in relation to business of assessee is ‘input service’.

Thus, though the words used in rule 2(l)(ii) are ‘used by the manufacturer, whether directly or indirectly, in or in relation to the manufacture of final products and clearance of final products from the place of removal’, in view of the word ‘includes’, the scope of definition is much wider than ‘in or in relation to manufacture’ and would cover even services unrelated to ‘manufacture’. This is also clear from the fact that service tax paid at Head Office and branches/depots can be utilised as Cenvat credit through the mechanism of ‘input service distributor’.
