The CBEC has also clarified this provision in Circular No. 97/8/2007-ST, dated 23-8-2007, in the following manner:

"8. CENVAT Credit

(c )ISSUE - Up to what stage a manufacturer/consignor can take credit on the service tax paid on goods transport by road?

COMMENTS - This issue has been examined in great details by the CESTAT in the case of Gujarat Ambuja Cements Ltd. v. CCE [2007] (6) STR 249/8 STT TRI-Delhi. In this case, CESTAT has made the following observations:—

"…The post sale transport of manufactured goods is not an input in manufacturer. The two clauses in the definition take care to circumscribe input credit by stating that service used in relation to the clearance from the place of removal and service used for outward transportation upto the place of removal are to be treated as input service. The first clause does not mention transport service in particular. The second clause restricts transport service credit upto the place of removal. When these two clauses are read together, it becomes clear that transport service credit cannot go beyond transport upto the place of removal. The two clauses, the one dealing with general provision and other dealing with a specific item, are not to be read disjunctively as to bring about conflict to defeat the laws’ scheme. The purpose of interpretation is to find harmony and reconciliation among the various provisions". (p. 127)

Similarly, in the case of Ultratech Cement Ltd. v. CCE [2007] 8 STT 152 (Ahd. - CESTAT), it was held that after the final products are cleared from the place of removal, there will be no scope of subsequent use of service to be treated as input. The above observations and views explain the scope of the relevant provisions clearly, correctly and in accordance with the legal provisions. In conclusion, a manufacturer/consignor can take credit on the service tax paid on outward transport of goods up to the place of removal and not beyond that.

The expression "reserves the right of disposal" as used in section 23(2) of the Sale of Goods Act, 1930 means "ownership", i.e., "right to sell/dispose". If the property in goods passes onto the buyer at the factory gate, i.e., seller no longer has the right to dispose of the goods as he likes, then credit is available only upto the factory gate.

However, if the seller retains the right to dispose of the goods till delivery, i.e., the property passed onto the buyer at buyer's premises (FOR sales) and the transit risk is of the seller, then the credit would be available upto the buyer's premises.

HEADNOTE: Rule 57G of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 - Modvat Credit - Gate pass endorsements--procedure cannot deny Mod vat so long as duty has been paid on the inputs. Three endorsements on original gate pass accepted

FACT: The appellants had taken Modvat credit for goods received against GP J, after it had been endorsed three times by different parties and a demand for Rs. 1,02,600.00 was confirmed. Their appeal was also rejected by the Collector (Appeals).

HELD: Modvat--cannot be denied in routine or by mechanical approach even if documentation is defective so long as duty has been paid on inputs, "... we are unable to appreciate the routine and mechanical approach of the authorities below in rejecting the claim of the Modvat credit only on the ground that more than one endorsement has been made. When the Board themselves have taken a decision to relax the procedural requirement by way of administrative instruction it should be the endeavour of the authorities to extend Modvat credit wherever the duty-paid nature of the goods is evident from the gate passes produced and quantum of duty paid on the inputs could be ascertained from them. A positive approach is called for in this regard."

2. Modvat--credit for goods received against GP I, after three endorsements by different parties can be allowed as long as duty-paid nature of the goods is established. "Rule 57G of the Central Excise Rules stipulates that inputs are to be received under the cover of a gate pass, an AR-I, a Bill of Entry or any other document as may be prescribed by the Board. ...However, when this requirement created some difficulties in the ease of Small Scale units to obtain the inputs through intermediaries, the Board appears to have made relaxation to this requirement by permitting one endorsement in the gate pass initially and subsequently based on the representations permitting upto two endorsements in the gate passes. This relaxation made by the Board appears to be purely of administrative nature based on considerations of implementing the Modvat scheme, so long as the duty-paid nature of the goods and duty paid thereon could be established. As seen from the Trade Notice cited by the learned advocate, it is evident that the Government is keen to extend the Modvat credit so long as the goods in factory packed condition as are covered by the gate passes are received by the parties intending to avail Modvat credit...... the department is entitled to make verification or investigation with regard to the genuineness of the gate pass and also on the question whether gate pass has been utilised for availment of Modvat credit at the earliest stages. In this case, no such enquiry appears to have been conducted and the Modvat credit has-been denied only on the ground that more than that of permitted endorsements have been made in the gate passes. Such an order cannot be sustainable in the context of the scheme of Modvat credit read along with the relaxation made by the Board. We, therefore, set aside the order passed by the authorities below and permit availment of credit and while doing so, we allow the liberty to the Assistant Collector to cause any inquiry or investigation to satisfy himself about the genuine nature of the gate passes and also about non-utilisation of the gate passes at the earlier stages of endorsements for availment of Modvat credit."

HEADNOTE: Rule 57 of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 - Cenvat Credit (Modvat) - Modvat - Raw material can be transferred to another unit which can get credit - Inputs need not be used directly as per settled law, as there is no requirement of direct use if inputs are fully utilised - CE Rule 57F(2)

FACT: The appellants have their factory at Mandideep in M.P. They have another factory at Ankleshwar in Gujarat. They manufacture Cephalexin and Cephadroxil falling under Chapter 29 of CETA. Penicillin GK is the main input for the final product, which the appellants import as also procure locally. With the approval of the Assistant Collector they sent Penicillin to Ankleshwar factory direct where the same was converted into "7ADCA", which was then received at the factory at Mandideep for manufacture of the final product. They had similar approval in respect of other raw materials used in the manufacture of "7ADCA" for being sent to the factory at Ankleshwar. They were availing of the Modvat credit in respect of all the raw materials at Mandideep when "7ADCA" along with other documents was received from Ankleshwar. The Collector of CE, Indore after issuing a show cause notice and hearing the appellants, held that appellants had wrongly availed of the Modvat credit at Mandideep by deliberately suppressing the fact by not making a proper declaration of use of inputs in as much as "7ADCA" was never declared as an input. According to the Collector, in the absence of such a declaration they were not entitled to Modvat credit which could have been availed of by the Ankleshwar factory which received the declared raw materials. He therefore disallowed Modvat credit of Rs. 79,38,597.50 and also imposed a penalty of Rs. 5 lakhs.

HELD: The appellants were legally entitled to send the raw material to Ankleshwar factory and to avail of Modvat credit when "7ADCA" was received at Mandideep factory. "Since the appellant had filed the declaration the appellant was legally entitled to send the raw materials to Ankleshwar factory and avail of the credit in respect of such raw materials when 7ADCA manufactured by the appellant at its Ankleshwar factory from such raw materials was received by the appellant at its Mandideep factory."

2. Since there was no requirement to use raw material directly in the manufacture of final product the denial of Modvat credit was uncalled for and contrary to judicial pronouncements. "Since there was no requirement to use raw materials directly in the manufacture of final product the denial of modvat credit by the Collector was clearly uncalled for and contrary to judicial pronouncements which has settled this position beyond any pale of doubt."

3. There was no violation of Rule 57F(2). "We, therefore, hold that there was no violation of Rule 57F(2) which postulates that a manufacturer assessee engaged in the manufacture of final product can send the raw materials directly to a job worker, request such job worker to convert the raw materials into an intermediate product and then receive such intermediate product in his factory for manufacture of final dutiable products."

4. No justification for denying the credit because all raw materials were used in the manufacture of final product. "There is no justification for denying the credit because it was not in dispute that the entirety of the raw materials were, in fact, used in the manufacture of final dutiable product. The appellant had filed before the Collector a certificate from the Chartered Accountant certifying that the total quantity of raw materials received at Ankleshwar was used in the manufacture of 7ADCA which, in turn, was used in the manufacture of Cephalexin at Mandideep. Every ounce of the material was thus fully accounted for."

5. Appellants entitled to Modvat credit of Rs. 79,38,597.50. Penalty imposed set side. "We, therefore, hold that the appellants are entitled to the benefit of modvat credit of Rs. 79,38,597.50. For the same reason, we also set aside the penalty imposed by the adjudicating authority."

FACT: The Tribunal denied Modvat to the applicant for 1.4.1986 on the ground that its declaration under Rule 57G was acknowledged by the Assistant Collector on 2.4.1986. The applicant has requested for rectification of the error in the Tribunal's order because its declaration was filed on 31.3.1986 and duly acknowledged by the Superintendent.

HELD: Modvat--the applicant is eligible for Modvat for 1.4.1986 because its declaration under Rule 57G was filed with the Range Supdt. on 31.3.1986. "The Tribunal has given a finding in the impugned order that the petitioner would not be entitled to the Modvat benefit for the inputs in question for the period prior to 2.4.1986 on the ground that the declaration under Rule 57-G has been acknowledged by the jurisdictional Collector only on 2.4.1986 and under Rule 57G(2) a manufacturer who has filed a declaration under sub-rule (1) may after obtaining the acknowledgement of the Asst. Collector take the credit of the duty paid on the inputs received by him. On going through the records we find that on 31.3.1986 the petitioner has addressed a communication to the Asst. Collector purporting to be a declaration under Rule 57-G of the Modvat Rules. This was presented with the Range Supdt., Hyderabad and has been acknowledged by him on 31.3.1986. It has been forwarded to the Asst. Collector, Hyderabad who had received it on 2.4.1986. It is not disputed that the inputs in question have suffered duty and the petitioner would be otherwise eligible to Modvat credit in respect of the inputs in question. Filing of a declaration under Rule 57-G is a procedural formality and in the present case the same has been done on 31.3.1986 itself to the Range Supdt. The fact that the Range Supdt. forwarded the same to the Assistant Collector in the same place only on 2.4.1986 cannot be a reason to deny the petitioner the benefit of Modvat credit. The Board has also given a clarification in this regard.........the impugned order is amended by rectifying the error holding that the petitioner would be entitled to the Modvat credit in respect of the inputs in question taken on 1.4.1986. The impugned order would stand modified accordingly after rectification of this mistake."

CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004 - Cenvat credit - Minor procedural lapses 23. In the case of L.M.L. Ltd. v. CCE, Kanpur, [2007] 8 STT 387 (New Delhi - CESTAT) the assessee availed MODVAT credit on the invoices issued by the dealers/traders during the period from July, 1994 to December, 1994. A show-cause notice was issued to the assessee denying the MODVAT credit on the ground that these dealers/traders were not registered dealers with the Central Excise department. Though the assessee contested the show-cause notice on the ground that these dealers/traders got themselves registered, yet the adjudicating authority confirmed the demand on the assessee and imposed penalty on the ground that addresses of the traders were different and duty paying documents did not show the required details. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals), in respect of the credit availed by the assessee on the invoices issued by the Indian Oil Corporation, allowed the appeal but in respect of other dealers/traders, denied the MODVAT credit and upheld imposition of penalty. He, however, reduced the quantum of penalty. The Tribunal held that the issue is squarely covered by the Larger Bench’s decision in the case of Kamakhya Steels (P.) Ltd. v. CCE 2000 (121) ELT 247 (Tri. - LB). The Larger Bench of the Tribunal in that case had held that minor procedural lapses like non-mentioning of the description of goods, duty paying documents number, registered number, etc., are to be condoned in view of the amendment which was done to rule 57G by Notification No. 7/99. It was also undisputed that the inputs covered under all the orders were received in the factory of the assessee and consumed by it in its factory. The Tribunal further held that from the plain reading of the Board’s Circular No. 441/7/99-CX dated 23-2-1999, it is very clear that the Assistant Commissioner should ignore minor procedural lapses as long as it is verified that inputs/capital goods have suffered duty and are being used in the manufacturing process. The Board, in the above Circular had clearly mentioned for disposal of pending cases accordingly. The Commissioner (Appeals), while disposing of the appeal, should have considered the Board’s Circular while dismissing the appeal filed by the assessee. Accordingly, the assessee demonstrated that it had received the duty paid inputs and consumed the same in its factory and, hence, it was held eligible for MODVAT credit.

The MODVAT Scheme was introduced by the Finance Minister with effect from 1-3-1986. The nature of the MODVAT Scheme is intended to be a revenue neutral. It was not the purpose to use the MODVAT to give substantial relief of excise. The shifting the effective burden of excise taxation away from inputs and on the final products is the heart of the said scheme. In short, the MODVAT Scheme allows the manufacturer to obtain instant and complete reimbursement of the excise duty paid on the components and raw materials which will result in considerable reduction in the cost of final product. The benefit of MODVAT is available only in respect of such raw material/components actually consumed in production of final goods actually sold. In the instant case, since only 50 per cent of inputs covered by the MODVAT Scheme were consumed in respect of which gate passes were obtained, MODVAT benefit available was only 50 per cent. Moreover, the issue had come up before the Tribunal in the assessee’s case for the assessment year 1987-88 where the Tribunal had upheld the deletion made by the Commissioner (Appeals).

In the light of above discussion and in the absence of additional material/evidence, the Commissioner (Appeals) was right in holding that there was no impact on the profit whether cost of raw material was debited at gross or at net of MODVAT. Therefore, the Commissioner (Appeals) had rightly deleted the said additions pertaining to the MODVAT.

FACT: The assessee was engaged in the manufacture of Vinyl Chloride Monomer, Poly Vinyl Chloride, High Density Polyethylene, Mono-Ethylene Glycol, Polyester Oriented Yarn, etc. at its integrated manufacturing under known as 'H'.

During the set up of 'H', the assessee purchased the complete Single Point Mooring System [SPM system] along with anchor chain, chain stoppers, anchor piles and anchor pipes and other items such as offshore bands, half shell brackets, anode pipes, etc.

SPM system was located by the assessee outside the factory.

HELD: The Single Point Mooring (SPM) buoy is located in mid sea (Arabian Sea), off. Suvail Coast, in Magdalla Port territorial water, at a distance of approx 12 kms from tank farm. SPM is a floating platform, held in place by 6 sets of suitable mooring chains which in turn are either connected to a pile or an anchor. SPM holds a vessel through a mooring hawser. SPM has an arrangement of inbuilt pipeline system with its entry/exit points, where subsea and floating hoses connect to facilitate the transfer of cargo between the vessel and the terminal. The floating hoses are connected to the vessel's manifold. Vessel pump the cargo through these hoses. [Para 9]

The subsea hoses are connected to a hard pipe lines at the bottom of the sea. This hard pipe is in turn connected to the tank farms located within the factory premises of the assessee. Accordingly SPM is connected to the tank farm through 2 pipelines. One pipeline is used for transporting Naphtha and other petroleum products from SPM to the tank farm. The second line is used to transport Paraxylene from SPM to the tank farm. These pipelines run underwater on the sea bed for about 4.85 kms and are then buried underground for another 7.15 kms to reach the assessee's tank farm. SPM is used for unloading of imported and coastal consignments and pumping the raw materials, namely, Naptha, Paraxylene and other petroleum products through the pipe lines directly to the tanks within the factory. [Para 10]

Part of the pipelines and SPM are integrally connected with the equipments and tanks within the factory through the pipelines and instrumentation. It is necessary to run the refinery of the size in question without installation of SPM used in connection with the import of crude by giant crude tankers. [Para 11]

The department contended that when the rule prescribes a particular document, the appellant is required to produce the said document only to enable himself to take credit.

The Tribunal held that the appellant clearly showed divergence in practice regarding generation of triplicate copy of the bill of entry, thus, necessitating prescribing the duplicate copy generated on EDI system also as document for the purpose of taking credit. Sub-rule (3)(k) prescribing such duplicate copy as the relevant document has been done with without amending sub-rule (3)(c) of rule 57G. The Tribunal found merit in the submission of the appellant.

u It follows from the above discussion that the credit is availed on the tax paid on the input service, which is advertisement and not on the contents of the advertisement. Thus, it is not necessary that the contents of the advertisement must be that of the final product manufactured by the person advertising, as long as the manufacturer can demonstrate that the advertisement services availed, have an effect or impact on the manufacture of the final product and establish the relationship between the input service and the manufacture of the final product. The manufacturer thereby can avail the credit of the service tax paid by him. Once the cost incurred by the service has to be added to the cost, and is so assessed, it is a recognition by the revenue of the advertisement services having a connection with the manufacture of the final product. This test will also apply in the case of sales promotion.

u Therefore, services of advertising and marketing procured by the assessee in respect of advertisements for aerated waters were covered by the definition of the words ‘input services’ as defined in rule 2(l) when admittedly the assessee manufactured concentrates which were exclusively used for the manufacture of the respective aerated waters which were advertised by the assessee. The original authority rejected the Cenvat credit and imposed penalty. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the order of original authority. It was found that some of the telephones were admittedly installed in the residential premises of the director and other employees. Credit had also been availed in respect of cellphones which were in the names of different individuals. The Commissioner (Appeals) had made a categorical finding that the landline phones were not installed in the factory premises registered with the Department and the cellphones were in possession of different individuals. As such, it could not be proved that such landline phones and cellphones were exclusively used in relation to the manufacturing or clearance activities. The assessee fairly conceded that some of the landline phones were installed in the residential premises of the directors and some of the cellphones were in the names of different individuals.

It fabricated a dry dock for manufacturing ship and repair services.

It availed cenvat credit on input services, input and capital goods used for fabrication of the dry dock amongst others. It utilised cenvat credit towards the output services mainly repair services and export of the goods and claimed refund of unutilised cenvat credit under rule 5.

The adjudicating authority denied the cenvat credit on input services, inputs and capital goods a on the ground that the final product 'ship' was classified under Central Excise Tariff Heading 8901 chargeable to nil rate of duty and, therefore, they were not eligible to avail cenvat credit for manufacturing of the exempted final product. HELD: Cenvat Credit on dry dock

The definition of 'input service' under rule 2(l) precisely covers any service used by a provider of taxable service for providing an output service, any service used by a manufacturer in or in relation to manufacture of final product and inclusive part of the definition, services used in relation to setting up, modernisation, renovation or repair of a factory, premises of a provider of output service or an office relating to such factory or premises, etc. The expression 'any service' read with 'for providing an output service' would cover wide encompass of the definition of input service. The Supreme Court in the case of Indian Chamber of Commerce v. CIT AIR 1976 SC 348 observed that the expression 'for' has to be interpreted as 'for the purpose of'. Cenvat credit availed on input service, input and capital goods for setting up dry dock would be allowed for providing output service namely repair/refit service. This is also covered in the inclusive part of the definition of 'input service'. Hence, the finding of the adjudicating authority, that the appellant is exclusively engaged in the manufacture of exempted final product 'Ships' and Cenvat credit on input, capital goods is inadmissible, cannot be sustainable. The first limb of the inclusive definition of the term ‘manufacture’ under section 2(f) has a very wide connotation. 8. Definition of ‘input service’ as per rule 2(1) of CENVAT Credit Rules is very wide in view of the inclusive part of the definition. Any service in relation to business is ‘input service’.

The second part of the definition of ‘input service’ covers various services like advertisement or sales promotion, market research, activities relating to business, such as accounting, auditing, financing, recruitment and quality control, coaching and training, computer networking, credit rating, share registry and security.

These input services have hardly any relation with ‘manufacture’ or ‘provision of output service’.

Main factory can ‘distribute’ entire credit to itself

9. In some cases, office and main factory are situated at one place and other factories are situated at different places. In such case, if the office is registered as ‘Input Service Distributor’, it is perfectly legal to distribute all CENVAT credit to the main factory itself. Thus, registering office as ‘Input Service Distributor’ and ‘distributing’ all CENVAT credit to the main factory itself is an exercise in futility. Instead of that, the credit of services at office can be utilised in main office itself. As explained above, definition of ‘input service’ does not require any relation with ‘manufacture’ or ‘provision of output service’. CENVAT Credit Rules do not require one-to-one relationship.

What is not required in the main definition cannot be brought in through the mechanism of ‘input service distributor’.

All provisions have to be read in cohesive manner

10. Any provision in law cannot be read in isolative manner. The provision of ‘Input Service Distributor’ cannot be read in isolation of other provisions relating to CENVAT credit.

Interpretation must depend on the text and the context . They are the basis of interpretation. One may well say, if the text is the texture, context is what gives the colour. Neither can be ignored. The interpretation is best which makes the textual interpretation match the contextual. A statute is best interpreted when we know why it is enacted. With this knowledge, the statute must be read, first as a whole and then section by section, clause by clause, phrase by phrase and word by word. If a statute is looked at, in the context of its enactment, with the glasses of the statute-maker, provided by such context, its scheme, the sections, clauses, phrases and words may take colour and appear different than when statute is looked at without the glasses of context. With those glasses, we must look at the Act as a whole and discover what each section, each clause, each phrase and each word is meant and designed to say as to fit into the scheme of the entire Act. No part of a statute can be construed in isolation. Statutes have to be construed so that every word has a place and everything is in its place - RBI v. Peerless General Finance & Investment Co. Ltd. AIR 1987 SC 1023/[1987] 1 SCC 424/[1987] 61 Comp. Cas. 663 (SC) - quoted with approval in J.K. Industries Ltd. v. Swaran Singh AIR 2004 SC 1531/[2004] 3 SCC 257, Prakash Kumar v. State of Gujarat AIR 2005 SC 1075.

Conclusion

11. In conclusion, it can be stated as follows—

u Input Service Distributor is a facility, not a compulsion.

u CENVAT Credit Rules do not require one-to-one relationship.

u Provision of ‘Input Service Distributor’ also does not envisage one-to-one relationship.

u Any service in relation to business of assessee is his ‘input service’.

u CENVAT credit can be utilised at one place without distributing it.

u Even if distribution is done, ‘distribution’ of credit can be in any ratio. Entire credit can be allocated to one of the factories/places of provision of output services, if assessee so desires.

u The only requirement is that ‘input service’ should be in relation to business of assessee. Any relation with ‘manufacture’ or ‘provision of output service’ is not required.

Rule 57G clearly shows that the credit of duty can be taken on inputs by establishing that the duty has been paid on the said inputs on the basis of documents such as invoice, AR-1, Bill on Entry, etc. In the instant case, it was not in dispute that the appellant had received imported shredded steel scrap from ‘E’ Ltd. on which countervailing duty had been paid by ‘E’ Ltd. It was also not in dispute that ‘E’ Ltd. had not taken credit of the duty paid on shredded steel scrap which was given on loan to the appellant. It was also not in dispute that the appellant had used the said shredded steel scrap taken on loan from ‘E’ Ltd. as inputs in its factory. The certificate issued by a Superintendent of Central Excise to the effect that ‘E’ Ltd. had not taken credit of duty paid on the said shredded steel scrap, was not doubted by the Excise authorities. Similarly, the certificate issued by another Superintendent to the effect that the quantity of shredded steel scrap received by the appellant from ‘E’ Ltd. had been used as inputs in the factory of the appellant, was also not doubted by the Excise authorities. In these circumstances, the appellant had established that the credit of duty on receipt of imported shredded steel scrap from ‘E’ Ltd. had been taken in accordance with law. [Para 9]

For availing the credit of duty, what is required to be established under rule 57G is that the inputs received are in fact duty paid. The procedure set out in rule 57G is to ensure that the credit is taken on the basis of duty paid documents. The bill of entry is one such document set out in rule 57G. The said rule does not require that the bill of entry should be in the name of the person claiming credit of duty. It is not in dispute that the goods imported and cleared on payment of duty by one person can be used as inputs and credit of duty can be claimed by another person by establishing that the imported duty paid goods have been received as inputs and that the importer has not taken credit of that duty. In the instant case, it was established that the duty paid goods were received as inputs, however, the credit was denied on the ground that the Bill of entry was not endorsed in the name of the appellant. Rule 57G does not require that for taking credit of duty, the bill of entry should be endorsed in the name of the claimant. In the absence of any provision regarding endorsement on the bill of entry, the credit of duty cannot be denied on the ground that the bill of entry is not endorsed in the name of the claimant. In the facts of the instant case, the evidence on record i.e., the bills of entry together with the certificates issued by excise authorities, clearly showed that the goods imported and cleared under the bills of entry on payment of duty were received and utilized by the appellant as inputs in its factory and that the importer had not utilized the credit of duty paid on the said goods. Thus, the appellant had established that the inputs received under the bills of entry were duty paid and, therefore, the authorities below were not justified in denying the credit of duty to the appellant. [Para 10]

INPUT SERVICE DISTRIBUTOR

In this article, the author has discussed the provisions relating to ‘input service distributor’ including amendment carried out in 2008.

Introduction

1. ‘Input service distributor’ is the beautiful and utilitarian concept introduced by the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004. In this article, we shall discuss the provisions relating to ‘input service distributor’.

Definition

2. Rule 2(m ) of the Rules defines ‘input service distributor’ as under :—

"(m)‘Input service distributor’ means an office of the manufacturer or producer of final products or provider of output service, which receives invoices issued under rule 4A of the Service Tax Rules, 1994 towards purchases of input services and issues invoice, bill or, as the case may be, challan for the purposes of distributing the credit of service tax paid on the said services to such manufacturer or producer or provider, as the case may be;"

Important criteria for input service provider

3. Important criteria for input service provider are :—

(i)It has an office as the manufacturer or producer of final products or provider of output service. In other words, an office of manufacturer of excisable goods or taxable service provider can be registered as input service distributor.

(ii)It has to receive invoices towards purchase of services. The services might have been received by one of the units manufacturing goods or premises providing services or other offices.

(iii)It can issue invoice or bill or challan for the purpose of distributing the credit of service tax paid on the services to the manufacturing unit or service providing unit.

It is to be noted that the input service provider can be registered as head office, registered office, branch, depot, regional office, zonal office, etc.

Regional marketing office was registered as input service distributor and credit was distributed to manufacturing units. It was held by the Tribunal in its prima facie view, that the distribution was in order in Jaypee Rewa Plant v. CCE 2007 (218) ELT 576 (Delhi - Trib.).

It is possible that one company may have many input service distributors.

Example

4. ABC Ltd. has three manufacturing units. Its head office has taken Fire Insurance Policy covering the manufacturing units and paid insurance premium and service tax of Rs. 10,300. Head Office can distribute the service tax paid by it to the manufacturing units and manufacturing units can take the credit on receipt of Invoice from the head office and utilise this amount like any other Cenvat credit.

Conditions

5. Rule 7 deals with distribution of credit by input service distributor. The input service provider can distribute service tax paid by it subject to the following conditions :—

(i)The credit distributed shall not exceed the amount of service tax paid by it. (Is it possible to distribute more than the credit availed?)

(ii)The credit of service tax attributable to service used in an unit exclusively engaged in manufacture of exempted goods or providing of exempted services shall not be distributed.

It is important to note that there is no requirement to distribute the credit proportionately. The input service distributor can distribute to various units as the circumstances warrants. There is no rule regarding periodicity of distribution and it is advisable to distribute monthly.

Registration

6. Input service distributors have to obtain registration from the service tax authorities. They have to apply in Form No. ST-1 and have to obtain Registration Certificate in Form No. ST-2.

Maintenance of records

7. Rule 9 of the Rules deals with maintenance of records by the input service distributor. The records maintained by it must contain the following :—

(i)Serial number and date of the document on which the Cenvat credit is availed.

(ii)Service tax registration number and name of input service provider.

(iii)Description and value of input service.

(iv)Service tax credit availed.

(v)Basis of allocation/apportionment of credit amount.

(vi)Service tax utilised for distributing the credit.

(vii)Balance credit available for distribution.

Issue of Invoice

8. After making the payment of service charges and service tax, input service distributor can avail the credit provided service received is input service and distribute it to various manufacturing units or service providing units.

Rule 4A(2) of the Service Tax Rules, 1994 deals with the issue of invoice by the input service distributor. The invoice shall be serially numbered and contain the following particulars :

(i)the name, address and registration number of the person providing input services and the serial number and date of invoice;

(ii)the name and address of the input service distributor;

(iii)the name and address of the recipient of the credit distributed; and

(iv)the amount of the credit distributed.

The case of the assessee was that TISCO did not supply original challans but only gave the carbon copies and same must be regarded as original within meaning of rule 57G. The appellate authority after considering various pieces of evidence had recorded a categorical finding in its order that it was incorrect to claim by the assessee that TISCO only issued carbon copies. The Tribunal in its finding observed that there were other manufacturers also who were receiving original challans issued by the stockyards of TISCO. [Para 3]

In the wake of the aforesaid findings, it was not possible to conclude that carbon copy was required to be regarded as original copy as per the claim made by the assessee.

A perusal of the provisions of the rule 57G shows that in order to claim Modvat credit, the original copy of the invoice is required to be produced. There is no provision for granting Modvat credit on the basis of carbon copy. If it is to be presumed that carbon copy in a case like the one in hand could be treated as original, then the finding of fact by the appellate authority or Tribunal has to be on the record. In the instant case, the finding of fact was against the dealer that TISCO did not issue invoice on a carbon copy so as to be treated as original for the purpose of rule 57G. The contention of the assessee that carbon copy had been properly verified and defaced was not impressive as in the instant case adjudication had to be only on the question of law. No merit was found in the contention raised by the assessee. Moreover, laying down a blanket principle permitting Modvat credit on carbon copy may result into setting up of false claims. On such a possibility of availing Modvat credit by many persons against one transaction would not be ruled out which will be highly damaging to the revenue. [Para 4]

Therefore, on the facts and circumstances of the case, the Tribunal was right in disallowing credit for Modvat on carbon copy of challans furnished by the assessee evidencing payment of duty. [Para 5]

There is absolutely no requirement that the capital goods at the time of receipt must be owned by manufacturer or that the same would cease to be capital goods, if they are installed in the factory and become fixed to earth. In fact, most of the capital goods the machinery, equipment or instruments covered by Chapters 84, 85 and 90, pipes and tubes, pollution control equipment refractories, and storage tanks are required to be installed and after installation, the same put together constitute a manufacturing plant, which is fixed to earth structure. Just because after being installed in the factory, the capital goods put together become a plant which is fixed to earth structure, the Cenvat credit cannot be denied on the basis that the plant which is fixed to earth structure, is not excisable. This preposition of the Department is, in fact absurd, as there is no such condition in rule 2(a) for capital goods.

For capital goods Cenvat credit, the items must be among those mentioned in this rule and should have been used in the factory of the manufacturer and how the items are not used relevant. The words used in rule 2(a) are "used in the factory of manufacturer of the final product" not "used in the manufacture of final product". Therefore, once any item received in the factory is 'capital goods' in terms of Rule 2(a) of the Cenvat Credit Rules, and is used in the factory, the manufacturer would be entitled to Cenvat credit of excise duty paid in respect of the same.

If the logic of the Commissioner in the impugned order is accepted, no capital goods Cenvat credit can be allowed in respect of any item of capital goods enumerated in rule 2(a) of the Cenvat Credit Rules, as all the items - various items of machinery covered under Chapters 84, 85 and 90 of the Tariff, pipes and tubes, tanks, pollution control equipments refractories, etc., have to be installed in the factory before being put to use and after installation, the same would become fixed to earth plant. Rule 6, of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004 makes it clear that the CENVAT Credit shall not be allowed on such quantity of goods which is used in the manufacture of exempted goods. However, exception is carved out in sub-Rule (2). Sub-Rule (2) of Rule 6 provides- where a manufacturer or provider of output service avails CENVAT Credit in respect of any inputs except the input intended to be used as fuel and manufactures such final products or provides such output service which are chargeable to duty or tax as well as exempted goods or services, then, an obligation is cast on the assessee to maintain separate accounts for receipt, consumption and inventory or input and input service meant for use in the manufacture of dutiable final products or in providing output service and the quantity of input meant for use in the manufacture of exempted goods or services. However he would be entitled to CENVAT credit only on that quantity of input or input service which is intended for use in the manufacture of dutiable goods. Therefore, it is clear that the assessee manufacturer is entitled to CENVAT Credit on "inputs" which is used in the manufacture of dutiable goods. [Para 11]

In view of clear language in the statutory provisions coupled with the fact that the factory includes more than one premises to be eligible for CENVAT Credit, an assessee has to use the input in the manufacture of dutiable goods in his factory. If the factory includes more than one unit and if the assessee uses this input in the manufacturing of excisable goods in both the units, he would be entitled to CENVAT Credit. [Para 12]

The definition of 'input' brings within its fold the inputs used for generation of electricity or steam, provided such electricity or steam is used within the factory of production for manufacture of final products or for any other purpose. Therefore, it follows the term "within the factory of production" cannot be confined to a single unit. In view of the definition of factory in the act which means more than one premises, it has to be construed as the factory owned by the assessee. If the assessee owns more than one unit, all the units if they are situated at a place would constitute "a factory". If the electricity or steam generated within the factory of production means within the factory premises which may include more than one unit. If such electricity or steam generated within the factory of production is utilized by the assessee in more than one unit and if those units are manufacturing excisable goods, then, the assessee would be entitled to the benefit of CENVAT credit to the entire extent of utilization of such electricity or steam in all the units of its factory premises. Therefore, whatever goes into generation of electricity or steam which is placed within the factory which may consists of more than one unit would be an input for the purposes of obtaining credit on the duty payable thereon. [Para 15]

In the instant case, the assessee is having two units; one DTA unit and another EOU unit. Both are situated in the same factory premises. Both are manufacturing excisable goods. The assessee has purchased furnace oil from which, the steam is generated within the said factory premises. The said steam is utilized by the assessee in manufacturing excisable goods in both the units which are situated within the same compound, which falls within the definition of the word "factory" and therefore, the assessee is entitled to CENVAT credit in respect of entire volume of steam used in the manufacture of excisable goods by both the units. That is precisely what the appellate authorities have held and granted relief to the assessee. [Para 16]

Hence, impugned order was confirmed. [Para 17]

[Para 39] Explanatory note by Harmonised System of Nomenclature (HSN) to Heading 21.06 proves the integral link between concentrate manufactured by the assessee and the beverage (aerated water) manufactured by the bottler from it. The concentrate manufactured by the assessee in question had been classified and assessed to Cenvat (excise duty) under heading 21.06 by the Schedule to the Central Excise Tariff Act, 1985. That heading is identical to heading 21.06 of organised system of nomenclature issued by WCO. In fact the Excise Tariff is based on HSN. Therefore, the Supreme Court has repeatedly emphasized that the Explanatory Notes of HSN are valuable material for understanding the scope of various headings in the Central Excise Tariff. The Explanatory Note of HSN of Heading 21.06 demonstrates that the concentrates contain the flavouring ingredient that are characteristics of a particular beverage. The beverage in question is obtained simply by diluting the preparation with water, sugar and carbondioxide gas. From the Explanatory Note it is, therefore, clear that there is a link between the concentrate and the beverage made from that. The above Explanatory Note also explains the rational for business being arranged in this industry in a particular manner. This method of doing business avoids unnecessary transport of large quantity of water. In addition, the bottles and crates have to be collected back from the shop keepers or dealers and taken back to the factory for filling the fresh batch on a constant basis. At all times, the quality of beverage was maintained and marketing support to the beverages was provided by the brand name holder-cum-concentrate manufacturer. [Para 42]

It follows from the above discussion that the credit is availed on the tax paid on the input service, which is advertisement and not on the contents of the advertisement. Thus, it is not necessary that the contents of the advertisement must be that of the final product manufactured by the person advertising, as long as the manufacturer can demonstrate that the advertisement services availed have an effect or impact on the manufacture of the final product and establish the relationship between the input service and the manufacture of the final product. The manufacturer thereby can avail the credit of the service tax paid by him. Once the cost incurred by the service has to be added to the cost, and is so assessed, it is a recognition by the revenue of the advertisement services having a connection with the manufacture of the final product. This test will also apply in the case of sales promotion. [Para 43]

Therefore, services of advertising and marketing procured by the assessee in respect of advertisements for aerated waters are covered by the definition of the words ‘input services’ as defined in rule 2(l) when admittedly the assessee manufactured concentrates which were exclusively used for the manufacture of the respective aerated waters which were advertised by the assessee. The advertisement or sales promotion of aerated waters undertaken by manufacturer of concentrate was covered by the inclusive part of the definition of ‘input service’ contained in rule 2(l ). [Para 43]

Freight also is paid by it up to the retail oulets/commission agents warehouses. [Para 7] In the appeal, the revenue contended that the services availed at retail outlets cannot be considered for credit to the assessee. The revenue contended that these services used in retail outlets had no remote connection in the manufacture of ready-made garments. The Adjudicating Authority did not appreciate the legal scope of rule 2(l). He presumed that the services should be in or in relation to manufacture of ready made garments, whereas rule 2(l) clearly talks about services used by manufacturers, whether directly or indirectly in or in relation to the manufacture of final products and clearance of final products up to place of removal. A plain reading of the said statutory provision will indicate that the presumption of the Adjudication Authority is not sustainable. [Para 8]

Regarding the dispute relating to registration of the assessee as ISD, one is in agreement with the findings of the Commissioner (Appeals). On examination of provision of rule 2(m), the Commissioner (Appeals) clearly recorded that a manufacturer who wants to avail benefit of service tax should get registered himself as service provider and then he will be able to account for all the input services tax paid in the headquarters and distribute the same to various units. After examining the provisions of rule 7, the Commissioner (Appeals) concluded that as the manufacturer was having various retail outlets and office besides the factory for manufacture, in order to utilise the credit of input service got registered with the department as ISD. [Para 10]

Another dispute in the appeal is relating to credit availed by the assessee on the basis of debit notes, which were found to be ineligible documents. One notes that the assessee issued challans under rule 4A of the Service tax Rule, 1994 which contain all the required details. Even in case certain particulars were found missing in the relevant documents, one notes that substantial benefit of cenvat credit cannot be denied on this ground. In this connection, one refers to proviso to sub-rule (2) of rule 9 which provides for discretionary powers to the Adjudicating Authority regarding allowing the credit in such situation. As such, mention of wrong address of the service tax department on the documents is not a bar to avail the credit. [Para 12]

In view of the aforesaid, the order to the Commissioner (Appeals) deserved to be upheld.

Authority failed to appreciate the difference between a civil appeal and a SLP filed before the Supreme Court. The civil appeal is a statutory appeal provided under the law and the decision of the Apex Court in such civil appeal is binding and the order of the Tribunal, which was appealed against merges with the decision of the Supreme Court. The same is a binding precedent for other lower Courts to follow. The observation of the Adjudicating Authority to the contrary is devoid of legal merit. [Para 10] Having considered the findings of the Adjudicating Authority and on perusal of the decision of the Tribunal in the case of Apitco Ltd. (supra) as affirmed by the Supreme Court one finds that the impugned order is devoid of merit in so far as it relates to tax liability of the assessee with reference to various works carried out by it for which consideration was paid by the Government through grants-in-aid. [Para 11]

The project works assigned to the assessee are in the nature of various welfare activities carried out by the Government in public interest. These are counseling, re-training and redeployment of rationalized employees of Central Public Sector Enterprises and Entrepreneurship Development Programme with reference to production of specific products, skill development training programme through Science and Technology, etc. The assessee was to submit full records of the expenditure with reference to each project to the concerned Ministry. Any surplus of the amount, given as grant should be returned to the Government. The decision of the Tribunal in the case of Apitco Ltd. (supra) is squarely applicable to the facts in the instant case. Therefore, the assessee was not liable to pay service tax in respect of these activities carried out, by using the grants-in-aid given by the various Ministries/departments of the Government. [Para 12]

With reference to demand created against the assessee on the ground that instead of paying service tax on the gross amount, the assessee paid service tax by treating the gross amount as cum-tax-receipt inclusive of tax, the assessee submitted that the invoices raised are inclusive of taxes. In terms of section 67(2) of the Finance Act, 1994, it is entitled for calculating the tax by treating the amount as inclusive of tax. The Adjudicating Authority did not give any detailed finding for demanding such short levy. He simply reproduced a case law, which states that section 67(2) will be applicable only in cases where the gross amount includes service tax. Though the assessee claimed in the appeal that the invoices indicated that the amount is inclusive of service tax, no evidence is submitted to support such contention. As such, the same requires verification of the actual invoices by the jurisdictional Adjudicating Authority. If the invoices issued during the relevant time specifically indicated that the amount is inclusive of service tax, then the benefit of section 67(2) is available to the assessee. [Para 13]

Regarding denial of cenvat credit, the assessee pleaded that such denial is only on the ground that the invoices were not in the assessee's name but were not in the name of branch/head office. This cannot be the reason for denial of credit. There is no allegation or finding to the effect that the input services were not received by the assessee or the said services were not covered under the scope of eligible input services in terms of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004. In such situation, the denial of credit only on the ground that the address of branch office or head office was mentioned instead of assessee's address cannot be the ground for denial of otherwise eligible cenvat credit. [Para 14]

HEADNOTE: Rule 2(l), read with rule 3, of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - Cenvat credit - Input service - Period February, 2005 to September, 2005 - Assessee availed Cenvat credit of service tax paid for GTA service, availed by it, for outward transportation of final product from factory to buyers’ premises - Revenue denied said Cenvat credit - Whether since duty was paid on ‘FOR’ destination basis and ownership of goods and property therein vested with assessee up to point of delivery of goods to customer, conditions laid down in Board’s Circular No. 97/8/2007-ST, dated 23-8-2007 were fulfilled and therefore, benefit of Cenvat credit was liable to be allowed - Held, yes [Para 5] Circulars and Notifications : Board’s Circular No. 97/8/2007-ST, dated 23-8-2007

FACT: The assessee availed Cenvat credit of service tax paid for GTA service availed by it for outward transportation of the final product from factory to the buyer’s premises during the period February to September, 2005. The revenue denied the Cenvat credit and imposed penalty under rule 15. The Commissioner (Appeals) set aside the penalty and sustained the remaining part of the order.

On appeal :

HELD: During the period of dispute, the assessee availed GTA service for outward transportation of liquefied gases (final products) from its factory to buyers’ premises. These gases were to be maintained in liquid form at sub-zero temperatures and, hence, cryogenic tanks were used for their storage. These cryogenic tanks containing liquefied gases were mounted on goods transport vehicles belonging to GTA who transported the goods from the factory to the buyers’ premises. The liquids were transferred into cryogenic tanks installed in the customers’ premises which, in some cases, also belonged to assessee and the customer paid rent in such cases. In all cases, the freight for the transportation of the goods was paid by the assessee and said amount was included in the assessable value of the goods for the purpose of payment of duty. In other words, duty was paid on ‘FOR destination’ basis. This fact was evident from the invoices available on record. A reading of a sample agreement entered into between the assessee and one of its customers showed that the ownership of the goods and the property therein vested with the assessee up to the point of delivery of the goods to the customer. On these facts, it had to be held that the conditions laid down in the Board’s Circular No. 97/8/2007, dated 23-8-2007 were fulfilled by the assessee and, therefore, the benefit of CENVAT credit is liable to be allowed to it in respect of GTA service availed for outward transportation of liquefied gases from the factory to the buyers’ premises during the period of dispute. [Para 5]

The adjudicating authority denied the Cenvat Credit of an amount of Rs.26,11,20,838/- on various grounds as ineligible Cenvat Credit, demanded interest thereof and imposed a penalty under Rule 15(1) of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004; also demanded interest on an amount of Rs.39,02,938/- reversed by the assessee during the scrutiny of the records admitting that such credit is ineligible. The Department submitted that the capital goods and other goods received during the construction period of the factory are eligible for availment of Cenvat Credit when the factory comes into existence. The assessee had started the commercial production from November, 2006 and has availed Cenvat Credit during that month only on the capital goods and other goods received during the construction of the factory/refinery. Provisions of Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 would be applicable as far as eligibility to avail duty credit is concerned and definitions relating to capital goods as appearing in Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 would alone be relevant.

Issue Involved

Whether credit of capital goods received during construction period will be governed by new rules prevalent at time of taking credit ?

HELD: The following facts were undisputed -

the capital goods/other goods on which Cenvat Credit was availed are received in the factory premises of the assessee.

the said capital goods/other goods were used/consumed for construction of or setting up of the refinery/factory.

the assessee had taken the Central Excise registration and discharging the duty liability on the finished goods manufactured and cleared from the assessee's factory premises from November 2006.

capital goods and other goods were duty paid. [Para 6]

As regards the denial of Cenvat Credit of Rs.20,61,57,657/-, Cenvat Credit was denied on the ground that the credit has been taken on the strength of invoices where owner is person other than the assessee and assessee be considered as person who had got the said capital goods/items from financing company since Essar Projects Ltd. (the owner of capital goods) was not financing company. In this regard, the duty paying documents clearly indicate the name of EPC contractors i.e. Essar Projects Ltd. and as also the name and address of the assessee as a consignee. It is not disputed that the said capital goods/other goods which were received at the site of the assessee, were used in refinery and the documents indicated correct duty paying nature. Since there is no dispute as to the receipt, consumption and duty paid nature of the capital goods or other goods in setting up of the factory of the assessees, demand was set aside. [Para 7(i)]

As regards the denial of Cenvat Credit of Rs. 38,74,887/-, the entire dispute was regarding the non-submission of intimation of the receipt of capital goods and other goods to the Jurisdictional Superintendent. As has been already accepted and undisputed that the capital goods and other goods were received and consumed in the setting up of the unit, mere non-filing of the declaration cannot be a ground for denial of credit. Subtantative benefits should not be denied to an assessee only on the ground of non-fulfilment of procedural conditions. [Para 7(ii)]

As regards the denial of Cenvat Credit of Rs.6,68,773/- and Rs.2,34,351/-, the adjudicating authority has sought to deny the Cenvat Credit only on the ground that the Cenvat Credit has been availed on the original copy and/or extra copy. As long as, there being no dispute as to the duty paid character of the capital goods/other goods, and the receipt in and consumption thereof, there cannot be the denial of Cenvat Credit to the assessee. [Para 7(iii)]

As regards the denial of Cenvat Credit of Rs.1,95,84,057/- and Rs.25,33,813/-, the credit was denied on ground that installation certificate as required under Rule 57Q of the erstwhile Central Excise Rules, 1944 was not submitted and the goods do not fall under Chapter 84, 85 and 90 as is envisaged in the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 for availment of capital goods credit. In this regard, the assessee has been able to demonstrate that HTPE sheets, insulation packages, domestic (refractory) anchors etc. though not falling under specific Chapters of 84, 85 and 90, are used in the refinery as either components or spares in the plant and machinery which are used for the manufacturing of the final products. The said detailed analysis as has been submitted by the assessee was not considered by the adjudicating authority, dismissed by a summary finding that these items cannot be in nature of capital goods and are not in nature of accessories of the main plant. The items and the usage thereof which has been demonstrated, from the documents on records, clearly indicate that these items were consumed/used as components, spares or parts of the various machineries which were either fabricated and installed alongwith bought out items for setting up of the refinery. HEADNOTE: Rule 9 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - Cenvat credit - Documents and Accounts - Period 1-4-2005 to 31-5-2005 - Whether branch offices are not registered with service tax authorities and they do not discharge service tax liability - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, if a person discharges service tax liability from registered premises for services provided by branches, benefit of Cenvat credit on service tax cannot be denied only on ground that invoices are in name of branch offices - Held, yes [Para 7]

FACT: The assessee was registered as provider of advertisement services. According to the adjudicating officer, it had contravened the provisions of rule 9 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 inasmuch as it had availed credit on the documents which were not addressed to its registered premises but addressed to the branch office of the assessee. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the order of the adjudicating authority. Before the Tribunal, the assessee’s case was that it had taken service tax registration with the authorities on the ground that it had got centralized accounting system and centralized billing was done from the address of its registered premises.

HELD: The assessee was not having any service tax registration in respect of branch office on whose name the invoices were issued by the service provider; it had centralized billing and centralized accounting system at its registered office. Rule 4 of the Service Tax Rules, 1994 provides for an assessee to get himself registered as service provider. It was seen that in the instant case, the assessee had taken registration under the category of ‘Service provider of advertising services’.

It can be seen from rule 4(2) that an option is given to an assessee to register the premises where centralized billing or centralized accounting systems are located. It was found from the records that there was no dispute that the assessee’s office at Manipal had got the centralized billing and accounting systems. If that be so, registration taken by the assessee was in accordance with the Rules. [Para 6]

If a person is discharging service tax liability from his registered premises, the benefit of Cenvat credit on the service tax paid cannot be denied only on the ground that the said invoices are in the name of branch office. There was no dispute that the branch office was not registered with the service tax authorities and it was not discharging the service tax liability, obviously, as the assessee was discharging service tax liability on the services provided by branch. [Para 7]

It was found that though the document on basis of which the assessee had taken the service tax credit was in the name of branch office, tax was actually paid from the premises wherein the service tax registration had been taken. [Para 8]

In view of the findings, the impugned order was unsustainable and the same was to be set aside and the appeal was to be allowed. [Para 9]

HEADNOTE: Rule 57G of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 - Modvat credit - Procedure to be observed by manufacturer - Appellant availed Modvat credit on basis of gate pass of goods consigned to job worker - Though duplicate copy of gate pass contained name of consignee, i.e., job worker, in original copy name of appellant was written after scoring out name of job worker - For said irregularities original authority denied Modvat credit to appellants and made demand of that amount - However, appellant stated that in order to avoid problem during transportation, said correction was made in gate pass - Whether when material had not been received by appellant, but by job worker, taking credit on such goods by changing name of consignee in original copy of gate pass was serious matter and such scant regard to rules could not be ignored - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, appellant would not be entitled for Modvat credit - Held, yes

FACT: The appellant availed Modvat credit on the strength of a gate pass which was not consigned to them but to their job worker. However, in the original gate pass the name of the job worker was scored out and name of the appellant was written but in duplicate gate pass name of the job worker was written. In these circumstances the department proceeded against the appellant for irregular availment of credit and the original authority disallowed the Modvat credit and demanded that amount with penalty.

In appeal the appellant contended that in order to avoid any problem during transportation, the correction was made by the consigner in original gate pass.

HELD: The goods, on which Modvat credit had been taken by the appellants irregularly, were consigned to the job worker. In other words the goods were not received by the appellant but by his job worker. The duplicate copy of the gate pass which had accompanied the goods contain the name of the job worker. However, the original which was sent to the appellants contains the name of the appellant, which was written after scoring out the original consignee i.e., the job worker. The adjudicating authority had given a very detailed finding to indicate that there had been manipulation of the consignee’s name in the original copy of the gate pass. But for that manipulation, the appellant would not have got the Modvat credit. In fact actual consignee was only the job worker. Further the adjudicating authority had found that there was no endorsement in name of appellant as rightly found in the duplicate copy of the gate pass in question. The adjudicating authority had observed that Modvat credit can be taken only when both the material as well as duty paying documents are received by the consignee as indicated in the gate pass. In this case, no fraudulent motive was found which could be attributed to the appellant. The appellant along with consigner have taken recourse to certain devices of expediency to avoid irksome procedures. However, when the material had not been received by the appellant and only by some job worker, taking credit on the goods received by the job worker by changing the name of the consignee in the original copy of the gate pass, was serious matter and such scant regard to rules could not be ignored. The appellant was not entitled for the Modvat credit. [Para 6]

[Para 8] In 2000, the MODVAT Rules were replaced by the CENVAT Rules by the Central Excise (Second Amendment) Rules, 2000. Basically there was a re-arrangement of the earlier rules which in substance remained the same.

It is clear that sub-rule (d ) of rule 57AA (as introduced in 2000) had merely reframed rule 57B to include all the ingredients of inputs while at the same time broadening the base not only by referring to ‘all goods’ but also by using the word ‘includes’. [Para 9]

Rule 57AC provides for the conditions for allowing CENVAT credit in respect of inputs received in the factory of the manufacturer. [Para 10]

Initially, rule 57J of the MODVAT Rules was deleted. Consequently, with the intention of re-introducing the benefit granted earlier under rule 57J, rule 57AB was introduced under the heading ‘CENVAT credit’. [Para 11]

Rule 57AB effectively duplicates the substance of rule 57J(1) and (2) and deals with a situation where inputs are received by a job worker for production of intermediate goods which are used in the manufacture of a final product. [Para 12]

In J.K. Udyog Ltd.’s case (supra), three reasons were given by the Supreme Court for holding that credit could be taken only on inputs received in the factory of the manufacturer of the final product. First, the Court held that the definition of input given in sub-rule(d) of rule 57AA was entirely different from the manner in which the said word had been expounded in the Explanation to rule 57A of the MODVAT Rules. However, there was only a re-arrangement of the several provisions of rule 57B in rule 57AA. Rule 57AA is in fact more broad based than rule 57B.

Second, the Court proceeded on the basis that under the CENVAT scheme, there was no provision similar to rule 57J of the MODVAT scheme. However, rule 57J was replaced in substance by rule 57AB. That provision was overlooked.

Another reason given by the Court in J.K. Udaipur Udyog case (supra ) for holding that the CENVAT scheme was different from the MODVAT Scheme was rule 57AC(1). However, that rule was limited to inputs received in the factory of the manufacturer and did not impinge on rule 57AB at all.

The schemes of MODVAT and CENVAT Credit are not, therefore, different and the conclusion of the Court in J.K. Udaipur Udyog that the decision in Jaypee Rewa Cement (supra ) would have no application to CENVAT Rules could not be accepted. [Para 14]

The CENVAT Rules in effect substitute the MODVAT Rules and the decision in Jaypee Rewa Cement would continue to apply. The decision in CCE v. J.K. Udaipur Udyog Ltd. (supra ) holding to the contrary, was not good law. [Para 15]

steam is utilized by it in it other unit in the same compound, it amounts to wheeling out or diverting the steam to another unit and the assessee is not liable for CENVAT Credit.

Issue Involved

When the assessee who manufacture the steam, use the same in the factory of manufacturing and also utilized the steam in its another unit which is situated in the same compound, is he entitled to CENVAT Credit proportionately to the extent which was used in the other unit ? HELD: The definition of "input" makes it clear that, "input" means all goods used in or in relation to the manufacture of final products whether directly or indirectly and whether contained in the final products or not and includes lubricating oils, greases, cutting oils, coolants, accessories of the final products cleared along with the final product, goods used as paint, or as packing material, or as fuel, or for generation of electricity or steam used in or in relation to manufacture of final products or for any other purpose, within the factory of production. [Para 8]

The word "factory" has been defined in the Central Excise Act at section 2(e). It is an inclusive definition. For the purpose of Central Excise Act, a 'factory' means more than one premises. [Para 9]

Rule 6, of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004 makes it clear that the CENVAT Credit shall not be allowed on such quantity of goods which is used in the manufacture of exempted goods. However, exception is carved out in sub-Rule (2). Sub-Rule (2) of Rule 6 provides- where a manufacturer or provider of output service avails CENVAT Credit in respect of any inputs except the input intended to be used as fuel and manufactures such final products or provides such output service which are chargeable to duty or tax as well as exempted goods or services, then, an obligation is cast on the assessee to maintain separate accounts for receipt, consumption and inventory or input and input service meant for use in the manufacture of dutiable final products or in providing output service and the quantity of input meant for use in the manufacture of exempted goods or services. However he would be entitled to CENVAT credit only on that quantity of input or input service which is intended for use in the manufacture of dutiable goods. Therefore, it is clear that the assessee manufacturer is entitled to CENVAT Credit on "inputs" which is used in the manufacture of dutiable goods. [Para 11]

In view of clear language in the statutory provisions coupled with the fact that the factory includes more than one premises to be eligible for CENVAT Credit, an assessee has to use the input in the manufacture of dutiable goods in his factory. If the factory includes more than one unit and if the assessee uses this input in the manufacturing of excisable goods in both the units, he would be entitled to CENVAT Credit. [Para 12]

The definition of 'input' brings within its fold the inputs used for generation of electricity or steam, provided such electricity or steam is used within the factory of production for manufacture of final products or for any other purpose. Therefore, it follows the term "within the factory of production" cannot be confined to a single unit. In view of the definition of factory in the act which means more than one premises, it has to be construed as the factory owned by the assessee. If the assessee owns more than one unit, all the units if they are situated at a place would constitute "a factory". If the electricity or steam generated within the factory of production means within the factory premises which may include more than one unit. If such electricity or steam generated within the factory of production is utilized by the assessee in more than one unit and if those units are manufacturing excisable goods, then, the assessee would be entitled to the benefit of CENVAT credit to the entire extent of utilization of such electricity or steam in all the units of its factory premises. Therefore, whatever goes into generation of electricity or steam which is placed within the factory which may consists of more than one unit would be an input for the purposes of obtaining credit on the duty payable thereon. [Para 15]

In the instant case, the assessee is having two units; one DTA unit and another EOU unit. Both are situated in the same factory premises. Both are manufacturing excisable goods. The assessee has purchased furnace oil from which, the steam is generated within the said factory premises. The said steam is utilized by the assessee in manufacturing excisable goods in both the units which are situated within the same compound, which falls within the definition of the word "factory" and therefore, the assessee is entitled to CENVAT credit in respect of entire volume of steam used in the manufacture of excisable goods by both the units. That is precisely what the appellate authorities have held and granted relief to the assessee. [Para 16]

Hence, impugned order was confirmed. [Para 17]

II. Minority View [per : Mathew John, Member (T)] - Credit allowable, but, only from 31-8-2006, after merger :

Scheme : Under the Cenvat Credit Scheme a manufacturer of excisable goods is allowed to take credit of excise duty paid on inputs and capital goods used in the manufacture of excisable goods and utilize such credit for payment of excise duty on final products manufactured by him. [Para 36]

Rule 4(4) - Credit only by person paying value/duty : There is no specific provision in the Rules to the effect that credit can be taken by a manufacturer only if duty is paid by him to the supplier of goods. There is a provision in rule 4(4) to the effect that CENVAT credit in respect of capital goods shall not be allowed in respect of that part of the value of capital goods which represents the amount of duty on such capital goods, which the manufacturer claims as depreciation under section 32 of the Income-tax Act, 1961. So prima facie it would appear that the person who is paying for the value of goods and duty thereon is relevant for taking credit. [Para 38]

Receipt in factory : On the other hand definition of capital goods as given in rule 2 (a) and the rule 3 (1) and rule 4 (2) (a) allowing taking of credit are clear enough that credit is to be taken on capital goods received in the factory of the manufacturer. Interestingly there has been amendment to rule 2(a) and rule 4(2) (a) by Notification 3/2011-NT dated 1-3-2011 to the effect that in the case of captive power plants credit can be taken even if the plants are outside the factory. [Para 39]

Payment of value and duty was made by JSWPL - JSWPL neither holding-subsidiary no job-worker : In this case Cenvat credit was taken by SISCOL during the period Sep 05 to July 06. (From 31-08-2006, SISCOL had taken over the power plant from JSWPL.). SISCOL had not paid for the value of the goods or excise duty payable thereon when credit was taken. Such payments could not be seen in the books of account of SISCOL, when credit was taken. The value of the goods and excise duty thereon were paid by JSWPL on the date on which credit was taken by SISCOL. These are two different companies. There is no relationship of one as the holding company of the other which fact existed in some of the decisions relied upon. There is no relationship of SISCOL as job-worker of JSWPL which was the fact in cases where persons not paying for the goods along with duty were allowed to take credit of duty. [Para 40]

HEADNOTE: Rule 57A of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 - Modvat Credit - Modvat - Procedural lapses cannot deny credit (substantive right) - Remanded for removal of omissions

FACT: The appellants availed Modvat credit for certain inputs used in the manufacture of their final product. The Asstt. Collector ordered reversal of credit taken on grounds that the original Gate Passes were not endorsed properly. The Collector (Appeals) rejected their appeal. Hence this appeal.

HELD: Modvat-Technicalities cannot deny a substantive right-credit admissible on removal of defects. Matter remanded for fresh decision. "........the defects referred to in the Show Cause Notices, on the basis of Modvat Credit has been denied, are remediable defects. On a query by this Bench Shri Willingdon Christian undertakes to get the defects rectified and also produce the requisite certificates from the suppliers about the fact of non-availment of Modvat Credit by them. In the circumstances, we hold that this technical requirement cannot come in the way in availment of the substantive benefit of Modvat Credit. Hence we set aside the order and remand the case back to the Assistant Collector before whom the appellants should produce the Gate Passes after rectifying the defects pointed out by the Department. The Assistant Collector may, thereupon decide the issue. So long as he is satisfied that the inputs has been received in the factory and utilised in the manufacture, modvat credit cannot be denied only on these technical aberrations."
