[Notification No. 15/94-C.E.(N.T.), dated 30.3.1994] It is seen that in a contingency where the goods were received not directly from the manufacturer but through the agency of the dealer, facility for taking modvat was taken care of by authorising the taking of MOD VAT Credit based on the invoice to be issued by the wholesaler, dealer, distributor etc. and for that reason it would appear the Government did not feel it necessary to issue any notification for acceptance of the endorsed invoices as was the case in case of Gate Passes. Even in the case of Gate Passes, a provision was earlier made for acceptance of subsidiary gate passes also. Thus, simultaneously the provision of acceptance of subsidiary gate passes and also endorsed gate passes was available. It is seen that at the time when the change over took place in the Central Excise documentation as above, there was some' confusion and some hardship and the Government issued Notification 16/94 dated 30th March, 1994 under which the endorsed Gate Pass, Subsidiary Gate Pass and certain certificates were notified as authorised documents for taking MODVAT Credit till 30th June, 1994. It would thus appear that upto 30th June, 1994 this facility of accepting endorsed Gate Pass was available along with the amended provisions in regard to taking of MODVAT Credit based on the invoices issued by the manufacturer or by the dealer. In the present case what has happened is that the full consignment as received by the dealer has been sent to the Respondents and the dealer has not issued any invoice of his own but has made an endorsement for the sale of the goods to the Respondents and sent the goods under the cover of this endorsed invoice. The question that arises is that whether in the circumstances which prevailed at the relevant time such a course was acceptable. It is observed that at the relevant time the dealers were not required to register while they were authorised to issue invoices as would be seen from Notification 15/94. In the present case what has happened is that instead of the dealer issuing invoice, he has made the endorsement in the invoice in respect of the goods he has received from the manufacturer. It is in the above context that the matter should have been examined by the learned lower authority. The learned lower authority does not appear to have examined the whole issue in depth and has held that the endorsements made later in the Gate Passes was adequate enough to give cover to the appellants for the purpose of MODVAT Credit. This, I am afraid, is not the correct way to look at things with the change of law and with the changed parameters and facilities which had been made available at the relevant time. The position should have been examined in the context of the same. This having not been done, I hold that the order of the learned lower authori ty is not proper and therefore set aside the same and remand the matter for denovo consideration of the factors set out above and after affording the Respondents an opportunity of being heard. The appeal is therefore allowed by remand.

Rule 57G of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 - Modvat credit - Invoice - showed appellants' two factories as consignees - inputs received in one factory - credit not deniable - assessee's appeal allowed (Para 7)

1. Cenvat credit of service tax paid has been denied to the factory on the ground that the invoice issued by the service provider is in the name of the registered office and not in the name of the factory. According to the Revenue, the registered office should have taken registration as in input service distributor and should have issued separate invoices to facilitate availment of cenvat credit by the factory.

2. Heard both the sides. Since the issue involved is short and both the sides were heard in detail and both the sides have no objection to decide the issue itself finally, the requirement of pre-deposit is waived and the appeal itself is taken up for final decision.

3. The learned counsel on behalf of the appellant submitted that the appellant has only one factory and therefore the question of distribution does not arise. He also submitted that it is not the case of the department, that service has not been received. He relies upon the decisions of the Tribunal in the case of CC&CE v. DNH Spinners [2010] 25 STT 295 (Ahd.-CESTAT) and Modern Petrofils v. CCE [2010] 29 STT 111 (Ahd.-CESTAT) to submit that just because credit has been availed on the basis of invoice not containing name of the factory, credit cannot be disallowed and when there is no dispute on receipt of services by the factory, credit cannot be denied on the technical ground that document is in the name of head office/registered office situated elsewhere. The learned SDR would rely upon the decisions of the Tribunal in the case of Khaitan Electricals Ltd. v. CCE [2011] 32 STT 234/12 taxmann.com 338 (Kol.-CESTAT), Philips Electronics (India) Ltd. v. CCE [2009] 22 STT 332 (Ahd.-CESTAT) and Vimal Enterprise v. Union of India 2006 (195) ELT 267 (Guj.). The learned SDR with the support of above decisions sought to submit that according to these decisions, registration of input service distributor is a must and if the input service distributor is not registered credit is not admissible.

4. After considering the submissions and records I find that the decisions relied upon by the learned SDR are not applicable to the facts of the case. In all these cases a view was taken that the input service distributor is required to be registered and the effective date of such registration was also required to be considered as held in the case of Philips Electronics (India) Ltd. (supra). In all those cases there was no dispute that input distributor was required to be registered. The dispute had arisen as to the effective date of registration, exercise of discretionary powers for allowing credit deficiencies in documents issued by the input service distributor etc. In the present case the dispute is totally different. The dispute is not as to whether the document issued by the distributor is a valid document or not. But the issue is whether the registered office of the appellant is required to be registered at all when they have only one factory and when the credit has been taken by the factory on the basis of invoices issued by service providers. There is also no indication or no allegation in the show cause notices or in the findings that appellant's factory did not receive the service. As per the position prevailing prior to 30-3-1994, when the purchaser resold inputs to third party, he would make an endorsement on the gate pass issued by the manufacturer of the input. Procedure had changed and instead of endorsement on the gate-passes, invoice was required to be produced as per Notification No. 16/94-CE(NT), dated 30-3-1994. Certain documents were prescribed for the purpose of giving credit of Modvat under the Rules. In Column No. 3 to the Entry No. 10 of the aforesaid Notification, prescribed documents were endorsed gate-passes/subsidiary gate-passes/certificates. Admittedly, gate-passes were required to be issued by the manufacturer under the procedure then prevailing and as and when the purchaser of the inputs resold inputs to third party, he would make an endorsement on the gate-pass, which would authorise the purchaser to take benefit of the credit of the duties paid on the goods. From the language of the said Notification, it is clear that benefit could be given if the documents would have been issued before 1-4-1994 and credit had been taken on or before 30-6-1994. From this, it was clear that gate-passes could be issued before 1-4-1994 and the benefit of credit could be taken on or before 30-6-1994. Transaction of sale or re-sale could take place any time prior to 30th June and on endorsement of same being made, benefit could be taken on or before 30-6-1994. The language of the Notification nowhere requires that the endorsement should also be made before 1-4-1994. [Para 1]

Therefore, gate-passes issued prior to 1-4-1994 but endorsed after that date would fall under the coverage of Entry No. 10 in the Table to the Notification No. 16/94-CE(NT), dated 30-3-1994 and would, consequently, be eligible documents for taking credit under the Modvat Scheme. [Para 3]

Assessee having only one factory or place of provision of service - Sometimes, an assessee has offices at various places but accounting is done centrally in the factory. Sometimes, there are various factories of assessee but accounting is done in main factory.

In such cases, in my opinion, if assessee has only one factory and/or one centralised registration of service tax, the HO or branches need not be registered and all Cenvat credit can be availed in the factory or place where centralised registration has been taken.

The reason is that Rule 7 of Cenvat Credit Rules reads, 'The input service distributor may distribute the Cenvat credit'. 'May' cannot be read as 'must'. It is nowhere stated that the utilisation should be only through mechanism of Input Service Distributor. A facility cannot be a compulsion.

Assessee having only one factory or place of provision of service - Sometimes, an assessee has offices at various places but accounting is done centrally in the factory. Sometimes, there are various factories of assessee but accounting is done in main factory.

HEADNOTE: Rule 57A of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 - Modvat Credit - Modvat - Procedural lapses cannot deny credit (substantive right) - Remanded for removal of omissions

FACT: The appellants availed Modvat credit for certain inputs used in the manufacture of their final product. The Asstt. Collector ordered reversal of credit taken on grounds that the original Gate Passes were not endorsed properly. The Collector (Appeals) rejected their appeal. Hence this appeal.

HELD: Modvat-Technicalities cannot deny a substantive right-credit admissible on removal of defects. Matter remanded for fresh decision. "........the defects referred to in the Show Cause Notices, on the basis of Modvat Credit has been denied, are remediable defects. On a query by this Bench Shri Willingdon Christian undertakes to get the defects rectified and also produce the requisite certificates from the suppliers about the fact of non-availment of Modvat Credit by them. In the circumstances, we hold that this technical requirement cannot come in the way in availment of the substantive benefit of Modvat Credit. Hence we set aside the order and remand the case back to the Assistant Collector before whom the appellants should produce the Gate Passes after rectifying the defects pointed out by the Department. The Assistant Collector may, thereupon decide the issue. So long as he is satisfied that the inputs has been received in the factory and utilised in the manufacture, modvat credit cannot be denied only on these technical aberrations."

Input Credit Distributor

Often invoices and bills in respect of inputs and capital goods are received at the head office while service is provided from some other place or site. In such case, the head office can distribute the credit of duty paid on such inputs and capital goods to the service provider by issuing an invoice. Such office will have to be registered with Central Excise and submit returns etc. similar to first stage dealer and second stage dealer [Rule 7A of Cenvat Credit Rules, inserted w.e.f. 1-4-2008].

HEADNOTE: Rule 57 of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 - Cenvat Credit (Modvat) - Modvat - Raw material can be transferred to another unit which can get credit - Inputs need not be used directly as per settled law, as there is no requirement of direct use if inputs are fully utilised - CE Rule 57F(2)

FACT: The appellants have their factory at Mandideep in M.P. They have another factory at Ankleshwar in Gujarat. They manufacture Cephalexin and Cephadroxil falling under Chapter 29 of CETA. Penicillin GK is the main input for the final product, which the appellants import as also procure locally. With the approval of the Assistant Collector they sent Penicillin to Ankleshwar factory direct where the same was converted into "7ADCA", which was then received at the factory at Mandideep for manufacture of the final product. They had similar approval in respect of other raw materials used in the manufacture of "7ADCA" for being sent to the factory at Ankleshwar. They were availing of the Modvat credit in respect of all the raw materials at Mandideep when "7ADCA" along with other documents was received from Ankleshwar. The Collector of CE, Indore after issuing a show cause notice and hearing the appellants, held that appellants had wrongly availed of the Modvat credit at Mandideep by deliberately suppressing the fact by not making a proper declaration of use of inputs in as much as "7ADCA" was never declared as an input. According to the Collector, in the absence of such a declaration they were not entitled to Modvat credit which could have been availed of by the Ankleshwar factory which received the declared raw materials. He therefore disallowed Modvat credit of Rs. 79,38,597.50 and also imposed a penalty of Rs. 5 lakhs.

HELD: The appellants were legally entitled to send the raw material to Ankleshwar factory and to avail of Modvat credit when "7ADCA" was received at Mandideep factory. "Since the appellant had filed the declaration the appellant was legally entitled to send the raw materials to Ankleshwar factory and avail of the credit in respect of such raw materials when 7ADCA manufactured by the appellant at its Ankleshwar factory from such raw materials was received by the appellant at its Mandideep factory."

2. Since there was no requirement to use raw material directly in the manufacture of final product the denial of Modvat credit was uncalled for and contrary to judicial pronouncements. "Since there was no requirement to use raw materials directly in the manufacture of final product the denial of modvat credit by the Collector was clearly uncalled for and contrary to judicial pronouncements which has settled this position beyond any pale of doubt."

3. There was no violation of Rule 57F(2). "We, therefore, hold that there was no violation of Rule 57F(2) which postulates that a manufacturer assessee engaged in the manufacture of final product can send the raw materials directly to a job worker, request such job worker to convert the raw materials into an intermediate product and then receive such intermediate product in his factory for manufacture of final dutiable products."

4. No justification for denying the credit because all raw materials were used in the manufacture of final product. "There is no justification for denying the credit because it was not in dispute that the entirety of the raw materials were, in fact, used in the manufacture of final dutiable product. The appellant had filed before the Collector a certificate from the Chartered Accountant certifying that the total quantity of raw materials received at Ankleshwar was used in the manufacture of 7ADCA which, in turn, was used in the manufacture of Cephalexin at Mandideep. Every ounce of the material was thus fully accounted for."

5. Appellants entitled to Modvat credit of Rs. 79,38,597.50. Penalty imposed set side. "We, therefore, hold that the appellants are entitled to the benefit of modvat credit of Rs. 79,38,597.50. For the same reason, we also set aside the penalty imposed by the adjudicating authority."

The respondent claimed Cenvat credit in respect of explosives used in the mines which was rejected by the revenue on ground that those goods were not used in the factory and, therefore, the respondents were not entitled to benefit of that credit. It is not in dispute that the assessee while making purchases in question has paid the applicable central excise duty. The only defect/lacunae in the process of availing Modvat credit was that the invoice was not marked as 'duplicate'. Rest of the particulars mentioned in that invoice are not in dispute nor its correctness is being disputed by the revenue. [Para 8]

In the instant case the assessee is the person who issues the invoice. Procedure to be observed by the manufacturer who wants to avail Modvat credit is provided by Rule 57G. The manufacturer who intends to take credit of the duty paid on inputs should file a declaration with the Assistant Commissioner having jurisdiction over his factory indicating the inputs intended to be used in the final product. Such a manufacture who has filed a declaration is allowed to take credit of the duty paid on the inputs received by him. Clause (2) states that no credit shall be taken unless the inputs are received in his factory or any other document as may be prescribed by the Central Government by notification in the Official Gazette in this behalf evidencing payment of duty on such inputs. By Notification No. 23/94, dated 20-5-1994, it was provided that this duplicate copy is the one to be used for taking credit under rule 57G and rule 57T. [Para 9]

Applying the principles laid down by the Supreme Court in various cases to the facts of the instant case, it was to be held that the amendment made in rule 57G of the Rules by insertion of sub-rule (11) vide Notification No. 7/99, dated 9-2-1999 relates to procedure for availing Modvat credit and does not effect any substantive right. [Para 35]

From the conjoint reading of rules 52A, 57G and the amendment made by Notification No. 7/99, dated 9-2-1999 by which sub-rule (11) was inserted in rule 57G, of filing of the documents for availing Modvat credit is only a procedural matter and the amendment made vide Notification No. 7/99, dated 9-2-1999 which inserted sub-rule (11) in rule 57G the position was made clear that Modvat credit should not be denied only on the ground that the documents referred to in sub-rule (2) does not strictly comply with the said rule but contains the details of payment dues, description of goods, assessable value, name and address of the factory or warehouse etc. This position has also been clarified by the Central Board of Excise and Customs by issuing a circular in exercise of its power under section 37B of the Act and made it applicable to all pending cases. [Para 36]

The submission of the revenue that the Notification No. 7/99, dated 9-2-1999 would come into effect on the date of its publication i.e., 9-2-1999 only, may be correct but the benefit of that Notification as directed by the Central Board of Excise and Customs has been extended to all the pending cases. The provision of sub-rule (2) is procedural for availing Modvat credit, the benefit of sub-rule (11) is available to the assessee. [Para 39]

22.6 A manufacturer or service provider may have head office/regional office at different place/s. The services may be received at head office/regional office, but ultimately, these will be indirectly used for manufacture or providing output service.

Similarly, a principal manufacturer (brand name owner) may send inputs to job worker who is manufacturing goods under brand name of brand name owner. These goods will be supplied by job worker to principal manufacturer. If the goods are covered under MRP valuation provisions, duty will be payable by job worker on basis of MRP. However, many of input services received by principal manufacturer are indirectly used by the job worker.

Provision has been made to avail Cenvat credit of services received and paid for at head office/regional office. Such head office/regional office can be registered with Central Excise as 'Input Service Distributor' and it can issue invoice on the manufacturer or producer or service provider or outsourced manufacturing unit [The words in italics inserted w.e.f. 1-4-2016]

Who is 'input service distributor' - As per rule 2(m) of Cenvat Credit Rules, "input service distributor" means (a) an office managing the business of manufacturer or producer of final products or provider of output service, (b) which receives invoices issued under rule 4A of the Service Tax Rules, 1994 towards purchases of input services (c) issues invoice, bill or, as the case may be, challan for the purposes of distributing the credit of service tax paid on the said services to such manufacturer or producer or provider or an outsourced manufacturing unit, as the case may be. [The words in italics inserted w.e.f. 1-4-2016].

An office of assessee (manufacturer or service provider) is 'Input Service Distributor' if it satisfies all the three aforesaid requirements. It is not that each and every office of assessee is 'Input Service Distributor' and must register. The office should be registered as 'Input Service Distributor' only if it wants to distribute. There is no law that 'distribution' is the only way of availing Cenvat credit of services received at office of assessee. There are various documents eligible for availing Cenvat credit. Invoice/challan issued by 'Input Service Distributor' is only one of the specified document.

In Jaypee Rewa Plant v. CCE (2007) 218 ELT 576 (CESTAT SMB), regional marketing office was registered as Input Service Distributor and credit was distributed to manufacturing units. In prima facie view, the distribution was held as correct.

Outsourced manufacturing unit - 'Outsourced manufacturing unit' means a job-worker who is liable to pay duty on the value determined under rule 10A of the Central Excise Valuation (Determination of Price of Excisable Goods) Rules, 2000 on the goods manufactured for the input service distributor or a manufacturer who manufactures goods, for the input service distributor under a contract, bearing the brand name of such input service distributor and is liable to pay duty on the value determined under section 4A of the Excise Act. [Explanation 4 to rule 7 of Cenvat Credit Rules inserted w.e.f. 1-4-2016]

Document eligible for Cenvat credit - As per rule 9(1)(g); 'invoice, bill or challan' issued by an 'input service distributor' under rule 4A of Service Tax Credit Rules is an eligible document for purpose of taking Cenvat credit.

In Shriram Pistons v. CCE (2012) 281 ELT 90 (CESTAT), it was held that Cenvat credit is allowable on the basis of letter issued by Head Office (as Input Service Distributor) even if not mentioned as invoice or challan, if it contains all required details.

Distribution of credit even if invoices prior to registration as ISD - There is no bar in rule 7 of Cenvat Credit Rules for distributing of credit of invoices prior to date of registration as Input Service Distributor - Beico Industries v. Hence, adjudicating authority has to apply its mind to this aspect of matter and thereafter to arrive at final conclusion.

Tribunal and Courts have consistently held that Cenvat credit cannot be denied for minor defects in Invoice.

Amal Rasayan Ltd. 1993 (68) ELT 446 (CEGAT), it was held that vital question is the receipt of inputs and their use in the manufacture of final product. The contention of the Revenue that since appellant has not made payment for purchase of the input of the manufacturer supplier, Cenvat credit is not admissible, is absurd for the reason that manufacturer supplier as per the invoices, sold the goods to the dealers and in turn dealers sold the goods to appellant in such transactions there are sale purchase transactions is involved, i.e., one from manufacturer supplier to dealers and second from dealers to the appellant. However, for taking Cenvat credit on input it is not mandatory that payment towards purchase of the input has to be made. Despite this position, Cenvat credit is admissible and cannot be disputed so long input is duty paid, received in the factory and used in the manufacture. HELD: There was no dispute that the goods in question were received by the assessee and were used in the manufacture of the final product and duly recorded in the register. The invoice issued by Swastika Pipes Limited mentioned that the goods were sold to Rameswar Das Devi Dayal, though the same were consigned to Gautam Steel Trader.

As per the definition of ‘First stage dealer’ given in rule 2(ii) of Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004, the ‘First stage dealer’ means the dealer who purchases the goods directly from the manufacturer or from the depots of the manufacturers or the premises of consignment agent of the said manufacturer or from any premises from where the goods are sold by or on behalf of the said manufacturer or from an importer or from the premises of consignment agent of such importer. In this case, Gautam Steel Trader had not purchased the goods directly from the manufacturer but had purchased the same from Rameswar Das Devi Dayal and the manufacturer’s invoice mentioned Rameswar Das Devi Dayal as the buyer, and, thus, Gautam Steel Trader cannot be called ‘First stage dealer’ within the meaning defined in rule 2(ii) of CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004.

Since Golden Steel Co. had purchased the goods from Gautam Steel Trader and Gautam Steel Trader was not ‘First stage dealer’, Golden Steel Co. would not be covered by the definition of ‘Second stage dealer’ as the term ‘Second stage dealer’ as defined in rule 2(s) of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 means a dealer who purchases goods from the first stage dealer.

In view of this, the invoice issued by Golden Steel Co. cannot be said to be a valid duty paying document for taking credit in terms of rule 9. Therefore, the Commissioner of Central Excise (Appeals)’s order permitting CENVAT credit on the basis of this invoice was not correct.

HELD: The goods, on which Modvat credit had been taken by the appellants irregularly, were consigned to the job worker. In other words the goods were not received by the appellant but by his job worker. The duplicate copy of the gate pass which had accompanied the goods contain the name of the job worker. However, the original which was sent to the appellants contains the name of the appellant, which was written after scoring out the original consignee i.e., the job worker. The adjudicating authority had given a very detailed finding to indicate that there had been manipulation of the consignee’s name in the original copy of the gate pass. But for that manipulation, the appellant would not have got the Modvat credit. In fact actual consignee was only the job worker. Further the adjudicating authority had found that there was no endorsement in name of appellant as rightly found in the duplicate copy of the gate pass in question. The adjudicating authority had observed that Modvat credit can be taken only when both the material as well as duty paying documents are received by the consignee as indicated in the gate pass. In this case, no fraudulent motive was found which could be attributed to the appellant. The appellant along with consigner have taken recourse to certain devices of expediency to avoid irksome procedures. However, when the material had not been received by the appellant and only by some job worker, taking credit on the goods received by the job worker by changing the name of the consignee in the original copy of the gate pass, was serious matter and such scant regard to rules could not be ignored. The appellant was not entitled for the Modvat credit. [Para 6]

5.1 Rule of harmonious construction - In Jagdish Singh v. Lt. Governor [1997] AIR SCW 2106 = AIR 1997 SC 2239, it was observed -

"It is a cardinal principle of construction that efforts should be made in construing the different provisions, so that, each provision will have its play and in the event of any conflict a harmonious construction should be given. Further, a statute or a rule made thereunder should be read as a whole and one provision should be construed with reference to the other provision so as to make the rule consistent and any construction which would bring any inconsistency or repugnancy between one provision and the other should be avoided. One rule cannot be used to defeat another rule in the same Rules, unless it is impossible to effect harmonisation between them. - - A construction that reduces one of the provisions to a ‘dead letter’ is not a harmonious construction as one part is being destroyed and consequently, Court should avoid such construction". - similar views in British Airways Plc.v. 8. Further, I find that that CBEC vide its Circular No. 179/13/96-CE dated 29.02.1996 has clarified that that the Cenvat Credit should not be denied to the branch office merely because the bill of entry is in the name of head office.

9. Further, I find that in the Tribunal in the case of Parekh Plast India (P.) Ltd. (supra), has observed as under:

"The tribunal's decision relied upon by ld. Advocate is clearly to the effect that the invoices, even in the name of head office, are eligible documents for the purpose of credit. INPUT SERVICE DISTRIBUTOR

In this article, the author has discussed the provisions relating to ‘input service distributor’ including amendment carried out in 2008.

Introduction

1. ‘Input service distributor’ is the beautiful and utilitarian concept introduced by the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004. In this article, we shall discuss the provisions relating to ‘input service distributor’.

Definition

2. Rule 2(m ) of the Rules defines ‘input service distributor’ as under :—

"(m)‘Input service distributor’ means an office of the manufacturer or producer of final products or provider of output service, which receives invoices issued under rule 4A of the Service Tax Rules, 1994 towards purchases of input services and issues invoice, bill or, as the case may be, challan for the purposes of distributing the credit of service tax paid on the said services to such manufacturer or producer or provider, as the case may be;"

Important criteria for input service provider

3. Important criteria for input service provider are :—

(i)It has an office as the manufacturer or producer of final products or provider of output service. In other words, an office of manufacturer of excisable goods or taxable service provider can be registered as input service distributor.

(ii)It has to receive invoices towards purchase of services. The services might have been received by one of the units manufacturing goods or premises providing services or other offices.

(iii)It can issue invoice or bill or challan for the purpose of distributing the credit of service tax paid on the services to the manufacturing unit or service providing unit.

It is to be noted that the input service provider can be registered as head office, registered office, branch, depot, regional office, zonal office, etc.

Regional marketing office was registered as input service distributor and credit was distributed to manufacturing units. It was held by the Tribunal in its prima facie view, that the distribution was in order in Jaypee Rewa Plant v. CCE 2007 (218) ELT 576 (Delhi - Trib.).

It is possible that one company may have many input service distributors.

Example

4. ABC Ltd. has three manufacturing units. Its head office has taken Fire Insurance Policy covering the manufacturing units and paid insurance premium and service tax of Rs. 10,300. Head Office can distribute the service tax paid by it to the manufacturing units and manufacturing units can take the credit on receipt of Invoice from the head office and utilise this amount like any other Cenvat credit.

Conditions

5. Rule 7 deals with distribution of credit by input service distributor. The input service provider can distribute service tax paid by it subject to the following conditions :—

(i)The credit distributed shall not exceed the amount of service tax paid by it. (Is it possible to distribute more than the credit availed?)

(ii)The credit of service tax attributable to service used in an unit exclusively engaged in manufacture of exempted goods or providing of exempted services shall not be distributed.

It is important to note that there is no requirement to distribute the credit proportionately. The input service distributor can distribute to various units as the circumstances warrants. There is no rule regarding periodicity of distribution and it is advisable to distribute monthly.

Registration

6. Input service distributors have to obtain registration from the service tax authorities. They have to apply in Form No. ST-1 and have to obtain Registration Certificate in Form No. ST-2.

Maintenance of records

7. Rule 9 of the Rules deals with maintenance of records by the input service distributor. The records maintained by it must contain the following :—

(i)Serial number and date of the document on which the Cenvat credit is availed.

(ii)Service tax registration number and name of input service provider.

(iii)Description and value of input service.

(iv)Service tax credit availed.

(v)Basis of allocation/apportionment of credit amount.

(vi)Service tax utilised for distributing the credit.

(vii)Balance credit available for distribution.

Issue of Invoice

8. After making the payment of service charges and service tax, input service distributor can avail the credit provided service received is input service and distribute it to various manufacturing units or service providing units.

Rule 4A(2) of the Service Tax Rules, 1994 deals with the issue of invoice by the input service distributor. The invoice shall be serially numbered and contain the following particulars :

(i)the name, address and registration number of the person providing input services and the serial number and date of invoice;

(ii)the name and address of the input service distributor;

(iii)the name and address of the recipient of the credit distributed; and

(iv)the amount of the credit distributed.

However, in cases where such documents could not be maintained and other sorts of documents are with the assessee by which he availed credit, then the following requirements are to be fulfilled—

u There shall be no dispute about the duty paid character of the input;

u Receipt of the goods in the factory of the assessee;

u Utilization for manufacture of the final product.

The authority, in such cases, has to satisfy the three tests, viz., integrity, dependability and relevancy as held in Kitply Industries Ltd. (supra). The Tribunal in Stelco Gujarat Ltd. case (supra) rightly held that the denial of credit on the procedural irregularity would not be justified. Eligibility of Transit sale – In case of transit sale, the Cenvat credit can be availed on basis of invoice of original manufacturer, which is eligible document under rule 9(1)(a)(i)(I) of Cenvat Credit Rules. The circulars only explain and confirm the legal provision. These are still valid as there is no change in that rule.

Intermediary dealer need not be registered - Since Cenvat credit is available on basis of invoice of manufacturer itself, the intermediary dealer is not required to issue any Cenvatable invoice. Hence, he need not be registered under Central Excise.

Invoice need not be in name of manufacturer – Tribunal has consistently held that invoice need not be in name of manufacturer, Even showing name of end user as consignee is not a statutory requirement. There is no such requirement of rule 9(1)(a)(i)(I) of Cenvat Credit Rules.

Proviso to rule 11(2) is only additional facility to registered dealer – The proviso to rule 11(2) of Central Excise Rules inserted w.e.f. 1-3-2015 is only additional facility to registered dealer. EN MAINTENANCE SERVICES

Whether garden maintenance service (With using materials/without using materials) is taxable? If yes, under which services it is taxable?

It should come under ‘Management, Maintenance or repair’ service , since that head covers both movable as well as immovable property. It does not make any difference whether it is with materials or without materials. You can claim deduction in respect of materials like plants, etc., but not in respect of consumables.

CENTRALISED OPERATIONS We are a Gas Distribution Company based at Gujarat. We are having CNG Station at various locations. We obtain excise Separate Registration of each CNG Station. Our queries are (1) Whether we are able to take CENVAT Credit on Excise Payable for Capital Goods? If yes, then whether only CENVAT credit on particular Capital goods used for a particular station only can be claimed? (2) Shall we claim excise on common pipe line which is partly used for CNG and partly for domestic gas, inspite of fact that domestic gas is not excisable goods? (3) Whether regarding the supplier invoice, the address of CNG Station has to be mentioned or not on that invoice or invoice made to Head Office address is sufficient to take Cenvat Credit?

(1) Since you have separate registration for each location, it is advisable to take separate credit only for each unit in respect of capital goods installed there. (2) Check tariff heading of pipeline. Mostly, it is 72 or 73 and, hence, does not fall within the definition of ‘capital goods’, as defined in the Cenvat Credit Rules. However, if some equipment does fall within the definition, you can take credit even if it is only partly used for taxable service. (3) It is highly advisable to mention address of CNG station in supplier’s invoice to avoid disputes and harassment from department. If this is not possible, invoice should be endorsed by HO in favour of CNG station with clear remark that these goods are for the particular unit and they have not taken any Cenvat credit at HO.

One of my clients has centralised registration. He has placed capital goods at various sites of the clients. Can the unit shift the capital goods to other sites of the clients after work at one site is completed ?

In respect of capital goods on which there was no credit taken, obviously no question arises. In other cases, if each unit is registered separately, then the first unit should pay ‘amount’ as per Cenvat credit rules and then other unit can take credit. However, in this case, since there is centralised registration, there is no problem, since there is no question of one unit paying duty and other unit taking credit. At the most, you may write letter informing department suitably (Don’t ask for permission. That will create a mess).

A unit having centralised registration is procuring inputs and input services at the sites where the work of the clients is going on. In view of the fact that the unit has taken centralized registration, will it be able to get credit of inputs and input services in the centralized office, if the billing of the supplier is addressed to this centralized office and inputs/input services are directly received at the work site? Or will the unit be required to avail service tax registration as a distributor for all these sites separately and then transfer the credit to centralized office? Here we would like to clarify that service tax registration certificate at present mentions the addresses of various sites at which work is going on.

Really, input service distributor is a facility and not compulsion. Further, Cenvat Credit Rules do not require one to one relationship. If there is centralised accounting and all records are available in HO, credit can be taken at HO. Of course, harassment from department cannot be ruled out. Hence, it is better to write a letter to the department about informing the procedure you are following.

We have branches at various places. Each branch is separately registered for purpose of service tax. In some cases, capital goods installed in one branch have to be shifted to other branch for various purposes like shortages, urgency, etc. We have received a demand that in such cases, Cenvat credit has to be reversed. Please advise.

It is true that technically, you should pay ‘amount’ while removing capital goods from one branch under ‘invoice’ and then take credit in other branch. However, practically, at operational level, such deep knowledge of service tax laws is difficult. You can argue that paying ‘amount’ in one branch and taking credit in other branch will be a revenue neutral exercise. There are many Tribunal decisions that substantive benefit cannot be lost for procedural lapses, particularly when the whole exercise is revenue neutral.

CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004 - Cenvat credit - Minor procedural lapses 23. In the case of L.M.L. Ltd. v. CCE, Kanpur, [2007] 8 STT 387 (New Delhi - CESTAT) the assessee availed MODVAT credit on the invoices issued by the dealers/traders during the period from July, 1994 to December, 1994. A show-cause notice was issued to the assessee denying the MODVAT credit on the ground that these dealers/traders were not registered dealers with the Central Excise department. Though the assessee contested the show-cause notice on the ground that these dealers/traders got themselves registered, yet the adjudicating authority confirmed the demand on the assessee and imposed penalty on the ground that addresses of the traders were different and duty paying documents did not show the required details. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals), in respect of the credit availed by the assessee on the invoices issued by the Indian Oil Corporation, allowed the appeal but in respect of other dealers/traders, denied the MODVAT credit and upheld imposition of penalty. He, however, reduced the quantum of penalty. The Tribunal held that the issue is squarely covered by the Larger Bench’s decision in the case of Kamakhya Steels (P.) Ltd. v. CCE 2000 (121) ELT 247 (Tri. - LB). The Larger Bench of the Tribunal in that case had held that minor procedural lapses like non-mentioning of the description of goods, duty paying documents number, registered number, etc., are to be condoned in view of the amendment which was done to rule 57G by Notification No. 7/99. It was also undisputed that the inputs covered under all the orders were received in the factory of the assessee and consumed by it in its factory. The Tribunal further held that from the plain reading of the Board’s Circular No. 441/7/99-CX dated 23-2-1999, it is very clear that the Assistant Commissioner should ignore minor procedural lapses as long as it is verified that inputs/capital goods have suffered duty and are being used in the manufacturing process. The Board, in the above Circular had clearly mentioned for disposal of pending cases accordingly. The Commissioner (Appeals), while disposing of the appeal, should have considered the Board’s Circular while dismissing the appeal filed by the assessee. Accordingly, the assessee demonstrated that it had received the duty paid inputs and consumed the same in its factory and, hence, it was held eligible for MODVAT credit.

CENVAT CREDIT

Input Service Distributor - Facility or compulsion

V.S. DATEY

Often, an assessee has office at a place different from the factory or place from which service is provided. Such small offices maintain only basic information. The accounting records including invoices, etc., are sent to main factory and final accounting and record-keeping is done in the main factory/office. Sometimes, office and main factory is at one place, but there are factories or places for provision of service in another places. In such cases, the input services received at main factory are recorded there itself and credit is availed in the main factory without ‘distributing’ to other factories or other places providing output services. It is learnt that in some cases, the department is taking a view that in such cases, registration as Input Service Distributor and distribution of credit is mandatory. This article examines the statutory provisions and concludes that Input Service Distributor is a facility, not a compulsion. Even ‘distribution’ of credit is a facility and not compulsion and the only requirement is that input service should be in relation to the business of the assessee.

Introduction

1. Often, an assessee has office at a place different from the factory or place from which service is provided. Such small offices maintain only basic information. The accounting records including invoices, etc., are sent to main factory and final accounting and record-keeping is done in the main factory/office.

Sometimes, office and main factory is at one place, but there are factories or places for provision of service in another places. In such cases, the input services received at main factory are recorded there itself and credit is availed in the main factory without ‘distributing’ to other factories or other places providing output services.

It is learnt that in some cases, the department is taking a view that in such cases, registration as Input Service Distributor and distribution of credit is mandatory.

The issue involved is whether such registration and/or distribution is compulsory or optional.

HEADNOTE: Rule 9 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - Cenvat credit - Documents and Accounts - Period 1-4-2005 to 31-5-2005 - Whether branch offices are not registered with service tax authorities and they do not discharge service tax liability - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, if a person discharges service tax liability from registered premises for services provided by branches, benefit of Cenvat credit on service tax cannot be denied only on ground that invoices are in name of branch offices - Held, yes [Para 7]

FACT: The assessee was registered as provider of advertisement services. According to the adjudicating officer, it had contravened the provisions of rule 9 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 inasmuch as it had availed credit on the documents which were not addressed to its registered premises but addressed to the branch office of the assessee. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the order of the adjudicating authority. Before the Tribunal, the assessee’s case was that it had taken service tax registration with the authorities on the ground that it had got centralized accounting system and centralized billing was done from the address of its registered premises.

HELD: The assessee was not having any service tax registration in respect of branch office on whose name the invoices were issued by the service provider; it had centralized billing and centralized accounting system at its registered office. Rule 4 of the Service Tax Rules, 1994 provides for an assessee to get himself registered as service provider. It was seen that in the instant case, the assessee had taken registration under the category of ‘Service provider of advertising services’.

It can be seen from rule 4(2) that an option is given to an assessee to register the premises where centralized billing or centralized accounting systems are located. It was found from the records that there was no dispute that the assessee’s office at Manipal had got the centralized billing and accounting systems. If that be so, registration taken by the assessee was in accordance with the Rules. [Para 6]

If a person is discharging service tax liability from his registered premises, the benefit of Cenvat credit on the service tax paid cannot be denied only on the ground that the said invoices are in the name of branch office. There was no dispute that the branch office was not registered with the service tax authorities and it was not discharging the service tax liability, obviously, as the assessee was discharging service tax liability on the services provided by branch. [Para 7]

It was found that though the document on basis of which the assessee had taken the service tax credit was in the name of branch office, tax was actually paid from the premises wherein the service tax registration had been taken. [Para 8]

In view of the findings, the impugned order was unsustainable and the same was to be set aside and the appeal was to be allowed. [Para 9]

A bare perusal of record would reveal that the Tribunal, having just ignored the admissions of the parties and the evidence on record, reversed the order of the Commissioner without any basis, particularly when, it in the impugned order, had noticed the fault of the assessee, that the invoices were incorrect for the purpose of taking Modvat credit, but it fell in legal error and observed that even if it was assumed that the goods had not been dispatched from premises of dealer, yet their receipts in the factory of the assessee and the other particulars relating to the quantum of duty, were not in dispute. [Para 15]

The Tribunal had also observed that if, according to the department, ‘S’ had committed certain irregularities at the time of issue of invoices, there could not be a case to penalize the assessee for someone else doing. Here, the Tribunal had fell in grave error and did not deal with the reasons recorded by the Commissioner in this relevant connection and therefore, the impugned order could not legally be sustained. [Para 16]

Again, it was not a matter of dispute that the assessee could only claim the Modvat credit on the basis of the invoices of the input duty paid goods, which had actually reached the premises of the assessee and not otherwise. Thus, the findings of the Tribunal were not only devoid of merit and misdirected but perverse and speculative as well. Therefore, the matter was to be remitted to the Tribunal for deciding the appeal afresh in the light of the aforesaid observations, admissions of the parties and evidence as relied upon by the Commissioner, so as to reach a definite conclusion, as to whether the assessee fulfilled all the requisite conditions to avail the Modvat credit, in the obtaining circumstances of the case. [Para 17]

Gate pass is a prescribed document under Rule 52A in respect of excisable goods cleared from a factory and this has been described as GP-1. Among other particulars in this form are - Name and address of the consignee, manner of transport, date and time of removal which should be shown in figures and words. All these particulars have been prescribed to ensure that the gate pass is not misused for double or treble transport of excisable goods and the gate pass is valid for transport of the goods in respect of consignees to whom these are consigned and the mode of transport etc. prescribed. We observe that the moment the goods have been received at the consignee's end the validity of the gate pass so far as the transport of the goods is concerned, can be taken to have run out and the gate pass only remains as evidence of clearance of the goods on payment of duty and the same gate pass can only be revived by following the procedure prescribed in this regard as set out under Rule 57G. Re-endorsement of gate pass in respect of part of the consignment sold is not one of the prescribed modes. For bringing the goods for MODVAT purposes, the proper course for the assessee was to have had the gate pass re-endorsed by the jurisdictional Central Excise officer after getting the particulars regarding consignment verified with reference to the gate pass if such a course had been prescribed under Rule 57G. This admittedly had not been done. We observe that a strict view has to be taken in regard to the documents under the cover of which the goods are brought in a factory for MODVAT purposes. The documents as have been prescribed are with a view to ensure that duty paid goods alone are received in the factory and it is obligatory that statutory documents as set out under Rule 57G alone are taken into consideration for the purpose of MODVAT Credit. There is possibility of misuse in case consignees on their own are allowed to endorse the gate pass after the goods have been cleared from the factory and received by them and a part of the same are resold. It would he difficult to verify the identity of the goods after the original consignment is broken up for sale. In this view of the matter we hold that the learned lower appellate authority has been in error in allowing the appeal of the Respondents. We, therefore, set aside the impugned order and allow the Departmental appeal.

Conditions for allowing CENVAT credit

6. (1) The CENVAT credit in respect of inputs may be taken immediately on receipt of the inputs in the factory of the manufacturer or in the premises of the job worker, in case goods are sent directly to the job worker on the direction of the manufacturer:

Provided that the manufacturer shall not take CENVAT credit after one year of the date of issue of any of the documents specified in sub- rule (1) of rule 11.

(2) (a) The CENVAT credit on inputs shall be allowed even if any inputs as such or after being partially processed are sent to a job worker and from there subsequently sent to another job worker and likewise, for further processing, testing, repairing, re-conditioning or for the manufacture of intermediate goods necessary for the manufacture of final products or any other purpose, and it is established from the records, challans or memos or any other document produced by the manufacturer taking the CENVAT credit that the inputs or the products produced therefrom are received back by the manufacturer, within one hundred and eighty days of their being sent from the factory:

Provided that credit shall also be allowed even if any inputs are directly sent to a job worker without their being first brought to the premises of the manufacturer, and in such a case, the period of one hundred and eighty days shall be counted from the date of receipt of the inputs by the job worker;

(b) if the inputs are not received back within the time specified under sub-clause (a) by the manufacturer, the manufacturer shall pay an amount equivalent to the CENVAT credit attributable to the inputs, by debiting the CENVAT credit or otherwise, but the manufacturer may take the CENVAT credit again when the inputs are received back in the factory.

(3) The Deputy Commissioner of Central Excise or the Assistant Commissioner of Central Excise, as the case may be, having jurisdiction over the factory of the manufacturer of the final products who has sent the input or partially processed inputs outside his factory to a job- worker may, by an order, which shall be valid for three financial years, in respect of removal of such input or partially processed input, and subject to such conditions as he may impose in the interest of revenue including the manner in which duty, if leviable, is to be paid, allow final products to be cleared from the premises of the job-worker.

Explanation I.—The amount mentioned in this rule, unless specified otherwise, shall be paid by the manufacturer of goods by debiting the CENVAT credit or otherwise on or before the 5th day of the following month except for the month of March, when such payment shall be made on or before the 31st day of the month of March.

Explanation II.—If the manufacturer of goods fails to pay the amount payable under this rule, it shall be recovered, in the manner as provided in rule 16, for recovery of CENVAT credit wrongly taken.

Explanation III.—In case of a manufacturer who avails the exemption under a notification based on the value of clearances in a financial year, the expressions, "following month" and "month of March" occurring in Explanation I shall be read respectively as "following quarter" and "quarter ending with the month of March".

HEADNOTE: Rule 57G of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 - Cenvat Credit - Modvat - Declaration within time--Benefit cannot be denied. Error in recording declaration date rectified

FACT: The Tribunal denied Modvat to the applicant for 1.4.1986 on the ground that its declaration under Rule 57G was acknowledged by the Assistant Collector on 2.4.1986. The applicant has requested for rectification of the error in the Tribunal's order because its declaration was filed on 31.3.1986 and duly acknowledged by the Superintendent.

HELD: Modvat--the applicant is eligible for Modvat for 1.4.1986 because its declaration under Rule 57G was filed with the Range Supdt. on 31.3.1986. "The Tribunal has given a finding in the impugned order that the petitioner would not be entitled to the Modvat benefit for the inputs in question for the period prior to 2.4.1986 on the ground that the declaration under Rule 57-G has been acknowledged by the jurisdictional Collector only on 2.4.1986 and under Rule 57G(2) a manufacturer who has filed a declaration under sub-rule (1) may after obtaining the acknowledgement of the Asst. Collector take the credit of the duty paid on the inputs received by him. On going through the records we find that on 31.3.1986 the petitioner has addressed a communication to the Asst. Collector purporting to be a declaration under Rule 57-G of the Modvat Rules. This was presented with the Range Supdt., Hyderabad and has been acknowledged by him on 31.3.1986. MODVAT--Detailed description in the prescribed manner of inputs is necessary to avail of MODVAT credit. "......the proforma for declaration to be filed under Rule 57G also has specific columns for the description of the final product and its Tariff classification as well as description of the inputs and its Tariff classification, besides the column to indicate the nature of the inputs whether raw material or component etc. When such is the legal position, and such is the requirement of the proforma for the declaration prescribed for the purpose, the contention of the appellants that broad description of the inputs will suffice for the purpose of availing MODVAT credit, is not tenable.'

In certain cases, direct dispatch of goods without bringing in the premises of dealer is permitted.

Direct despatch from manufacturer to final buyer, but sale is through dealer i.e. Transit sale - If whole consignment is despatched to buyer from manufacturer, Cenvat will be permissible, if name of the final buyer is shown as consignee. Applicability of proviso to Rule 11(2) of Central Excise Rules

3. Rule 9(1)(iv) of Cenvat Credit Rules states that invoice issued by a first stage dealer or a second stage dealer, as the case may be, in terms of the provisions of Central Excise Rules, 2002.

Rule 11 of Central Excise Rules makes provisions in respect of invoice issued by manufacturer.

Rule 11(7) of Central Excise Rules states that the provision of rule 11 shall apply mutatis mutandis (i.e., after making necessary changes) to goods supplied by a first stage dealer or second stage dealer.

Rule 11(1) of Central Excise Rules are applicable for removal of goods from the factory. As per rule 11(2) of Central Excise Rules, the invoice is required to contain various details like, range, classification, time and date of removal, mode of transport and registration number, rate of duty etc.

Thus the rule expected that goods should be dispatched from the godown of the registered dealer (so that time and date of removal, mode of transport etc. can be indicated in the invoice).

Thus, a registered dealer was required to bring goods to his godown and then dispatch goods to his customer under his Cenvatable invoice.

This required double transport of goods, which increased transportation costs. Hence, as a facility to registered dealer, direct dispatch of goods has been permitted vide proviso to rule 11(2) of Central Excise Rules, w.e.f. 1-3-2015.

Thus, the proviso is applicable only to invoice issued by registered dealer, who is issuing invoice under rule 9(1)(iv) of Cenvat Credit Rules.

The new proviso only provides that Cenvat credit can be availed on basis of invoice of registered dealer even in case of transit sale. Of course, Cenvat credit can be availed on basis of invoice of original manufacturer also.

3.1 Providing additional facility does not mean that earlier facility withdrawn: In UOI v. Rajasthan Spg. & Wvg. Mills 2004 (174) ELT 42 (Raj.), it was held that merely providing an alternative method or additional method for availing Cenvat Credit does not take away the entitlement to avail Cenvat credit on the basis of original document evidencing payment of duty on inputs.

In this case, the issue was relating to eligibility of Cenvat credit on basis of endorsed invoice. However, the principle is fully applicable here.

Thus, proviso to rule 11(2) of Central Excise Rules is only additional method of availing Cenvat credit on basis of invoice of registered dealer, in case of transit sale.

[Para 9] For availing the credit of duty, what is required to be established under rule 57G is that the inputs received are in fact duty paid. The procedure set out in rule 57G is to ensure that the credit is taken on the basis of duty paid documents. The bill of entry is one such document set out in rule 57G. The said rule does not require that the bill of entry should be in the name of the person claiming credit of duty. It is not in dispute that the goods imported and cleared on payment of duty by one person can be used as inputs and credit of duty can be claimed by another person by establishing that the imported duty paid goods have been received as inputs and that the importer has not taken credit of that duty. In the instant case, it was established that the duty paid goods were received as inputs, however, the credit was denied on the ground that the Bill of entry was not endorsed in the name of the appellant. Rule 57G does not require that for taking credit of duty, the bill of entry should be endorsed in the name of the claimant. In the absence of any provision regarding endorsement on the bill of entry, the credit of duty cannot be denied on the ground that the bill of entry is not endorsed in the name of the claimant. In the facts of the instant case, the evidence on record i.e., the bills of entry together with the certificates issued by excise authorities, clearly showed that the goods imported and cleared under the bills of entry on payment of duty were received and utilized by the appellant as inputs in its factory and that the importer had not utilized the credit of duty paid on the said goods. Thus, the appellant had established that the inputs received under the bills of entry were duty paid and, therefore, the authorities below were not justified in denying the credit of duty to the appellant. "8. CENVAT Credit

(c )ISSUE - Up to what stage a manufacturer/consignor can take credit on the service tax paid on goods transport by road?

COMMENTS - This issue has been examined in great details by the CESTAT in the case of Gujarat Ambuja Cements Ltd. v. CCE [2007] (6) STR 249/8 STT TRI-Delhi. In this case, CESTAT has made the following observations:—

"…The post sale transport of manufactured goods is not an input in manufacturer. The two clauses in the definition take care to circumscribe input credit by stating that service used in relation to the clearance from the place of removal and service used for outward transportation upto the place of removal are to be treated as input service. The first clause does not mention transport service in particular. The second clause restricts transport service credit upto the place of removal. When these two clauses are read together, it becomes clear that transport service credit cannot go beyond transport upto the place of removal. The two clauses, the one dealing with general provision and other dealing with a specific item, are not to be read disjunctively as to bring about conflict to defeat the laws’ scheme. The purpose of interpretation is to find harmony and reconciliation among the various provisions". (p. 127)

CCE [2007] 8 STT 152 (Ahd. - CESTAT), it was held that after the final products are cleared from the place of removal, there will be no scope of subsequent use of service to be treated as input. The above observations and views explain the scope of the relevant provisions clearly, correctly and in accordance with the legal provisions. In conclusion, a manufacturer/consignor can take credit on the service tax paid on outward transport of goods up to the place of removal and not beyond that.

The MODVAT Scheme was introduced by the Finance Minister with effect from 1-3-1986. The nature of the MODVAT Scheme is intended to be a revenue neutral. It was not the purpose to use the MODVAT to give substantial relief of excise. The shifting the effective burden of excise taxation away from inputs and on the final products is the heart of the said scheme. In short, the MODVAT Scheme allows the manufacturer to obtain instant and complete reimbursement of the excise duty paid on the components and raw materials which will result in considerable reduction in the cost of final product. The benefit of MODVAT is available only in respect of such raw material/components actually consumed in production of final goods actually sold. In the instant case, since only 50 per cent of inputs covered by the MODVAT Scheme were consumed in respect of which gate passes were obtained, MODVAT benefit available was only 50 per cent. Moreover, the issue had come up before the Tribunal in the assessee’s case for the assessment year 1987-88 where the Tribunal had upheld the deletion made by the Commissioner (Appeals).

In the light of above discussion and in the absence of additional material/evidence, the Commissioner (Appeals) was right in holding that there was no impact on the profit whether cost of raw material was debited at gross or at net of MODVAT. Therefore, the Commissioner (Appeals) had rightly deleted the said additions pertaining to the MODVAT.

The issue involved is whether such registration and/or distribution is compulsory or optional. Who is Input Service Distributor ?

2. As per rule 2(m ) of CENVAT Credit Rules, an entity is ‘input service distributor’ if it satisfies the following three conditions—

"(a )office managing the business of manufacturer or producer of final products or provider of output service,

(b )which receives invoices issued under rule 4A of the Service Tax Rules, 1994 towards purchases of input services and

(c )issues invoice, bill or, as the case may be, challan for the purposes of distributing the credit of service tax paid on the said services to such manufacturer or producer or provider, as the case may be."

The word used is ‘and’. Thus, an entity is ‘input service distributor’ only if all the three conditions are satisfied. If an assessee has office or premises which receives invoices and it does not issue any invoice, bill or challan for distributing credit of service tax, it is not ‘Input Service Distributor’.

Service Tax (Registration of Special Category of Persons) Rules, 2005 issued vide Notification No. 27/2005-ST, dated 7-6-2005 provide for registration of ‘Input Service Distributor’. Rule 2(c) of these Rules states that ‘input service distributor’ shall have the meaning assigned to it in rule 2(m) of CENVAT Credit Rules.

It is, thus, clear that the Service tax (Registration of Special Category of Persons) Rules, 2005 apply when an entity falls within the definition of rule 2(m). If the office or main factory does not issue any invoice or challan for distribution of CENVAT credit, it does not fall within the definition of ‘Input Service Distributor’. In such case, the rules in respect of registration and issue of invoice by Input Service Distributor do not apply at all.

Provision is not a mandatory requirement

3. Rule 7 of the CENVAT Credit Rules uses the words ‘Input Service Distributor may distribute credit’. ‘May’ cannot be read as ‘must’.

Rule 9(1) of CENVAT Credit Rules gives list of seven types of documents eligible for availing CENVAT credit, out of which invoice of input service distributor is one of the eligible documents. Thus, the invoice of input service distributor is not the only eligible document for availing CENVAT credit. Credit can be availed on basis of other eligible documents also.

As discussed below, distribution can be in any ratio. Thus, even if main factory is registered as ‘Input Service distributor’ it can legally allocate entire CENVAT credit to itself, which would be an exercise in futility.

Facility cannot be a compulsion

4. ‘Input Service Distributor’ is a facility provided to assessee. It is nowhere stated that it is a mandatory requirement. This ‘facility’ cannot be thrust upon an unwilling assessee.

In CIT v. Mahendra Mills [2000] 243 ITR 56/109 Taxman 225 (SC), it was observed, ‘A privilege cannot be to a disadvantage and an option cannot become an obligation’.

8. Definition of ‘input service’ as per rule 2(1) of CENVAT Credit Rules is very wide in view of the inclusive part of the definition. Any service in relation to business is ‘input service’.

The second part of the definition of ‘input service’ covers various services like advertisement or sales promotion, market research, activities relating to business, such as accounting, auditing, financing, recruitment and quality control, coaching and training, computer networking, credit rating, share registry and security.

These input services have hardly any relation with ‘manufacture’ or ‘provision of output service’.

Main factory can ‘distribute’ entire credit to itself

9. In some cases, office and main factory are situated at one place and other factories are situated at different places. In such case, if the office is registered as ‘Input Service Distributor’, it is perfectly legal to distribute all CENVAT credit to the main factory itself. Thus, registering office as ‘Input Service Distributor’ and ‘distributing’ all CENVAT credit to the main factory itself is an exercise in futility. Instead of that, the credit of services at office can be utilised in main office itself. As explained above, definition of ‘input service’ does not require any relation with ‘manufacture’ or ‘provision of output service’. CENVAT Credit Rules do not require one-to-one relationship.

What is not required in the main definition cannot be brought in through the mechanism of ‘input service distributor’.

All provisions have to be read in cohesive manner

10. Any provision in law cannot be read in isolative manner. The provision of ‘Input Service Distributor’ cannot be read in isolation of other provisions relating to CENVAT credit.

Interpretation must depend on the text and the context . They are the basis of interpretation. One may well say, if the text is the texture, context is what gives the colour. Neither can be ignored. The interpretation is best which makes the textual interpretation match the contextual. A statute is best interpreted when we know why it is enacted. With this knowledge, the statute must be read, first as a whole and then section by section, clause by clause, phrase by phrase and word by word. If a statute is looked at, in the context of its enactment, with the glasses of the statute-maker, provided by such context, its scheme, the sections, clauses, phrases and words may take colour and appear different than when statute is looked at without the glasses of context. With those glasses, we must look at the Act as a whole and discover what each section, each clause, each phrase and each word is meant and designed to say as to fit into the scheme of the entire Act. No part of a statute can be construed in isolation. Statutes have to be construed so that every word has a place and everything is in its place - RBI v. Peerless General Finance & Investment Co. Ltd. Conclusion

11. In conclusion, it can be stated as follows—

u Input Service Distributor is a facility, not a compulsion.

u CENVAT Credit Rules do not require one-to-one relationship.

u Provision of ‘Input Service Distributor’ also does not envisage one-to-one relationship.

u Any service in relation to business of assessee is his ‘input service’.

u CENVAT credit can be utilised at one place without distributing it.

u Even if distribution is done, ‘distribution’ of credit can be in any ratio. Entire credit can be allocated to one of the factories/places of provision of output services, if assessee so desires.

u The only requirement is that ‘input service’ should be in relation to business of assessee. Any relation with ‘manufacture’ or ‘provision of output service’ is not required.

FACT: The assessee was engaged in the manufacture of crushing machines and screening machines.

It availed cenvat credit on certain input services.

The Adjudicating Authority denied cenvat credit on input services.

On appeal to Tribunal:

HELD: The Adjudicating Authority has denied cenvat credit alleging that the assessee has not obtained registration as Input Service Distributor (ISD). The assessee has submitted that it has obtained ISD registration in 2008. A copy of the ISD registration is also furnished. Therefore, the disallowance of credit for the reason that the assessee has not obtained ISD registration is unjustified and requires to be set aside. [Paras 9.1 and 9.2]

The Adjudicating Authority has further denied cenvat credit stating that the invoices were raised in the address of Bangalore and Pune office and the credit has been availed in Hosur Unit. The assessee has taken centralized registration incorporating Bangalore and Pune units. In such circumstances, the revenue cannot deny the credit availed on invoices raised in the address of Bangalore and Pune unit. [Para 9.3]

The Adjudicating Authority has also denied cenvat credit on the plea that clearing and forwarding agent services are availed by the assessee outside the factory/place of removal. The definition of input service does not state that the services have to be availed within the factory. The Board Circular No. 999/6/2015-CX, dated 28-1-2015 has also clarified this point. Therefore, the disallowance of credit is unjustified. [Para 9.4]

The assessee has availed credit on debit notes which has been disallowed on plea that these are not valid documents to avail credit. Debit notes can be considered to be valid documents for availing credit when there is no dispute with regard to the service tax paid and the services consumed. In the instant case, the department does not have a contention that the assessee has not discharged the service tax on the said services on which credit has been availed. Therefore, the disallowance of credit on this ground is unjustified. [Para 9.5]

The assessee has availed cenvat credit on photocopies of invoices. The assessee has submitted that the original invoices were misplaced and, therefore, it has availed credit on photocopies. This submission does not find favour. The assessee cannot avail credit on photocopies. These are not valid documents for availing credit. Further if such practice of availing credit on photocopies of invoices is allowed, then it will lead to false claims of credit made by assessees. The claim of assessee on this ground is disallowed. [Para 9.6]

The Adjudicating Authority has disallowed credit on various input services stating that these services are not availed in relation to the activity of manufacture. The assessee has submitted that these services include services like membership charges which are paid for taking membership in industrial association, exhibition stall charges, delegate fee, sales commission, etc. According to assessee, all these services have an integral connection with the manufacture of finished products. These services were consumed to carry out the activity of manufacture effectively and also to provide export of services/goods. The Adjudicating Authority has not made adequate discussion in this regard. The assessee has submitted that it would be able to establish the nexus of the services with the output services/manufacturing activity, if it is given a further chance. Therefore, this issue requires to be remanded to the Adjudicating Authority. [Para 9.7]

In the result, the impugned order is modified to the extent of allowing the credit in respect of the services availed except on photocopies of invoices. The issue with regard to credit disallowed alleging that the services do not have nexus with the manufacturing activity is remanded to the Adjudicating Authority leaving this issue open. [Para 10]

[Para 8] In 2000, the MODVAT Rules were replaced by the CENVAT Rules by the Central Excise (Second Amendment) Rules, 2000. Basically there was a re-arrangement of the earlier rules which in substance remained the same.

It is clear that sub-rule (d ) of rule 57AA (as introduced in 2000) had merely reframed rule 57B to include all the ingredients of inputs while at the same time broadening the base not only by referring to ‘all goods’ but also by using the word ‘includes’. [Para 9]

Rule 57AC provides for the conditions for allowing CENVAT credit in respect of inputs received in the factory of the manufacturer. [Para 10]

Initially, rule 57J of the MODVAT Rules was deleted. Consequently, with the intention of re-introducing the benefit granted earlier under rule 57J, rule 57AB was introduced under the heading ‘CENVAT credit’. [Para 11]

Rule 57AB effectively duplicates the substance of rule 57J(1) and (2) and deals with a situation where inputs are received by a job worker for production of intermediate goods which are used in the manufacture of a final product. [Para 12]

In J.K. Udyog Ltd.’s case (supra), three reasons were given by the Supreme Court for holding that credit could be taken only on inputs received in the factory of the manufacturer of the final product. First, the Court held that the definition of input given in sub-rule(d) of rule 57AA was entirely different from the manner in which the said word had been expounded in the Explanation to rule 57A of the MODVAT Rules. However, there was only a re-arrangement of the several provisions of rule 57B in rule 57AA. Rule 57AA is in fact more broad based than rule 57B.

Second, the Court proceeded on the basis that under the CENVAT scheme, there was no provision similar to rule 57J of the MODVAT scheme. However, rule 57J was replaced in substance by rule 57AB. That provision was overlooked.

Another reason given by the Court in J.K. Udaipur Udyog case (supra ) for holding that the CENVAT scheme was different from the MODVAT Scheme was rule 57AC(1). However, that rule was limited to inputs received in the factory of the manufacturer and did not impinge on rule 57AB at all.

The schemes of MODVAT and CENVAT Credit are not, therefore, different and the conclusion of the Court in J.K. Udaipur Udyog that the decision in Jaypee Rewa Cement (supra ) would have no application to CENVAT Rules could not be accepted. [Para 14]

The CENVAT Rules in effect substitute the MODVAT Rules and the decision in Jaypee Rewa Cement would continue to apply. The decision in CCE v. J.K. Udaipur Udyog Ltd. (supra ) holding to the contrary, was not good law. [Para 15]

It is in fact the assessees who will be foregoing the benefit of the credit in case they choose to take the credit after a lapse of time as they will be deprived of the benefit of the MODVAT Credit due till they take the credit. In view of the above and in the absence of any specific provision in the Central Excise Rules in regard to time limit for taking MODVAT Credit, we hold that the plea of the Revenue is not maintainable in law."
