Cenvat Credit : Where there is no dispute that assessee had received input services and utilised them for providing output services, credit cannot be denied merely on ground that address of assessee was not mentioned on invoices on which credit was availed

Rule 9(2) provides for the availment of Cenvat credit by a manufacturer or provider of input/output services on the basis of the documents, which are enumerated in rule 9(1). The said documents on which credit was availed was not in dispute, inasmuch as the delivery invoices on which credit had been availed by the assessee fell within the category of ‘Invoices’ issued by a service provider. The only question was as to whether the provisions of rule 9(2) were attracted in the instant case. Provisions of rule 9(2) can be pressed into service for denial of cenvat credit to the assessee, only if the document does not contain the particulars as required. In the instant case, it was seen from the show-cause notice that only the contravention of rule 9(2) had been indicated, but it was not very clear as to what was the contravention. Proviso to rule 9(2) talks about non-mention of the particulars and the corrective action that can be taken by the jurisdictional Assistant Commissioner and the Deputy Commissioner in the absence of such details. The credit of service tax leviable under section 65 of the Finance Act, 1994 is eligible to be taken as Cenvat credit on any input services received by the manufacturer of the final product. The plea of the assessee on provisions of credit rules, invoked for denial of cenvat credit, was not at all addressed by the Commissioner (Appeals) while rejecting the appeal filed by the assessee. It could be seen from the finding of the Commissioner (Appeals) that the Commissioner had recorded that the invoices in question were received under the Service Tax Rules, 1994. As per rule 4A(1)(ii), the invoices should indicate the name and address of the person who is receiving the taxable services. There was a strong force in the contention of the assessee that the provisions of rule were very clear; it only requires person receiving the taxable services and only address where the taxable services are provided. [Para 7]

It could be seen from the impugned order that the Commissioner (Appeals) had tried to apply rule 2(1)(ii ) to deny Cenvat credit. That allegation was not made out in the show-cause notice and the finding recorded by the Commissioner (Appeals) to reject the appeal filed by the assessee, on that ground, was beyond the allegations made in the show-cause notice. [Para 8]

In sum, the assessee had made out a case for credit of service tax paid on the service to its branch offices. In view of the foregoing reasoning, the impugned order was unsustainable and was to be set aside. The appeal was to be allowed. [Para 9]

CENVAT Scheme The Cenvat Credit Rules allow credit of duty paid on (i ) capital goods used in the factory of the manufacturer of the final products and (ii) inputs used in or in relation to the manufacture of final products. There are provisions in the Cenvat Credit Rules which deny credit of duty paid on inputs and capital goods if the same are used for manufacturer of exempted final products. The Cenvat scheme enables a manufacturer to take credit of duty paid on the inputs and capital goods and utilize the same for paying duty on excisable goods manufactured by him which are called ‘final products’. If the scheme was to be limited to granting credit only on capital goods and inputs, it would be advantageous for a manufacturer to buy capital goods on payment of duty but it would be disadvantageous if he manufactured the capital goods himself by procuring inputs for the same (such as parts and components) on payment of duty as he would not be able to take credit of duty paid on such inputs because these are not inputs used for manufacturing the final products. It is clear that to obviate such a disadvantageous situation, the scope of ‘input’ has been extended to include goods used in the manufacture of capital goods, which are further used in the factory of the manufacturer. This provision has been made by way of inserting Explanation 2 to the definition of ‘input’ under rule 2(k ), of the Cenvat Credit Rules and, thus, the scheme provides for credit of duty paid on :-

(i)Capital goods used in the factory of the manufacturer of the final products;

(ii)inputs used in or in relation to the manufacture of final products; and

(iii)inputs used in the manufacture of capital goods which are further used in the factory of the manufacturer. [Para 38]

Capital goods

There are other details to the Cenvat scheme and the definition of ‘capital goods’ primarily includes machinery items; components, spares and accessories of the same; and a few other things which have been specifically added such as pollution control equipment; moulds, dies, etc.; refractories; tubes and pipes and fittings thereof; and storage tank. The moulds, dies, refractories, tubes and tank have been specifically added as they would not get classified and included as machinery items, but the rule makers in their wisdom have specifically and additionally included these perhaps considering their functional utility to the manufacturing process. By specifically including these items, credit in respect of duty paid on such items has been allowed which would not otherwise get coverage under the term ‘capital goods’. Secondly, credit of duty paid on inputs used in the manufacture of such specifically listed items has also been allowed. However, factory shed, building foundation and structures (in the manufacture of which the goods, namely, cement and steel items are used) have not been specifically listed under the definition of ‘capital goods’. [Para 39]

FACT: The assessee was engaged in the manufacture of Vinyl Chloride Monomer, Poly Vinyl Chloride, High Density Polyethylene, Mono-Ethylene Glycol, Polyester Oriented Yarn, etc. at its integrated manufacturing under known as 'H'.

During the set up of 'H', the assessee purchased the complete Single Point Mooring System [SPM system] along with anchor chain, chain stoppers, anchor piles and anchor pipes and other items such as offshore bands, half shell brackets, anode pipes, etc.

SPM system was located by the assessee outside the factory.

It availed Modvat credit of duty paid on SPM system stating that it was capital goods in terms of rule 57Q.

The lower authorities including the Tribunal disallowed the Modvat credit.

On appeal to High Court:

HELD: The Single Point Mooring (SPM) buoy is located in mid sea (Arabian Sea), off. Suvail Coast, in Magdalla Port territorial water, at a distance of approx 12 kms from tank farm. SPM is a floating platform, held in place by 6 sets of suitable mooring chains which in turn are either connected to a pile or an anchor. SPM holds a vessel through a mooring hawser. SPM has an arrangement of inbuilt pipeline system with its entry/exit points, where subsea and floating hoses connect to facilitate the transfer of cargo between the vessel and the terminal. The floating hoses are connected to the vessel's manifold. Vessel pump the cargo through these hoses. [Para 9]

The subsea hoses are connected to a hard pipe lines at the bottom of the sea. This hard pipe is in turn connected to the tank farms located within the factory premises of the assessee. Accordingly SPM is connected to the tank farm through 2 pipelines. One pipeline is used for transporting Naphtha and other petroleum products from SPM to the tank farm. The second line is used to transport Paraxylene from SPM to the tank farm. These pipelines run underwater on the sea bed for about 4.85 kms and are then buried underground for another 7.15 kms to reach the assessee's tank farm. SPM is used for unloading of imported and coastal consignments and pumping the raw materials, namely, Naptha, Paraxylene and other petroleum products through the pipe lines directly to the tanks within the factory. [Para 10]

Part of the pipelines and SPM are integrally connected with the equipments and tanks within the factory through the pipelines and instrumentation. It is necessary to run the refinery of the size in question without installation of SPM used in connection with the import of crude by giant crude tankers. [Para 11]

The Adjudicating Authority has denied cenvat credit alleging that the assessee has not obtained registration as Input Service Distributor (ISD). The assessee has submitted that it has obtained ISD registration in 2008. A copy of the ISD registration is also furnished. Therefore, the disallowance of credit for the reason that the assessee has not obtained ISD registration is unjustified and requires to be set aside. [Paras 9.1 and 9.2]

The Adjudicating Authority has further denied cenvat credit stating that the invoices were raised in the address of Bangalore and Pune office and the credit has been availed in Hosur Unit. The assessee has taken centralized registration incorporating Bangalore and Pune units. In such circumstances, the revenue cannot deny the credit availed on invoices raised in the address of Bangalore and Pune unit. [Para 9.3]

The Adjudicating Authority has also denied cenvat credit on the plea that clearing and forwarding agent services are availed by the assessee outside the factory/place of removal. The definition of input service does not state that the services have to be availed within the factory. The Board Circular No. 999/6/2015-CX, dated 28-1-2015 has also clarified this point. Therefore, the disallowance of credit is unjustified. [Para 9.4]

The assessee has availed credit on debit notes which has been disallowed on plea that these are not valid documents to avail credit. Debit notes can be considered to be valid documents for availing credit when there is no dispute with regard to the service tax paid and the services consumed. In the instant case, the department does not have a contention that the assessee has not discharged the service tax on the said services on which credit has been availed. Therefore, the disallowance of credit on this ground is unjustified. [Para 9.5]

The assessee has availed cenvat credit on photocopies of invoices. The assessee has submitted that the original invoices were misplaced and, therefore, it has availed credit on photocopies. This submission does not find favour. The assessee cannot avail credit on photocopies. These are not valid documents for availing credit. Further if such practice of availing credit on photocopies of invoices is allowed, then it will lead to false claims of credit made by assessees. The claim of assessee on this ground is disallowed. [Para 9.6]

The Adjudicating Authority has disallowed credit on various input services stating that these services are not availed in relation to the activity of manufacture. The assessee has submitted that these services include services like membership charges which are paid for taking membership in industrial association, exhibition stall charges, delegate fee, sales commission, etc. According to assessee, all these services have an integral connection with the manufacture of finished products. These services were consumed to carry out the activity of manufacture effectively and also to provide export of services/goods. The Adjudicating Authority has not made adequate discussion in this regard. The assessee has submitted that it would be able to establish the nexus of the services with the output services/manufacturing activity, if it is given a further chance. Therefore, this issue requires to be remanded to the Adjudicating Authority. [Para 9.7]

In the result, the impugned order is modified to the extent of allowing the credit in respect of the services availed except on photocopies of invoices. The issue with regard to credit disallowed alleging that the services do not have nexus with the manufacturing activity is remanded to the Adjudicating Authority leaving this issue open. [Para 10]

The appellants have their factory at Mandideep in M.P. They have another factory at Ankleshwar in Gujarat. They manufacture Cephalexin and Cephadroxil falling under Chapter 29 of CETA. Penicillin GK is the main input for the final product, which the appellants import as also procure locally. With the approval of the Assistant Collector they sent Penicillin to Ankleshwar factory direct where the same was converted into "7ADCA", which was then received at the factory at Mandideep for manufacture of the final product. They had similar approval in respect of other raw materials used in the manufacture of "7ADCA" for being sent to the factory at Ankleshwar. They were availing of the Modvat credit in respect of all the raw materials at Mandideep when "7ADCA" along with other documents was received from Ankleshwar. The Collector of CE, Indore after issuing a show cause notice and hearing the appellants, held that appellants had wrongly availed of the Modvat credit at Mandideep by deliberately suppressing the fact by not making a proper declaration of use of inputs in as much as "7ADCA" was never declared as an input. According to the Collector, in the absence of such a declaration they were not entitled to Modvat credit which could have been availed of by the Ankleshwar factory which received the declared raw materials. He therefore disallowed Modvat credit of Rs. 79,38,597.50 and also imposed a penalty of Rs. 5 lakhs.

The view seems correct for the following reasons.

The words used in rule 4A(1) of Service Tax Rules are 'invoice, challan or Bill'. Rule 11 of Central Excise Rules specified the document as 'Invoice'. This indicates that in case of service tax, specific nomenclature is not essential.

In fact, first and second proviso to rule 4A(1) uses the term 'any document, by whatever name called'. Thus, rules do envisage flexibility in nomenclature depending on trade and business practices. Different practices are followed in different trades. Nomenclature can vary from trade to trade or business to business.

As per rule 5(1) of Service Tax Rules, the records maintained by assessee including computerised data maintained by assessee in accordance with various other laws are acceptable. Thus, private documents maintained in normal course of business are acceptable. No special records or registers or change in business practices is envisaged. This also indicates that law does not envisage that trade should change its normal business practices.

As per Explanation (c) to section 67 of Finance Act, 1994, "Gross amount charged" includes payment by cheque, credit card, deduction from account and any form of payment by issue of credit notes or debit notes and book adjustment. Thus, charging of any amount by debit note and credit note has been accepted.

V S DATEY

There is controversy raging in respect of eligibility of Cenvat credit in respect of transit sale through dealer not registered under Central Excise and also through dealer registered under Central Excise. The issues discussed in this article.

Background of the issue

1. Often the end user (manufacturer consumer) purchases goods through dealer and not through the original manufacturer. If the goods are purchased by dealer and then sold on piecemeal basis, there is provision to issue Cenvatable invoice by first stage dealer and second stage dealer.

However, when entire consignment is to be sold as it is, the dealer instruct the original manufacturer of excisable goods to dispatch the goods directly to the end used (consumer manufacturer). Invoice of Manufacturers invoice is in name of dealer as the buyer. Name and address of end user (manufacturer consumer) is shown as consignee.

The end user (consumer manufacturers) avail CENVAT credit on the basis of such invoice of original manufacturer.

This is standard practice, going on at least since 1995.

In the recent budget, a proviso has been added to rule 11(2) of Central Excise Rules w.e.f. 1-3-2015, which reads as follows - "Provided also that if the goods are directly sent to any person on the direction of the registered dealer, the invoice shall also contain the details of the registered dealer as the buyer and the person as the consignee, and that person shall take CENVAT credit on the basis of the registered dealer's invoice:"

1.1 Controversy arising out of this proviso: On the basis of this proviso inserted w.e.f. 1-3-2015, a view has been expressed that the Cenvat credit cannot be availed in case of transit sale, if the intermediate buyer is not registered under Central Excise.

A view is also expressed by some assessees that Cenvat credit cannot be availed on basis of invoice of original manufacturer, if sale is through registered dealer. The registered dealer has to issue another Cenvatable invoice.

In my view, there is no such change in rules. In case of transit sale, Cenvat credit can be availed on basis of invoice of original manufacturer, even if the intermediate buyer is not registered dealer. Even if intermediate buyer is registered dealer, he need not issue Cenvatable invoice as Cenvat credit can be availed on basis of invoice of original manufacturer.

Reasons for my view are stated below.

Statutory provisions

2. Rule 9(1) of Cenvat Credit Rules prescribes that Cenvat Credit can be taken on the basis of any of the documents prescribed in that sub-rule. The relevant extract from the rule are as follows –

Rule 9(1) Documents and accounts - The CENVAT credit shall be taken by the manufacturer or the provider of output service or input service distributor, as the case may be, on the basis of any of the following documents, namely:–

(a)

An invoice issued by -

(i)

a manufacturer for clearance of— (I) inputs or capital goods from his factory or depot or from the premises of the consignment agent of the said manufacturer or from any other premises from where the goods are sold by or on behalf of the said manufacturer (II) inputs or capital goods as such

(ii)

not relevant

(iii)

not relevant

(iv)

a first stage dealer or a second stage dealer, as the case may be, in terms of the provisions of Central Excise Rules, 2002.

2.1 Invoice of manufacturer is eligible document for Cenvat credit: It can be seen that invoice issued by manufacturer for clearance of inputs or capital goods from his factory is eligible document for availing Cenvat credit, as per rule 9(1)(a)(i)(I) of Cenvat Credit Rules.

The rule does not state that the invoice should be in name of buyer-manufacturer or consumer-manufacturer. The rule even does not state that name of end user (final consumer-manufacturer) should be shown in the invoice.

Of course, it has to be 'input' or 'capital goods' of the consumer-manufacturer.

2.2 Transit Sale through dealer not registered under Central Excise: In transit sale, goods are despatched directly from place of original manufacturer to final user manufacturer (end user) though invoice is in name of the intermediary dealer.

In that case, Cenvat credit is available on basis of invoice of manufacturer under rule 9(1)(a)(i)(I) of Cenvat Credit Rules itself.

Cenvat Credit : Where three separately registered units are using a common input in continuous, interconnected and integrated process for common share, they constitute a single factory and CENVAT cannot be denied on ground that credit is being availed by one factory and material inputs are used by three factories
2006 taxmann.com 993 (New Delhi - CESTAT)[30-09-2005] Collector of Central Excise, Ghaziabad vs. Modi Tyre Factory

write off of physical stock. Accounting for income tax purpose require following of accounting standards prescribed under law. Mere diminishing of value of goods in books of account could not itself permit department for reversal of Cenvat credit [This decision was for period prior to amendment to rule 3(5B) of Cenvat Credit Rules w.e.f. 7-7-2009. However, in my view, principle applies even today if only a general provision is made in books of account]. Removal of obsolete inputs is removal 'as such' - Removal of obsolete inputs is removal 'as such' and entire Cenvat credit is required to be reversed. Mere paying excise duty on scrap price is not sufficient - Panasonic AVC Networks India Co. Ltd. v. CCE (2014) 301 ELT 624 (CESTAT SMB).

Recovery if the 'amount' not paid - If the 'amount' payable under rule 3(5), 3(5A) or 3(5B) of Cenvat Credit Rules is not paid, the same can be recovered in the manner provided in rule 14 of Cenvat Credit Rules, as if it is recovery of Cenvat credit wrongly taken - Explanation to rule 3(5B) of Cenvat Credit Rules, inserted w.e.f. 1-3-2013.

Inputs from outside godown should move under challan in prescribed form. As per Chandigarh-II Commissionerate TN No. 13/97-CE dated 17-11-1997, intimation in D-3 form is necessary within 24 hours of receipt of each consignment. Monthly stock statement should be submitted to Range Office. Cenvat credit can be taken only when entire inputs covered by an invoice are received in the factory - similar procedure in CCE, Ahmedabad II TN No. 93/2004 [179 ELT T15].

See Appendix for text of circular issued by CCE, Ahmedabad.

No assessee would like to store goods outside factory except under compelling circumstances as storage outside is open to many vagaries of nature including theft, pilferage etc. Hence, shortage of space outside factory is an exceptional circumstance, and application for storage of goods outside factory should be considered, as per guidelines of CBE&C vide Circular No. 206/40/96-CE dated 1-5-1996 - Anutone Accoustics v. CCE (2010) 250 ELT 590 (CESTAT).

Even if permission is not obtained, confiscation is not sustainable if there was no mala fide, but penalty for technical breach of law without intent to evade duty is sustainable - Sanchit Polymers v. CCE (2009) 241 ELT 240 (CESTAT SMB).

In British Biologicals v. CCE (2011) 266 ELT 217 (CESTAT), inputs were stored outside in rented premises without even reversing Cenvat credit. It was held that no demand is sustainable as situation similar to sending inputs to job worker.

In Priyadarshini Polysacks v. CCE (2014) 307 ELT 136 (CESTAT), it was held that Cenvat credit is available even if permission was not obtained for taking out inputs outside the factory.

If permission is refused, appeal can be filed, as it is adjudication order - GKN Sinter Metals v. CCE (2015) 324 ELT 153 (CESTAT).

4.2-3 Input Credit Distributor

Often invoices and bills in respect of inputs and capital goods are received at the head office while service is provided from some other place or site. In such case, the head office can distribute the credit of duty paid on such inputs and capital goods to the service provider by issuing an invoice. Such office will have to be registered with Central Excise and submit returns etc. similar to first stage dealer and second stage dealer [Rule 7A of Cenvat Credit Rules, inserted w.e.f. 1-4-2008].

4.2-3A Distribution of credit by warehouse of manufacturer

A manufacturer may have central warehouse from which he may be distributing inputs to his various factories.

The case of the assessee was that TISCO did not supply original challans but only gave the carbon copies and same must be regarded as original within meaning of rule 57G. The appellate authority after considering various pieces of evidence had recorded a categorical finding in its order that it was incorrect to claim by the assessee that TISCO only issued carbon copies. The Tribunal in its finding observed that there were other manufacturers also who were receiving original challans issued by the stockyards of TISCO. [Para 3]

In the wake of the aforesaid findings, it was not possible to conclude that carbon copy was required to be regarded as original copy as per the claim made by the assessee.

A perusal of the provisions of the rule 57G shows that in order to claim Modvat credit, the original copy of the invoice is required to be produced. There is no provision for granting Modvat credit on the basis of carbon copy. If it is to be presumed that carbon copy in a case like the one in hand could be treated as original, then the finding of fact by the appellate authority or Tribunal has to be on the record. In the instant case, the finding of fact was against the dealer that TISCO did not issue invoice on a carbon copy so as to be treated as original for the purpose of rule 57G. The contention of the assessee that carbon copy had been properly verified and defaced was not impressive as in the instant case adjudication had to be only on the question of law. No merit was found in the contention raised by the assessee. Moreover, laying down a blanket principle permitting Modvat credit on carbon copy may result into setting up of false claims. On such a possibility of availing Modvat credit by many persons against one transaction would not be ruled out which will be highly damaging to the revenue. [Para 4]

Therefore, on the facts and circumstances of the case, the Tribunal was right in disallowing credit for Modvat on carbon copy of challans furnished by the assessee evidencing payment of duty. [Para 5]

Background

1. In industries like pharmaceuticals and agro-chemicals many times near-about expired goods, defective goods or damaged goods (for the sake of convenience let us say "defective goods") are sent again by various marketing depots (not registered under excise) for reprocessing. Usually it happens that the original goods have been manufactured by let us say factory A, B and C but the defective goods are returned to only one factory, let us say factory D for reprocessing. This is so because it will be impractical to send the defective goods for reprocessing to the very same factory which had manufactured the original goods due to logistical costs as well as difficulties in identifying them on one-to-one basis.

In such scenario, only document available will be copy of excise invoice issued by the original factory. Had the defective goods been returned to the same factory, manufacturer could have easily claimed CENVAT credit on the basis of originally issued invoice (as the excise invoice was issued by the same factory). However, here the case is different. Factory D wants to claim CENVAT credit of returned defective goods on the basis of excise invoice issued by other factories.

Critical Issues

2. Following critical issues arise in this set-up:

2.1 Whether CENVAT credit can be claimed by factory D when the invoices on the basis of which credit will be claimed has been issued by factory A, B and C ?

2.2 W.e.f. 11-07-2014, third proviso has been added to rule 4(1) of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004 which provides that credit cannot be claimed after a period of six months from the date of issuance of any document (in our case excise invoice) on the basis of which credit is claimed. In our case, as we are dealing with near-expired or defective goods, in all likelihood excise invoice issued by original manufacturer would have been dated beyond statutory period of six months. Issue is whether the third proviso will apply to the present case ?

2.3 What are the procedures one needs to follow to claim the said credit ?

3. Legal Analysis

3.1 To answer the first question, i.e., whether factory D can avail CENVAT credit on the basis of invoices issued by factory A, B and C for defective goods which are received back, one has to refer to rule 16 of the Central Excise Rules, 2002. Relevant extract is reproduced below for ready reference:

"Rule 16. Credit of duty on goods brought to the factory.—(1) Where any goods on which duty had been paid at the time of removal thereof are brought to any factory for being re-made, refined, re-conditioned or for any other reason, the assessee shall state the particulars of such receipt in his records and shall be entitled to take CENVAT credit of the duty paid as if such goods are received as inputs under the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2002 and utilize this credit according to the said rules.

(2) If the process to which the goods are subjected before being removed does not amount to manufacture, the manufacturer shall pay an amount equal to the CENVAT credit taken under sub-rule (1) and in any other case the manufacturer shall pay duty on goods received under sub-rule (1) at the rate applicable on the date of removal and on the value determined under sub-section (2) of section 3 or section 4 or section 4A of the Act, as the case may be.

[Explanation.—The amount paid under this sub-rule shall be allowed as CENVAT credit as if it was a duty paid by the manufacturer who removes the goods.]

3.2 Careful reading of above rule provides that CENVAT credit will be available of any goods on which duty has been paid and are brought to any factory for re-making, refining, re-conditioning or for any other reason as inputs. Thus, only condition to be fulfilled for claiming credit is that duty should have been paid on said goods. It is not necessary that goods should be received back in the same factory. It can be received in any factory. Further, goods can be brought back for reprocessing under rule 16 even if shelf life has expired (CCE v. Rako Agrochem (P.) Ltd. 2010 (260) ELT 479 (Trib. - Delhi)). Thus, credit can be claimed of goods received by factory D on the basis of invoices issued by original manufacturers. One may also refer to Board's Circular 607/44/2001-CX, dated 13-12-2001 which confirms the above view. Thus, CENVAT credit can be claimed on basis of manufacturers invoice available with depot to the extent of quantity received by factory D.

FACT: The assessee availed Cenvat credit of service tax paid for GTA service availed by it for outward transportation of the final product from factory to the buyer’s premises during the period February to September, 2005. The revenue denied the Cenvat credit and imposed penalty under rule 15. The Commissioner (Appeals) set aside the penalty and sustained the remaining part of the order.

On appeal :

HELD: During the period of dispute, the assessee availed GTA service for outward transportation of liquefied gases (final products) from its factory to buyers’ premises. These gases were to be maintained in liquid form at sub-zero temperatures and, hence, cryogenic tanks were used for their storage. These cryogenic tanks containing liquefied gases were mounted on goods transport vehicles belonging to GTA who transported the goods from the factory to the buyers’ premises. The liquids were transferred into cryogenic tanks installed in the customers’ premises which, in some cases, also belonged to assessee and the customer paid rent in such cases. In all cases, the freight for the transportation of the goods was paid by the assessee and said amount was included in the assessable value of the goods for the purpose of payment of duty. In other words, duty was paid on ‘FOR destination’ basis. This fact was evident from the invoices available on record. A reading of a sample agreement entered into between the assessee and one of its customers showed that the ownership of the goods and the property therein vested with the assessee up to the point of delivery of the goods to the customer. On these facts, it had to be held that the conditions laid down in the Board’s Circular No. 97/8/2007, dated 23-8-2007 were fulfilled by the assessee and, therefore, the benefit of CENVAT credit is liable to be allowed to it in respect of GTA service availed for outward transportation of liquefied gases from the factory to the buyers’ premises during the period of dispute. Rule 57G clearly shows that the credit of duty can be taken on inputs by establishing that the duty has been paid on the said inputs on the basis of documents such as invoice, AR-1, Bill on Entry, etc. In the instant case, it was not in dispute that the appellant had received imported shredded steel scrap from ‘E’ Ltd. on which countervailing duty had been paid by ‘E’ Ltd. It was also not in dispute that ‘E’ Ltd. had not taken credit of the duty paid on shredded steel scrap which was given on loan to the appellant. It was also not in dispute that the appellant had used the said shredded steel scrap taken on loan from ‘E’ Ltd. as inputs in its factory. The certificate issued by a Superintendent of Central Excise to the effect that ‘E’ Ltd. had not taken credit of duty paid on the said shredded steel scrap, was not doubted by the Excise authorities. Similarly, the certificate issued by another Superintendent to the effect that the quantity of shredded steel scrap received by the appellant from ‘E’ Ltd. had been used as inputs in the factory of the appellant, was also not doubted by the Excise authorities. In these circumstances, the appellant had established that the credit of duty on receipt of imported shredded steel scrap from ‘E’ Ltd. had been taken in accordance with law. [Para 9]

For availing the credit of duty, what is required to be established under rule 57G is that the inputs received are in fact duty paid. The procedure set out in rule 57G is to ensure that the credit is taken on the basis of duty paid documents. The bill of entry is one such document set out in rule 57G. The said rule does not require that the bill of entry should be in the name of the person claiming credit of duty. It is not in dispute that the goods imported and cleared on payment of duty by one person can be used as inputs and credit of duty can be claimed by another person by establishing that the imported duty paid goods have been received as inputs and that the importer has not taken credit of that duty. In the instant case, it was established that the duty paid goods were received as inputs, however, the credit was denied on the ground that the Bill of entry was not endorsed in the name of the appellant. Rule 57G does not require that for taking credit of duty, the bill of entry should be endorsed in the name of the claimant. In the absence of any provision regarding endorsement on the bill of entry, the credit of duty cannot be denied on the ground that the bill of entry is not endorsed in the name of the claimant. In the facts of the instant case, the evidence on record i.e., the bills of entry together with the certificates issued by excise authorities, clearly showed that the goods imported and cleared under the bills of entry on payment of duty were received and utilized by the appellant as inputs in its factory and that the importer had not utilized the credit of duty paid on the said goods. Thus, the appellant had established that the inputs received under the bills of entry were duty paid and, therefore, the authorities below were not justified in denying the credit of duty to the appellant. [Para 10]

Conclusion 4. The Finance Act, 2008, has modified and rationalised the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004 and removed some anomalies. These amendments would significantly reduce the uncertainty in relation to utilisation of credit and would also solve the issue of attribution of common credits to a large extent. There are, however, certain open issues which are required to be addressed on priority. For example, issues like how a trading activity is to be recognised and valued - whether or not as an exempted service or how the opening balance of the CENVAT Credit is to be recognised in the new attribution formula. There are other such issues as well. It is hoped that the CBEC would come out with appropriate clarifications on these open issues to ensure a uniform application of the amended rules across the country.

The material on record clearly discloses that the dealer who has issued the invoice has shifted the premises and that the premises from where the invoices are issued are the premises where the dealer did not have any office or business activity going on. However, there is no denial of the fact that the inputs which were procured by the assessee are duty paid and they were received and consumed by the assessee in the factory premises. The assessee is required to give all the particulars of the goods procured by it and the details of the duty paying documents. The invoice produced by the assessee contains all the necessary particulars. The authority has not recorded any finding that there is no such dealer in existence or that no inputs are supplied by him or that no duty is paid on such inputs. There is also no finding that the inputs are not received in the factory premises or same are not used in the manufacturing process. In absence of any such finding and all those facts having been established, the Tribunal held that the benefit of Cenvat credit cannot be denied. In that view of the matter, there is no justification to interfere with the well-considered order passed by the Tribunal. [Para 3]

FACT: The assessee, a 100 per cent export oriented unit (EOU) was granted permission for manufacturing ship building and the services of ship repairs/refit within the private bonded warehouse as per Letter of Permission (LOP) issued by the Development Commissioner. It fabricated a dry dock for manufacturing ship and repair services.

It availed cenvat credit on input services, input and capital goods used for fabrication of the dry dock amongst others. It utilised cenvat credit towards the output services mainly repair services and export of the goods and claimed refund of unutilised cenvat credit under rule 5.

The adjudicating authority denied the cenvat credit on input services, inputs and capital goods a on the ground that the final product 'ship' was classified under Central Excise Tariff Heading 8901 chargeable to nil rate of duty and, therefore, they were not eligible to avail cenvat credit for manufacturing of the exempted final product. It had further been alleged that the assessee availed the cenvat credit wrongly on the basis of ISD invoices, issued by its Head Office, whose name was not mentioned in LOP. Input service credit was denied mainly on the basis that the input service credit availed on the input services was shown in ER-1 return instead of ST-3 returns. It was also alleged that the assessee availed cenvat credit on the capital goods fixed with earth.

On appeal:

HELD: Cenvat Credit on dry dock

The definition of 'input service' under rule 2(l) precisely covers any service used by a provider of taxable service for providing an output service, any service used by a manufacturer in or in relation to manufacture of final product and inclusive part of the definition, services used in relation to setting up, modernisation, renovation or repair of a factory, premises of a provider of output service or an office relating to such factory or premises, etc. The expression 'any service' read with 'for providing an output service' would cover wide encompass of the definition of input service. The Supreme Court in the case of Indian Chamber of Commerce v. CIT AIR 1976 SC 348 observed that the expression 'for' has to be interpreted as 'for the purpose of'. Cenvat credit availed on input service, input and capital goods for setting up dry dock would be allowed for providing output service namely repair/refit service. This is also covered in the inclusive part of the definition of 'input service'. Hence, the finding of the adjudicating authority, that the appellant is exclusively engaged in the manufacture of exempted final product 'Ships' and Cenvat credit on input, capital goods is inadmissible, cannot be sustainable. [Para 7]

The revenue denied credit on the grounds that shared service center was not registered as Input Service Distributor and that the ISD invoices were not valid documents as they did not contain the information as required under rule 4A(2) of the Service Tax Rules, 1994. The Tribunal held that the credit was taken by the assessee almost after more than two months of applying for centralized registration and it showed that the revenue had enough time to take a decision. Thereafter, the application was wrongly rejected and, later restored, based on the clarification issued by the Board. As regards other defects, they were mainly procedural and rectifiable. Further, the effective date of validity of the registration certificate is also required to be considered in terms of the statute. It is also necessary for the Commissioner to decide whether the defects are rectifiable and if yes, have been rectified. 5. The assessee purchased bottles of country spirit from the licensees who were engaged in the manufacture and supply of country liquor in sealed bottles pursuant to the license issued by the competent authority of the State Government under the provisions of the M.P. Excise Act, 1915 and the Rules framed therein. The rectified spirit was manufactured by the process of distillation in the distillery. It was blended in the warehouses, bottled, sealed, labelled and was supplied to the retail contractors. The assessee was granted a bottling license in respect of the excise year 2005-06 for supply in respect of the areas mentioned therein. Service tax was demanded from the assessee for activity of bottling of liquor as packaging activity under section 65(76b). The assessee challenged the validity of said section in writ petition. In the course of hearing, the assessee contended that the Division Bench in Vindhyachal Distilleries (P.) Ltd. v. State of MP [2006] 5 STT 254 (MP) had not appropriately considered the decision rendered in case of Som Distilleries & Breweries (P.) Ltd. v. State of MP 1997 (1) JLJ 319 and various other aspects which deserved consideration. The Division Bench thought it apposite to refer the matter to a Larger Bench referring the question as to whether bottling of liquor amounts to manufacture of liquor or only packaging so as to attract service tax.

The High Court held that on a scrutiny of the definition of ‘packaging activity’, it is quite clear that packaging activity means packaging of goods including pouch-filling, bottling, labelling or imprinting of the package but the definition does not stop there, as the provision expressly shows that it does not include any packaging activity that amounts to manufacture within the meaning of clause (f) of section 2 of the 1944 Act. In Circular No. 249/1/2006, it was mentioned that as alcohol beverages are not covered under the Central Excise Law, the production of beverages would not fall within the meaning of the term ‘manufacture’ as conceptualized under clause (f) of section 2. The Board re-examined the matter in detail after receipt of the response and issued Circular F. No. 249/1/2006-CX.4, dated 27-10-2008 which relates to levy of service tax on production of alcoholic beverages on job work basis.

As per High Court, the basic aspect of manufacture as contained in section 2(f) conveys that the term ‘manufacture’ would include ‘any process incidental or ancillary with the completion of manufactured product’. The definition clause further expands the scope of manufacture to include certain goods which are specified in the section. The first limb of the inclusive definition of the term ‘manufacture’ under section 2(f) has a very wide connotation. As the definition clause lays down an inclusive facet, the term ‘manufacture’ has to be construed in a natural and plain manner and would include any process incidental or ancillary to the completion of a manufactured product. Keeping in view the context in which the term ‘manufacture’ has been used, it would take in its fold the incidental or ancillary process in the manufacture or finishing of any manufactured product. It does not leave any room for doubt that an allied process should be an integral and inextricable part of manufacture for completeness and presentability of the manufactured product.

Issue Involved

Whether unconfirmed demand can be set-off against unconfirmed refund claim ? HELD: It is seen that vide Order-in-original No. 44/R/2007, the Assistant Commissioner sanctioned the entire amount of refund sought by them. In other words, the Assistant Commissioner sanctioned the refund of Rs.11,79,720. Having sanctioned the entire amount as refund, the Assistant Commissioner, recording that Rs.11,18,182 availed and utilised by the assessee was not found admissible on the ground of its availment on the strength of improper documents under rule 9 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, went ahead and deducted Rs.11,18,182 from the sanctioned amount.

In this regard, it is pertinent to state that while confirmed demand can be adjusted from the amount of refund, there is no provision to adjust unconfirmed demand from the amount of refund.

There has been no show cause notice given to the assessee for showing cause as to why the cenvat credit amount of Rs.11,18,182 (adjusted from the amount of refund sanctioned) was inadmissible to them and how the same was recoverable under what provision of law and how it was not hit by time bar inspite of having been taken in the year 2005-06.

Even if the corrigendum issued on 17-7-2007 is attempted to be treated as a show cause notice, the said corrigendum falls fatally short of the requirement of a notice under section 73 of the Finance Act, 1994 inasmuch as the said corrigendum does not even mention section 73 ibid anywhere at all and it also does not contain any grounds to allege as to how the recovery, even if the said credit was held to be inadmissible, was not hit by time bar. Indeed the said corrigendum nowhere requires the assessee to show cause as to why the said amount should not be held inadmissible and why / how the same is recoverable without being hit by time bar. It merely stated that the said amount appeared to be not admissible to them and then straightaway called upon the assessee to show cause as to why the refund claim should not be rejected to the extent of Rs. 11,18,182. [Para 2]

While it is arguable that the amount of Rs. 11,18,182 taken as cenvat credit on the strength of the document received by the Head Office of the assessee is clearly admissible as has been held in several cases of the assessee themselves, in the instant case, this point is beside the issue. [Para 3]

Having sanctioned the full amount, there was no legal authority to adjust the amount of Rs. 11,18,182 as the same cannot be held to be a confirmed demand. [Para 4]

In view of the above, the impugned order was set aside and refund of the remaining amount of Rs. 11,18,182 was granted alongwith applicable interest. [Para 5]

However, the adjudicating authority rejected said claim of the assessee and confirmed the demand along with interest and penalty. Appeal of the assessee before the Commissioner (Appeals) was allowed.

On appeal : HELD: It was an admitted fact that the lorryloads of HR Coils which were received at the assessee's factory were weighed on its weighbridge and the net weights of the materials were recorded in the ‘HR Coil receipt register' maintained by the assessee. Often these weights were found to be less than the quantities mentioned in the corresponding invoices. In some cases, the weight entered in the said register was higher than that indicated in the invoice. In both the cases, the MODVAT/CENVAT credit was availed of the duty paid on the materials as indicated in the invoices. These facts, noted by the lower appellate authority, were also not in dispute. The only dispute was with regard to the credit availed on the differential quantity of input where the weight of material entered in the material receipt register was less than that mentioned in the corresponding invoice. According to the revenue that differential quantity of input was not received in the factory and was not used in the manufacture of the final product and, hence, was not eligible for the MODVAT/CENVAT credit as per the relevant rules. According to the assessee, the variation in the weight was on account of two different weighbridges having been used for weighing the materials, one at the supplier's end and another in its own factory. These weighbridges were of different capacities and their tolerance limits worked out to be 0.075 per cent to 0.1 per cent. The actual shortage of material, as found on comparison of the invoices with the ‘HR Coil receipt register', was from 0.02 per cent to 0.04 per cent only, which variations were within the abovesaid tolerance limit. These facts pleaded by the assessee and accepted by the lower appellate authority had not been disputed by the revenue. The contention of the revenue was that the rules did not permit any tolerance limits of weighbridges to be taken into account in the determination of admissibility of the MODVAT/CENVAT credit. A similar contention of the revenue was considered by the Larger Bench in the case of CCE v. Bhuwalka Steel Industries Ltd. [2010] 24 STT 436 (Chennai - CESTAT) wherein it was held that minor variations arising due to weighment on different machines will have to be ignored, if such variations are within tolerance limits. [Para 6]

In the instant case, the variations due to weighment on different weighbridges, undisputedly, were only from 0.02 per cent to 0.04 per cent and were within tolerance limits prescribed under the Standards of Weights & Measures Act and the Standards of Weights & Measures (General) Rules, 1987 and, hence, could be ignored as held by the Larger Bench in the above case. As it was not the case of the revenue that the so-called differential quantity of HR Coil was lost in the transit or had been diverted or that it was not duty paid, it was to be held that the entire quantity of the material covered by the invoices was received in the assessee's factory and was used in the manufacture of the final product and, therefore, credit of the duty paid on such quantity would be admissible to it. [Para 7]

Therefore, the decision of the Commissioner (Appeals) was to be sustained and the instant appeal was to be dismissed. [Para 10]

Authority failed to appreciate the difference between a civil appeal and a SLP filed before the Supreme Court. The civil appeal is a statutory appeal provided under the law and the decision of the Apex Court in such civil appeal is binding and the order of the Tribunal, which was appealed against merges with the decision of the Supreme Court. The same is a binding precedent for other lower Courts to follow. The observation of the Adjudicating Authority to the contrary is devoid of legal merit. [Para 10] Having considered the findings of the Adjudicating Authority and on perusal of the decision of the Tribunal in the case of Apitco Ltd. (supra) as affirmed by the Supreme Court one finds that the impugned order is devoid of merit in so far as it relates to tax liability of the assessee with reference to various works carried out by it for which consideration was paid by the Government through grants-in-aid. [Para 11]

The project works assigned to the assessee are in the nature of various welfare activities carried out by the Government in public interest. These are counseling, re-training and redeployment of rationalized employees of Central Public Sector Enterprises and Entrepreneurship Development Programme with reference to production of specific products, skill development training programme through Science and Technology, etc. The assessee was to submit full records of the expenditure with reference to each project to the concerned Ministry. Any surplus of the amount, given as grant should be returned to the Government. The decision of the Tribunal in the case of Apitco Ltd. (supra) is squarely applicable to the facts in the instant case. Therefore, the assessee was not liable to pay service tax in respect of these activities carried out, by using the grants-in-aid given by the various Ministries/departments of the Government. [Para 12]

With reference to demand created against the assessee on the ground that instead of paying service tax on the gross amount, the assessee paid service tax by treating the gross amount as cum-tax-receipt inclusive of tax, the assessee submitted that the invoices raised are inclusive of taxes. In terms of section 67(2) of the Finance Act, 1994, it is entitled for calculating the tax by treating the amount as inclusive of tax. The Adjudicating Authority did not give any detailed finding for demanding such short levy. He simply reproduced a case law, which states that section 67(2) will be applicable only in cases where the gross amount includes service tax. Though the assessee claimed in the appeal that the invoices indicated that the amount is inclusive of service tax, no evidence is submitted to support such contention. As such, the same requires verification of the actual invoices by the jurisdictional Adjudicating Authority. If the invoices issued during the relevant time specifically indicated that the amount is inclusive of service tax, then the benefit of section 67(2) is available to the assessee. [Para 13]

Regarding denial of cenvat credit, the assessee pleaded that such denial is only on the ground that the invoices were not in the assessee's name but were not in the name of branch/head office. This cannot be the reason for denial of credit. There is no allegation or finding to the effect that the input services were not received by the assessee or the said services were not covered under the scope of eligible input services in terms of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004. In such situation, the denial of credit only on the ground that the address of branch office or head office was mentioned instead of assessee's address cannot be the ground for denial of otherwise eligible cenvat credit. [Para 14]

1999 taxmann.com 1062 (CEGAT- NEW DELHI)[09-04-1999] Modipon Ltd. vs. Collector of Central Excise, Meerut

The assessee had set up a petrochemical complex for manufacture of naphtha based on petrochemical products.

For the purpose of meeting its requirement of electricity and steam, a power plant was set up by the assessee in a joint venture with HPLCL and power agreement for a period of 20 years was signed between the assessee and HPLCL. In terms of this agreement, the assessee was required to supply Naptha, as such, or partially processed Naphtha (CLP) and start up fuel free of cost to HPLCL through pipeline for generation of electricity and steam, which would be returned to the assessee for use in the manufacture of its final products. As per the terms of the power agreement, the assessee was required to pay conversion charges to HPLCL for carrying out the aforesaid operation. The land on which the power plant was situated had been assigned by the assessee to HPLCL for a period of 20 years. The power plant was situated within the factory complex. Cenvat credit would be available on naphta used as input for generation of electricity. The Superintendent informed the assessee that Cenvat credit on Naptha used for generation of electricity and steam by the power plant would not be allowed.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) held that the power plant was under the ownership of a different company, HPLCL, and the land on which the power plant was situated was assigned by the assessee to HPLCL by way of a deed of assignment and, as such, it no more remained the part of the factory premises of the assessee; that the factory of the assessee and the power plant of HPLCL were in two separate premises; that the Modvat credit was permissible only in respect of the duty paid on the inputs used for generation of electricity or steam used for manufacture of the final product or for any other purpose within the factory of production; and that since the input was being used for generation of electricity or steam outside the factory of production, Modvat credit was not available.

Thereafter, the Commissioner issued a show-cause notice to the assessee raising duty demand.

What is the import of the words "reserve the right of disposal" ? Please clarify. The expression "reserves the right of disposal" as used in section 23(2) of the Sale of Goods Act, 1930 means "ownership", i.e., "right to sell/dispose". If the property in goods passes onto the buyer at the factory gate, i.e., seller no longer has the right to dispose of the goods as he likes, then credit is available only upto the factory gate.

However, if the seller retains the right to dispose of the goods till delivery, i.e., the property passed onto the buyer at buyer's premises (FOR sales) and the transit risk is of the seller, then the credit would be available upto the buyer's premises.

Scheme : Under the Cenvat Credit Scheme a manufacturer of excisable goods is allowed to take credit of excise duty paid on inputs and capital goods used in the manufacture of excisable goods and utilize such credit for payment of excise duty on final products manufactured by him. [Para 36]

Rule 4(4) - Credit only by person paying value/duty : There is no specific provision in the Rules to the effect that credit can be taken by a manufacturer only if duty is paid by him to the supplier of goods. There is a provision in rule 4(4) to the effect that CENVAT credit in respect of capital goods shall not be allowed in respect of that part of the value of capital goods which represents the amount of duty on such capital goods, which the manufacturer claims as depreciation under section 32 of the Income-tax Act, 1961. So prima facie it would appear that the person who is paying for the value of goods and duty thereon is relevant for taking credit. [Para 38]

Receipt in factory : On the other hand definition of capital goods as given in rule 2 (a) and the rule 3 (1) and rule 4 (2) (a) allowing taking of credit are clear enough that credit is to be taken on capital goods received in the factory of the manufacturer. Interestingly there has been amendment to rule 2(a) and rule 4(2) (a) by Notification 3/2011-NT dated 1-3-2011 to the effect that in the case of captive power plants credit can be taken even if the plants are outside the factory. [Para 39]

Payment of value and duty was made by JSWPL - JSWPL neither holding-subsidiary no job-worker : In this case Cenvat credit was taken by SISCOL during the period Sep 05 to July 06. (From 31-08-2006, SISCOL had taken over the power plant from JSWPL.). SISCOL had not paid for the value of the goods or excise duty payable thereon when credit was taken. Such payments could not be seen in the books of account of SISCOL, when credit was taken. The value of the goods and excise duty thereon were paid by JSWPL on the date on which credit was taken by SISCOL. These are two different companies. There is no relationship of one as the holding company of the other which fact existed in some of the decisions relied upon. There is no relationship of SISCOL as job-worker of JSWPL which was the fact in cases where persons not paying for the goods along with duty were allowed to take credit of duty. [Para 40]

Thus, any item which is covered by the list of the items mentioned in rule 2(a) of the Cenvat Credit Rules, except for office equipment or office appliances, and is used in any manner in the factory of the manufacturer of the final products, would be covered by the definition of the capital goods and, accordingly, would be eligible for Cenvat credit. There is absolutely no requirement that the capital goods at the time of receipt must be owned by manufacturer or that the same would cease to be capital goods, if they are installed in the factory and become fixed to earth. In fact, most of the capital goods the machinery, equipment or instruments covered by Chapters 84, 85 and 90, pipes and tubes, pollution control equipment refractories, and storage tanks are required to be installed and after installation, the same put together constitute a manufacturing plant, which is fixed to earth structure. Just because after being installed in the factory, the capital goods put together become a plant which is fixed to earth structure, the Cenvat credit cannot be denied on the basis that the plant which is fixed to earth structure, is not excisable. This preposition of the Department is, in fact absurd, as there is no such condition in rule 2(a) for capital goods.

For capital goods Cenvat credit, the items must be among those mentioned in this rule and should have been used in the factory of the manufacturer and how the items are not used relevant. The words used in rule 2(a) are "used in the factory of manufacturer of the final product" not "used in the manufacture of final product". Therefore, once any item received in the factory is 'capital goods' in terms of Rule 2(a) of the Cenvat Credit Rules, and is used in the factory, the manufacturer would be entitled to Cenvat credit of excise duty paid in respect of the same.

If the logic of the Commissioner in the impugned order is accepted, no capital goods Cenvat credit can be allowed in respect of any item of capital goods enumerated in rule 2(a) of the Cenvat Credit Rules, as all the items - various items of machinery covered under Chapters 84, 85 and 90 of the Tariff, pipes and tubes, tanks, pollution control equipments refractories, etc., have to be installed in the factory before being put to use and after installation, the same would become fixed to earth plant. Reading the impugned order gives an impression that the same has been passed without any application of mind.

Therefore, prima facie, impugned order is not sustainable and as such the assessee have strong prima facie case in their favour. The requirement of pre-deposit of the Cenvat credit demand, interest thereon and penalty is, therefore, waived for hearing of the appeal and recovery thereof is stayed till the disposal of the appeal. The High Court held that even as a matter of first principle on a plain and literal construction of rule 3(1) the Tribunal was not justified in holding that Deepak Fertilisers was not entitled to avail of the CENVAT credit in respect of services utilized in relation to ammonia storage tanks on the ground that they were situated outside the factory premises. The High Court further observed that rule 2(l) initially provides that input service means any services of the description falling in sub-clauses (i) and (ii). Rule 2(l) then provides an inclusive definition by enumerating certain specified services. Among those services were services pertained to the procurement of inputs and inward transportation of inputs. The first part of rule 2(l), inter alia , covers any services used by the manufacturer directly or indirectly, in or in relation to the manufacture of final products. The inclusive part of the definition enumerates certain specified categories of services. Whereas rule 3(1) allows a manufacturer of final products to take credit of excise duty and service tax among others paid on any input or capital goods received in the factory of manufacture of the final product, insofar as any input service is concerned, the only stipulation is that it received the final product. This was needed to be read with the broad and comprehensive meaning of the expression 'input service' in rule 2(l).

The Court finally held that the input services in this case were used by Deepak Fertilisers, whether directly or indirectly, in or in relation to the manufacture of the final products and the storage and use of Ammonia was an intrinsic part of that process.

4.1 Final verdict/Judgment - The High Court allowed the input tax credit on the services received in connection with the activity of installation of storage tanks.

Conclusion

5. A manufacturer/service provider uses capital goods such as plants and machinery, inputs such as raw materials and input services such as security services, management, maintenance or repair services, etc., to make a final product. The excise duty/service tax paid on any of these three items is credited and accumulated under a CENVAT credit account. Whenever the manufacturer has to pay duty on finished goods and service tax on output services, it can utilise the accumulated CENVAT credit for the payment, subject to fulfilment of certain conditions. This ensures that the inputs are taxed only once.

Input services also include services used in relation to: modernisation, renovation or repairs of a factory, premises of provider of output service or an office relating to such factory or premises, advertisement or sales promotion, market research, storage up to the place of removal, procurement of inputs, accounting, auditing, financing, recruitment and quality control, coaching and training, computer networking, credit rating, share registry, security, business exhibition, legal services, inward transportation of inputs or capital goods and outward transportation up to the place of removal.

Since inputs may be stored outside the factory as per rule 8 of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004, therefore, any services availed in relation to such storage should also be allowed as credit.

Rule 15 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 contains provisions regarding confiscation and penalty. Rule 15 has been amended to rationalize penalty.

12. Changes in provisions relating to supplying of goods

Under rule 11(2) of the Central Excise Rules, 2002, under mentioned provisos have been inserted which are self-explanatory:

If goods are directly sent to a job worker on the direction of a manufacturer or the provider of output service, the invoice shall also contain the details of the manufacturer or the provider of output service, as the case may be, as buyer and the details of job worker as the consignee.

If the goods are directly sent to any person on the direction of the registered dealer, the invoice shall also contain the details of the registered dealer as the buyer and the person as the consignee, and that person shall take CENVAT credit on the basis of the registered dealer's invoice.

If the goods imported under the cover of a bill of entry are sent directly to buyer's premises, the invoice issued by the importer shall mention that goods are sent directly from the place or port of import to the buyer's premises.

CENVAT CREDIT RULES

13. Increase in time-limit for availment of Cenvat credit from six months to one year

Till 10.07.2014, there was no restriction on availment of Cenvat credit. From 11.07.2014, the Cenvat credit can be taken only upto six months from the date of issue of document as contained in rule 9(1) of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004. From 01.03.2015, the time-limit for availment of Cenvat credit has been increased from six months to one year.

14. Credit on goods directly dispatched to job worker

As per rule 4(1) of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004, 'the CENVAT credit in respect of inputs may be taken immediately on receipt of the inputs in the factory of the manufacturer or in the premises of the provider of output service'.

In case where the goods are directly dispatched to the premises of job worker on the direction of the manufacturer or the provider of output service, credit can be taken only when the said goods are received in the factory of the manufacturer or in the premises of the provider of output service. This was the interpretation done by the department and various Courts.

In order to streamline the said provision, rule 4(1) of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 w.e.f 01.03.2015 states that the CENVAT credit in respect of inputs may be taken immediately on receipt of the inputs in the factory of the manufacturer or in the premises of the provider of output service or in the premises of the job worker, in case goods are sent directly to the job worker on the direction of the manufacturer or the provider of output service, as the case may be;

Similarly, w.e.f 01.03.2015, with respect of capital goods, rule 4(2)(a) now states that the CENVAT credit in respect of capital goods received in a factory or in the premises of the provider of output service or outside the factory of the manufacturer of the final products for generation of electricity for captive use within the factory or in the premises of the job worker, in case capital goods are sent directly to the job worker on the direction of the manufacturer or the provider of output service, as the case may be at any point of time in a given financial year shall be taken only for an amount not exceeding fifty per cent of the duty paid on such capital goods in the same financial year.

3. Registration procedure changed

Registration procedure has been changed by amending Notification No. 35/2001-CE(NT) dated 26-6-2001 w.e.f. 1-3-2015.

Online application for registration is mandatory. Applicant must have Income Tax PAN. Online registration through website is adequate proof, even if not signed. After application, prescribed documents should be submitted and post facto verification should be carried out. If required clarifications are not provided by assessee, registration can be cancelled after granting personal hearing. If premises are non-existent, registration can be cancelled.

[Thus, opportunities of recovering 'amounts' by excise officers have been retained. There is no relief from that].

4. Existing registered persons to furnish details electronically within three months

Existing registered persons shall submit details of e-mail address and mobile number. Registration with customs (BIN), IEC, State Vat number, CIN shall be submitted. Amendment application shall be submitted electronically within three months from 1-3-2015.

5. Amendment to Cenvat Credit Rules

Following are important amendments to Cenvat Credit Rules, mostly w.e.f. 1-3-2015 [except in few cases].

Inputs can be dispatched directly to place of job worker, but should be received within 180 days - Manufactured or imported goods can be sent by supplier manufacturer or importer directly to place of job worker. The invoice issued by supplier manufacturer or importer should contain details of purchaser manufacturer (or purchasing service provider) and job worker. – second and fourth proviso to rule 11(2) of Central Excise Rules, inserted w.e.f. 1-3-2015.

The purchasing manufacturer can avail Cenvat credit as soon as goods are received in the factory of job worker. – rule 4(1) of Cenvat Credit Rules amended w.e.f. 1-3-2015.

If the goods were sent directly to job worker, goods should be received by purchasing manufacturer after job work, within 180 days from the date at which inputs were received by first job worker – proviso to rule 4(5)(a)(i) of Cenvat Credit Rules w.e.f. 1-3-2015.

itself. The Commissioner (Appeals) had denied the benefit on paint on the ground that the same was not used for painting the final product, but was used for painting machinery or the floor. The appellant had specifically contended that paint in question was not an ordinary decorative paint, but was epoxy paint used for industrial purpose for making floor dust free for easy movement of goods. As such, it became a commercial necessity to paint floor so as to enhance the effective manufacturing activity. [Para 11] Viewing the use of paint in the appellant’s factory in the light of the observations made by the Supreme Court in Maruti Suzuki Ltd. v. CCE [2009] 22 STT 54, it was found that the issue to be addressed was as to whether the use of the paint was in or in relation to manufacture of final product or not. Admittedly, if paint is not used in relation to manufacture of final product, the same would not become an input merely because the same is mentioned in the inclusive part of the definition. The Supreme Court in the above judgment has referred to oils and lubricants mentioned in the definition required for smooth running of machines, as eligible input as they are used in the manufacture of final product. By applying the same criteria, it could be said that the paint which was required for smooth running of machineries, by repeatedly painting them and also for floor for smooth movement of raw materials, semi-finished goods and final product by making floor dust-free, had a nexus with manufacture of final product. [Para 13]

In view of the above definition of ‘input’ during the relevant period, the appellant was entitled to the benefit of Modvat credit in respect of paint in question. The impugned order was set aside and appeal was allowed. [Para 14]

The assessee had taken on lease a plot of land for establishing and running the factory from Madhya Pradesh Audyogik Kendra Vikas Nigam (MPAKVN).

It availed cenvat credit of service tax paid on maintenance charges to MPAKVN.

The Adjudicating Authority denied the credit of service tax paid on maintenance charges.

The Commissioner (Appeals) confirmed the order of the Adjudicating Authority.

On appeal to Tribunal:

The following facts were undisputed -

the capital goods/other goods on which Cenvat Credit was availed are received in the factory premises of the assessee.

the said capital goods/other goods were used/consumed for construction of or setting up of the refinery/factory.

the assessee had taken the Central Excise registration and discharging the duty liability on the finished goods manufactured and cleared from the assessee's factory premises from November 2006.

capital goods and other goods were duty paid. [Para 6]

As regards the denial of Cenvat Credit of Rs.20,61,57,657/-, Cenvat Credit was denied on the ground that the credit has been taken on the strength of invoices where owner is person other than the assessee and assessee be considered as person who had got the said capital goods/items from financing company since Essar Projects Ltd. (the owner of capital goods) was not financing company. In this regard, the duty paying documents clearly indicate the name of EPC contractors i.e. Essar Projects Ltd. and as also the name and address of the assessee as a consignee. It is not disputed that the said capital goods/other goods which were received at the site of the assessee, were used in refinery and the documents indicated correct duty paying nature. Since there is no dispute as to the receipt, consumption and duty paid nature of the capital goods or other goods in setting up of the factory of the assessees, demand was set aside. [Para 7(i)]

As regards the denial of Cenvat Credit of Rs. 38,74,887/-, the entire dispute was regarding the non-submission of intimation of the receipt of capital goods and other goods to the Jurisdictional Superintendent. As has been already accepted and undisputed that the capital goods and other goods were received and consumed in the setting up of the unit, mere non-filing of the declaration cannot be a ground for denial of credit. Subtantative benefits should not be denied to an assessee only on the ground of non-fulfilment of procedural conditions. [Para 7(ii)]

As regards the denial of Cenvat Credit of Rs.6,68,773/- and Rs.2,34,351/-, the adjudicating authority has sought to deny the Cenvat Credit only on the ground that the Cenvat Credit has been availed on the original copy and/or extra copy. As long as, there being no dispute as to the duty paid character of the capital goods/other goods, and the receipt in and consumption thereof, there cannot be the denial of Cenvat Credit to the assessee. [Para 7(iii)]

As regards the denial of Cenvat Credit of Rs.1,95,84,057/- and Rs.25,33,813/-, the credit was denied on ground that installation certificate as required under Rule 57Q of the erstwhile Central Excise Rules, 1944 was not submitted and the goods do not fall under Chapter 84, 85 and 90 as is envisaged in the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 for availment of capital goods credit. In this regard, the assessee has been able to demonstrate that HTPE sheets, insulation packages, domestic (refractory) anchors etc. though not falling under specific Chapters of 84, 85 and 90, are used in the refinery as either components or spares in the plant and machinery which are used for the manufacturing of the final products. The said detailed analysis as has been submitted by the assessee was not considered by the adjudicating authority, dismissed by a summary finding that these items cannot be in nature of capital goods and are not in nature of accessories of the main plant. The items and the usage thereof which has been demonstrated, from the documents on records, clearly indicate that these items were consumed/used as components, spares or parts of the various machineries which were either fabricated and installed alongwith bought out items for setting up of the refinery. [Para 7(iv)]

Rule 4 of the Service Tax Rules, 1994 provides for an assessee to get himself registered as service provider. It was seen that in the instant case, the assessee had taken registration under the category of ‘Service provider of advertising services’.

It can be seen from rule 4(2) that an option is given to an assessee to register the premises where centralized billing or centralized accounting systems are located. 5. In Hindustan Coca Cola Beverages (P.) Ltd. v. CCE 2010 (255) ELT 94 (Trib. - Delhi), the appeal was against the order of Commissioner of Central Excise (Appeals) upholding the bill of entry generated on EDI system. The original authority denied the credit holding that in terms of rule 57G(3)(k), the credit can be taken only on the basis of duplicate copy of the bill of entry generated on Electronic Data Interchange (EDI) system installed in the Customs of Central Excise Commissionerate.

The appellant submitted that rule 57G(3)(c) has prescribed ‘triplicate copy of bill of entry’ as relevant document for the purpose of taking credit. There is no stipulation that the triplicate copy referred to in rule 57G(3)(c) relates only to triplicate copy of the bill generated in manual system. Since the initial stage of the EDI system some of the Commissionerates were not generating second copy of the bill of entry, the Central Government included the duplicate copy of the bill of entry generated in EDI also as document for the purpose of taking credit.

The department contended that when the rule prescribes a particular document, the appellant is required to produce the said document only to enable himself to take credit.

The Tribunal held that the appellant clearly showed divergence in practice regarding generation of triplicate copy of the bill of entry, thus, necessitating prescribing the duplicate copy generated on EDI system also as document for the purpose of taking credit. Sub-rule (3)(k) prescribing such duplicate copy as the relevant document has been done with without amending sub-rule (3)(c) of rule 57G. The Tribunal found merit in the submission of the appellant.
